_childDocuments_.review: I just want to begin this review by saying that, unequivocally, this game is worth your time and money. I highly recommend going in with as few spoilers as possible, I promise it's worth it. If that's not enough to persuade you, continue reading.Never before have I been so emotionally invested in a game's characters and the desire for a happy ending; not Undertale, not Omori, not Celeste, not Jimmy and the Pulsating Mass. Nothing has compared to this. The writing is fantastic and all of the characters have incredible amounts of depth. I fell in love with all of them. There is one particular moment where you unintentionally break a promise to a character in a horrific manner, and it is devastating in a way that I have never felt from any piece of media before. Two of the characters in particular struggle with negative self-talk in a way that would frequently make me pause so I could cry my eyes out at how painfully relatable their dialogue was. I don't particularly struggle with depression, but I am in a difficult time in my life right now, where I find myself saying these awful things about my own character. To see the things that I say to myself mirrored by characters that I had grown so attached to left me with the some of the strongest emotions I've ever experienced.I want to briefly discuss some of the flaws in this game. While there are some annoying aspects of this game that you will notice in reviews (as well as more serious criticisms to be made on rare occasions), I would argue that the less serious annoyances are intentional and, most importantly, meaningful to the experience. That may sound like a cop out defense, and before finishing I would've agreed. However, in retrospect, I see what these annoying, repetitive mechanics are there for. I don't really want to divulge that purpose, because I think you need to realize it for yourself. As I mentioned, this game is best experienced spoiler-free, so I hope you will trust me when I say that no part of this game is pointless. You will fall in love with this game. It has the potential to be healing and life-changing. All you have to do is give it your trust.

You simultaneously understand them completely, while also going "Siffrin NO" every other line of dialogue. _childDocuments_.review: I got this game after seeing some recommendations for it online and trying out the free demo (not the Start Again Prologue, which I haven't played).  I soon fell in love with the party characters and their dynamic, reached the end of the demo, and just had to go for the full game right after.  I thought the demo had given me a good taste of what to expect, but I was happy to find that it had only scratched the surface of what this game offers!Where In Stars and Time stands out most is the character writing and in just how well it goes into working with the time loops.  I don't want to go too much into it because I don't want to spoil anything about that, but I do want to say one thing that really stuck out for me.  There are moments where I felt absolute dread and fear over what was going to happen next in the story.  The content warning at the start of the game is not a joke.  It can take a while to reach those points, depending on your progress playing through, but when those moments happen you will know... and it does not hold back.  Pair with that with the game's stellar soundtrack and you've got a great game experience that will stay with you for a long, long time.Aside from the story, the main gameplay of In Stars and Time is about what you'd expect from a classic RPG.  The Rock-Paper-Scissors nature of the combat is pretty interesting, and helps it not get too annoying when repeating everything as the time loops continue.  And those loops will continue on and on and on as you figure out what to do and experiment here and there.  It can feel like it's droning on at times when repeating parts that have already been done, but I would not have it any other way.So, overall, I highly recommend this game.  If you like the look of it and think it would be up your alley, go for it!

_childDocuments_.review: I finished the game after 16 hours, and can give my impressions.  I don't know if there are multiple endings, and I definitely found most things but didn't find everything (all accessories/weapons but not all memories).  This is a great game if you like emotional stories, light RPG mechanics, the art style, and are queer or an ally.  The game uses its timeloop format intertwined with the story and characters in a smart way to approach difficult themes and guide the characters through them.  It is similar to Undertale, but while the game is goofy when it wants to be and not every joke will land with you, it is not nearly as "internet-humor", "lol so random" as parts of Undertale are.  Characters in this are far, far more relatable and their issues are grounded, approached, solved in an intelligent and mature way.  Or not ultimately solved! Some things don't get fixed right away and that's ok, in fact a refreshing take on how real life works. In my opinion the game is written very well, overall. You will see aspects of yourself and the people you know in these characters, hell you may BE one of these characters.  As you can see in one of the main tags of the game, the game does feature a lot of LGTBQ+ characters and themes, and like I mentioned above, it handles this in a very respectful, intelligent, mature way.  Being LGTBQ+ is not what the game is all about, the game instead tells the story centering around the main character of Siffrin, and just happens to star characters that mirror the LGTBQ+ community and aspects of our own lives.  I mean this game takes place in a country that worships change as a religion, and changing your entire physical makeup is magically as easy as the equivalent of going to get a fancy haircut.  So in a setting like this, the question you explore is what are the issues that the characters face?  Are they similar/different? What really matters to them?So how does the actual gameplay fit in?  You'll explore the small town as well as the House, the big RPG-ish dungeon where you ascend to fight The King.  Obviously stuff happens and you end up repeating this activity in a time loop.  The goal is to figure out why and how to get out, so you will follow clues and try new things in areas with new knowledge, picking up new items to use in different spots, etc.  The game will give you shortcuts as you go along, from skipping dialogue to skipping entire floors of the dungeon and skipping finding keys, etc.  Items can be forwarded in time, but not back, equipment is always saved between loops, and your party's XP is saved to the highest point it has been at on each floor.  The biggest drawback to the game is that despite the numerous shortcuts it gives you, there is far too much backtracking and "fetch-quest" style traveling that it becomes frustrating past the point of the intended "wow it must be frustrating repeating the same two days".  Sometimes the shortcuts don't work the way you thought, or you have to do an entire sequence again just to keep an item with you, etc.  Even with the dialogue skip I eventually turned the message speed to the max setting just to mash through so much repeated dialogue.  The combat system is quite simple and basic, and I rarely found myself challenged even when not bothering to level the party up, which made combat more of an annoyance after not too long.  While the art style is great in cutscenes and pictures, the pixel art itself in the overworld is quite basic, and while the music is quite suspenseful in certain moments, the same old overworld and dungeon tracks will begin to grate.  If the built-in skipping and time saving mechanics were not there, this game would be difficult to get through.  Overall I highly recommend the game to anyone who enjoys the premise and a good story.  Just go into it prepared to read and think of it more like a long puzzle adventure game than an RPG.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm fine. I'm fine. I'm fine. Actually, I'm MORE than fine because this game is outstanding. A heartfelt, sincere, and emotionally impactful turn-based RPG that made me care about the characters from the jump, In Stars and Time is now one of my favorite games in recent history. I rarely feel the need to immediately hop back in and replay a game, and yet as soon as I finished ISAT, I knew I needed to go back in to discover all of the secrets and quests I had left unfinished. Yes, it does explore -- in sometimes painfully accurate detail  -- anxiety, disassociation, and the dark mental health spiral that can cause us to feel isolated and alone... but it also has some of the most beautiful moments of catharsis, laughter, joy, and love in how these characters interact with one another. I think I cried with joy and sadness in equal amounts (perhaps even MORE tears of joy, to be honest).The battle system is simple and straightforward. Quite literately, it's turn-based rock-paper-scissors, and it's definitely a backdrop to the character arcs and moments that you're meant to pay attention to. If I had to call out a weakness of the game, I would say that sometimes, even with the quality of life elements to keep the loops moving briskly, I felt like it was a bit slower going. There were perhaps one or two moments in the story I wasn't sure exactly what I needed to trigger to move the plot forward, and it resulted in me taking a lot of time to interact with everything to see what was different. But, for the vast majority of my time, the pacing and story seemed to move in a way that felt natural and allowed themes to have their moment to breathe. Best of all? You could probably finish this game in about 30-35 hours, making it a very approachable title from a time perspective. I'll be putting this on my list of games to regularly recommend to folks, for sure. Thanks to the devs for making this!

_childDocuments_.review: Originally, my review of this game was negative owing to the technical issues I was experiencing. After several months of waiting for an update that claims to properly fix these problems, I decided to experience In Stars and Time on another platform. I will say this first and foremost- my issues were most likely due to having a low quality laptop to play this on. If you don't have a particularly capable device you would probably want to pass on this game. I crashed multiple times by simply going through basic actions. If you have a Playstation or Nintendo Switch, play on those instead.With that being said, this game is a narrative experience above all else. The gameplay is passable but if you are looking for an RPG with deep, fleshed out mechanics then you will not find it here. There is very little difficulty in the combat. When you find an enemy you either simply spam abilities until it's dead, or you throw out attacks to see what works and then employ the best strategy every encounter afterwards.  The bosses function similarly. The game simply does not throw enough at you to make battles challenging. You don't even get to fight multiple enemies at once (save for a few rare encounters), something that could easily help with this problem. This is a baffling design decision. The only enemy I found truly challenging and particularly enjoyable was the final boss, but even that loses its novelty after a while.The gameplay problems are further exacerbated by the lack of equipment and skills you can employ. You find some weapons here and there, but most of them don't have interesting mechanics associated with them barring one memorable exception. The memories (a unique sort of equipment) you can get suffer similarly. Most of them just allow you to use higher level skills at lower levels. The issue with this is that they are entirely unnecessary, because once again the game does not throw enough at you to make things challenging. All that remains beyond that are just a few memories, and even then some clearly outclass others so you only bother equipping one or two usually.The skills (or crafts as they're called) suffer from the same problem. You only use a handful of them because combat consists solely of exploiting enemy weakness. You might employ a buff or two to help out, but almost never in a normal fight. Certain crafts are also outright useless. Why only buff one person's attack and slightly heal them when someone else has far better crafts to do both? Why bother making something weak to an element when they already have a perfectly exploitable weakness, one which you are already encouraged to spam the same elements for to launch your ultimate attack? Overall it feels like the game outright forbids you from experimenting and experiencing new things. Leveling up mostly just gives you higher numbers and the skills you get usually don't matter. Combat also loses most of its fun when you have to redo fights and realize what lack of depth it truly has. And combat is especially prevalent in this games, as the only other thing left to really experience is the story. There are no puzzles to solve, no minigames to enjoy, and it forces you to engage in battles often even when you dont want to. Certain plot points make you fight whether you like it or not, and even outside of that the corridors of the only dungeon in the game are narrow enough that you can't escape enemies easily. All of this is extremely important to mention since the combat is what fills in the downtime between story beats, and if the combat isn't good it will leave a lot of people bored and frustrated. Even if the game is supposed to be story based anyways, even if it's supposed to get you into the mindset of the protagonist or whatever, I don't believe letting your players feel like this is good game design.Now, it might shock you to be reminded that I still recommend this game. Even if it feels like a chore to get through with all the gameplay features it lacks, I think that this game's writing is definitely some of the most unique and interesting I've experienced in a while. Each main character has many unique facets to their personalities and their backstories are fun to explore. Even after numerous loops you can still discover more about these people, making them feel more and more real. You would think focusing on only a mere handful of characters would make them boring but it's instead used to develop very well written people. Spending time with every individual main character already teaches you a lot about them, but seeing everyone comfort and banter with each other elevates it significantly. It feels like there's a long history that everyone has with each other regardless of how long their actual journey was. All their experiences have given them intricate understandings of each other than are intriguing to see and think about. For a game that isn't nearly as long as some other story based RPGs, I think the characters in this game are far more memorable compared to some other series.Not only all of that, but the amount of world building that has been done is absolutely shocking. You only spend time in one town and one dungeon throughout the entire game, yet you learn so much about the world around you. The characters constantly discuss cultural aspects with each other, and even though it may come off as just exposition to some people, it makes the world feel far more alive. It also contributes to the characters personalities as well. You see more of their perspectives on certain things and it lets you understand them even more. I would have never expected this game to deliver so well on such things and yet I have been pleasantly surprised.Unfortunately however, in spite of singing praises for this game's writing, it does have notable problems. I can't get too deep into it without spoilers, but there are surface level things I will mention. Firstly, the protagonist Siffrin feels strangely written at points. Some of the things he does doesn't make sense and feel like they should have been changed or better thought out. Second, the pacing of the main story feels iffy and I think it ends up going too fast. It actually starts out really well, but over time the quality becomes more shaky and eventually leads to points in the story that I feel are just poorly written. This leads to certain things not being resolved and leave me feeling kind of irked. It feels rushed and it makes enough of a mess that towards the end that it felt like it tripped over itself.As for other things that don't quite work for me, there are certain parts of the time loop mechanic that are annoying. Namely, being forced to loop back because the game simply forces you to. At some points the game will make you repeat certain sections just because. It wants you to understand that sometimes looping is inevitable, but there are parts where you have to loop because you made the wrong decision without any hints or ability to know what the right thing to do was. Moreso, even if you do make the "correct" decision you can be forced to loop anyways because the game has decide there was something in a previous location you need to do or obtain. There are also moments where you think you you're on the right path, but it turns out the game wants you to do something different that it didn't elaborate on.To sum it up, I feel like In Stars and Time is maybe an 8/10, or a 7/10 if we're being more cynical. This game is meant more for a specific type of person, one who focuses mostly on the story of a game and is patient enough to trudge through the bad parts so that they may see the ending. If you don't like reading too much, and if you can't handle the repetition of certain parts of this game then you won't enjoy it. Regardless, this game is a unique experience and I feel that it is unfortunate that it isn't more popular than it already is.

_childDocuments_.review: Phenomenal game, easily among my favorites now. This is largely a story told through a game and it leverages its medium fantastically. _childDocuments_.review: In Stars and Time (which I'll be calling ISAT from now on) is a game in which you play through a time loop at the end of your character's journey, rather then the start. As the time loop aspect implies, you will need a  of patience. The game removes a lot of menial aspects, thankfully, but you will still need quite a lot of it if you wish to see the ending of the game. If this is not your style, I would suggest against it. Now, without further ado, let me get into:This game is absolutely LOVELY in terms of storytelling, as well as gameplay. It's criminal just how underrated the game is. Your journey will be one of patience and will, but it will be one worth telling and experiencing. This game does a wonderful job at portraying just how much despair a time loop will cause, instilling a sense of dread in both the writing, art, and OST. You will reach amazing highs, and despairful lows, as is the point of the game.

_childDocuments_.review: RPG Maker type games are really hard to pull off correctly, let alone having it be actually interesting but this game really manages to capture my brain in just the right way.Its been awhile since i've played a game like this and have it make me want to actually explore and talk to people, the interactions are just so interesting that it made me want to see everything the game had to offer, and even then i still missed stuff!The Timeloop mechanic is one of my favorites in the genre, its done so well in a way that i just cant describe. _childDocuments_.review: I can't recommend this game enough for those looking for an experience they will remember. If you're nervous about getting into  an rpgmaker game, don't be- The strengths of In Stars and Time lies in its amazing writing, pitch-perfect atmosphere, and lovingly crafted emotional scenes that make it one of the best stories to be found in video games. The battle mechanics, while not the jewel in the crown, still stand as an enjoyable take on the genre. The battles themselves were well balanced for me, with the threat of defeat never too far away in the early-mid game but always preventable, and the jackpot system actively promotes more tactics than mindlessly attacking. Outside of battles, the game revolves around the time loop mechanic, how it allows you to progress through failure and grow more adept at exploring the heights of the castle each time you venture in. The game does an excellent job of both allowing you to gain information and strength through loops without losing the sense that you are starting over each time.Of course, that lends itself perfectly to the story being told. The characters are immediately lovable, with the dynamic of an rpg party that has already worked through the cliches and introductions that other games spend all their time setting up. Its what makes the descent into much more powerful emotional scenes all the more engrossing. This game portrays a descent into madness through repetition, one you can't help caring immensely because of how believable every character is. It's difficult to convey how well the story hits its marks, but it made me feel mirthful joy, shocking dread and cathartic sadness in equal measure. There are so many things to love about this game, and so much to discover. If you're at all on the fence, give the demo a shot. Trust me, the character writing is always that good.

_childDocuments_.review: An interesting game that takes place in a well-built world with well-written characters. While the looping mechanic can make the dungeon crawl part of the game feel a bit repetitive, the attention to little details tends to give the player lots to explore over their various loops. The ending felt a bit rushed, but overall a good experience. Just be warned that if you're a story-focused player, you absolutely should take the time to track back and talk to EVERYONE in the epilogue (multiple times in the case of party members), and that some interesting questions raised in the game remain unresolved, with the devs stating they have no intention of answering them, rather leaving it to fans to theorize.The devs tried very hard to make the game inclusive... to the point where it can feel heavy-handed at times. Whether this is a net positive or negative will depend on the player's personal views and personality.

_childDocuments_.review: Very nice concept - good art style, decent writing, intriguing story - but the fact you have to redo *so much stuff* each time you loop back ruins it. I love time loop games - I've played basically all of them and almost always review them positively because the concept is so appealing. But this game doesn't really capture the fine line between immersing oneself in the idea of a time loop vs. pure tedium.I have a recommendation to the dev:- Make it possible to instantly skip a dialogue line rather than waiting for the text to finish appearing. I know there's the "SHIFT" mechanic but there's a ton of dialogue in the game that's pure fluff and I hate having to wait for the lines to finish when I can read much faster than the text scrolls. Almost all JRPGs have this - there's no excuse not to have it here.

_childDocuments_.review: I want to like this game and I'm squarely in an audience that loves representation of LGBTQ+ issues; but... gah time loop games just aren't for me. The review on RPS pretty much is an example how I feel about this game - I'm just too old for this. The combat is ludicrously simple rock-paper-scissors style; you won't lose a battle (unless the random number gods are very unfriendly) once you get the system. OK. Fine. The narrative then, right? The mechanics don't matter if the narrative is great!But... the narrative seems geared towards a much younger audience than I. Which is cool, I'm an old man past 30 but... the time loop mechanic is just too much. It's boring. It's repetitive. It's padding. The game, honestly, which had a cool story, would have been so much more enjoyable as a short game where I just went through and experienced the "ending" without having to sit there and press the "X" button on my controller to skip a dialogue that I might have seen 10 times before - BUT - the game assured me, I might find hidden meaning if I kept looking and playing and looping and...I didn't. Finishing was more of a grudge work. I can't recall the last game I just wanted to rage finish but this might be it.

_childDocuments_.review: My main gripe about this game is the gameplay itself. It is EXTREMELY repetitive. Even if you interact with an object to progress the story, you must backtrack through countless encounters that are meaningless to fight, just to inspect a book or key that you already interacted with before.Since this story is all about time looping, you are forced to rewatch the same interactions over. And over. And over. This causes all characters relevant to the story completely lose their humanity and it sucks because the ending of this game was genuinely pretty cool.The RPG elements feel forced. Since XP is basically meaningless in this game, you are forced to kill enemies for other means, such as fast traveling... Why do you have to pay currency to fast travel in a game that literally barely changes? Beats me. Spamming buffs and the same attack type without sense of urgency makes battling even more boring.The writing is corny. Exclamation marks are overused!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!! (Even in the 4th screenshot on the store page) And tired-out jokes like "Oh crab" was shockingly less funny the 100th time.In conclusion, the game's content feels extremely padded out. Scripted deaths and forced backtracking even prohibit someone paying close attention to the environments. From pointless backtracking, to spreading out keys and locked doors as far apart from each other as possible, you wonder if just quitting the game and just watching the ending on youtube is worth it. For a couple reasons, I can see why people like this game, but the 98% rating is misleading. The concept is cool, and the ending is unique, but is it really worth 26 dollars?

_childDocuments_.review: If you like captivating, entrancingly flawed characters, mysterious, engrossing stories, or clever, innovative RPG mechanics, In Stars and Time is a must-play!(I’m listed as getting the game for free via a fanworks contest, but I plan to buy many a copy in the days to come! It’s that good!!!)I'm only a few hours in so far, so I'll be coming back once I finish the game to write a more full-scope review, but in quick fashion the constant drip of fascinating developments, charming and beautifully human characters, hilarious and heart-wrenching writing and engrossing, tactical gameplay have grabbed me by the heart and refused to leave my thoughts for a single second.Some key points!-The core cast is the core strength of the game, both in how staggering the characterization is, and how on-hooks you’ll be from moment one to see their journeys over the course of the game- both in how they evolve, and what delicious secrets they’ll reveal. Their friendships, how they get along and butt heads, their interrelationships, and, yes, the incredible potential for capital-S Shipping all drive this game forwards in the best of ways-ISAT is, as has been noted many a time, incredibly LGBT+ focused! The core cast are all various flavors of queer, but so are many of the NPCs you’ll meet! Disability-positive too, and with a fantasy-flavored highlighting of a number of real-world cultures, all handled with obvious love, care and passion. Feels good!-The mystery of the time loop that the game centers around, as well as the various mysteries surrounding Siffrin, the main character, and King, the enigmatic antagonist, are as puzzling as they are enthralling. I’ve seen in reviews, too, that there may be even more, Gaster-esque behind-the-curtain mysteries waiting in the distance... I don’t know about you, but I love that stuff so freakin much-I haven’t seen it praised enough, but there’s so much to love about the Rock-Paper-Scissors-based RPG battles! More than just a classic triangle of type-matchups, thanks to the Active Time Battle-esque system, the ability for some characters to give their turns to other teammates, the need to keep your buffs rolling and hp maxed, and the only limit on skill use being turn cooldowns, there’s an amazing amount of Optimization and delightful RPG fiddlyness in mastering the battles that you’ll run into. Ass in some very clever and tricky Time Loop shenanigans to the mix, and the RPG side of this Narrative RPG is just as special as the rest of it!-It’s funny as hell!!! I bust out laughing IRL multiple times in the first hour alone, and many more as the game’s gone on. I know it’s gonna get sad and tug at my heart like nobody’s business later on (especially if the amazing prequel game START AGAIN is anything to go by), but seriously, the writing is 10/10 on all fronts.-It inspired me to create fanwork again for the first time in years! I don’t know if that means anything to you, kind stranger, but it sure as hell does to me.Again, I’ll write more detail into this once I’ve beaten the game, but as of now, a loud, resounding GET THE GAME! PLAY THE GAME! LOVE THE GAME!7777777/10

_childDocuments_.review: Wow.The characters are so crabbing colorful and fun to get closer to and spend time with.The world feels big and rich even though you only see a tiny fragment of it.The art is stunning.The music is delightful.I normally hate playing a game multiple times, but In Stars And Time really makes the monotony melodious.Every major act feels punctuated by an emotional gut punch.And the dev wisely decided to give us a character whose sole purpose is telling us where to go when we're lost. Bless.Oh and the combat! The combat. Absolutely fascinating. You loop, but your main party doesn't level up, so you never get to the point of being stupidly overpowered, which makes every combat feel challenging, and somehow the extremely simple rock-paper-scissors damage types and +/- att/def/spd buffs end up feeling remarkably nuanced.Very fun. Very emotional. And opens the door to some very interesting conversations about the Change belief. Play this.

_childDocuments_.review: I think all the other reviews have cover this, but, like... Love yourself. Play this game. Also heed the content warnings because the game is behind you, and it has a folding metal chair and it will use it wrestling style on you -- but it knows what it's doing, and it's done so well. Don't worry. You're fine.It's a simple premise, executed SO well. It will resonate with you in one way or another -- and if a theme doesn't resonate with you because you haven't experienced the things the game is working through, it will gently help you understand. It will explain it in ways that fit with the universe but allow you to understand the context and in turn, understand what Siffrin is going through. It's something very impressive for a game to manage to give you that much understanding and empathy, but it does let you go through it again and again and again so you learn. The cast is incredible. You will laugh, cry, and smile at their antics. I hunted for every scrap of new dialogue I could find, wanted to see every scene because I genuinely wanted to know these characters and their stories more. The battle system is very simple, but it's also fun. Pay attention to everything, because the devs sure did and it pays to look at the same thing in many different contexts just to see if you get new chatter about it, or what people's reaction to it is. Read your profile often. Double check the portraits, the punctuation. Everything feels deliberate and thought out, and you will be rewarded for looking for what the devs have added in places you might not expect.I honestly don't really have the words to fully explain how this game impacted me, because I'm terrified of spoiling it in any way. You have to play this! Don't look up anything else about it! Don't do it! Don't do yourself a dirty like that!! Go in with no knowledge and let the game pile drive you with emotions from on high! IT'S INSERTDISC5 WITH THE SUPLEX. LET THEM DO IT. I will say this though -- as soon as I told a friend I was playing this game, I heard, from an entire ocean and eight hour time distance away, the sound of them scrambling to their PC and telling me I had to stream it for them. They sat with me for a combined total of 29 hours over a few days as I played through this, listened to me reading all the lines with different voices for the characters and didn't tease me when I was too emotional to keep doing that, or when the game hit me so hard I had to just sit and stare at the screen for a few minutes before continuing. They love this game that much. And now I love it that much too. I hope you love it too. (Honestly, I'd love to be as funny as that France review down there, 10/10 kudos to that reviewer, but I am unfortunately a BIG SAP. Anyway go buy this game.Also if you listen closely, you can hear the sound of every non-heterosexual woman shaking in their boots when Madame Odile hits low HP for the first time. It's incredible.)

_childDocuments_.review: My complaint is that the game is *really* insistent on you never missing a single detail, as it will repeatedly, for dozens of times in a row, tell you, that you can, indeed, use the A button to select an attack. There's never any downtime to absorb a situation by yourself; it is always narrated and commented on by the other characters.Every line is written like I've never encountered fiction in my life, hammered down to the point of exhaustion for even the most trivial notion that I've been told fifteen times over. When you see an enemy, a tutorial is almost certain to come up, in which five paragraphs are expended to tell you that yes, this is a indeed video game.The characters each speak like 8-year olds, which is obviously meant to be endearing, but it gets grating fast. Everything in the narration "feels like" something. You "feel there's no key here", you "feel the weird presence", "it feels the room is safe", without justification as to why such a feeling would arise. Another example of why the writing didn't land with me was that seemingly the only way the story could convey an intense feeling is the *very* visual novel trope of going "it hurts it hurts it hurts it hurts" ad nauseam, forgoing actual description. This happened a lot. Speaking of visual novel tropes, if you don't enjoy... a certain amount of anime influence in your story, you might not enjoy parts of this. Nyaa~ onigiri thousand needles and anime tropes galore.

_childDocuments_.review: I would 100% recommend this game to anyone at all regardless of their opinions on RPGs. In Stars and Time is the most perfect storytelling game I have played, placing it at the top of my favorite games of all time next to other indie classics like Hollow Knight. The central premise of this game is that you loop through the same twoish days over and over, and the attention to detail and wholehearted care that goes into every possible element of this game can fully absorb you in a few minutes. The writing is the best part of this game, second best is the worldbuilding (in a 20ish hour-long game!), third is the level/puzzle design and art, and last is the combat. They all work in harmony to deliver what I can only call an experience you can't get anywhere else. It's fully unique and fully worth 20$.

_childDocuments_.review: In Stars And Time is a well-written time loop story. It has a cast of colorful characters you get to know quite thoroughly throughout the game.Before playing I thought that constantly looping through the same scenes would be tiresome, and it is but that's the point. The main character experiences a slow descent into madness and you help them break free from the loops before they turn full coo coo. You learn more about their friends, the world, and the loops. It becomes this puzzle of finding where you have to loop in time to find the next piece of information to progress.I did get stuck a few times and needed to see a walkthrough.The rock-paper-scissors-derived combat is shallow. The same tactics work on the same enemies every time. Only the final boss has some mechanical depth.Graphically it's what you would expect from an RPG maker game. The character designs are minimal and appealing. The lack of noses is a bit suspect but you get used to it.Overall, I would say that In Start And Time's moment-to-moment gameplay is subpar but it compensates with excellent writing and characters. Also, everything was solved with  in the end which earns it a positive review from me <3.

_childDocuments_.review: This was a wonderful game.   I laughed and I cried and got really invested in the characters by the end. I ended up playing the last 8 or so  hours in a single sitting because I was so pulled in.  The combat is a pretty fun literal rock/paper/scissors dynamic but its never particularly hard, you're not likely to ever die to a random enemy, and some of the eventual power ups and upgrades feel pretty satisfying. The timeloop aspect may be offputting to some people, especially early on where there's a handful of "well you trapped yourself, have to restart now" puzzles, but there's not too many of those and once you've experimented and solved them once its never an issue again.   It kept doing new things and keeping it interesting and played with a lot of themes and ideas.  Probably a 15-20 hour game for most people but I put in 35, cause I did everything.If a timeloop rpg with great characters sounds at all interesting to you, don't look up any other reviews or trailers, (Why are you even reading this review?) they ALL give away a ton of stuff including a bunch of early surprises and jokes while trying to sell the pitch, and there's things I wish I'd been surprised by or just discovered on my own.If I have one complaint it's in the achievements. A couple of the achievements have missable elements that you're almost certainly going to miss without following a guide, I 100%ed and did everything in the game, but missed something in the sequence which kept a few things from popping because I missed a single character dialogue at some point between hour 3 and hour 25, and another I missed because there's an RNG event you pretty much have to save scum to trigger,  I had multiple save files and was able to go back and do these things to see them once I knew about them, but since they're not in the same run as everything else they don't count.

_childDocuments_.review: i finished this game a couple weeks ago and have not stopped thinking about it since. i don't often leave reviews but i will leave one here because i would love for this game to become more popular! if you find the premise interesting at all, which you likely do if you're reading the reviews, i'd say it's well worth giving this one a try. i want to give siffrin a hug so bad, i  haven't been quite this attached to a game protagonist in a while. possibly ever. the rest of the party is great too! i love them all very dearly. it is a lot more focused on characters and narrative than on gameplay - not that the gameplay is bad but it is constructed to serve the narrative rather than the other way round. which for me is a positive but for some people might be a negative. also do definitely mind the content warnings. this one gets pretty freakin dark, the second half especially is emotionally draining like woah. but there's plenty of lovely soft moments too to offset the depressing stuff, and the ending is super satisfying! i've seen a lot of people compare it to undertale and omori, and while i don't like to just compare games to other games - i think it doesn't really do it justice, it's its own game - i do think if you like those two games there's a pretty good chance you'll like this one.i've talked enough, there's a lot more i could say but i think it's all been said better by others. if you're still reading this honestly just play it. if you're anything like me it'll find a place in your heart and not leave there anytime soon.

_childDocuments_.review: There's a lot I want to praise about In Stars and Time. How it's full of charming and immediately lovable characters. That it's got adorable and visually stunning artwork. About its gripping story that keeps you hooked and eager to see what's next, while also questioning what's happened before. The way it's precisely tuned to put you in the same mental headspace as the main character; almost uncomfortably so. The fact that it's a turn-based RPG where I gave a damn about using buff and debuff skills. All of those, I could write about. But there's one specific aspect to it I think encapsulates this game more than anything else. Here's a message I sent to my friend while playing In Stars and Time:Other games have stressed me out. But, they always stressed me out due to gameplay. Maybe an intense boss fight where I could only take one more hit. Maybe a speedrun where I knew I'd have a tiny frame perfect window to execute the strat. Maybe a clutch moment where the other players were riding entirely on me. You get the idea - every other time I've been stressed from a game, it was because of high intensity gameplay that would make anyone's heart flare up.In Stars and Time stressed me out purely from its writing. I was on the verge of pulling my hair out, because the dialogue and story were making me that anxious.That's In Stars and Time.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is delightful. I played the prologue when it was released a while back, and have been waiting for the full game to come out ever since. It has been truly worth the wait! If there's anything to truly highlight out of the entire experience, it's the characters and how they're written. Everyone's unique and delightful, and their interactions with one another are so charming you can't help but falling in love with them all immediately.Of course, there's more to it than just them; the story overall is incredibly engaging, and the time loop factor is taken so well into account that, even if you have the option to skip over dialogues, there's ways to make things interesting if you don't, so you can get to enjoy the dialogues over and over again if really refreshing ways.I am far from the end of this game, but I have been having a blast and these characters and the world, plus the mystery happening behind the mission they're after, have me completely hooked. I cannot recommend this game enough; and I haven't stopped recommending it to everyone on my path! It's just that kind of game. The kind that catches you and you just don't want to let go, the kind that tugs at your heartstrings and you feel for each and every character because you can't help but feel close to them with how real their experiences feel.Loving this experience, and I can't wait to find out more!EDIT: Despite Steam saying I've played for 41 hours, my game says it's been over 44 and I choose to believe the latter. I had 7 hours in only when I left my initial review, and I have now finally reached the end. The entire journey was worth it, and every emotion it threw at me reached and tugged and played with my heartstrings, threatening to cut them out, make music with them, make them dance or make them wish to rot and decay. And every single emotion, feeling, event, action or scene was worth every bit of the story.There's still so many mysteries left behind, but at the end of the day, does that truly matter? Do the mysteries matter when your journey is over and you're able to look back and not regret any single bit? For now, breath in, breath out. The journey's over.

_childDocuments_.review: this game is best experienced blind, so beware of spoilers!A tifully illustrated RPG with VN-elements, ISAT starts out simple at first and becomes the right amount of difficult to tell the story it wants to tell. The gameplay  is simple and engaging, the characters feel alive and complex, there are lots of little details and hidden secrets, and I’d argue that, even if you don’t engage to the fullest with all the elements of the game, you’d still enjoy yourself. As someone who related maybe a bit too much with Siffrin, I also love how the game kinda pushes you into behaving like him ()Probably not of interest to everyone, but this game also lends itself fairly well to being played by taking turns with a friend. I personally played it like that and we both enjoyed it a lot. (the only problem is achievements, of course, but even then, the many save slots make that less of a problem)Probably could have afforded to be more angsty at s.Can get somewhat repetitive, but that's kind of the point, so I personally didn't mind it too much.No special dialogue for interacting with stuff you're not supposed to know about (which I get why, but still, it could have been hidden away by, like, clicking 10 times, or be a speedrunner extra). It is true, though, that the whole point of the game is Siffrin's arc as he learns what he's supposed to be doing, so doing everything right the first time would probably make the game very different and boring, but still.All in all, I really enjoyed it, so I had trouble finding something to nitpick ^^;Definitely one of my favorite games of all time, looking forward to insertdisc5's next (not ISAT-related) project(s) :D

_childDocuments_.review: This is my favorite time loop media, and it's not even close. It's witty, it's heartfelt, it's terrifying.Just stop reading and play it already, I'll be here pouring more of my emotions in this textbox.This game refuses to end, and I mean this in the best way. Can you believe I thought It would have three acts? Lol. Lmao even. It's relentless in it's goal to explore every nook and cranny of the time loop trope- more then anything I've ever seen. Like the protagonist, I was kept in a constant state of "okay, surely this is the one." (It wasn't.)This game cares so much about the story it tells, the characters with all their complexity, the rich world and it's cultures, it's philosophies, and the hard, often disturbing emotions this scenario would drive anyone to. The time loop gives all of these the space to be explored genuinely and thoroughly. The amount of detail, variation, and depth it's willing to go to dwarf all the other similar stories I've seen.This is an interactive visual novel first and rpg second, but every element of the rpg medium is used cleverly to elevate the story and themes. If you're not much for reading (you dork) this might not be for you. It's a slowburn, but oh boy does it deliver.Surface level stuff- Art is great with a very strong visual choices (obvious), dialogue is fantastic, the pacing reveal of the text is practically acting. I can hear these gremlins in my mind. Get them out. The music is great, and the repeating aspect of it connects me to the protag inherently. "Here again.", "Oh, it's this part", and so on and so forth. The battle system is engaging, and invites you to avoid enemies for time- with a price to your exp, of course. Quality of life out the wazoo. If you think "this will get annoying to redo" shut up no it won't they thought of that.This is a full, long, LONG game, polished in every aspect. An absolute masterpiece of the genre. Buy it. Heck, why not, buy it a second time, it's on theme.

The things that make you reset are forced - there's no way to avoid dying to them the first time, and mostly they just feel like their purpose is to add playing time. _childDocuments_.review: One of the things about this game that I found the most interesting is how much my experience playing it matched Siffrin's journey. Early on I was determined to not skip dialogue and make sure to do all the things every loop as much as possible, but eventually I found myself just ignoring certain things completely and using the skip function liberally, which matched Siffrin's mental state at that point incredibly well.This was a fantastic journey and an incredibly enjoyable game. The mechanics are simple and fun and quick to pick up, and I love exploring how the little moments changed through every loop. I do wish Acts 5 & 6 had a bit more breathing room/time to explore the culmination of the story, but I still enjoyed the whole game overall and definitely recommend giving the game a try.

_childDocuments_.review: A truly wonderful experience, carried entirely by its writing and excellent characters. Although flawed, I wholeheartedly recommend this game.Pros:- Top class writing, with outstanding, multi-dimensional characters that you will care about by the end of the game. - Pulls you into the plot by bringing the player along for the gradual decline of the protagonist. Things get worse, and you are always there for the transition.- Although I do think there was too much backtracking, there us a slow build up of tension over loops that has some incredible emotional payoffs, some of which hits you by surprise and keeps you engaged despite how repetitive the gameplay is.- The music is limited, but what is in the game is pretty good.Cons:- You are here for the writing, there isn't much else to see. Gameplay is boring and monotonous. Enemy design is uninspired. Art, outside of character portraits, is mediocre. Combat is brain dead. It does not get better with time.- The core plot has a bit of hand waving in the final acts that left a bad taste in my mouth.- Some quests have excessive backtracking. This was absolutely required to express themes, but it could have been even more streamlined in ending acts after the message had been conveyed.- Because the writing is so consistently excellent, flaws stand out and distract. Loop is an excellent character, but they have a lot of canned dialogue that doesn't evolve with the plot. The game almost always shows instead of tells, but the end sections have a lot of monologuing and it was a bit obnoxious. There's rule changes to the lore in the last acts that didn't make sense. Relatively small things that build up over time. I really enjoyed this game despite its flaws, and I think it'll stick with me for a while. I thought the writing was smart, the characters were compelling, and the protagonist to be relatable. However, what's disappointing for  me with this game is that it feels like it's on the cusp of being a masterpiece. Good writing is the hardest part, and it has it. If the gameplay was more unique and interesting, if the game didn't run long after conveying themes, if the backtracking was not so much of a chore, if there was more varied enemy types, better music, if just the whole package was better I think this game could be a 10/10. Not everyone has the patience or time for the monotonous backtracking and boring gameplay. That is such a shame. I hope more people play this.

_childDocuments_.review: I've been putting off writing a review for this game because I didn't know how to start or how to put my feelings into a small enough amount of words that anyone would read my damn review. But here I am and here are my thoughts.FIrst of all, 10/10 character writing. The dialogue has so much character and it feels so organic. The party all have distinct personalities and the way they talk and joke with each other feels incredibly organic. This game just has tons of charm across the board. It's funny, the little conversations with side characters are fun, I have no notes.This is supplemented by EXCELLENT use of text boxes. The dev drew I believe it was 429 different sprites for characters to show how they feel when they speak. These are not only really cute but also make it very great to read the tone of any given line. The writing itself plays with punctuation to show all kinds of emotion in a way I don't often see. This can mean several exclamation points or a classy creeping ellipses. What do I mean a "creeping ellipses"? Great question hypothetical reader! The text moves across the screen at varying speeds not infrequently going character by character to show pauses. You will also see large breaks in a word to show mid-sentence or word pause, jumping text, and shaking text. All of this combined with the character sprites lets you read the so much emotion in the lines. It's like good voice acting in text form if that makes sense.The combat system is simple but fun but simple, it has turn-pass mechanics my beloved and potential to make some smart plays but it's not the main focus of the game in my eyes.The story of the game itself is pretty interesting. There is a lot of mystery to work through which can at times feel tedious (though there are very nice QoL features regarding the timeloop), though there was only one part of the game where I felt that this was to its detriment. That moment being when I had to find an object and it wasn't clear enough to me what it was. There was also a non too small plot point that I felt didn't have a real resolution but it's possible I missed something. Those are only real gripes with this game which is pretty good by my standards. Learning new pieces of the story was a good driver for me to keep playing the game. But, at least for me, the lore is not what kept me playing for most of this game.The protagonist, Siffrin, is, expectedly, the beating heart of this game. They are as subject to all of the great writing I mentioned before but it goes to another level here. All of the work that sprites and text movement does for the rest of the game is with him but just, more. And it's great. On top of that, I have never in my life had any character be as in my own head is Siffrin. There were several moments where I thought something only to see that exact sentiment reflected in dialogue, internal monologue, or hell even the sprite art. These are levels of he's literally me previously unknown to the human mind. The flipside of this is that I was also subject to a substantial amount of the character angst this game had to offer. This is a personal thing really so        LOOK AWAY FOR PEAK BLIND GAMEPLAY        TLDR: Cute game, great writing, emotionally powerful, play it NOWbut only if you wanna :)

_childDocuments_.review: First of all: This game is critically underrated and deserves so much more attention and praise. I feel as though this game goes over the theme of time loops in its own unique way than what other games and movies will do when using it. With most games that use the sense of a "time loop", the character you play as is, in a sense, the player. With the player and character being one, there is never sort of a negative impact on the player's character.  In Stars and Time uses a form of reality with the idea that living the same timeline over and over without being able to see the goal is destructive to one's mental health as Siffrin who has his own history and personality. In a sense, the game goes deep into how that implication affects not only yourself but the people around you as well. In my own personal experience, representing mental health this way is so important to me. The further you go into the game, the deeper the story becomes and the situation you find yourself in. The actions you choose don't have consequences in your loop, but it will have consequences on yourself- and I think that's such an interesting take on the "actions have consequences" portion of time loops. Its such a wonderful story and world built with so many mysteries and questions to still be answered. I love this game so much and will be playing it over and over to see things I missed out on in my first run.

_childDocuments_.review: Words cannot express how much I love this game. I already played through it once on Switch and wanted to play it again to see what all I missed and to go through certain dialogues and scenes with the new insight. Ended up buying it on Steam because my Switch barely made it through before it kicked the bucket. Was totally worth getting again and doing another playthrough. I've already found things that I missed the first time around. Okay a more useful breakdown about this game: The gameplay's weakest element is repetition, which doesn't come as a surprise given that it's about a time loop. However, this is greatly eased by a lot of quality of life features. You can fast forward through repeat dialogue. This can impact small scenes, but is never punished so you can be as patient (or not) as you want. You can also skip entire sections if you don't want to repeat parts of the game's dungeon crawl. You will also need to revisit sections so it does create somewhat of a large puzzle, which i found myself really enjoying. The combat is straightforward, but not so simple that it's completely mindless. I found it had a good amount of strategy for engagement, but simplicity so as to not get too time consuming with the time looping.: It starts simple enough that it's very easy to get into, but had enough elements and complexity that I didn't get bored despite repeating the same two days. If anything, unearthing hints, lore, and character information had me making a lot of theories about the world, story, and characters. It's very engaging when you immerse yourself in the details.: My goodness do I absolutely adore the cast. I didn't dislike a single member of the party. They're all lovable as individuals and only get better through their dynamics with each other. My biggest worry was about Bonnie as younger characters can often be written as a bit obnoxious, but they're also an absolute delight. Everyone felt believably their age with (mostly) charming flaws and traits. Siffrin desperately needs therapy, but that's a whole other can of worms. I won't talk about Loop too much, but I will say that I started out disliking them and grew ever more conflicted as the game went on.Speaking of therapy, I did find this game (or more specifically Siffrin) to be a bit of a black mirror at times. This was honestly a good thing and while a bit of an emotionally rough ride for me and my roommates who also got sucked into watching my playthrough, it lead to some pretty healthy introspection. For the sake of spoilers, I won't get into the ending or finer details, but I found the overall message to be a blunt but necessary hit between the eyes lol. An overall phenomenal game that I'm so happy to have played.

_childDocuments_.review: Indie gaming is entering its kitsch era. That's not to day In Stars And Time is kitsch, but it's part of a phenomenon beginning to plague gaming: a "that's the point" approach to defending fundamental failures in game design.In Stars And Time has a message for you, and the gameplay exists in service of that message. What your character is experiencing is an inescapable whirlpool of existential suffering, and if the game can make you feel that, you've connected to its themes and its characters.My issue is that I don't think capturing suffering is as cut-and-dry as that. You can convey a feeling of suffering without making gameplay itself suffering, AND you can make gameplay itself suffering without making the experience unenjoyable. I feel In Stars And Time misses both these marks.In the former camp, we have genre games which inspired this game's style. Omori understood that pain can be experienced alongside depth of environment; the consistently fresh and varied progression through plot and areas achieved suffering through the behaviour of the protagonist. Everhood understood that an excellent foundation of gameplay can guarantee a vehicle for whatever emotions you wish, retaining fun in the face of grim work. Undertale understood that if your gameplay and environments are not your draw card, you need alternatives to keep engagement - humour, novelty, and alternate options in combat.Sadly, In Stars And Time understands none of these things. Its environments and story progress are distressingly samey, with plot reached by pilgrimages of character interaction hoping to make us like the (admittedly likeable) cast, through the exact same hallways and rooms looking for keys. Its core gameplay showed promise, but immediately boils down to routine - see the hand type, choose the attack type. And in a game emphasising comedy, this core gameplay is sterile; no jokes, no interesting mix-ups, just the same approach to a different blob.Worse, these fights are then heavily pushed onto the player. Each time a room is entered enemies respawn, and once spotted the chances of avoiding them are slim. They can hit hard, requiring frequent use of heals or buffs that slow down these already stagnant fights. And above all, you get skills and stats through the shockingly slow levelling which are nigh-on required to progress, demanding grinding.On top of that, the loop is actually handled terribly in a gameplay sense. Unlike other frontrunners of time loop games, you are not discovering opportunities to loop back organically, you are stonewalled by set occurrences like your character missing something in a cutscene. It has some utility as a tool in finding little side-content, but its most common use is forcing you back when the game feels like it, not you.All of this is a shame because yes, the characters are funny, and the handling of the protagonist's attitude is refreshingly adaptive. But their bonds and development are the only rewards for a gameplay loop bereft of well-paced plot progress. The bulk of your time will be walking through the exact same dark hallways, trapped into fights that all feel that too-simple-same. It's an existential dread, but one we know already as distinct from the game's message. Every time you've had to reload a save after losing, had to play through that part you hate again. And as a player your end point isn't "how much more can I fight for the people I love", it's "why am I still playing this waste of time?"This game is not even close to the best use of a time loop - its claim to fame, if any, is the best encapsulation of the pain a time loop would be like. Outer Wilds and The Forgotten City are both exceptional merges of gameplay with time loop, and I strongly recommend checking them out if that's your thing. As for this game, I'd recommend asking yourself: do I care if I'm not having fun as long as it's for a reason?Some will love this game, which is great, and I respect that opinion, just as the above is my opinion. But defending frustrations of gameplay as part of the message, as "the point", is just as much an opinion. I get it, the suffering is the point. It just doesn't excuse that it's not fun.

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to like this game, but its not quite clicking for me and truthfully I feel the game about time ironically commits the sin of not respecting the players time. I have too many games to play and not enough time in this life to play them, so when I find myself thinking "why am i playing this when i could be playing x instead", at that point its time to put the game down and go play something else. First, why the game didnt click for me. I agree so heavily with the opening line of  on this game. "Have you ever felt like you're at least ten years too old to be playing certain video games?" This game has both wonderful and terrible writing, primarily from the dialogue being absolutely childish at times. Sometimes the characters are endearing or the jokes are funny and get a chuckle. But more often than I like, there's just silly childishness for the sake of it. The game treats the "actual" child of the group, Bonnie, very differently than the group and yet i cannot help but feel the way that Mirabelle and Isabeau behave, they should be right in there with Bonnie. And with the game being like 90% dialogue and 10% gameplay, the only "draw" is failing to land for me.Secondly, lets talk about the game not respecting players time. You can read pretty much any other negative steam review to get the gist, but I think that the steam user "Some Guy" who also left a negative review really summed things up rather well. I will copy an excerpt of their review here:The hallways are narrow, the enemies are very hard to dodge, and I honestly don't find the combat interesting or engaging enough to warrant the amount of fighting that it seems users encourage you to do (aka grinding) to get to the point where you can 1shot monsters. Add on that the main thing you are doing when you arent in dialogue is basically exploring looking for keys so you can backtrack to the door that they unlock, and each time you walk into a room monsters will respawn, you are going to be fighting a lot.While important things are kind of sparkly in the overworld so you can see them, in order to find other types of items items, you need to search many different things, which often all have some dialogue from the characters. This is nice and all but sometimes the characters just talk too much. Far far too much. And finally, I feel as though theres some sort of... i cannot put my finger on it, but delay/lag when interacting with items, talking to people, starting/finishing combats, etc. It could be my brain screaming "give me more now faster" at the game drip-feeding you content, but I find myself spamming A far too frequently for this kind of game. I dont need a text box every combat saying "(you breathe in and out)" "(gained 200 exp)" at the end of every combat, adding another second of delay to my exploring. Perhaps this is being nitpicky but I think its a symptom of general frustration at other areas of the game just taking far too long. And also, dialogue speed. I cannot even make the dialogue go faster as it started in the highest speed there was available, and the only higher tier of "instant" ruins the interesting way the characters say/reveal dialogue to fit their moods. All in all theres just a bit of frustration at every turn here.I see often parroted around reviews that the game is intentionally designed to make you tired of time looping, to feel what the main character feels, etc. Okay thats great that you feel that way, but as the steam user "Some Guy" also pointed out that this mentality is just defending fundamental failures in game design (). If you like that, fine, but again, I have hundreds of games to play and not enough time to play them, and in the next few years ill have hundreds of more games to play, and still not enough time to play them. I am all for games trying to push the boundaries of gaming, but failing to respect the the players time is not one of them.

_childDocuments_.review: I don't know that I can accurately summarise how much I adore this game, but I will try. The story is incredible, the characters are captivating, and the game is meticulously mechanically tuned to avoid many of the hurdles one might run into with making a game about time looping. This is, as many time loop and story-driven games are, best experienced with as little prior knowledge as possible, so if this review is at all swaying you to buy and play the game, I urge you to do so immediately. But I also want to braindump about it, so I'm gonna. (It's going to be *wordy*, and I will *not* apologise for that.)One key piece of advice I would have is to follow your impulses with this game. If you have an idea of something interesting you want to try, to see how a character might react to something, what using [x] item at [y] location might do, what might work to break out of the loop, try and explore it, in many cases you will be rewarded for your efforts. The game may even help you keep track, depending on what you come up with!I've played a lot of time loop games, and I adore looping as a narrative device. Unlike a lot of time loop games, like Outer Wilds or The Sexy Brutale, In Stars And Time expends a lot of effort exploring what being stuck in such a situation would be like for the person experiencing it. Our PC, Siffrin's, inner monologues and conversations with himself paint a strong picture of his evolving mental state, but to be honest, a lot of the time I found I already shared those thoughts. I had a theory of how to end the loops, and some time later Siffrin would come up with the same idea. When I began to feel myself becoming impatient with repeating the same sections, Siffrin's behaviour had often already started to adapt in a way that mirrored my frustration (not quite the right word, I always enjoyed it, but frustration's the closest approximation). Because I loved the characters and the writing, I often found myself wanting to repeat things anyway, to see what new dialogue may have been unlocked, but I think surrendering part of my impulse to wade through repeated content helped immerse me more into Siffrin's mindset. If you also like time loop games and enjoyed the final ending of Elsinore, you will enjoy what this game explores.That said, the looping is handled very well mechanically, in my opinion. The developer obviously realised that an RPG in which your progress is constantly reset would eventually get tedious, and you could never just blaze your way through easy encounters, and these are mitigated by game mechanics () These mechanics then also play into the narrative in interesting ways that I won't spoil.While the looping is handled mechanically well, the battle system is very simple. This isn't necessarily a point against or in favour of the game, but people looking for a very mechanically dense RPG battle system may find themselves disappointed (it's mostly literally Rock, Paper, Scissors with some extra things to bear in mind like status ailments). At the same time, with the number of loops you're going to be required to do, a battle system that is too complex would likely become a hindrance, but I feel like this is a point worth mentioning for anyone who doesn't typically enjoy games for their narratives.Aside from the incredibly immersive way in which the game manages to make you relate to and identify with Siffrin, the rest of the party members (and, indeed, many of the random NPCs) are incredible. The humour is on point, with each character's traits carrying through strongly and consistently, bouncing off one another or working in harmony to great comedic or emotional effect. The writing is very successful at making this seem like a party of disparate people drawn together by circumstance who have grown incredibly close. And while the comedy is on point, the characters are far from quippy, one-note trope heroes, each of them has hidden depths that are emotionally resonant and compelling, and the player is justifiably rewarded for trying to connect more with their party members.It's also super gay, so that's a point in its favour.I cried multiple times during this game, and it has genuinely changed how I view the world, how I view myself (I'm tearing up as I write this review!) The developer clearly wrote this game from somewhere deeply personal within them, and I want them to know that it has definitely impacted me greatly.If you like games for their stories, In Stars And Time is undeniably one you should not miss out on for any reason. If you only like games strictly for their gameplay, you may find it lacking, but regardless I still recommend it, perhaps you'll find something in this game that resonates with you.

_childDocuments_.review: I am a person that absolutely loves games with a rich story. In stars and time is no exception to this. The game offers a nice array of characters and has some really good dialogue. It got me feeling horrible in certain moments when the MC broke down and had me actually feeling my heartbeat during the silence. If you enjoyed things like Undertale, Omori or Oneshot, you would definitely enjoy this. I only have a few major gripes with the game1:During the game, you get access to a "zone out function" (skip previous dialogue). On the surface, it's fine. You get booted during imported moments and when your character talks. However, things can change and you might miss information. If the game had some sort of dialogue log then this wouldn't matter but sometimes i find it annoying to try and find missed dialogue. 2:During the game's mid point, there is a certain part of the main quest where you need to find something specific. During other parts of the game, it's something quite big or you get a blatant hint (it's in the library, its with specific npc in the starting village, etc). However, this one was just "find it in the dungeon". It's the only thing i needed an actual guide for and it might get other stuck as well. 3:The game is split into sections (otherwise known as acts). It gives you a warning for when you pass the point of no return but because of the acts system i assumed that i could start from a certain point like in other games (I hate the fact that the only game i can think of is bloody minecraft story mode). This is not the case. I finished the game and didn't have access to the point where i could get all the achivements so i need to redo the entire game... It is my fault but i feel like it could've easily been avoided with a "start from act x" in the new game option. Overall, this game is awesome. The music is pretty good, characters are awesome, dialogue is funny and it hits you in the feels when it wants to. If you like story games, try it. If you mainly want game play, it's still worth it in my opinion. TLDR: Game has good story, a few minor issues that don't really matter and overall is a 9/10

_childDocuments_.review: In Stars and Time is a game I cannot recommend enough. It's charming, witty, and gratifying. It's a character driven story with a heavy focus on dealing with trauma and relationships. While I was initially apprehensive of the game because it uses rpgmaker, it's very much worth looking past that. What is here is amazing world building, fleshed out characters, and an interesting take on time looping.I think it's really ambitious to tackle time looping in a game, because it is so easy to do wrong. You miss something, you don't add in enough detail, you make it feel like your actions don't matter. This is one of those games that has managed to pull it off. Every loop is working towards a goal, bit by bit, into smaller and bigger pictures. The mystery is untangled, the world is fleshed out, context is given. You might reach a dead end, you may be free to do as you wish. It's a series of puzzles that you need to figure out.It's important to point out that one of the reasons the time looping story works so well is that the game is actually repetitive and monotonous. It does not hold that back, and while you can use a system to move quickly between floors and areas, you will absolutely be spending a lot of time backtracking. Your entire area of play is limited in areas, and you will be revisiting them countless times. While this might sound like a large negative, it honestly adds to the experience. What the MC feels becomes more authentic when you are also experiencing it with them, eager to find out what's next and feeling frustrated by what you missed the first time.While I'm giving a pass to the repetitive nature, I do have some gripes. The game can be at times a little too cryptic with what it wants you to do next, and sometimes you'll just end up brute forcing the game by interacting with anything you can possibly think of being related until you find what it wants. As well, the combat is simple, almost to a satirical degree, and it's unlikely you're going to be looping from dying in battle.  While it's simple, it is still enjoyable, and to be fair, you are not playing this game for deep rpg mechanics. This is a story that I will absolutely be experiencing again some day, and hopefully you will too.

_childDocuments_.review: Have you ever found a piece of media that makes you dread the moment it's going to be over? Be it comic, television, animation, gaming, whatever, it's a sign of designer pedigree, or at the least something you as an individual connects with deeply. I have felt this way only a handful of times, and I can safely attest that In Stars And Time is a newcomer to the club. I fell in love with the cast, and it only grew more as the game continued. Character interaction is, in my mind anyways, should be the forefront of any RPG. This does it with flying, pride flag colors. I never skipped any interaction with the cast as I was going through, because even the minute details and changes in conversation with the people and the world around you kept me hooked. The little ways you uncover more about a character's personality through conversation or their observations. I understand how The King felt, I didn't want it to end.Is the constant backtracking tedious? Yeah, but that's the very nature of Time Loop games honestly. Or at least ones of this nature. Though it didn't feel like it had nothing to add to the game. If it was maddening, then it was doing its job right. Imagine the sheer torment of having to repeat the same lines, move the same way, eat the same food every single day, on the same day for eternity? I felt it in the gameplay. The way the torment of a Groundhogs Day incident is portrayed in its narrative and gameplay? Amazing. The cast is also fantastic. So often do groups of characters in works of fiction often feel stiff when you contrast them with the rest of their group. Sure, you may have a straight man and the wise guy, but if they say they're friends and you can't feel the dynamic between them, their interactions are falling flat. Everyone in ISAT works off of one another in exceptional ways that made me fall in love with them the more I saw them. I don't care if I saw the Tree-mendous joke 100 times, I'd give my left nut to protect Isabeau's smile. Tl;dr: 10/10, I enjoy.

_childDocuments_.review: Memes aside, this quickly became one of my top five favorite games probably just within the first hour of playing, and then it got . It's an absolute masterclass in writing--in writing character relationships, in writing timeloops, in writing casual representation, and in writing stories that tug at your heart (or stomach?) and stay with you long after you've finished. It's been maybe a week since I finished the game for the first time on the Switch; not long after I bought it here as well to give a second playthrough, and for all the time in between I've been thinking about it, watching other people play it, discuss it, writing fanfiction, writing songs about it...pretty much everything I can do to keep the experience with me and to try to put into words how much it's meant to me. I don't really think this review is going to be the thing that does it, but it's worth a try! The music is wonderful and very fitting for the game and infinitely replayable, the art is gorgeous and the character portraits in particular are an absolute delight at every turn, and again, the writing is amazing. Right away you fall in love with the characters and with the world they inhabit, and every moment you spent with them is one you fall in love a little harder...and what's more fantastic is that all of this, this experience with the characters and more broadly the gameplay itself, only echoes the main character's feelings. It's very immersive and very beautiful, and I cried a whole bunch and then thanked the dev for it. One hundred percent recommended. Play it play it play it!
