_childDocuments_.review: In Stars and Time is yet another experience in what I want to call the "Undertale" genre. Memorable games that come to mind are, obviously, Undertale, and Omori. I am usually pretty picky and wary of these types of games, because there are others out there who want to be like Undertale, perhaps too much, and fall short of being its own unique adventure. Omori was inspired by Undertale but was its own product and identity, and a very memorable one, one that I enjoyed immensely.Then comes In Stars and Time.To start off with the bad, there is really one aspect of the game that really impacted my enjoyment; the lack of respect for player's time. There is a lot of tracing back, and while the game does help speed parts of these up, in my opinion it's not enough. It feels like padding. The more guilty part of the game though is there's a resource used to be able to fast travel, as I'll say call. This resource is farmable, but you need a special item equipped to efficiently farm it. I found that I needed to grind quite a bit to have enough of this resource to fast travel comfortably throughout my playthrough, and it felt like a drag at times. There is also a character you'll meet that you'll talk a lot with, and there were times where you had to go back and forth between this character and other destinations which just added to the tedium. Most importantly, the messages had no way of being mashed through. There is an option to make messages instant, and this is perhaps more of a petty inconvenience, but I like to have messages just be fast, but instant when I press a button.But despite the flaws, I thoroughly enjoyed the game, its theme and its story. I can see inspirations of Undertale, but the game I feel shaped its own unique identity just like Omori, and became something to be remembered on its own. The unique concept of its fighting system is simple, but interesting, and the storytelling of in-game events is what really shines, in my opinion. The more I played, the more engrossed and curious I was to see what happened next. In fact, there are parts of the story that I wish I could've see more expansion on that were very interesting. I am hoping to see more information on the "world" of this game in the future from the creator, maybe even a sequel!Overall the game demands you put in some sweat to make progress at times, but does it make it worth playing through to the end? I would say yes, at least for me. I won't be forgetting the Memories of In Stars and Time

_childDocuments_.review: What all the other reviews are saying. The game is charming, well-written, funny, emotional, and everything you could really want from games as a storytelling medium in general. Never before have I ever felt so... well-anticipated by a game, both from a story perspective and mechanically. A solid 9/10 experience that's well worth a play even if you (like me) totally spoiled yourself on pretty much the whole thing by watching complete playthroughs... multiple times.PROS:- The game is consistently well-written, both from an overarching story perspective and just in the little moments during interactions, etc. that are easy to miss. Pretty consistently nails its humor. A distillation of the best of internet humor's charm without the abstract non-sequiturs that often gunk up modern internet humor and rapidly lose their shine.- The game is really smart about how it uses its limited mechanics. It's a time loop game, but it does a fantastic job of calling you out on your complacency. The number of times I was cursing myself because I autopiloted through a chunk of the game and then realized I had forgotten to do something important had me sold on the way the game is set up. It's tedious on purpose, and that creates a game that sells me more on the story through its gameplay.-  The characters and the art are good, yeah yeah yeah every review mentions it but it's worth a shout here.- The OST bangs. Enough said.CONS- It's not a game you are really playing for the gameplay. The gameplay itself is... fine, I guess, but really just serves as a delivery device for the game's true strengths. It's not going to blow your mind with revolutionary turn-based combat, and it wears RPG Maker on its sleeves with pride.Go into it blind if you can, but even if you know the story there are lots of little things that are even more impactful with 20/20 hindsight. It's also a pretty meaty game for its price - 20-25 hours long and none of it feels like filler. Worth your time and money, 100%.

_childDocuments_.review: This is the third time I've bought this game—I already beat it on Switch with 35 hours logged. I also played START AGAIN: A Prologue back in 2021. This game is so much more than I expected it to be. I was blown away by the passion and attention to detail. I cried, I laughed, Act 5 literally had me gaping in awe after entering the House... there's so much I want to say but can't, because I want everyone to feel the same feelings I did on my first blind playthrough.Things I WILL say about this game:- Undertale vibes for sure, can't speak for Omori since I never played it but I'd also compare it to the anime RE:Zero with it's combination of timetravel and focus on trauma/character growth.- Lots of varied queer rep! It never felt forced to me, and I love how the fantasy setting is designed to tie that queer rep into the story's themes without making it a focus on discrimination/bigotry. I never knew until this game how badly I wanted more aroace rep in gaming, so thanks for that.- You will repeat a lot of the same dialogue (of course!) but I always felt rewarded for poking at the same stuff over and over again. The party's dialogue doesn't always change, but Siffrin will often have new comments to add as the loops go on. Make sure to rexamine everything and read the dialogue at least a couple times each new act!- Combat is simple but still provides some strategy to chew on early on. That said, it's largely inconsequential by Act 3/4 of the story, which DOES feel accurate to the story but does turn encounters into an annoyance. Luckily, you don't have to grind at all past a certain point since mandatory fights give plenty of EXP for the party and Siffrin can otherwise hard carry the team. You can run from battles by pressing X/Cancel during a character's turn.- One small gripe is that it's easy to miss the "true" ending conditions, which adds a LOT of context to the end of the story. Pro tip: look at your silver coin in your inventory! Use it around town and in front of the Favor Tree! Make sure to talk to Loop a bunch after! Trust me!!- Love the music!! Also love the art. Also love the characters. I would die for everyone in this party.- I put 35 hours into this game and I still feel like I missed so much, so I am probably going to put like another 30 or so hours into it. it's fine im normal dwbi hahaThis game did irreparable damage to my brain chemistry. I have not stopped thinking about it for a solid week. Sorry to all of my friends who will have to listen to me gush about this all the time now. Please suffer with me... please.... the blorbos...... please.....

_childDocuments_.review: One of those games you wish you could play for the first time over again. Go into this as blind as possible. This review won't spoil specific plot points, but you should still play the game before reading it.Part JRPG, part visual novel, In Stars And Time is a contender for the best time-loop game ever made. Outer Wilds, its only competition, is more fun; but ISAT isn't exactly trying to be "fun". This is a long, exhausting, emotionally and even physically  experience, but the catharsis you get for all your effort is nearly unmatched.The gameplay is standard JRPG fare. Combat is ATB-based, but auto-pausing when a character's turn comes up makes it work more like a turn-based system. Spells have turn-based cooldowns rather than an MP bar, so you're incentivized to speed up your turns as much as possible. When not in combat, you can walk around the world & dungeon and examine things, talk to people, etc. There are no random encounters, instead utilizing Chrono Trigger's method of wandering enemies in the world that you can avoid if you choose.The story focuses on Siffrin, an introverted yet cheerful rogue, as he finds himself trapped in a time loop that starts the day before fighting the final boss of an RPG with his gang of friends. As you inevitably fail on your first few attempts to take on the House of Change, things begin opening up for you to experiment and try to alter events to bring you and your party victory.But victory is a long time in coming. As the loops and hours go by, the gameplay's charm eventually wears off. Fights become tedious, to the point where even waiting for the 1 second buff animations feels like a waste of time. What's the point in grinding when your teammates' experience doesn't even carry over between loops? Easier to just run past the enemies. Finding keys becomes first a chore, then a punishment. Knowing exactly where they are only makes it more excruciating when you realize that their placement requires you to run back and forth across the entire floor--running into more annoying enemies--rather than quickly ducking into a room that you know has the final required item to progress. Listening to your friends repeat the same lines over and over and  starts to fray on your nerves, even with the help of a zone-out fast forward button. Speed up, speed up, speed up, skip, skip, skip. After fifteen  of this you'll have all the layouts memorized and be effectively speedrunning the loops, hoping every time to find the next breadcrumb of lore, or a clue, or an interaction with your friends that's  just to remember when they didn't feel like robots.And Siffrin feels exactly the same way. Never before has a game protagonist so precisely echoed the player's growing thoughts, emotional state, and even boredom. His inevitable mental decline was paced out more perfectly than I could have expected, matching the player's deteriorating experience and keeping you locked in and interested in the greater mysteries that slowly, SLOWLY piece together over the dozens and eventually hundreds of loops. His frustrating, total inability to ask for help or let the others see his pain doesn't feel like plot railroading--it feels authentic. While nothing in the world ever changes, Siffrin's experience inevitably shapes him, and that's what the heart of the game is about.I have only two complaints, both so minor I'm not sure I'd even knock a point off for them. One is a particularly vague puzzle involving a book where the in-game hint is exceptionally unhelpful, which took a few hours longer for me to find than I think might have been intended. The other is that the ending, while satisfying, does feel a little bit too neat and pat--I was hoping for a more grounded confrontation than what eventually occurs. But there was still enough of the game's customary bittersweet realism to make it land well enough.Where many JRPGs build to an external apocalypse, ISAT is all about an internal one. This is a character study on par with the greats. Though the scope is intentionally much narrower than Evangelion, that was the comparison that kept coming to mind the further in I got. I'll be thinking about this game for years.

_childDocuments_.review: "Land of The Great Horses" is a 1967 short story written by Robert A. Lafferty for the anthology Dangerous Visions, a collection of stories from various authors on topics deemed "unpublishable" by the mores of the time. "Land of The Great Horses" paints a picture of the land of the roma people being returned to them, and a deep instinct awakening in anyone of their descent to return to a home they never remembered. The official German translation of this story is titled "Heimkehr der Heimatlosen," translating literally to "The Homesickness of The Homeless."In Stars & Time is about many things. It's about being touch starved, depressed, so convinced others hate you, could easily hate you, that you hide your entire self. It's a story about patterns of habits and how the only way to break a depressive cycle is to love, and be loved. In Stars & Time is a game about a person who cannot remember their homeland, but is homesick for it anyway, and expects to lose the things they've come to love just as easily. It is a gripping story with genuine lovable characters, and a protagonist that is far too easy to see myself in. I hope one day to create art like this, that captures emotions of isolation and despair and anxiety so easily, while also showing there is a light out of the tunnel.

_childDocuments_.review: A well crafted story with middling gameplay, I love every character in this thing--from the cute as hell main group to the npcs and the worldbuilding makes me want more stories in this setting. However, while i'm giving this a thumbs up for all the soul infused in the game's writing I do want to warn anybody looking for a straight up RPG that ISAT is more of a story game with an RPG as it's background. Yeah there's actual battling mechanics, equips, leveling, skills, element advantages/disadvantages and so on but compared to the work put into making the player care for the main party and the world they inhabit the actual playing aspect of it is not the best. Enemies respawn the instant you return to an area, tight corridors make dodging them a pain in the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ ass so going between the same hallways back and forth is always a hassle, and all of the game's events take place in the same three floor castle environment (not counting the small hub town) with there only being a handful of interesting side areas.  You can skip whole areas using your looping powers but there will be times you need to start from the beginning in order to see certain events or get certain achievements. You can get several memories (special equips you gain from completing certain objectives or from seeing certain events) that make it all less tedious however.tldr; this is basically Backtracking: the Game I nearly left this game unfinished around the halfway point but i'm glad I stuck through it to the end. The characters are wonderful and consistently written, the psychological elements were creatively implemented, and the final half of the game more or less made all the backtracking worth it.

_childDocuments_.review: “Change is destruction.”One of my favorite concepts is time travel, and so I was drawn to In Stars and Time, an indie RPG. The basic gist is that the story picks up at the *end* of a regular RPG. The party is high level and at the point-of-no-return. They are at the last village before fighting the final boss in the castle. In this case, the King as they call him, has frozen an entire country in time, and Dormont (I just realized this is a play on the word “dormant” heh) is one of the few places left where people aren’t frozen. The protagonist is Siffrin, a rougish type character. He wakes up from a nap in a field and goes about his business getting ready for the battle in the castle. Except there’s one hiccup: anytime he dies he loops back where he first woke up from his nap. He doesn’t want the rest of the party to find out what’s happening so the rest of the game is the player looping through the same two days of the plot trying to uncover the mystery of why they are trapped in the loop. Luckily, there are a lot of things the game does to make the looping feel less repetitive but part of the experience is feeling frustrated along with Siffrin. It goes WAY into depth about what would actually happen if someone experienced hundreds of time loops. Siffrin slowly goes mad over the course of the game. While much of the game is lighthearted, it explores dark topics like self-hate, suicide, despair, disgust, apathy, dissociation etc. It’s basically like if Groundhog Day happened in a JRPG. The writing is absolutely outstanding. There is so much attention to detail and characterization. If you like games like Undertale or Omori, this will be your bag. The battle system isn’t fancy, it uses literal rock-paper-scissors rules, but honestly, it’s more about the story anyway. The entire game is in black-and-white as an artistic choice and it definitely has that RPGMaker kinda aesthetic, but there’s a lot of fantastic hand drawn art as well. I absolutely loved it! Expect to cry tho.I’m being intentionally vague because this game is best going in blind, it REALLY goes to some places.

_childDocuments_.review: Okay, this review has been a long time coming.There's so, so much good stuff I could say about this game, but I'll try to keep this kind of brief.I found this game back in June of this year and I have been absolutely hooked by it for months since. Even after playing the game three times all the way through, I am still so deeply enamored with the characters, the story, the visuals, the music, etc. etc. Siffrin and Loop specifically my absolute beloveds.From a gameplay standpoint: this is one of the only games I have ever 100%ed. The quality of life for this game is impeccable, and it enables the gameplay to really make you FEEL the effects of the timeloop without completely burning you out by making you do the exact same thing over and over again. Getting achievements in this game is an INCREDIBLY gratifying experience as well; the sidequests and achievements lend themselves to really cool expansions to the story and the characters. I wholeheartedly believe that if you like this game even a little bit, you should do all the sidequests. That's how good they are.From a sappy personal standpoint: This games messages and themes really stuck with me. The incredibly casual and expansive LBGTQ+ rep was so refreshing to see, and the deeper emotional journey that Siffrin undergoes through this game really resonated with me as someone who experiences a lot of similar anxieties to him. The ending of this game had me SOBBING, so. Do with that what you will.All this to say: If the premise of this game interests you at all, if you like character-driven RPGs, if you like INSANELY tight and well-written worldbuilding, you have GOT to check this game out. This game is easily one of my all-time favorites now, and it will mean so much to me for a very long time to come.

_childDocuments_.review: I have yet to even beat this game and it has marked itself as one of my favorite RPGs of all time, and the best time loop story ever. Usually with time loop stories, things end up changing or speeding up with each run through due to the story not wanting to annoy or aggravate the user, so it feels less like a time loop and more like a linear story with occasional recaps. This game however, does not fall under this category of time loop stories, it does have features to make it less annoying, but these do not take away from the looping aspect and that exact looping aspect is so important to the story and how it makes you feel. Only through forcing the player to restart over and over again does it make the final fight of act 2 so enthralling and makes you want to make sure you don't fail. Then once you complete act 2, the events that open act 3 hit the player so much harder because of everything they went through, connecting you with the main character even more. All in all, really excited to finish the game and hope this review can convince others to buy this game.

TEDIOUS TIME LOOP GAME. this game is very very long because of how repetitive it is. despite that, i enjoyed it. i personally didnt mind the repetitiveness that much, and loved the story along with the characters. yeah, the writing can be cringy and corny, and yeah i did get bored, but i personally think it was worth it for watching the story play out how it did.the game takes place at the end of a journey as a character on a quest with their friends. time loop stuff happens, and you have to go through "the dungeon" to find pieces of the puzzle to eventually figure out how to get out.this game drives hard on its story and its characters, and if you're someone who enjoys reading dialogue between characters and seeing their dynamics, along with some really nice world building, and someone who doesnt mind repetitive gameplay, then this is for you. otherwise, i recommend finding another game.isat does a spectacular job of putting you in the main character's headspace and as someone who can relate on some level, it does a good job of representing trauma and how someone without proper help might cope with that. thats another thing it hinges on, though, the character. siffrin, the character you play as, probably wont stick with you unless you relate with them. its targeted at a specific group of people, and unless you are that group of people i dont think you will enjoy this game. if you dislike the repetitiveness, i recommend watching a playthrough of the game rather than playing it yourself.tldr; long repetitive game with very good story and characters, though its a game targeted for specific people who can relate to mental illness and general neurodivergency, and unless you are part of that group you likely wont enjoy it

_childDocuments_.review: I've bought this game a couple weeks post release and it took me 61 Loops to beat it (it turned out to be such a high number cuz I was a bit stupid at times) and I've loved the experience. I've started the game during a time where a lot of big changes happened at once in my life, so the message of the game hit close to home. Things happened so fast and I had to let go of so many things so suddenly when i wasn't ready. It brought me comfort, accompanying Siffrin on their journey. And boy what a journey it was! The time loops were a bit frustrating at times but that was due to the fact that i always played through the whole thing in fear of missing any new tidbits and interactions. The game provides enough features to skip the parts you've already experienced i simply didn't use them. But honestly? It enhanced the experience for me to a certain degree. As the loops kept continuing i grew more and more frustrated which made me really feel for Siffrin who had to go through this over and over and over again. In a way my frustration was also Siffrin's. That thought was really cool to me. All in all a really interesting and lovely character-focused story with beautiful worldbuilding. If you enjoy seeing a lil guy go bananas while trying to figure out what's going on and slowly losing the grip on reality this game is for you!

_childDocuments_.review: This was a really well written story that revealed its hand gradually and with a lot of skill that, as a fellow writer, I really found not only incredible on a technical level, but an emotional one. It was only during act 5 that I was worried I might hate the game (I thought the ending was going to take a turn down a much darker path but I was proven wrong :) ). Overall this is a game I had so much fun playing. If I would recommend anything it's not to try and play this game all in one sitting. I'd recommend taking a break for a few days if you feel yourself finding the game to be a chore. One of the really well done parts of this game is how it tries to minimize the annoying parts of time loop stories, which is having to sit through the same thing a thousand times. That said, it's still a time loop game so there is slog, but that slog feels well utilized because it really puts you in Sirrifin's shoes and makes their emotions a lot more understandable then they would have been otherwise. Breaks are important, especially because this is a really amazing story that I almost missed out on myself and I would hate to see someone miss out on what could be there next favorite game! I highly, highly recommend checking this out. It's one of those games that doesn't come along very often but when it does it makes sure to leave a lasting impression.

_childDocuments_.review: In Stars and Time is a game i can only recommend on the condition that the player knows what they are getting in to.I was gifted the game by someone who loved it very much. Someone who spent more than triple the amount of time in the game i have, just to find all the little details and secrets within. I could never do this because my patience is thoroughly worn out.In Stars and Time loves to waste your time. It loves to repeat events, enemies, music and puzzles over and over and over and OVER again. All of this to find the one extremely well hidden thing to progress. You begin to forget things and places where things are due to the repetition which wastes even MORE of your time! While the game is great fun the first time you go through these things, by the 5th or 30th or 80th time you've done it in a row it completely loses its charm and just becomes infuriating and exhausting to get through.This is all for a purpose though. Siffrin, the main character, is stuck in a Groundhog Day like time loop. In Stars and Time purposefully irritates or angers the player on purpose because that is EXACTLY how the main character feels if not worse. The game is absolutely brilliant because this causes every little advancement to be rewarding and every single story beat to resonate with the player as they know exactly how Siffrin would be feeling. It puts you in Siffrins perspective and emotional state completely. I have never seen a game do this in all my years and it truly is clever game design.That's why you need to know what you're getting into before you try In Stars and Time. It's such a huge red flag because a lot of people simply will not have the patience to play through something that actually wastes your time on purpose even if it is for a very good reason. Lord knows i almost got annoyed enough to quit at times..... but then something would keep bringing me back.The story is simple on the surface but packed with detail and emotional moments with a beautiful ending that left me emotionally worn out. The characters are charming, funny and genuinely well written so nothing they do ever feels contrived or out of place. Special mention to Bonnie for being the best written child character i have ever seen in a game: someone who is immature and overly emotional but never annoying or too stupid. The combat, although repetitious on purpose, actually has moments of genuine challenge that surprised me and made me want to keep going. The "representation" for LGBTQ is very tactful, feels like genuine parts of their character and most importantly: felt completely natural and not pandering at all. In Stars in Time is a really good game in all parts. Just with a massive asterisks next to an otherwise glowing recommendation. In some ways it's actually a better piece of art than a game because a lot of the time it is just not fun. The important questions are: Do you have the patience for it? Is it all worth it in the end?I barely had the patience to finish In Stars and Time. It drove me up the wall at times. In the end though? It was absolutely worth it and has left me with the sinking feeling that i will never be able to play it again and feel the same way i did playing through it the first time. It's a trying and emotionally draining experience but something truly special.

_childDocuments_.review: Hoo boy. That "Not Recommended" looks bad next to the Overwhelmingly Positive reviews. Let me explain.First: If the art, characters, and humor of the trailer are what's drawing you to this game, this review does not apply. You will likely enjoy it! It's a very lovingly crafted game and the vibes of it are pretty obvious just from the trailer. Just stop reading, grab the game, and enjoy. There will be some mild spoilers just from context from here on; nothing to any degree of ruining actual content, but you'll probably prefer going in blind. There is one caveat, here, that I'll put in spoiler text before going on - just as mild as other spoilers, but it relates to the direction of the story.  But: if the appeal of this game to you was the time loop aspect, as it was for me... you may be disappointed, like I was. Having finished the story, I am pretty underwhelmed.So - there's generally two directions a time loop video game can generally focus on. One is in mystery: why is this happening? What's causing it? What can I discover by viewing events from different angles? These are your Zero Escapes, your Steins;Gates, etc. They usually work with the visual novel format best, because that lets them neatly divide into separate "routes." The second is experimentation-based. What are the possibilities available to me? How can I accomplish my goals using information and tricks I pick up from previous loops? These are your Majora's Masks, Deathloops, Returnals, etc. In Stars and Time  it'll be the "experimentation" type, but this is a misdirect. You get the basic idea if you've watched through the trailer: you're in a typical RPG party, at the end of your journey, but you start dying and looping. Gotta try things out, dungeon crawl, and determine a way to finish your journey! But after, say, 8 loops? You already know how to accomplish this. There are no alternative routes, there are just 5 or so roadblocks where if you make a mistake, you have to start over. Most of these are unavoidable your first time through, to teach you how to avoid them. For context, by the time I finished, I was at 53 loops total, by the game's standards. That counts fast forwarding and intentionally ending them early, but *far* beyond one run.So! Mystery focus, that's the actual direction. And here's where we run into our first main problem: our protagonist. They are, without question, the most deeply incurious character I have ever seen in a story like this. Their tagline once you've done something once is "Follow the script," and hoo boy does it show. You check out an obvious clue, they'll note that it's there, and not care at all or consider it. There is a story reason that explains that, once you're ~15 hours into the game or so - but that's well past the point where it becomes infuriating, from a player's perspective. There's two reasons for this: first, the obvious problem of the player's goals clashing with the character's, and that just being frustrating. But second, it creates extremely tedious gameplay. After you have finished your first run (which, again, happens very early), it becomes a pattern of doing the one thing the protagonist can think of, another character saying something that triggers them going "wait, haven't I seen something like this before?" and running through the dungeon back to the clue that you, the player, already noticed hours prior. Past the point where the dungeon crawling is any actual obstacle, this is the only gameplay loop. It is the worst parts of Phoenix Wright logic, on repeat, with little else. This train is firmly on the railroad tracks, and you may only investigate when Siffrin SAYS you may investigate, one clue at a time, good sir!Okay, okay. So maybe not the type of game that would attract people who are into time loop stories and the possibilities those stories create. That's not...  considering that's the thing the game is ostensibly about, but come on. Look at it. This is clearly a character-based, story-driven, RPG Maker game, the sort whose inspirations are kinda beating you over the head when you look at it. How does it measure up when you look at it from that angle?It fares a lot better from that perspective, obviously. There's a reason so many people love it. And hell, I love games like that too, even if it wasn't what I came in for. The thing is, though. I'm not sure if it actually delivers in that area, either. If I had to describe it... the best comparison I could find is fanfiction? That may sound weird for an original story, but: we start with a fully-formed cast of characters, with established relationships that aren't gonna change much, they'll just be revealed to us, and it feels like most of the sharp edges are filed way down. Everyone gets along for the most part, conflicts are the sort that can be hashed out in a brief conversation, and the characters fully have the reins of the story, not the player. It definitely has the vibes of something from Ao3 over anything else. There isn't much "role-playing" to do, and you don't get much in the way of choice. It very neatly could have been a web novel, or a comic, and might have been better for it. But it is a game, and compared to other games in this sort of genre (let's be clear, Undertale and OMORI), the railroading  the direction the story is trying to take at the end. This is tough to write. I can tell the game is a labor of love. It just isn't a fun game to play, and it completely turned me off of its cast of characters based on the game's direction. It was not for me, and if you're reading this and any of these frustrations resonate with you, it might not be for you either.

_childDocuments_.review: A review I saw said something along the lines of, "if this seems interesting to you at all, buy it," and that is true. Best impulse buy of my life. I've written this review and am going back to edit it because I need a short, concise way to express how I feel about this game. The characters, story, worldbuilding, and mystery are amazing. Anytime I thought I knew where the story was going, I was wrong.The main "issue" with this game is the time looping. Eventually, it becomes repetitive, boring, and, in certain sections, a little boring. It has some mechanics that help with that, but inherently, it's a lot. But that's the thing; that is the point. I've never had a game immerse me in the story as much as this. You are on a ride with the main character, and it's amazing. The best story beats were when I was bored, going through the motions, looping, and then something *different* happened. My main warning is that this game goes dark and will keep going darker as you go. If you think you can take it, buy this game.

_childDocuments_.review: This was a great pickup to fill the void in my brain while I wait for  chapter 3.Please leave all your tired jokes about quirky indie RPGs about depression at the door, thank you very much.With that out of the way, this is a really cool take on the idea of time-loop games. It's less of a proper RPG and more like  That is to say- you aren't going to be getting much in the way of engaging gameplay. Without giving too much away, I can confidently say that  intentionally forgoes this to add to the feelings of tedium, being trapped, and mindless repetition that are so intertwined with the time-loop concept.The characters are excellent across the board. I love all of them, and I thoroughly enjoyed learning more about all of them and interacting with them as I went.  Also, they are pretty much all queer in one way or another, which is really nice to see. I won't get specific, as it's relevant to a particular plotline, but seeing my own identity and some experiences associated with it shown so genuinely, accurately, and without infantilization was a very pleasant surprise.If you're anything like me,  By the end, I was actually shocked at how much my perspective of the story and the other characters was warped to match that of Siffrin, rather than one of my own, an objective viewer outside of the game. It's wonderful, unique, and heart-wrenching.The soundtrack is nothing particularly mind-blowing, but it's still quite good, and makes clever use of numerous different leitmotifs and tricks that help the music add to the narrative in subtle ways. Visually, the game takes its monochrome palette in stride, and insertdisc5's non-pixelated art- which appears plenty often to break apart the fairly standard pixel-art overworld and UI- is an absolute treat.One last thing before the final verdict- I'd like to note that  I can only describe it, affectionately, as "tumblr user comedy." Not at all in a bad way. If you're unsure what I mean by this, there are a couple of achievement names that might help you see what I mean. If you're at all familiar with the site, its users, and its sitewide running gags, you'll definitely recognize a line or two here and there. I definitely appreciated this game's humor more as someone who's used tumblr for about 7 years, but So, finally... You won't be disappointed. It unquestionably deserves more love than it's currently receiving. :)

_childDocuments_.review: Every so often, a piece of media comes along that changes your brain chemistry forever. This game is that for me. The characters are all fantastic and live rent free in my head. The dialogue is well-written and conversations between the main characters feel very natural. Despite the premise having the potential to make things annoyingly repetitive, there are so many different little nuggets of information and juicy tidbits to discover that keep things from getting stale. The dev clearly put a lot of work into making the game fun to play and avoiding any potentially frustrating mechanics. There are laughs. There are gut punches. The ending made me cry like a little baby and I immediately bought the game for my best friend so that I could infect her with the same brain worms.TLDR: This game is so good, please buy it. 10/10 would loop again.

_childDocuments_.review: Not only is In Stars And Time an incredibly charming and heartfelt story with a lovable and very fleshed-out cast of characters, it's also one of the most harrowing and downright nightmarish depictions of time loops and mental illness I think I've ever seen. Take heed to the content warnings, this game does *not* pull its punches; but the tale the game weaves with these themes is an incredibly rich and emotional one, and was worth every second. It is a turn-based RPG with interesting mechanics as well, but at a point it does largely take a backseat to the narrative.Also the game has very fun and hilarious dialogue a lot of the time, and I absolutely love pretty much the entire cast of characters. By the end I'm left wanting more stories with these characters, which I think is a testament to how good the story and writing here is.Definitely pick up this game if you're interested, just do keep the content warnings in mind because, yeah, the story gets really grim (but worthwhile, still).

_childDocuments_.review: I love weird indie games, so when I bounce off a clearly well-loved one it feels like there's extra pressure to pinpoint why; I'll give it a go.<the hopefully more objective bit>I think the story and characters need to hook you in - and quickly! - for this game to land. I'm surprised this held true for so many. Not because I think the writing is bad - at all - but it's on the mature side of YA drama, which isn't for everyone (what writing is?). I didn't dislike it, but nor was I that taken with it - being in my late 30s I'm more of a pretentious litfic / classics reader, but I do like other genres and even VNs when they do really out-there and interesting stuff e.g. I loved Steins;Gate and the Zero Escape series.<the definitely subjective bit>And this is where it falls flat for me - I just didn't find the mysteries that interesting. And the process of getting those story breadcrumbs were too much work for too little payoff. I like the conceit of 'the tedium is the point', but I need something more to keep me going than 'one mundane interaction in an earlier area is now available, start again and go do that'. There's a fine line between being teased along and being jerked around, and I felt firmly in the latter camp throughout.<6 hours might not be a fair shake, but it was enough for me (and you can read some fantastic books in that time*). I've looked up the rest of the story, and I don't regret throwing in the towel. Hard to expound on that without spoiling anything, so I'll just conclude: odds are if you're reading this you'll love the game, but there's also a modest chance it'll fall totally flat for you.* I'll throw Piranesi (Suzannah Clarke) or Exhalation (Ted Chiang) out there if you're interested in recent recommendations from a total internet rando

_childDocuments_.review: I remember first hearing about this game through the release trailer on Nintendo's YT channel. Last week, I was finally able to buy the game and play it. And I could. Not. Stop! I loved every second of this game! Yes, the time loop aspect can make the monologues and dialogue feel repetitive sometimes, but there are FREQUENT altercations to them showcasing the changes that Siffrin goes through over the course of the two days that they loop over. The writing and pacing of this game is incredible overall! I was immediately endeared to all of the characters, each one of them having their own unique and likable personality. Siffrin and their party all have fantastic chemistry with each other! Also! The world building!!! You, the player, only ever experience the town of Dormont and the House, but scattered throughout are bits and pieces informing you of the world outside of where you are playing. Given enough time, you can find even the most elusive pieces of this charming universe! It makes the game feel truly alive. Also, Siffrin. God, I love him so much. Such a fantastic main character. I loved watching their character grow and change and decline and grow again as time passed. Their progression felt so organic as they tried and failed to cope with their past, present, and future.In short: 10/10 game, if you got 20 bucks to spare, use it on this, please!

_childDocuments_.review: Disclaimer that I played this on Switch first and logged about 24 hours there, so I don't have much time yet on the Steam version. But I enjoyed the game so much that I know I'll be playing it again, and I thought it was more than worth the $40 to buy it twice!As for the actual review:In Stars and Time is an absolutely captivating game, with a delightful cast of characters and an engaging story. The art is lovely--especially the character dialogue sprites and the overworld sprites--and the music is solid. I also ended up enjoying the battle system a lot! The amount of care and detail put into the writing, character development, and minute changes throughout each loop was my favorite part, though (and clearly the driving force of the game). I could see some players finding the main time loop mechanic repetitive, but I had so much fun finding new tidbits of information each loop and puzzling out what to investigate next that it didn't bother me. If you're like me and enjoy time loop stories or the found family trope, this game was MADE for you. If you're on the fence and aren't going to be upset by a very organic inclusion of queer characters, please give it a shot. It has lived in my brain rent-free ever since I finished it.

_childDocuments_.review: There aren't really words to truly express how wonderful this game is. I could write paragraphs upon paragraphs trying to capture all the emotions I'm feeling after finally seeing the credits roll, but I don't feel like anything I say will truly do it justice.In Stars and Time is a game about joy, sorrow, and learning to accept love. It reminds us to be kind to the people we care about, and more importantly to ourselves. Pushes us to understand others, even if we might not always be able to find common ground. Most importantly though, it reminds us that although life is messy, occasionally cruel, and frequently unforgiving, that that's okay, because it's also joy, and love, and hope. And those things make all the difference.

_childDocuments_.review: REALLY good game, loved the storytelling a lot, definitely recommend it if you are autistic. but even if you aren't you should still play this because who DOESN'T want to get stuck in a torturous time loop for like a good weekEDIT: okay SERIOUSSSS review time. SPOILERS BELOW !!!game is still really good, the story is evocative and the art is GREAT (all the poses and expressions are so fun!! loved the character designs so much!!) and all the teeny tiny details are incredible. you can really tell a lot of thought went into it!!a lot of the reviews are right though, this will NOT be a game for everyone. you will have to be willing to forgive it some things! some rushed story beats, some awkward dialogue, some frustrating gameplay mechanics. but if you’ve got the patience and the openmindedness then it’s totally worth it!! it utilizes the medium perfectly for a story about timeloops, you really get into the main character’s head and feel everything they’re feeling (also, is it really an rpg if you’re not gradually losing your mind every other fight?) Amazing execution and i LOVED the horror parts!! this is less criticism and more of a personal thing but i wish there were more subtle horror parts!!! because they were SO GOOD!!!!! i do want to share some thoughts on what i think could’ve been done better. first of all, we started at the end of the characters’ journey—which is fine! it’s a unique take and very interesting!! BUUUUT it really could’ve used some more setup. i didn’t connect with the characters as much as i would’ve liked to, because we’re just kinda thrown into this journey with them and told to care about them? and we’re told that we’re close with them and that we’ve got so much history with them and yadda yadda? i know that siffrin is quite forgetful, but they DO dream between loops, so it would’ve been cool for them to have flashbacks during their dreams!! it would’ve been really nice to find out more about the party and all their relationships, it would make it WAY easier to get invested in!! and the whole plot point of siffrin wanting to stay with them and treating them like family would’ve hit much harder and been more compelling i think!!! the flashbacks/dreams could even become gradually more messed up and Wrong as siffrin goes trough the timeloop over and over again and starts forgetting things more (and just becoming crazy). it also would’ve added some variety between the loops, and would’ve given you more motivation to keep going even if you were frustrated :)second of all, i felt like the epilogue came a bit suddenly. we were really at the rock bottom of siffrin’s mental state to the point that he was hallucinating his friends, so i think what would’ve worked is to 1. have his friends calling out to him and gradually getting louder (during the whole Homesick fight, or after it, in the darkness) instead of just suddenly appearing 2. not have siffrin believe they’re real at first, because that’s what *i* thought. we spend half the act seeing messed up visions of our friends!! it would’ve made sense for sif to not believe they ACTUALLY came to save him at first, for him to act like they weren’t real, and then maybe have him or them touch each other so that siffrin can have the Realization. and it would’ve fit the themes! of sif’s relationship with physical contact and with unreality!! (could’ve brought back the ‘They’re real, they’re here, you’re real, you’re here’ lines) personally i think that would’ve made the epilogue a bit more seamless!!! and more compelling too!! that’s pretty much all my ‘gripes’ i have with the game, like i said some of the dialogue is awkward but i don’t mind. i still liked it a lot! i’d rather have a messy and imperfect but still fun game than have no game at all!! i can tell it’s a really personal project and i’m glad it was made!! i do definitely recommend it if you think you’d like the game, it’s a solid 8/10 from me!EDIT 2: don't play this

_childDocuments_.review: Having beaten In Stars and Time once on Switch, I've returned to PC to give the most helpful review I can for people still feeling unsure. To give you fair warning, there will be some (hopefully) light spoilers in this. If anyone can guess what character I'm imitating to write this I will be extremely impressed. If you want the basics, just skip to the last two paragraphs, but if you want an idea of my emotional impression of the game, try this on for size:In Stars and Time is an RPG about the power of friendship in which you play as Siffrin, a quiet and introspective rogue out to save the country of Vaguarde from the evil King, who seeks to freeze the world in time. With them are their friends Mirabelle, Odile, Bonnie, and Isabeau, and they all draw strength from the wonderful bonds that their little group has. Arriving in the town of Dormont, you and your friends charge up the House of Change to meet the King, ready to defeat him using the power of...Uh oh. Something seems to have gone wrong here. I'm pretty sure that you weren't supposed to die this early. If it was the final battle and this was some kind of grand sacrifice I would get it, but as of right now... let's just try this again.In Stars and Time is a game about time loops. Specifically, the one that you, Siffrin, are stuck in. It turns out you may have been less prepared to fight the King than you thought. Don't worry though; you have all the time in the world to figure it out, even if it's a little more difficult than it first appeared. Just remember to rely on your helpful guide Loop, who's here to help you make it through the best they can, even if they don't know how or why the loop started in the first place. But as if getting through the House of Change wasn't hard enough, what with its traps, locked doors, and vicious Sadnesses standing in your way, you have to manage your party members too. As it turns out, they aren't looping with you. But don't worry! While you may have felt a little lost at first, eventually you discover the perfect things to do and say to make them like you even more than the first time around. With your bonds stronger than ever and your route through the House perfectly memorized, you charge up to face the King in a heated battle with the fate of Vaguarde on the line! It's difficult, but in the end you triumph over the King and head into the final room of the House to celebrate with your friends- no, your family.That's odd. You've defeated the King with the best possible ending, but there's still another 3 Acts left in the story. What's going on here?In Stars and Time is actually just another trash indie game. Sorry, but it's true; this game should be 10 hours shorter and cut right after you beat the King with your family in tow. It hurts to play, because now that things have gone wrong, things seem to have gotten worse in your head, too. Where's the resolution to this story? When does it end? You said all the right things, you made all the right moves and your family members have never been happier! By any other game's logic, this would be the end point. You may have struggled to make it through the time loop, but since you managed to keep your sanity intact and be nice to your friends, you get a gold star and the true ending. For some reason this game refuses to let you have that success, and I'm infuriated on your behalf. I suppose you'll have to keep looking for a solution somewhere within the House, even though I know you're getting a little sick of it by now. Try not to get too frustrated by all this, okay? It would be quite awful if you did something you'd regret because you were feeling...Ah. Well. That changes my opinion on things, I suppose. I have no words that could do justice to what happened there. What a finale, eh? Let's try this review one more time, with a more... holistic view of things. No more of this "describe what happens in the game step by step" malarkey. Everyone knows that's bad review writing anyways.In Stars and Time is an RPG about memory, communication, and the mortifying ordeal of being known. (It'll make more sense when you play it). With a lovely sound track and both beautiful hand-drawn and pixelated artwork, In Stars and Time manages to convey one the best stories I have ever experienced in the history of gaming. If you're the sort that likes comparisons, I would describe this game as a combination of the the humor and surprising depth of the Stanley Parable, the intense emotional characters and tight writing of Undertale, and the incredible worldbuilding of Harry Potter (without having to suffer through J. K. Rowling). I felt genuinely mystified by the unexplained and had a strong desire to learn more about the world during my unfortunately brief time within it. 3 weeks after completing the game, I'm still stewing in the things I felt and the realizations I came to while playing it. This is one of the few games I can say genuinely changed my life; after playing it I found the strength to reach out and connect to the friends I have in the real world on a level I never thought I'd be able to achieve. I feel a moral obligation to recommend this game; if it can do the same things for you that it did for me, it would be evil of me to deny you them. For the incredibly modest price of 20$, you will experience approximately 20 hours of soul-gripping gameplay that might stick with you for the rest of your life. This is something worth your time.

_childDocuments_.review: One of my favorite time loop stories ever. The gameplay starts cute and descends into intentional tedium (with just enough QoL features to make the game not an outright chore) in a way that's difficult to pull off but perfectly complements the narrative here. The graphics are cute and great, the music is perhaps not the most memorable ever but still has plenty of really good tracks, and the writing really steals the show. The worldbuilding is fascinating and the perfect combination of detailed but not bogged down in those details. The characters are so charismatic and interact with each other so well that it's easy to see why even through their flaws and endless repetition Siffrin continues to love them. The plot is compelling, with a strong emotional arc.It's not a game for everyone, admittedly. The tedious gameplay is a purposeful method for getting the player into Siffrin's mindset, but that makes it no less boring once you get into the weeds of achievement hunting or not realizing which book exactly you're supposed to be checking. The story is heavily reliant on Siffrin being allergic to communication--something made more bearable by this also being the game's central tragedy, but which can nevertheless be frustrating to watch. (Siffrin is also weirdly allergic to deviations from their self-imposed script, but then you see what happens when they DO improvise and it becomes yeah, the script worship makes sense actually.) A ton of major mysteries brought up are simply never solved. There's just enough information that you can get the general gist of what might have happened, but you'll never get a full answer even in dev interviews.But if none of those things are automatic dealbreakers, the execution and charisma this game has easily make up for them. I cannot recommend this game enough.

_childDocuments_.review: I have been trying to figure out how to write this review since I finished the game a month ago. I wish steam had more complex options of recommendation than do I recommend it or not because well;This game's story is really well written and emotionally impactful. Even with its odd mixture of wanting to be PG in its dialogue and arguably with the cartoony art style but yet will deal with heavy emotional themes that are just dealt with such care and passion. Every step along the way of this story is really good, man. Every character is fantastic and I love Siffrin I want to protect that boy with my very everything man he deserved better. Now, that said,It just...Hmm.Okay okay. So what did I didn't like? The story is really good, even if I am not the biggest fan of the use of the cartoony elements to some parts of the story the story was still really good -- What's the issue? This is a game. Simply put, you have to have an enormous amount of patience to deal with the backtracking of ISaT. This is a game about time loops. You will have to beat the final boss bare minimum three different times with it being fairly the same just you know what to do slightly better. This is the game's biggest weakness and biggest strength. If you are like me, it will take over 100 loops to solve the mystery of the castle and break the curse. You will (not want to) try again. But wanting to know just where this story goes is what keeps you going. It kept me going. The madness that the backtracking creates is absurd, but it in a sense puts you perfectly in the shoes of the protagonist. This is, as the description of the game has stated, is a time loop game. The frustration that having to do everything again and again and trying just one thing different until you get it perfect or find just one more piece of info to the puzzle to go further in the castle and solve its secrets is what *has* to keep you going. If it doesn't, this game isn't for you. You see why this game is hard to recommend? I have been wanting to recommend it but the bit of you have to be able to sit down and suffer *with* the protagonist instead of idly watching the protagonist suffer is what makes this such a compelling story. By the time you are getting the point of the later acts, of really trying everything, slamming your head against a wall, and then experiencing actual mania, both yourself and the protagonist, it is truly *really, really* hard to go through. The cute, silly text becomes more and more of a chore to get through, the silly jokes become more and more white noise and then, at some point, you realize you have the entire map of the entire castle memorized. One more run through it will be it. This is the run where you figure it out, right?Then it isn't. One more try. One more try, one more try...The last stretch is one of the most emotionally satisfying moments in the entire game, in any game, honestly. I tried to binge through this game in a couple of sessions and getting to the finale of the game I started reaaal late into it, past 2 am or so. Finally figuring out what exactly I was supposed to do, to say, and then, the game will tell you one thing simple: One more run.The final run of the game is really good, man. At this point the connection I felt with the protagonist of "why am I even bringing the rest of my party members. I am stronger than them by a mile." and the increasing frustration of what was once charming jokes just perfectly clicked. This frustration is intended. The headache of figuring things out is intended. You have to suffer with Siffrin. You have to suffer with them. This IS intended. So, again, if this game doesn't sound like a good time? Avoid it. It is not for you. If you are willing to put in the effort and have far too much patience or at least stubbornness? This game is probably for you. The finale is peak. I have been thinking about this game for the last month since completion despite having a fairly negative and frustrating time. That is like, art, man. This is like the Pathologic of RPG Maker games. This game sucks and I really didn't enjoy myself. 10/10

_childDocuments_.review: this game changed my brain chemistry. holy. what the hell. play it play it play it. more advanced review following:this game is phenomenal in so many ways. the chemistry between the party (family) members is phenomenal- everyone loves everyone else, and in different ways. odile may not like touch but she does join in on group jokes and really values everyone's input on Vaugardian customs, even if she already researched them. she calls bonnie "boniface" and everyone else by full names, but isn't above calling someone else cute or ragging on them playfully. isabeau can't get enough of the whole team, but especially siffrin (siffrin. I love you. you are blind as a bad when it comes to isa) for obvious reasons. he's happy to hug people and do group jokes, like Team Beauty or the funny noises squad. when mira panics he's the first one to comfort her, and the first one to worry if he did it well. mira loves everybody, appreciates them all, and she has a lot on her plate and, like siffrin, doesn't want to burden everyone with it, but she still appreciates the help when it comes. bonnie thinks caring is icky but still does it anyway. glorious snack leader etc.and the themes!!! the way that, following your core objectives, the thought of 'maybe you should tell someone what's happening' is never even a thought pass the 1-2 times Loop brings it up to mirror the fact that siffrin doesn't even consider it an idea. it's not a thought he'd have. he doesn't want to burden them- he will not burden them. you're in a time loop, so it's your job to do everything right! the way words change slowly to mirror siffrin's deteriorating mental state- "close your eyes" turns to "close your eye", mirabelle appearing turns to "enter mirabelle," you start to have "lines" and a script. this has become a play because no one ever changes even though you do. you're stuck here. they're fakes. reality starts to fade away.the plights the rest of your party has, too. bonnie is still caught up over siffrin's eye, and it makes sense. it was their mistake, and siffrin lost an eye- but siffrin doesn't mind it. they'd do it again. it wasn't anything to them, and therein lies the problem of why they "aren't getting along." bonnie, like siffrin in the end, feels like siffrin should be mad or something, but siffrin barely thinks about it anymore. mira is struggling with her sexuality / romantic attraction (me too girl < ace aro) but she feels like she can't talk to anyone about it because. who's like that right??? but siffrin is like that. odile being not accepted in one hegemonic culture and too embroiled in it to find identity in her other half really connected with me, and the way she tries to find that in researching Vaugaurdian customs and such just to see if she can find a place. and she does! she finds it in the family, in a way. her place isn't a place but with people. and, of course, isa just wants to hang out with siffrin, because they've been working so hard! helping everyone! running around and everything!god, and the section of loops where you're just throwing yourself into the king fight over and over and over again, desperately searching for answers, and you remember the loops but the king doesn't. he only figures it out when you start speaking nonsense, you mention things he's never said to you. he knows now. and he can take advantage of it. this isn't the man who, with you, tried to scream your home country's name until the world bled out- this is a man who sees a weak link in the only thing that could destroy him and will take advantage of it. but you forgot that.and the use of monochrome and color by the way!!!!!!! everything being in monochrome is fitting, and makes the use of red at the end hit so hard. it fully realizes the idea of a cosmic entity you can't understand, a power foreign to you, by making a world where something we have in the real world doesn't exist, and therefore you can introduce it and show a world where that is foreign and strange and wrong. you can't imagine something that doesn't already exist, so make the world less than what exists and then add to it. genius.even the little details! the conversations around the house. the mirror. the way during the final loop, siffrin remembers the conversations so well they play out in their head without anyone there. they can't even be bothered to pick up the sharpening stone. you've slept long enough. they should restart to make everyone happy- but they're tired. they can't. they  do another one. the house is distorted because finally, what the head housemaiden said is happening is finally happening- you're losing it and so is your wish, confused and distorted. why are you in the house alone? you wanted the journey to never end, didn't you? you wanted to stay with them? this place shouldn't even be considered yet, because they aren't here.I could write more but what else could I write that I have not wrote in fanfiction. lmao. anyway. to summarize: siffrin plush CANNOT come quick enough I need squeeze him and pat him on the head and tell him to smile baby boy you're out of the loops

_childDocuments_.review: No game is perfect. I absolutely have some reservations about In Stars and Time, which I'll get to. But I think it comes close enough that the term "Masterpiece" is one I feel comfortable in dragging out of the attic to describe this game.I'll try to address the negatives first. The spunky, amateurish art conveys tons of character, but it can be inconsistent, and there are places where it can come across as simply unpolished. The traditional turn-based RPG combat also has fairly little going for it in terms of depth. There's a simple three-"element" system in play wherein every enemy (and character!) has an element they're vulnerable to and another they're resistant to, which gets a little elaborated upon with the way you can build "jackpot" combos by using moves of the same element in succession, which may require some strategic turn-skipping, keeping an eye on ability cooldowns, or benefit from certain equipment. But that's about it. Aside from some buffs of not-necessarily-remarkable utility, your main tool is grinding for levels, which can get tedious. My main complaint, I think, is that the story leaves enough questions with answers at best only alluded to, that I'm really unsure all of it was actually thought through. There are facts in play that the story depends on, but it often felt like there were aspects the developer just gave up on figuring out. One particular character decision () is required for the story to function at all, yet never really analyzed or clearly justified in the story itself. Secondary to that, some of the mechanics for when you keep or lose certain elements of progress are a little ambiguous and require some trial and error to make sense of. (The entire "" mechanic, for example, raises a LOT of questions in terms of what it skips or doesn't, and why.)With those missteps qualified, the fan ranting begins here.There are two brilliant ventricles in the beating heart of ISAT. The more obvious one is its characters. The story lives through its superb cast. A given player will definitely like some characters more than others, but every one of them has believable, complex, human emotions and motivations, right down to those little self-contradictions and seemingly out-of-character behaviors of real people that are so often overlooked in even good fiction.The other, less overtly, is the structure and gameplay. I have never in my life agreed with the idea of making part of a game "unfun" to make a point about a story or character. I've always been firmly of the opinion that the same thing could be achieved without making it a drag. Until now. There are parts of this game that are definitely unpleasant to experience, in a variety of ways. But every single time, it is done impeccably in service to helping the player understand what the protagonist is experiencing, with no heavyhanded expository dialogue required. Where the game is frustrating, or tedious, or horrifying (not a problem for me as a horror fan, but possibly for some players), or outright psychologically brutal, it uses these to align the player's experience with the protagonist's. The game's length is reasonable enough (maybe around 20-25 hours for a relatively casual playthrough) that it didn't become grueling or feel like the same points were being hammered incessantly. This certainly won't work for everyone, but it did for me.While the story is, at its heart, not particularly complex or even original, it's driven powerfully by a sense of emotional reality that it exists in a class of its own. It plays every note on the scales, from sincerely funny and silly to horrific and heartbreaking. A superb soundtrack certainly doesn't hurt either. In Stars and Time gracefully avoids the pitfall of being saccharine or mawkish and delivers an emotionally honest experience that I found to be among the most memorable and moving of any games I've ever played.Disclaimer: I have done my best to avoid letting my unhinged fixation on Odile color this analysis, but cannot make any guarantees.

_childDocuments_.review: An excellent RPG that manages to show the frustration of time loops while staying focused throughout its playtime. The writing in this game is great, keeping optimistic even when the main character is at their wit's end trying to solve the main mystery. I loved hanging out with the main cast and seeing how they changed in response to how I acted between loops. While I still recommend checking out the content warnings if you're sensitive to those, the writing remembers to balance the tone and reminds players why they want to save everyone in the first place.Even if you have to loop over a hundred times (an actual possibility), there's plenty of mechanics that remove the worst of the tedium: fast-forward, instant restarts, and even an in-game hint system! All of these help the game world feel open and nothing is actually stopping you from progressing forward or backward even when the main dungeon is completely linear. The combat serves more of a quick obstacle than an actual threat, and I always knew where I needed to go to find my next clue and it was never long before I arrived there. I absolutely recommend this game if you're a fan of RPGs with a focus on characters, world-building, and overworld puzzles!

_childDocuments_.review: Impressively heartfelt, incredibly well-designed (ludonarrative harmony, wow!), and a great ride from start to finish. The kind of game that takes an hour or two to get interesting, but before you know it it's 3am and you're pushing for ONE MORE LOOP, dying to uncover the mystery behind it all. You will notice things changing. You will forget things ever happened. You'd think it's an experience that's hard to replicate the second time around, but I found it worth replaying (twice!), just to see how much love and nuance is squeezed into each dialogue and sprite, in everything from item interactions to order of events. I don't write reviews, ever, but this game...... man. Don't sleep on it, thinking it's just another simple, party-based rpg. It really is something special. (10/10 would experience heartbreak and catharsis and heartbreak and catharsis all over again. Encore!)

_childDocuments_.review: Evidently this game was made for me. It's extremely rare for a game or written work to make me cry. The creators of this game can now proudly say they've created one of the handful of works that's succeeded. I adore this game, all the build-off and payoff is wonderful. You can tell the creators had a very strong idea of what sort of emotions and themes they wanted to evoke throughout the game and everything from the worldbuilding to the gameplay helps create those emotions and feelings. The humor may not be for everyone, but personally I quite liked it--especially the contrast between the goofy antics of other characters and Siffrin's deteriorating mental state. It felt jarring, but in a good way? Like everyone else was in a completely different genre than Siffrin for much of the game, which felt like an apt metaphor for his worsening depression. I also loved the worldbuilding! This is one of the stories I've come across where it feels like there was the perfect amount of worldbuilding, and the creators knew EXACTLY how much they needed to show or hide to get across the story's message and make the world feel 'real,' without getting bogged down in it. They knew where it was safe to leave gaps and blank spaces--though I'm sure a handful of those gaps are probably because I'm not always very great with exploring. At any rate, a wonderful game well-worth the hype! Definitely not for everyone because they are NOT joking about the subject matter. Emotionally, this game cuts like a hecking knife, it's long, it's grindy and annoying and sometimes it's not obvious what you're meant to do next. But for me, it all contributed positively to the experience and took me on a hell of a ride. As someone who's been thinking a lot about gameplay itself as a story vehicle and how I might make use of it as a writer and creative, it gave me a lot to think about in the best possible way!

_childDocuments_.review: This was such an incredible experience. The exploration of mental health, queer identities, and relationships is really unparalleled to anything I've played yet. I played a few hours of In Stars & Time after graciously receiving a review copy of the game, and then I thought, "before I continue, I should give 'START AGAIN: A Prologue' a try first." After completing that in a few hours and loving it, I knew I was in for a treat with this game but just didn't know how much this game would get into themes and ideas touched on in the Prologue. Answer was really above and beyond!!Siffrin, as a kind of travelling wanderer who seems very *outside* the party but at the same time really a part of the family is a very interesting perspective to give the player. I found myself consistently being driven to push forward through more loops to figure out the time looping mystery, and sort out why it was happening to them! All of the characters were equally as unique as Siffrin, all having their own special qualities that the game allows you time to explore.As well, the music? Animation? Phenomenal. I found myself cheering for characters during big battles or revelations as the music swelled, and humming familiar themes throughout. Also super glad to see characters of color and queer identities represented in a lovely and soft kind of style.Having finished the game last night while streaming, and learning there is a 'perfect ending' to aim for, I'm more determined than ever to go back and get that ending now! This motivation to replay games, especially after finishing one, is a rare thing for me. So that's really exciting!Please consider giving ISAT and SA: A Prologue a try! Thank you so much for this review copy. This game will remain as one of my absolute favourites.

_childDocuments_.review: I am not finished with the game but I wanted to warn people what they are about to get into. This game is fantastic but it is absolutely not for everyone!This game is very similar to Pathalogic in a lot of ways. The game play itself can be tedious and make the experience a slog at times. But it's all in service of the greater narrative. Because of it's time loop nature there is a lot of back tracking. Sometimes the game specifically putting you in scenarios you cannot win in order to make you back track to prove it's narrative's point. It strongly puts you in the main character's shoes, experiencing the agony of doing something over and over. Stuff that seemed emotionally touching the first time around becomes an annoyance the second time around. Easily skip able and forgotten. It's game play is not fun, but god does it pay off big time with its emotional beats. It's a narrative work of art first and a game second. And that really works for In Stars And Time. It would not be the same experience without the game being sometimes tedious to play. But that kind of artistic expression isn't for everyone, some people are rightfully looking for a fun game to play. They are games after all.I highly suggest if the back tracking sounds annoying to you or if you picked it up and realized this wasn't for you, to try playing with a glitchless speed running guide. It tells you clearly where to go for the interesting stuff, making it so you have to do less loops, and you can easily stop following the guide if you figure something out on your own. I have not finished it yet but from what others have said and what I have seen already, the emotional pay offs are amazing and life changing. The writing is extremely charming and the world is well realized. I've loved it so far.

_childDocuments_.review: Great writing, simple but fun combat, great art style. The story is very interesting and pretty original from my experiences. It apes on Groundhog's Day but with a wildly different pay off.  The looping mechanic also gives a plot reason for the limited settings. That being said, the story feels like it lasts a little longer than it needs to. That's not to say there are things i would cut (maybe trim) but because the story necessitates a few too many repeat trips through the House, later in the game I resorted to using a guide because I did not want to be bothered to search high and low for the story checkboxes that would let me proceed. On the story, there are a couple story beats that never really got resolved..My biggest nitpick, the nature of the looping leads to a lot of repeated dialog. That is eased by a skip (nod off) function, but it is limited in weird ways. If the text is something Sif is thinking then it can't be skipped, some of the dialog in the town can't be skipped, the mini quests with your team mates can't be skipped until you talk to them for a while making it tedious to do over and over again. I think this should absolutely be addressed as this felt like the most annoying time waster in this otherwise pretty great game. Also I found Bonnie pretty annoying and unlikeable but the game made sure to tell me that I do like Bonnie, which I did not. This is important for some scenes that should have been more emotionally impactful than they ended up being in practice.

_childDocuments_.review: Ok, so, I played Start Again: A Prologue back when it first came out so I have been eagerly awaiting this game. This means I am biased, but also I LOVE IT. VERY GOOD. THANK YOU FOR THE MEAL. Just finished the game and intend to go achievement hunting -- this play time is reflective of a completionist playthrough.More seriously, you will enjoy this game if you like character driven story and playing spot-the-difference with dialogue, with subtle shifts in characterisation.For comparisons I'd say to look at visual novels and RPGs in the vein of the Trails series, where there's mountains of optional dialogue and attention to detail. And I do mean optional - there's a healthy amount of QoL features so you can skip and skim to the 'new' core content if you don't enjoy seeking small changes. But if, during the game, you think "I wonder if X has changed know we know Y".... Yes! Probably!The characters are very lovable. You're very much watching SIffrin's world, and nudging them along diverging paths, with a front row seat to the consequences in his mind. I think if you're wavering, the demo is a good taste of what's to come. Obviously it's just scratching the surface but if you /hate/ the demo, then you won't like the full game... I hope you do like it! I hope lots of people do! There's a lot to love and resonate with.
