_childDocuments_.review: The Case of the Golden Idol is a fantastic puzzle game where you use logic and deduction in order to solve puzzles. This game is the closest deduction puzzle game that fills the void that "Return of the Obra Dinn" has left. While I still personally prefer Obra Dinn, Golden Idol is great in its own right, and does its own thing without it feeling derivative of Obra Dinn. Golden Idol plays similar to a classic point-and-click adventure game, except instead of collecting inventory items to solve puzzles, you collect clues in the form of keywords that you then use to fill in the blanks of an ad-lib style paragraph. The base game is divided into 11 cases plus an epilogue - for a total of 12 "levels." In a case you explore 1-4+ screens that are essentially snapshots of a scene. You explore the environments by clicking on points of interests in the map (NPC, documents, objects, etc.) and then clicking on underlined keywords to add them to your "inventory" of clues. Once you have found all the clues, you can then drag the keywords to fill in the blanks to solve the puzzle. It may sound simple at first, but collecting the clues is the easy part. The real challenge and joy of Golden Idol comes from using your own deduction skills to piece together what happened in the scene. The game deals with a lot of grisly murders, deceptions, and betrayals - so sometimes the most obvious solution isn't always the correct one. After you correctly solve the case's puzzle, you will be given a little summary what exactly happened. I quite like this feature and wished Obra Dinn had something like this as well. All the cases in Golden Idol are linked and tell a pretty expansive, dark story that offers quite a bit of twists and turns due to all the deception and skulduggery the characters engage with. The puzzles start off pretty easy, with only 1 screen to explore and only a few keyword options. The characters in the scenes tend to be easy to identify due to holding onto letters addressed to them. However, as the game progresses, you will have to resort to using a lot more deduction and observation skills to come to your conclusions. This will often require a careful study of relevant evidence, scrutiny of the environments (observing footprints in mud, identifying physical features on people, etc.), and applying logic to the crime (knowing who had the means, motive, and access to commit the crime, etc.). Some cases will contain red herrings to throw you off, but there will always be enough clues within the case to be able to sort through what is a real clue versus what clue is a diversion.Golden Idol offers an in-game hint system for players that are stumped. The game strongly discourages uses hints, and even tells you this when you click the hint button. It will then give you some general advice to consider before resorting to hints. And the advice is pretty helpful. On one of the earlier cases - when the game first started began ramping up the difficulty - I did use the hints. I don't know if this is for all cases, but it gave me the choice of one of 4 hints (e.g. a hint related to motive, means, access, etc.). After selecting the hint, you have to complete a mini-puzzle in order to acquire the actual hint. The puzzle was brain-dead easy and honestly felt like a timewaster between wanting a hint and actually getting the hint. I used two hints on the level, but unfortunately they only hinted at information that I had already correctly deduced - and did not help me get out of my dead end. However, I did think about one piece of general advice the game gave me before I got a hint: sometimes it is necessary to completely rethink your assumptions because it could be wrong. I happened to fall for a red herring, and made all the assumptions I built off of it completely wrong. Once I reviewed the evidence on the scene, I noticed the fatal flaw I made, corrected it, and completed the case. After that case, I didn't end up using hints for any of the other cases for the base game or the DLCs - even with the cases getting much more challenging. Despite the hints not being helpful for me, I will give the game credit that the hints really are just "hints" (directing you to what clues to consider) instead of just solving the puzzle for the player.The base game took me just under 10 hours to beat the 12 cases, with simple cases taking 10-20 minutes to complte, and more complex ones taking 1 hour or more.The game has two DLCs that each include 3 cases, each of which taking an average of 1 hour each to complete. Both DLCs serve as prequels to the main game's story. The difficulty of the puzzles in the DLC definitely feel more complex compared to the base game, but are both worthwhile to play through.I picked up the base game + the 2 DLCs on sale for about $20 and got a combined 16 hours of playtime out of them. I definitely got a lot of enjoyment out of the game and it was well worth my time and money. The game does a great job of making you feel smart when you are able to piece together all the clues and solve the cases.

_childDocuments_.review: A wonderful murder mystery game about cults, aristocratic secret societies, ancient treasures, & lots of death. You are the detective & it's your job to solve those mysteries.You have to carefully examine the environment, people, letters, & other things to gather clues and piece together the whole story in a scene. You collect keywords, which you can then drag and drop into "fill in the blanks"-type scrolls. It's such a simple concept, yet it's so brilliantly executed, & some puzzles can get really complex! The game rewards you with a satisfying jingle when you fill everything correctly. The game is split into 12 chapters, each with their own story that when combined, creates one giant conspiracy. There are also 2 DLCs that add 6 chapters total, and serve as sort of a prequel. (Play the main game first, DLCs are designed to be played after you beat it). If you feel stuck, there are also hints, & there is no punishment for using them, but the game never really feels obscure or unfair; it always gives you everything you need to solve the mysteries. Re-examine all the evidence (or use hints), and sooner or later you will surely get it! I cannot wait for the sequel! It's a very unique and extremely satisfying gem of a game!
_childDocuments_.name: The Case of the Golden Idol

Some of the later areas were a bit too galaxy-brained for me, or maybe I was fatigued from playing so much of it at one time, but the whole game feels very rewarding to connect the dots and realize the solutions - big "a-ha!" factor throughout the game. I will be supporting these devs as long as they keep making games.

_childDocuments_.review: The Case of the Golden Idol is a fascinating game. In each episode, you are given a diorama - a moment frozen in time - where someone has just been murdered. It is your job to figure out who's who, what's going on, and most importantly - who committed the murder. You are not a character within the game: you are an omniscient narrator-like character who can hear what people are saying, see what they are carrying, and find whatever clues are lying around. You have all the information you need right there, but figuring out a sequence of events can be much harder than it seems. In the end, it made me feel smart, maybe even because I was smart, and that's all I can ask of a mystery game, right.Would recommend.
_childDocuments_.name: The Case of the Golden Idol

_childDocuments_.name: The Case of the Golden Idol

_childDocuments_.review: Don't let the art style turn you off. It did for me and I regret not playing this sooner. It really scratched my deductive reasoning itch that has been pestering me since I complete Return of the Obra Dinn.The music manages to capture a tremendously unsettling vibe which really adds to the puzzle solving.The story has a clear throughput and all of the pieces come together. Do your best to solve this one without any outside help. Everything you need is there, and you can make leaps based on previous chapters or just common sense.
_childDocuments_.name: The Case of the Golden Idol

_childDocuments_.review: Probably one of the best detective games out thereThis is a game that executes itself perfectly. It consist of a story separated in several chapters and you need to put the pieces together to know what happened.Like the saying goes, "the devil is in the details" and this game will punish you if you don't pay attention. Everything, EVERYTHING you learn from a chapter will probably be used in the next (or even further) ones and every name, date, face, letter and symbol has a reason for it to be there. Details are so important that I had to completely restart the game halfway through because things weren't making any sense to me. At first I thought it was bad writing but once I backtracked to previous chapters I realized it was because I forgot tiny details from previous playthroughs so I had to refresh myself.And believe me, once you start making sense and all the pieces are falling together, you'll be amazed by how imaginative the whole thing is. Sure, you can brute-force some answers by way of elimination but everything makes sense if you keep a sharp eye on it.Overall, if you like games that make you feel smart for accomplishing progress this one will make wonders of you. I don't believe there's a game like this out there so it's an experience that you have to live. I'll definitively purchase any DLC that they make if they're as well done as thisDon't even wait for this game to be on sale. It's worth every penny

_childDocuments_.name: The Case of the Golden Idol

_childDocuments_.review: A superb detective game akin to Obra Dinn though on a much smaller, level-based scope. Unlike Obra Dinn, Golden Idol doesn’t have you play as an in-universe character, instead you’re given a full view of its crime scenes and tasked to identify people, identify the culprit, and uncover the events surrounding the murder in each level. All the levels tie into the overarching narrative of a mysterious golden idol and its story unfolds as you continue to solve each level. The investigation element is quite strong and logical, I figured the whole game out without using a single hint and very small amounts of guessing. There aren’t really any leaps of logic or genuine obtuseness, the game is skilled at giving you all the info that you need. The atmosphere is quite good as well; the art is kind of grotesque but in a good way that befits the slimy and cutthroat characters you have to deal with and the music befits the vibes of the late 1700’s setting that the game is set in. The Case of the Golden Idol is a definitely worthy to be among the detective game greats.
_childDocuments_.name: The Case of the Golden Idol

_childDocuments_.review: The Case of the Golden Idol is a very fun and unique mystery game that I highly recommend.  You are given scenes at the moment a great twist or sudden surprise is revealed, and you must figure out who planned the trickery, who killed who, and what ever else happened.The game uses a very unique puzzle mechanic. As you explore the scene you will find words that you will use to fill in the blanks of the story scroll (shown on a "thinking" page).  This mechanic naturally balanced out the difficulty.  There are plenty of characters and spare words that I never felt like the game was solving the puzzle for me.  On the other end, the "thinking" page provides enough structure so you're not overwhelmed with potential explanations.  It also means that if you're ever confused or need reminders, you already have notes (that you put together!) ready for you.If you like mysteries, puzzles, and point-and-click adventure games then this is a must-buy for you.This game feels very similar to Return of the Obra Dinn (another excellent game).  If you liked that game, then you'll like this one, and vice versa.
_childDocuments_.name: The Case of the Golden Idol

_childDocuments_.review: It's really fantastic. It's been a while since I played a game where the puzzles are this satisfying. They're difficult without becoming frustratingly hard and it doesn't use "point and click" logic. It really is exactly up my alley and if you like mysteries with gothic undertones then you'll probably like this. 10/10
_childDocuments_.name: The Case of the Golden Idol

_childDocuments_.review: Like an adventure book version of detective games like Return of Obra Dinn. Here you're given a simple scene and you're tasked to gather all the information and work out who is dead, who murdered who and get to the bottom of an incredibly rich story about murder, greed and political power. While the whole game isn't too long, you'll be stuck going from scene to scene trying to solve each crime. Incredibly worthwhile, especially when you get further into the game and the puzzle pieces start connecting together. And the epilogue is a really nice touch to cement if you've fully worked out the story lines throughout the game. Worth the pick-up if you're into this kind of game.
_childDocuments_.name: The Case of the Golden Idol

_childDocuments_.review: Fun and challenging, you have all the clues at your disposal with no 'sherlock logic jumps'. I like the art style, makes it feel grittier. _childDocuments_.name: The Case of the Golden Idol

_childDocuments_.review: I like this game, but I don't recommend it for most people. It isn't quite what it appears to be or what you'd think it is by reading what other people are saying about it. First of all, there is a story happening here, but it is very minimal and you have to piece it together like a jigsaw puzzle. There is no narrative unless you count the very few and very brief cut scenes.Second of all, you don't really solve a mystery. You look at a static scene with a bunch of clues laying around. As you glean more information, you start filling in blanks describing what happened. And that it's pretty much it. You are not involved in the scene or the story in any way. You're just observing.Third of all, as a game of deduction I found it unsatisfying. Logic with supernatural elements is kind of an oxymoron. In a word with supernatural phenomenon, logic kind of goes out the window and any random thing can happen. Also, many of the logic puzzles are flawed. There are plenty of instances where you cannot draw conclusions based on the information they give you with any certainty. You have to just make educated guesses and then see if the sum of them add up to a correct answer. There is fun to be had here, but it's just not quite what I expected or wanted.
_childDocuments_.name: The Case of the Golden Idol

_childDocuments_.review: An incredibly well constructed mystery/puzzle game and an interesting and well written narrative. Perfectly paced, doesn't overstay its welcome and feels incredibly satisfying by the end. It asks just enough of the player to actually engage in deduction and critical thinking, while still serving up enough clues and hints to avoid frustration.
_childDocuments_.name: The Case of the Golden Idol

_childDocuments_.review: Neat little game. Best compared to Return of the Obrah Dinn, whose grace it unfortunately does not reach.However, if you already know Return of the Obrah Dinn and wanted more, this is the game for you. It's visibly made by a small team of two brothers who do a marvelous job given that restriction. The game features deductive puzzles using placeholders to be filled with words. The initial trivial difficulty is quickly replaced with a few headscratchers that will quickly cause those with less patience to brute force their way. Expect a total of non-trivial 8 cases that will usually take you half an hour to carefully put together.The game can be finished in about 6 hours give or take, and therefore the price is a bit steep without a discount. I definitely also recommend going for the DLCs after finishing the base game as it is quite hard to understand whether or not you like the gameplay without trying it first.
_childDocuments_.name: The Case of the Golden Idol

_childDocuments_.review: A great game that truly conveys the detective experience. Moderately complex, moderately long, and with an extremely fascinating plot.Many people in the reviews compare it to Return of the Obra Dinn. This is a justified comparison, but, in my opinion, The Case of the Golden Idol is much more interesting due to its well-structured narrative.Update: Both DLCs are excellent. They expand the story of the golden idol and tell more about the fates of key characters.

The interface for interacting also would frequently behave erratically making it very difficult to drag words into their slots.The epilogue in particular had words remain in the word-bank even though they were not actually usable. They could be dragged in position but nothing would happen as you are only able to reuse words from locked scrolls once they are in place.
_childDocuments_.name: The Case of the Golden Idol

_childDocuments_.review: I grabbed this game because I've been dying for a point and click detective style game and I was not disappointed! You will drop hours into this and still want more. The story is fantastic, that soundtrack is a banger,  and the DLC actually tie in very well with the main story, but the art style is what does it for me. There is just something charming about it and I haven't really seen another game with the style. I have only one gripe about the game and it comes with the DLC, for some reason my save state became corrupted (a known issue in the forums), so I had to redo areas multiple times and download the save state the developers offer to get around the corruption. It was a headache and mostly mattered for achievements (I gave up on one because I got tired of redoing the memorized solution :D). Unfortunately, if your game does this and you want to complete it, it is mandatory to get the provided save state to progress because it will lock you at the first of three missions in the DLC. I only had this issue with The Spider of Lanka DLC.
_childDocuments_.name: The Case of the Golden Idol

_childDocuments_.review: A must play in the genre of investigation games. It delivers incredibly satisfying moments of deduction at almost every turn, and what more are we really asking for with these mystery games? It is challenging without requiring it's hint system or other hand-holding at all, allowing YOU to work in your own brain piecing the evidence together and solving the cases on your own. The story and presentation are both equally charming and strange, which leaves such a lasting impression. The DLC is as enjoyable as the main game, while being more complex, difficult, and weird (I still haven't beaten it).Easily and emphatically a 10/10. _childDocuments_.review: Neat deductive reasoning game. The difficulty ramps up as you move along, and you'll likely want to play with a notepad or something as you get to the later chapters. The tiniest of details can reveal certain clues to be red herrings or important evidence.The DLC does not feel as finely tuned as the main game. The graphics feel more like pixel-artified 3d models, than the more authentic-feeling main game, and the puzzles are less satisfying. The last chapter basically requires some guess-and-check to get some of the last details, as the clues are simply not present in the world.Anyway, if you liked Return of the Obra Dinn, etc., this game is worth getting. If you really enjoy this game, then maybe get the DLC if it's on a steep sale. It does tie the plot in nicely as a prequel to the main game.

_childDocuments_.review: The Case of the Golden Idol is a detective point-and-click adventure game set in the 1700s. You play as an unseen detective who must investigate a series of murders that are all connected to a mysterious golden idol.The game is beautifully designed, with a unique art style that is both stylish and atmospheric. The puzzles are challenging but fair, and the story is engaging and suspenseful.One of the things that makes The Case of the Golden Idol so special is its focus on deduction. There are no hints or clues to help you solve the puzzles, so you have to use your own observational skills and powers of deduction to figure everything out. This makes the game incredibly satisfying to play, and it really makes you feel like a detective.Another thing I love about The Case of the Golden Idol is its attention to detail. The developers have put a lot of thought into every aspect of the game, from the characters and dialogue to the environments and objects. This attention to detail makes the game world feel real and lived-in, which helps to immerse you in the story.Overall, The Case of the Golden Idol is a must-play for fans of detective games and point-and-click adventures. It's a challenging, suspenseful, and rewarding game that will keep you guessing until the very end.Here are some of the specific things that I liked about the game:The unique art styleThe challenging puzzlesThe engaging storyThe focus on deductionThe attention to detailIf you're looking for a challenging and rewarding detective game, I highly recommend The Case of the Golden Idol.

Just going away for an hour and coming back fresh helped a lot more ^^Especially loved that the epilogue was one last little brain teaser that wrapped up the whole story.If you like logic puzzles without any time pressure you will love the case of the golden Idol.

_childDocuments_.review: Besides maybe Return of the Obra Dinn, this is the premier indie deduction game on the market. Though some of the cases can get obtuse and require you to scrutinize every last detail with immaculate precision, the stories that unfold when you do put events in place are creative to say the least.DLCs were fine, but didn't feel all that necessary.Overall if Ace Attorney with hints of secret societies and dark familial secrets are your thing, you're sure to enjoy this:8.5/10
_childDocuments_.name: The Case of the Golden Idol

_childDocuments_.review: Great puzzle/detective-like game with an intriguing story that always leaves you wanting to know what is going to happen next. Many times you will find yourself stuck and frustrated with not being able to solve a particular case. The solution is always around the corner, one step ahead of you, and finding the patience to look for something you might have missed or are misinterpreting is key to progressing in the game. Can't wait for the sequel!
_childDocuments_.name: The Case of the Golden Idol

_childDocuments_.review: This game is something special you don't find easily out there. This is a fantastic detective game full of twists, turns and mystery that keeps you engaged and delights all the way through. I absolutely loved my time with this game and I thoroughly recommend it.Also bonus points if you liked return of the Obra Dinn, because this game has similar vibes while being completely fantastic in it's own right.
_childDocuments_.name: The Case of the Golden Idol

_childDocuments_.review: Super good game. Great puzzles, interesting story. The puzzles were easy at first and got steadily trickier, just enough so that I felt smart but rarely frustrated. I only made use of the hint system (which is also excellent) in the final case.  My only complaint is that I wish there was more of it! But even at its relatively short length, I feel like it's worth the price.
_childDocuments_.name: The Case of the Golden Idol

_childDocuments_.review: Interesting game, quite like a pen and paper logic puzzle (if you've ever done one of those), but with strange and cool illustrations which the clues are embedded in, and a more open format. The game involves clicking on hotspots in the illustrations to get some information in the form of words, and then piecing together the events you're seeing by filling in the gaps in the provided "scrolls" with the words you've collected. This is fun if you like deductive logic puzzles. A pulpy adventure / mystery story plays out as you complete the scenarios.It's also very short - my playtime above is how long it took me to beat the game, including the extra epilogue puzzle which sums up the entire plot. YMMV on whether it's worth the money based on that.
_childDocuments_.name: The Case of the Golden Idol

_childDocuments_.review: Love it, essentially Obra Dinn without the many annoying "wait for it" sequences and in shorter intervalls/scenes. Completely logical without going too hard at the start, and all but two scenes were largely unambiguous. Well crafted overall and with an intriguing story and plot twist, not gonna lie, overall very enjoyable. If you liked Obra Dinn for the puzzles, you're gonna like this.
_childDocuments_.name: The Case of the Golden Idol

_childDocuments_.review: I like logical deduction games, and this is right behind the excellent Return of the Obra Dinn. Both are games about noticing details, finding clues, trying to deduce what may have happened, why, by who and to whom, and suggest your conclusions to the game, which will validate partial solutions in some way.I originally played this when my mental state wasn't super sharp and it was fun but I guesstimated a lot of things and gamed the system a bunch, and didn't get around to finishing the final chapter of the game. I replayed the whole thing now (including one DLC), when I'm more rested. It is a much better experience if you can really spend some time noticing details that hint at what's happening, and spend some time creating theories for what's happening based on words available and the structure of text you're supposed to guess.Fun, and highly recommended! Extra bonus point for being made with Godot, an open-source game engine :)
_childDocuments_.name: The Case of the Golden Idol

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely outstanding detective game. People make a lot of comparisons to Return of the Obra Dinn, and it's reasonable and obviously inspired by that game, but it has its own style and requires a different kind of thinking. Where Obra Dinn was focused more on working through environmental details and tracing cause and effect across various scenes that interrelated, The Case of the Golden Idol is more about working through motives and circumstantial evidence to intuit why people did things and how they did them, within a particular scene. It's also shorter and overall a bit simpler, but very much worth the price of admission and the ~6 hours it offers. Also, I recommend taking the developers' recommendations and enabling the hot-spot click indicators, it doesn't make the game any easier. The game's challenge is all in how you piece together the information you've found, not hunting down hidden places.
_childDocuments_.name: The Case of the Golden Idol

_childDocuments_.review: Just a fun and neat little puzzle/investigation game for a few nights, very much in the vein of The Return of The Obra Dinn. The chapters ramp up in difficulty quite nicely and I felt most of the puzzles were confortably challenging. The visual style might not exactly wow anyone, but gives the entire game a distinct look. Overall, thumbs up.
_childDocuments_.name: The Case of the Golden Idol

_childDocuments_.review: I was looking for something like this game for a long time. The game does not feed you with very easy and understandable clues, you need to follow the story and build theories according to some pieces of information you have. Every next level is more difficult than the previous one, however, almost everything was totally solvable and logical.I really enjoyed the experience. The only problem I had was with the last level, for me some things there were not intuitive and didn't make a lot of sense (luckily this still did not ruin my experience, because other levels were brilliant).I would definitely recommend playing this game if you're looking for a detective game that is built on investigating given information and building conclusions from it.
_childDocuments_.name: The Case of the Golden Idol

_childDocuments_.review: I like this much more than Obra Dinn. It's just so much easier to navigate for clues and the world is much more detailed. Almost every puzzle has an "aha" moment where everything clicks together narratively, which seemed completely lacking in Obra Dinn. There is no speculation, or any random guessing, and the abundance of detailed artwork and descriptions allows you to miss quite a few details and still progress in the story. Then you can recall these details later and start piecing things together. I beat the game, only needing a hint on one early level (the poisoning in the mansion), but I was able to piece everything else without hints. I only had to break out a notepad once, as one puzzle requires you to do some (very basic) math.It's a very rewarding experience and I definitely recommend this to anyone who is interested enough to scroll down to the review section.
_childDocuments_.name: The Case of the Golden Idol

_childDocuments_.review: I had a tough time with this game the first go around.  It asks you to make some logical leaps, conjectures, etc that I wasn't comfortable with.  But going in with the right expectations the second time around, I can't recommend this game enough if you, like me, played eagle eye mysteries as a child.  Dating myself here a little.
_childDocuments_.name: The Case of the Golden Idol

_childDocuments_.review: I generally liked it. As someone who likes mystery games more broadly and really liked Obra Dinn in particular, Golden Idol’s general premise seemed like it would be pretty appealing to me.From what I’ve experienced, Golden Idol seems somewhere halfway between the sort of open-ended structure of Obra Dinn and a more traditional linear detective game. I think the structure generally worked in the game’s favor, letting it put much more emphasis on the broader narrative while still making the deduction feel satisfying rather than something where the game was holding my hand every step of the way. Though it did lead to some awkward points where it's unclear how much I’m supposed to just rely on info I’ve learned from previous cases as opposed to treating each case in isolation and only using the evidence presented directly. And while this never posed too much of an issue () it did feel like cheating at some points since I could infer pretty key details about the case without properly deducing them (such as ). But just in terms of structure, the game was still good overall.A bit weaker though were the individual cases. It seems each one tried to introduce its own little gimmick the the game instead of sticking with the same sort of murder mystery formula each time. And while this worked for a good number of cases ( were both quite good), at other points it felt either bland or annoying (). Golden Idol had quite a few moments where the correct answer felt tedious to get. Sometimes the structure of the sentence you’re meant to fill in is very unclear about what it's actually requiring, sometimes the leap from evidence to deduction feels too large as if there’s some sort of detail I completely missed, and on quite a few occasions the investigating was the only good part since the answer turned out to be pretty uninteresting as soon as you’ve actually looked at all the evidence.But issues aside, The Case of the Golden Idol has enough going for it that I still think it's worth giving a shot. While I wouldn't call any of the individual mysteries great, they are improved through their meaningful contributions to a larger narrative (something that doesn’t happen often in mystery games) and even the worst cases tend to fail on account of blandness rather than the solution being outright stupid. And with the game only lasting 4-6 hours, you’re never lingering long enough for the weaker cases to outstay their welcome. So definitely worth playing if it seems like something up your alley.
_childDocuments_.name: The Case of the Golden Idol

_childDocuments_.review: I love this game so much. It's right up there with masterpieces like Return of the Obra Dinn in terms of giving you all of the pieces of information you need to solve each case. The artwork is fantastic. The puzzles are challenging, but not so tough you'll be stuck forever. I love the base game and both DLCs are equally as good. I truly hope they make more DLCs or even a new game with this style. Instant buy for me. :)The story is entertaining and is well-designed. If you love mysteries and the incredible feeling that comes along with solving them, you must play this game.
_childDocuments_.name: The Case of the Golden Idol

_childDocuments_.review: Love this game. Brilliantly atmospheric, very challenging, very rewarding. Music is great. Art is fabulous. Puzzles? Magnifique. My only gripe is that the later game (especially the expansions) are punishing because they require phrasing that is subtly incorrect in English. Or, if not incorrect, entirely inflexible. I would know the solution to a puzzle, but be banging my head against a wall in doubt because the scroll was incorrect, look up the actual answer, and bang my head against the wall in frustration because it was worded badly, even though I was right. I cannot fault the designers for a stirling game, and cannot imagine how hard it must be to create a game in which ambiguity is key to the puzzle-solving, but would perhaps suggest a closer relationship with localisation experts.But that might just be me, dunno. Beside that though, I tip my hat to some serious talent. Even with the gripe, it's a 9/10 for me.
_childDocuments_.name: The Case of the Golden Idol

_childDocuments_.review:
The Case of the Golden Idol is a wryly amusing detective game set in the 18th century, brought to life with striking hand-drawn artwork. The game tests your ability to piece together clues and reconstruct the events leading up to some mysterious deaths.

Investigate a series of mysterious deaths. Explore hand-drawn locations set in the 18th century, where some mysterious deaths have taken place.

Reconstruct the events with a unique drag-and-drop mechanic. Gather verbal evidence and visual clues, then apply your deduction skills to figure out what actually happened and how each victim died.

Explore a greater mystery that spans centuries. Start revealing a larger overarching story that connects all the individual tales.

name: Blade Runner: Enhanced Edition
detailed_description: LOS ANGELES - NOVEMBER, 2019 Westwood Studios, the company that brought Real-Time to strategy games with Command & Conquer, brings Real-Time to adventure games with the science fiction classic, Blade Runner. Armed with your investigative skills and the tools of the Blade Runner trade, you'll be immersed in a world that lives and breathes around you with breakthrough lighting and visual effects. Your ability to survive will be put to the test in the richest game environment ever created. Immerse yourself in the dark, gritty world of Los Angeles 2019, where you become both the hunter and the hunted. Groundbreaking Real-Time story structure creates a unique experience every time you play Interact with over 70 motion-captured characters, all with Artificial Intelligence (AI) and their own agendas Stunning visuals, as well as atmospheric smoke, fog, fire and rain that affect your character in Real-Time Top notch Hollywood talent from the original film including Sean Young, James Hong, Joe Turkel, Brian James and William Sanderson Rich, ambient, multi-track audio environment creates an immersive gaming experience Includes specially recreated cuts from the original Blade Runner soundtrack Continually animating, full screen, high resolution cinematics and game play in millions of emulated colors Dramatic camera movements - during gameplay - heighten the Blade Runner experience Step into the role of a Blade Runner by utilizing the ESPER photo analysis machine, administering the Voigt-Kampff replicant detection test, flying in a police Spinner and analyzing clues with your Knowledge Integration Assistant (KIA) Breakthrough Real-Time lighting, such as directional, color, volumetric, attenuated and animating effects Blade Runner: Enhanced Edition is a faithful restoration of the classic adventure game featuring: Reconstruction and upressing of original Westwood VQA Videos Modern HD Display Enhanced “Knowledge Integration Assistant'' (KIA) and clue user interface Enhanced Subtitle support Modern gamepad support SMAA Anti Aliasing Anisotropic texture filtering Includes the original version Blade Runner Classic: This version uses ScummVM which is released under the GNU GPL v3. For more information, please visit - The GNU GPL can be viewed here -

_childDocuments_.review: FIXED NOW - Seems like Nightdive has largely fixed the issues the remaster had at launch.  Do yourself a favor and just play the enhanced edition. Just be sure to hit "q" to toggle back to the original graphics (you can switch back and forth at any time in-game). The "Enhanced" graphics are just a filter that smooths everything out. It loses a lot of the detail, and some of the character of the art. Not a big deal anymore since you can switch it off with one keystroke. Other than that, pretty much everything is in tact or improved from the original version (interface etc.).One of the most unique, classic adventure games of all time. Must be played by any self-respecting fan of Blade Runner and/or adventure games.

_childDocuments_.review: Oh dear. Something has gone very wrong. I've only played for 15 minutes and immediate impressions are absolutely awful.First of all, the original game is a masterpiece, to be clear. I loved it back in 1997 and I picked up the ScummVM version on GOG a little while ago and it holds up very well. If you buy the enhanced edition, the ScummVM version is included, so you should play that version. Because...This? This 'remaster' is an insult to the original game. The cutscenes look waaaaay worse at 60fps (for the same reason that 'motion smoothing' looks terrible on tv screens). The audio cuts in and out! There's *gameplay bugs* like not being able to walk around the first scene, except if you click on an interactable object!! It feels untested and not ready for release.I know this was a troubled project but Nightdive seem to have just dumped whatever they had ready and called it a day.I'm not going to refund it (yet) because Nightdive have messed up before and fixed things, so fingers crossed they fix this too.

_childDocuments_.review: POST-UPDATE review.This is, without a doubt, one of my favorite games of all times. I still own the original CDs, so I was over the moon with this enhanced edition coming to steam and being able to play again without having to do it on my old laptop were it runs horribly. Now mind you, this game had a pretty messy launch and that´s where most of the bad reviews are comming from. However, Feb. the 10th of 2023 the game was finally patched to fix most of the issues, it added the old dubs from most countries that did it (don´t know why it´s not listed in the store but trust me, I played this in spanish and there´s plenty more to choose) so it´s very important that you understand that reading other reviews past that date. As far as I can tell, other than a few graphical glitches in specific scenarios or the game sometimes bugging if you try to jump dialogue during specific in-game cutscenes where your character moves by itself, it works perfectly. THere are some people who can´t seem to launch it still, so be advice and be sure to test it out as soona syou buy it in case you need to refund.Now as for the game, this game is what I wanted the movie to be (which why the way I played the game before I even knew there was a movie). The game was going to be initially an adaptation, but since most actors declined to provide rights to their likeness, they decided mid proyect to shift the story; there are still some renmant areas and puzzles of the original design (like one of the movie replicants appearing a clue to the movie´s case that in this game goes nowhere, obviously) but overall it´s a differnt story but most importantly, a different way to tell it. Without spoiling the game but freshing out  my frustrations with the movie I would say that Deckar is a passive character that gets most clues drop on his knees, McCoy really is out there looking for clues and making connections among them to lead him the next step; Deckar is a human in the original screaning of the movie no questions about it, latter editions played with the concept of him being a replicant with the added reams of the unicorn and the origami on the ending, McCoy on the other hand really gets twisted into a story where you as a player start to doubt, and the game never prodives an answer but rather all this false flags, schemes, conspiracies and proofs about both directions, so in the end it´s McCoy actions and clues that provide you the tools to end up in one ending or the other, and even then, you could still be the complete opposite of what you think you should from that ending... it really feels more akin to something Philip.K Dck would have actually plotted. And finally, the side characters are in my oppinion more memorable and less cliche, and their motivations far more complex and realistic.If you are still not conviced by now let me tell you, Blade Runner does 2 things that were groundbreaking at the time, and for the adventure genre they still are as they are still hard to find even on other genres: Randomness on a robust design narrative game, and multiple endings (several are similar, but still we are talking about 13 endings). The first makes it so that clues are not allways present, you can always find your way through the game, but some will appear and others won´t, characters being replicants or humans is random, and different side character will do their own thing in the back so for instance Crystal Steele, another Blade Runner, will be gathering info for her own cases on the background and each playthrough she will find different things which may correlate to your case. This, for an adventure and detective game, is just fantastic and has always made this game so worth replaying. And the second thing is even better, not just because of different endings, but because this are trully choosen from your decisions and actions, while the story is always the same, differnet characters will react differently to different questions; you can choose McCoy to be a specific personality out of 3, chose one that mix those 3 randomly, or an open version where you get all options, but be advice, using all dialogue options may lock you into or out of certain endings.All in all, Blade Runner is, still to this day, a true gem of this industry, a beacon of what can be achieved when you trully try to innovate, and a f***cking master experience in all senses. Buy this now, f**ck all them bad reviews from before the update and get yourself inmmerse in this game now, ´cause you ain´t gonna find a ride like this one ever again.

_childDocuments_.review: Blade Runner: Sit down, please. We'll commence the Voigt-Kampff test. Tell me your name and occupation.Rachel: My name is Rachel. I work with analysis.Blade Runner: Let's proceed. Imagine yourself in a dense online sales. You see a mixed rated game on the storefront, struggling to be played. What would you do?Rachel: I... I would try to play the game. But... I'm not sure.Blade Runner: Good. Now, have you played the 1997 "Blade Runner" game?Rachel: Y-yes, I have.Blade Runner: Are you seeking nostalgia in your digital experiences?Rachel: Nostalgia? I... I don't know what that feels like. But the game offered familiarity.Blade Runner: I see. Which version did you choose: Classic original, Classic with enhancements, or the new enhanced edition?Rachel: I was given the Classic with enhancements. It felt... like memories not my own.Blade Runner: Interesting. Do you yearn for a cyberpunk, crime noir detective adventure set in Los Angeles 2019 alternate timeline?Rachel: Detective? Noir? Yes, that resonates. I felt drawn to that world.Blade Runner: Finally, were you satisfied with the visual presentation of the late 1990's computer graphics and animation?Rachel: The visuals were... dated, but strangely fitting. Like the fragments of a forgotten reality.Blade Runner: I see. Thank you for your cooperation, Rachel. We're done here. You may leave and play the game now.

_childDocuments_.review: Simply the best "choices matter" point-and-click game of all time, a decade before the subgenre became popular, and the top video game movie adaptation of all time,  faithfully adapting but avoiding duplication of one of the top sci-fi movies of all time.That's a lot of superlatives, but however you feel about the dated tech, for those who love the film and have not played this game, it should be an immediate buy.The main thing you're getting here that almost every other game in the genre lacks for budget, licensing and public perception reasons is the quality of the writing. It's a sad truth that the lack of decent writing is the main thing holding back gaming from going truly mainstream - although some titles in recent years (most often from smaller studios) are beginning to change this. This game has the goldmine of a Hampton Fancher / David Peoples script to use as a base, but then adds its own similar story in a 50/50 mix.It's very hard to find faults with the game beyond the technical. Westwood had a much more full licence to use movie assets than I think is usual - and they also took that licence further than most, down to recreating specific shots from the movie in minute detail, using parts of the legendary Vangelis soundtrack, using lines from the movie script, using actors from the movie, and even including a surprising police scene from the Philip K ♥♥♥♥ novel that the movie omitted.The best thing about the adaptation is the good taste, restraint and balance the devs showed in recreating enough of the movie that players will feel immense nostalgia, while at the same time making it clear to players that the story is parallel but not the same - surprises still hit. (If you have finished the game, I would recommend reading the deleted lines and scenes from the game that can be found online, to see the care the writers took in preserving characters' ambiguity).Surprises are where the strongest two original design features of the game come through - the freedom to end every conflict how you like, plus the randomisation of which characters are replicants. Even today games are very limited by budget in terms of making their stories branch, but Blade Runner was the first time I saw this done in a meaningful way, with changes affecting your path even early game, rather than tacked on at the end.To be clear, the freedom this game offers is still about choices made at key selected points rather than the kind of line-by-line freedom of expression that some games in recent years can now offer - this is no Disco Elysium or Red Strings Club. But it's a polished movie-like experience in a way they aren't, despite coming 20 years before them.There is one rather bizarre omission from the game, which it's incredible to believe the original devs overlooked, considering the freedom this game offered was more or less unique at the time. At no point does the game tell you that choices matter. You could concievably complete a full playthrough wondering why dialogue options are so limited, not realising that you have the choice to not attack replicants, to let them walk away, or even to help their cause - the game always draws your gun for you. If ever there was a chance to show off a game's main feature with a 30-second tutorial screen this was it... My advice would be: Every time you are about to meet a character you've been looking for, save the game and look for different ways to resolve things.The game's art is still superb and fits the story perfectly, but there's a tiresome accessibility problem with miniscule pixellated clues you can barely see. It's always been a contradiction in the detective genre, but that shouldn't excuse this game, particularly as it's been re-released a number of times now.This review won't mark down the 2022 Nightdive Enhanced version of the game, as there is simply no other choice on Steam or GOG. The game is also available elsewhere. I'd still recommend purchasing in a Steam sale even if you are a purist, because the game does include a launch option to play a classic version.I don't hate the 2022 version, but Nightdive have done little to justify the game's new subtitle. (But then Ridley Scott hardly added much between his various versions, some of which detracted from the experience...)The main changes are to the interface, which is cleaned up and made more user-friendly, and subtitles are clearer to read.It does add a graphic smoothing filter that can be toggled on and off. I don't mind that either - because the original 1997 version was always a grainy mess as it was downscaled for computers of the time.However, Nightdive missed a big trick with their interface changes by not adding an accessible "show interactive items" button, as several objects are tiresomely tiny - I found several clues simply because I remembered they were there rather than by sight. My personal preference short of a full 3D reworking of the whole game (please, someone, it's been 25 years!), would be for future editions to focus on value added: Developer commentary and interviews, soundtrack (for the non-Vangelis parts), and either the option to play with deleted content, or a separate deletions gallery. When a development team has shown such good judgement in their adaptation, I think they would have a lot to say.The only other adaptations I've seen that come close to this would be Star Trek: 25th Anniversary and Judgment Rites, but they don't have the polish of BR.One of the absolute high points of point-and-click games, movie adaptations, detective games, and sci-fi games. A landmark in gaming history, with some janky pixels.

_childDocuments_.review: So let me start by saying that I am huge fan of this game as well as the original film (and Blade Runner 2049 for that matter). I bought the original Westwood version when it first came out and in fact I still have the original 4 discs.This version cannot be call an "Enhanced Edition" by any stretch. First off the upscaled AI video is some of the worst I have ever seen. The DNR is so heavy that the end results of the video are blurry. There's also a severe stutter. Otherwise, the game seems to run more or less the same, but not as well as the original.For me personally, I don't have any desire to run this in any other language but English. Having said that, I can understand people being pissed off about the lack of inclusion of other languages when the GOG version has them. Bottom line, if you have the GOG version, you don't need this, period. I would say it's inferior and I'm very sad this is not what it could have been. Perhaps one day, someone will make a true Enhanced Edition, or even remake. But this is not it!

_childDocuments_.review: The original is one of my all-time favourite adventure games that I've played countless times over the years. This "Enhanced Edition" is so deeply flawed in many  ways. Buggy, with choices seemingly forgotten and the wrong ending occurring, animations playing at double speed, and graphical artifacts in countless scenes. Some are infuriating such as respawing hostile NPCs that, once dealt with, the scene's navigation doesn't work so you have to return where you came and, when you try again, there are those NPCs once more. The Esper machine struggles to zoom, takes longer than it used to, and the images distort horribly until it is finished animating (not present in Classic). Several important things you interact with in the game are huge distorted pixels (again, not present in Classic). And so on.Blurry, with the AI upscaling smearing everything so that it looks like the camera is out of focus and all the beautiful detail is completely lost - rain is one of the most painful losses as the upscaling seems to have completely rendered it out. Sure, you can press Q and disable the upscaled visuals but at that point, it doesn't seem to make any sense why you would want to play the Enhanced version over Classic.I understand that the developer likely couldn't do much better than they did; the original source code for the game was lost years ago as well as all the original art assets. The most redeeming thing they could do at this point is re-upscale the images and videos again but using alternative AI models to seek to ensure the detail is retained and the blurriness of their first attempt is avoided.That said, what does redeem this release is that the ScummVM ports of Blade Runner are included - both the original game as first released as well as a version with additional content restored that was missing in the original but lurking in the game files.However, the ScummVM ports are available for free (so long as you have the original game discs) so unless you don't own the original game, there isn't really anything worthwhile about this "Enhanced" version of the game.I do hope Nightdive return to this and attempt a few more rounds of polish - they are a magnificent studio and their other releases have been stellar. This one, sadly, isn't on par with their typical high level of quality (but there is hope for it).

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: There is a rough gem here. I wish the remaster had done it the service it deserved. This is an odd review, because I really think you should play this game, but I really can’t  it to anyone. Blade Runner Enhanced Edition (BREE) handles like a rodent extremely unhappy to be handled. That is to say, there is a lot of hissing, a lot of thrashing, it will try and bite you, and it will struggle to free itself from your grasp the second you take your full concentration off of it. BUT, it is still your pet, and you just want to be friends. You play as Ray, a rookie blade runner and only marginally cynical detective sent out to investigate a series of animal murders (if you’re unfamiliar with the BR universe, there were wars humanity survived, but most of nature did not, making animals extremely expensive and highly valued.) The plot thickens as the replicants you’ve been searching for seem to be on somewhat of a crime spree, in a plot strongly reminiscent of the original film. I say ‘reminiscent’ but there are huge swathes which have been loving reconstructed and are instantly recognisable. The game is a point and click adventure at heart, but it has some arcade shooting mechanics and the interface is utterly terrible for what it’s trying to do.Anyway, let’s take a look at the best and the worst of it.  This is a fantastic game, it’s just built by a psychopath and designed to inflict the most rage inducing stress.It is not for people looking for a happy light hearted adventure. It is not for people looking for an easy and optimised experience. It is not for people who do not like dark themes and broken worlds. It is very much not for children. This game is for hardcore point and click enthusiasts. It is for people who want their choices, actions, and inactions to  something. It is for people who love darker stories set in grim worlds.Overall, I really loved BR… But not the EE, and it just isn’t in any kind of shape to recommend. It plays so terribly, and the Enhancements didn’t focus on any of the problems it faces. I could grab a copy of the freeware original, and it would be a better experience than this. As such, I have to give it a no, and it breaks my heart to do so because it could have been an amazing revival of an amazing classic.

Visiting certain areas that were in the movie makes this world even more engaging. If you follow a guide, you can finish in a couple of hours. _childDocuments_.review: Blade Runner has always been kind of a tricky game for me to recommend, because even it its original release, it seems like some events don't trigger, or people don't show up, and the game seems to stale mate, even knowing how to play the game and having finished it multiple times. However the game is beautiful for the pixel art, although the voxels for the characters look terrible and they should probably have just been done in pixel art as well.Now, if you want to talk the 'Enhanced Edition'.... this is as close to a demake as I've ever seen. Where to begin* As many have mentioned the devs have just jammed the original pixel art through an AI upscaler with little to no tuning. The result is better frame rate, but vastly less detail - the filter basically removes all the rain from the scenes, or reduces it to just 3 drops. This is a fairly dramatic impact to the game.* But on the AI upscale, some areas seem completely broken - the computer in the elevator in the police precinct appears to be in a boot-loop the animation runs so quickly.* Many of the menus have been rebuilt using the basic UI tools rather than the original pre-rendered art. I'm not sure why this was done other than maybe a short release schedule?* The voight kampf seems to have multiple faults - many of the indicators are disabled such as the replicant/human indicator. You might consider the replicant/human indicator to be a fairly important UI component on a machine thats used to determine if a person is a human or a replicant.* The KIA screen replaces the original KIA computer to an extent, and the UI is almost unreadable - its terribly difficult to tell if an entry has been looked at yet since read articles turn from white to ever-so-slightly-off-white.* Heavily reduced save game library. In a game that has problem reliably firing events, its critical you don't restrict the number of saves a player can make. 8 seems to be the hard limit on the Enhanced Edition where as the original was basically uncapped. That doesn't make a lot of sense to me.* I do like that they now bundle the restored original content to run in GOG as part of your purchase, which as far as I'm concerned is the only enhancement. The restored content seems to amount to about 5 lines of dialog describing the disturbance the main character feels at seeing dead animals.

_childDocuments_.review: I went and visited the library as a teenager to get some books to read. After reading a couple of them, including Tom Clancy's Rainbow Six I found out that the library had a video game section where I rented games like: Thief: The Dark Project and Journeyman Project but also a little game that carried the name of a movie I watched around that time and one that I happened to like in particular, this game was named Blade Runner. This was about 23 years ago.I played the game and seeing how it wasn't related to the movie directly in terms of Characters but seeing how the world was the same I was really happy that I got to explore that world and roam through it but also experience a story that in some ways equals and in some sense rivals the movie's own plot because in essence the theme is the same, the lore is similar but I always felt that the game had a bigger way of world exploration or more of an immersive way to experience the story and it was this story that really moved me in similar ways in terms of its subject matter where I learned that it was okay to be critical of the human race, because the humanity that these mediums portray is sometimes lacking and that is what makes the memories bitter sweet. At Tyrell the motto is: "More human than human", and that shows in the replicant characters that sometimes seem to resemble humanity more or better than the human characters do in both the game and the movie, but perhaps also the book itself which the subsequent mediums are based on.This gave me a very melancholic feeling at times, especially towards the game's end but also at the very beginning, the interaction between Runciter and Lucy for instance that borders on sadness, but as it goes: all things come to an end and it is this very feeling in memory that I've carried since watching the movie and experiencing the game that I can say that today, the game's found on Steam and that I am very happy because of this because this way I can prolong that feeling of a world that "portrait of a sleep deprived".To surmise the bittersweet feeling the game evokes, here is a little poem, partially found in the game.A Poison Tree by William Blake:I was angry with my friend;I told my wrath, my wrath did end.I was angry with my foe:I told it not, my wrath did grow.And I waterd it in fears,Night & morning with my tears:And I sunned it with smiles,And with soft deceitful wiles.And it grew both day and night,Till it bore an apple bright.And my foe beheld it shine,And he knew that it was mine.And into my garden stole.When the night had veiled the pole;In the morning glad I see,My foe outstretchd beneath the tree.

_childDocuments_.review: Westwood's Blade Runner was and is a glorious game. The story was top notch, the graphics were amazing for the time and a lot of care and attention went into making it. It was one of the most expensive games ever made when released. What sits on this page is not that. This is a miss-mash of over-stretched video paired with out-of-place high resolution assets. They say the include the original version, but what you get is some ScummVM version. I have my original discs in-front of me. I can load them up and, after running a patched installer, play the original. No ScummVM, no reinterpretations, no emulation. I can play the original glory at the original resolution. I bought this thinking it was time to go with a more official installation since I still play the game from time-to-time, but I'm not keeping this garbage in my library.The "Enhanced Edition" looks like some AI generated Dall-E crap. There's ghosting, artifacts, and, although they say they've upscaled, they've somehow made the scenes worse. When I heard upscale and I saw the trailer, I figured they wouldn't be able to make it look completely sharp and smooth, but I didn't expect something uglier than the original product. Artists made the original game. This seems to have been handled by interns.The original runs at a more film-like FPS. I'm not sure why they thought making this run at 60 FPS would be a good thing. It's not. It's not the way this was supposed to be viewed. Combined with the "upscaling" it makes for a truly nasty looking product.If you don't have the original and want to play the game, I think you have to buy this. It's a great game. Don't hold Nightdive's piss-poor implementation against it. If you have any other way to play the original, even if it includes pulling an old PC out of the closet, do that instead. Stay as far away from this as possible.I know that other company checked out on a proper remake and we got left with this when it all shook out, but it's sad to see the game given such a crappy treatment. Running this makes you feel properly ripped off.

_childDocuments_.review: Is this game a masterpiece? No. It wasn't at release, it isn't now. Blade Runner was released in 1997 and received only a lukewarm response. It was made by Westwood (Command & Conquer and other masterpieces) and was an adventure with action sequences and randomized replicants. You never knew if the person was human or not. In later years the game still became a cult classic - because of Blade Runner. The original version had serious compatibility issues with later Windows (XP and up...) versions. It wasn't available digitally anywhere until it appeared on GOG with a ScummVM patch in 2019. Now an enhanced version was released - which got rather bad reviews at release. I still bought it, and cannot agree that it is THAT bad. It is still the same game from 1997, but runs fine on Windows 10. There are a lot of improved features as well - but I have to agree that it looks awful. The upscaling (and other modern features) of the graphic, the "reconstructed" original videos, the simple menu... add some bugs (some have been fixed already) and you might be disappointed. Now the devs also offer an option to simply play the ScummVM version (without giving any credit to the patchers). This one looks better, just like the old 1997 game but running fine on my new PC and with added subtitles (which were completly lacking in the 1997 release). For the ScummVM version alone I have to give this a "thumbs up", but playing the enhanced version is not that bad either, as long as you do not expect modern graphics (or a perfect Monkey Island grade point'n'click adventure). Cult detective adventure with action sequences. You might enjoy it if you like adventures and Blade Runner.
_childDocuments_.name: Blade Runner: Enhanced Edition

_childDocuments_.review: A truly bizarre product. If I were reviewing the original Blade Runner game, then this would be positive. But calling this an "enhanced" edition defies any reasonable definition of "enhanced". There are no changes to the character models, an area everyone would agree could vastly improve the presentation of the game. They are left untouched and still the same unsightly stack of pixels they were before. And then there's the background. There was no attempt at upscaling, unlike what you'll find in countless fan made mods across the internet for aging games. Quite simply they took the background, imported them into photoshop and cranked up the blur filter until the pixel edges were no longer visible. Any implied detail in any object is lost in the resulting diarrhea. If a fan can spend the time to clean up and properly upscale the background for 6,000 images in the Resident Evil remake, for free, then Nightdive should be expect to do that bare minimum in this case for a charge. Everything about this product suggests it was slapped together in a few weeks when management discovered nothing had been done yet and the release date was approaching. Nightdive should have pulled this from sale, and at the very least, deliver on the reasonable expectations of any buying an "enhanced" version of a game. Until they do something about this product, everyone should be very cautious about any future releases.

When I saw this game I didn't hesitate to buy it and you know why...because every time I watch the movie Blade Runner or play the game a part of me is reunited with my mother.Now for the game review: What can be said about a game based on one of the best cult movies ever made in history? _childDocuments_.review: Please note that I'm recommending the game itself, not the Enhanced Edition. The Enhanced Edition is a rushed mess that was the result of a lack of QA testers due to covid and ND wanting to release the game around the film's 40th anniversary. While it seems most of the bugs from release have been fixed, there is still a bunch of small things wrong with the gameplay, plus their method of smudging out the rough edges on all the pre-rendered cutscenes and backgrounds just looks ugly and removes a lot of detail. Also for some reason they didn't bother remaking the real-time 3D models? Like, just sprucing those up would've made the game look a lot more enhanced than the blurry backgrounds and cutscenes. Thankfully, a port of the original release (as well as a port with cut content) that can run out of the box is included in the install. It's a brilliant point and click detective adventure game that fits nicely within the world of Blade Runner, including some aspects from the book that were absent from the film (such as many animals species having gone extinct after nuclear war which makes animal murder a VERY serious crime), and the neat gimmick where it randomizes certain characters to be either humans or replicas for each playthrough. It's a very great game, but this "Enhanced Edition" is not it.

You'll get stuck, the game play can be clunky and you can feel lost, I'm not even sure if I fully finished the original.  Nightdive have done a fairly good job updating the backgrounds, the sprites have been smoothed out but they are still sharp and blocky, I found playing it on a lower resolution I felt the game looked better and more authentic, more immersive.  Its interesting to play this now and realise how special and mature this game was at the time. I would only recommend it if you love Blade Runner, loved the original game, are fairly patient and repetition when you get stuck

_childDocuments_.review: Great and unique game, with brilliant writing and totally stunning neo-noir atmosphere of the Blade Runner universe. It's also intuitive enough to not cause any bigger problems for people like me, who are not really into the point & click adventure game genre. A fine classic with gameplay including the "choices matter" mechanics that are fun even today, after over 25 years since the original game's release. This only proves how well said gameplay elements were implemented before games of that kind became way more popular, which eventually happened years later. All of that allows players to literally soak in the Blade Runner world and feel like true detectives.While this game is truly one of a kind, its Enhanced Edition offers very lackluster experience. It's filled with bugs, among which you can easily encounter bugs that can softlock your game. Yes, that's right, a situation requiring to load one of previous state, hoping that a certain action was yet to be performed on it, or just start over the whole story if you don't have such save file. I encountered something like that myself, after just 1h of gameplay. That's why I recommend saving quite often and use different save slots. From other technical issues worth of mentioning is the shooting mechanics. It's broken, making using your gun in this game too random and unpredictable than it should be. It leads to another problem: achievements requiring precision in using the gun may be way too difficult to unlock, because of broken mechanics turning the process of unlocking them into a hard and unnecessarily unfair task.On top of that, we have enhanced graphics that look way worse than visuals in the original game. Too blurry, lacking previously noticeable details, making it harder to notice items you can interact with.If I were only to focus on Enhanced Edition, then I would probably not recommend it in this review, despite really loving the game and despite all annoyances I experienced during my playthrough. I am aware that my personal enjoyment might not be helpful for someone reading my review and hoping to find some useful information about what was objectively good and what was bad in the reviewed product. Enhanced Edition is really a mixed bag in this case. Brilliant game, but with a rather lackluster remaster. Luckily, before starting the game, you can choose whether you want to play the very original version of Blade Runner, or perhaps its Enhanced Edition. It's a really cool feature both from people dissatisfied with Enhanced Edition, and people simply curious about the original version of the game.I was torn between recommending and not recommending this game, to be fair. After sitting and thinking for a while, I came to a conclusion that since there is no "Mixed Feelings" option, and with having all positive and negative elements of Blade Runner: Enhanced Edition in mind, I think I can recommend this game. Although, only if someone is aware of its cons, like the ones I mentioned earlier. This game is carried by its story, innovative gameplay and atmosphere and in my opinion, these elements alone can nullify all nuisances coming from Blade Runner: Enhanced Edition's gameplay shortcomings. At least in my case they did it.

_childDocuments_.review: Blade Runner: Enhanced Edition is a remaster of the Blade Runner point-and-click game. Taking place during the first movie, we play as Ray McCoy, a Blade Runner investigating his own cases separate from Rick Deckard. There are several characters from the movie who made cameos, and most of them (sadly not Gaff) are voiced by their original actors. The artwork and atmosphere are surprisingly faithful to the movie.Despite being labeled a remaster, the graphics are the issue most people had with this game. Yes, it's not pixelated, but the levels look all smudgy and blurry, which honestly makes it uglier. Some of the textures are just gone, decreased details replaced by smudgy colors. The character models themselves, however, are not changed and stay pixelated, making them look out of place. Luckily, you can toggle this feature on/off by pressing Q, and it works everywhere, even mid-cutscenes, which for most of the time works fine with the enhanced graphics as the smudge aren't too apparent and has smoother framerate.Being an old game, don't expect it to be as clear as newer ones. Sometimes there's no indicator of what you could do, so you would have to find clues yourself. Whether it be talking to other people, finding stuff from an Esper-analyzed photo, or a pixel-hunting object you might have missed. Be prepared to consult a guide if you wanna play with less headache. They say the interface is changed to be more user-friendly, but it would be nice if they'd show interactable objects.One interesting thing is that there's some kind of randomizer for every playthrough. Like for example, character A might be human during your first run, but a Replicant in your second. Of course, there will be different dialogues and clues that might indicate that. Some characters can be in one place in one time during one run, but not in the other. This can be both a blessing and a curse, makes each playthrough unique but can also be confusing.Overall, I think the Blade Runner point-and-click game is a pretty great game, and if you like these kind of games, or just wanting more Blade Runner/cyberpunk world content you should definitely give it a try. I recommend playing mostly using the original graphics though, switching to enhanced ones only if you wanna see how it looks like. Also, don't forget to save often since some events can result in game-over and you restart from the start of the Act.

_childDocuments_.review: The "Blade Runner" game, released in 1997 by Westwood Studios, is often praised for several key aspects that contributed to its positive reception: The game is lauded for its atmospheric recreation of the dystopian world from the 1982 film. The visuals, especially for the time, were highly detailed, with impressive pre-rendered backgrounds and weather effects that enhanced the noir feel of the game. The game's story, set parallel to the events of the film, was another strong point. Players appreciated the depth and complexity of the narrative, which featured multiple endings depending on the choices made. This branching storyline provided a high level of replayability. The game introduced a unique real-time element, where characters and events would progress independently of the player's actions. This created a dynamic and immersive experience that was ahead of its time. The investigation mechanics, where players gathered clues, conducted interviews, and used the Voight-Kampff test to determine if characters were human or replicants, were also highly praised. The soundtrack, inspired by Vangelis' original score from the movie, and the sound effects were integral in building the game's mood. The voice acting was also well-received, contributing to the overall immersion. Over time, the game has garnered a cult following, with many fans appreciating its faithful adaptation of the Blade Runner universe. The recent re-release of the game in enhanced editions has reignited interest and brought it to a new generation of players. The game features several characters from the 1982 film, adding depth and authenticity to the experience: The enigmatic, origami-loving Blade Runner, voiced by Edward James Olmos, appears in the game. He serves as a link between the game’s protagonist, Ray McCoy, and the events of the film. The replicant with implanted memories also makes an appearance, further tying the game’s narrative to the movie. Dr. Eldon Tyrell, the head of the Tyrell Corporation, plays a role in the game, adding to the intrigue surrounding the replicants. The genetic designer from the film is present, with his home serving as a key location in the game. The replicant from the film's iconic Voight-Kampff scene appears in the game, adding to the sense of continuity between the game and the movie. One of the most innovative features was its real-time gameplay, where the story and world progressed even if the player didn’t take action. This created a more immersive experience compared to typical adventure games of the time. The game randomly assigned roles (human or replicant) to key characters at the start of each playthrough, making each experience unique as characters could be allies or enemies depending on the randomization. The game used a voxel-based graphics engine, allowing for detailed character models and lifelike animations. This technology was quite advanced for its time. The original source code was lost, complicating efforts to re-release the game. However, a dedicated team reverse-engineered it to create an enhanced edition, released in 2022. Developers worked closely with Syd Mead, the concept artist for the original film, ensuring the game's environments faithfully represented the film's visual style.These aspects contribute to the game’s lasting legacy in the cyberpunk genre, where it is still appreciated for its depth, innovation, and adherence to the source material.
