_childDocuments_.review: Very disappointing.The good:- Character and world design is decent. The game would have been quite pretty if it performed well, but it does not...- The core cast of characters is also not bad.The bad:-The main feature of the game, which is the main character's power, is the worst part of the game. Any mystery in the game is solved by repeatedly highlighting the interactables around you, clicking them in order and reading walls of text that immediately give you the answer. No thinking is involved. Neither by you nor by the main character. -The game is designed around highlighting the interactables. Which is not unlinke other CRPGs. Here is the difference: in other games you can highlight the interactables on your screen with the press of a button. Here, the MC has Perception, which he activates by loudly clicking his fingers, and this spreads a ring of red particles which collect around interactables in a short range. And there is a ton of garbage lying around in the world, and this garbage gives you XP when you interact with it. Surely you see the problem? The game is designed around you constantly spamming Right Click when running around to highlight stuff in a small range around you, which results in endlessly repeating clicking.-The previous issue is exacerbated further by the location design. When you get a quest, you are usually given an address. How the hell are you supposed to use a Polish street name to navigate a city divided into multiple completely disconnected locations? You are not, which means the game has to point you in the correct direction. And it does that when you, you guessed it, click your fingers. The game is designed around the player doing what the game tells you to do. You are no longer exploring, you are following an annoying red pointer.-The dialogue is quite bad, and again, for a very fundamental reason. I don't know who came up with the idea, but in dialogue you are not offered to choose a line for your character to say, you are only given a description of a line. As an example, you might be offered a line like "mention X's wife" which results in your character accusing X's wife of infidelity and X himself of being a cuckold. Why? Who came up with this???-The combat is awful. It poses no challenge whatsoever even on the highest difficulty, and is incredibly repetitive. Think of Pokemon, but you only have a few pokemon, and the enemies are all the same, except for some week points which the game highlights for you. -The game is set in alternate history Poland. The problem is, outside of the magic shenanigans, it's not immediately clear just how "alternate" it is, unless you know history. The truth is, it is really, really alternate. It is in this weird limbo where it is inaccurate enough to be completely uninteresting from a historical point of view, and not weird and distinct enough to be captivating on its own. Nevertheless, you have reviews here saying that "they learned a lot about Polish history from this game". Learning Polish history from a game called The Thaumaturge is obviously not a very good idea. I could go on about the bad, but I think I am done with the game. And I am exactly the target audience of this game, too.
_childDocuments_.name: The Thaumaturge

_childDocuments_.review: The year is 1905, and you are Wictor Szulski (that’s Wictor with a “W”). A grimoire-totin' Polish Pokémon hunter of sorts, only the Pokémon are “salutors” that feed on your innermost emotional flaws and catching one turns you into a mentally-shattered lunatic.  Luckily, divisive Russian mystic Grigori Rasputin (that’s the Rasputin) whom you meet in a muddy Georgian village, can hypnotize you back to health and get you back to catching those ♥♥♥♥♥♥ up Pokémon monster demons. But, when you receive word of a family tragedy, you’re called back to Warsaw and before long find yourself knee-deep in a political powder keg of Russian expansionism and Polish pride... and it turns out that Rasputin’s burgeoning godlike complex might just be the fuse.  In other words, DAMN this game is cool! In fact, think it’s the most-engrossed I’ve ever been in a video game’s plot, thanks in large part to its fascinating cast of semi-historically accurate characters and wonderfully-voice acted dialogue that’s equal parts witty, believable, and thought-provoking.   But, while I’ll most remember The Thaumaturge for its storytelling, that's not to say the remainder of the game is any less compelling. Far from it, in fact, as the game features a complex and creative turn-based combat system that pits you and your army of salutors against any ♥♥♥♥♥♥ or ♥♥♥♥♥ stupid enough to piss you off. As you level up, you’ll gain Thaumaturgy points that you can allocate to four dimensions (Heart, Mind, Deed, and Word), each of which has a salutor associated with it. As you allocate points into this skill tree, you’ll unlock new combat skills and modifiers that you can experiment with before any encounter. And you’d better, because certain enemies have powerful traits that you’ll need to disable with the salutor they’re most susceptible to, meaning in each fight you might end up rotating multiple times through your entire assortment of demon pals. But that’s only half of the fun! The other side of this game’s combat coin is timing. Up here you’ll see each round’s order of attacks. Your best bet when outnumbered will be attempting to interrupt the next enemy in line, either with a direct attack or by breaking their focus (pictured here with these little diamond dots). Reducing an enemy’s zero focus to zero results in a guard break, opening your foe up to a devastating super attack. The combat here feels like a deadly dance between attacking, interrupting, disabling traits, and healing, and I just couldn’t get enough of it.  Which is saying something, because the game throws a LOT of it at you, at times feeling a bit forced, even, like the game was worried of boring you with its at times slow burn story and general lack of non-combat mechanics. While it’s hard to get bored running around such a committed historical recreation of Warsaw at the ugly turn of the 20th century, especially when you factor in all the fun little touches that make the city feel alive and lived in, there is, admittedly, not a whole lot for Wiktor to do outside of punching, talking, changing his haircut for the twentieth time, and catching a carriage to the next quest. Luckily, the game has a dizzying number of interesting side quests that complement the main story nicely, peeling back the curtain of high society before plunging you headfirst into the city’s criminal underworld.   But no matter where you go, you’ll look good doing it. The Thaumaturge features crisp UE5 textures and nice lighting on Epic settings, not to mention some awesome creature designs. However, the steady barrage of choppy cutscene animations and clipping kill some of the immersion. That’s not the case for the game’s incredible soundtrack. Accordions, clarinets, strings, and even the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ Hurdy Gurdy combine to create unusual and atmospheric Polish horror folk music that my ears just gobbled up.   Before we conclude, a few tiny gripes. First, boss fights in The Thaumaturge (which occur whenever you attempt to capture a new salutor) are surprisingly “mid” for how strong the combat system is; they’re really just normal encounters with an extra wave of damage thrown at you every few turns—I think it would’ve been much more interesting to fight the actual salutor head on applied directly to the forehead. Second, while the User Interface here is sleek, helpful, and easy to navigate, I often lost track of where side quest locations were—would love to see them added to the main map in a future update. Finally, the game’s load times are lightning fast—so fast, in fact, that I often couldn’t appreciate the loading screens for their art or historical details. More importantly, I did encounter two crashes during my playthrough, but they were ultimately insignificant thanks to the game’s reliable autosave feature.   In conclusion, I beat The Thaumaturge in 18 hours without touching much of the optional content, meaning there are several salutors out there that I still haven’t tamed. Between them, the game’s multiple endings, and a dialogue system that locks a significant number of options depending on your level of pridefulness, The Thaumaturge feels like it was built to be a two or even three-playthrough kind of experience. At $35 and for this level of excellence, consider me more than impressed with the game’s value, which leaves us with a second-best all-time aggregate MEGA score of 4.43/5 (full scoring breakdown, from “Plot” to “Sound” available in video form). Thank you for reading, and please let me know if you have any questions about the game or my review.

Particularly the effects and animations for pistols and rifles is cool to observe. The Salutors (demons) in the game have very detailed character models and all look much different compared to each other. Cons: Some woke themes. Example your sister being a feminist and potentially being LBGQT++. She is also the competent one in the family with your player character at times being portrayed as the incompetent brother. This is typical western anti male ideologue. And most game companies are following these trends. There is a woke disclaimer at the start of the game. Do developers not realise actual gamers look at things like that and roll their eyes out of exasperation. We only care about having fun. Not covering ones back for political reasons or virtue signalling. In 14.7 hours I had one Unreal Engine 5 crash. That said "Fatal error". If a character you are speaking to has one dialogue option and that dialogue options is inaccessible due to your applicable flaw not being high enough. _childDocuments_.review: The Thaumaturge is an original, turn based RPG, that excelled in the narrative sections of the game and I loved it.If you are someone who enjoys a good story with lots of side quests and exploration then I am sure you will love this too. The combat sections were beautifully portrayed with some interesting and imaginative fighting scenes, but ultimately you'll want to play on a harder difficulty if you require a challenge. Overall, after completing the game with most endings, I would highly recommend this for its atmospheric story and vivid locations. It's a strong game of the year candidate for me personally. There are a generous amount of locales to visit, all within easy travelling distance by tram or coach. I appreciated the quickness of going from one district to the next, whilst pursuing quests, and locating where you had to go was a breeze with Viktor's sixth sense of direction taking you straight to the heart of the quest. This only becomes a little confusing when you have more than one quest active, as I noticed sometimes that multiple points of interest were located on the map, and it can leave you visiting the wrong place because you visit the wrong quest. There is no more instruction than a red exclamation mark which pinpoints which district you need to visit, so perhaps this could be a little clearer. When you reach destinations they are wonderfully rich with characters going about their daily lives in bustling environments. Sometimes, a text based comment, usually rude I might add is said, but there are a surprising amount of characters you can talk to with branching narratives. Viktor can explore places and use his senses to detect traces of emotion on everyday objects which can help him deduce what happened in certain situations. He can then use this information in conversations, often giving him an advantage by opening up branches that would otherwise be closed. The mechanic is very interesting to begin with but it tends to get a bit stale towards the end of the game, and I realised it was just the conclusion I needed to read once all the objects had been found and examined.  It is definitely worth using Viktor's sixth sense as much as possible whilst you are running around locales as often unexpected items can be detected which trigger side quests. Besides the main quest, which has eight different endings depending on which factions you swear your allegiance to, there are a multitude of side quests which can be discovered. A lot of these will result in being awarded a stereograph photograph, which is sometimes a disappointing conclusion, but needs to be collected if you want that achievement. Some of these side quests have time limits or can only be performed at certain times of the day or night, but there is an easyy waiting mechanic and as long as you pay attention to your quests, I never ran out of time. There are also achievements for collecting clothes patterns, which you can change into throughout the game, and why not get a haircut at the barber shop too. There are gramophone records to find and listen to, and local landmarks which can be found and admired. There are lots of collectibles to find if that is something you enjoy. I absolutely loved the narrative in the game. Everything is just so atmospheric. Rasputin is an intriguing character, who keeps you guessing his intentions throughout the game, and every character is professionally voiced with believable emotions and a wealth of different avenues to follow in the branching narratives. If a branch is closed, it will either display that previous decisions have caused this branch to close, or it will tell you that you need more information, so you will need to search the area for further clues. Talking to characters effects the story line and options open to you, so I happily found myself talking to everyone to maximize the possibilities. There is a lot of lore in the game and characters are very well developed. I think if you love conversations and characters you will do the same as me and just explore as much as you can. You can get rewarded for more knowledge, and may open up possibilities to manipulate characters using your senses. There is quite a deep examination of yourself and your relationship with your father and your sister in the game which I enjoyed, and there is an unusual connection with your salutor, a demon that is attracted and latches to flaws in a character. Viktor can have conversations with his salutor, although he doesn't say much in return, and use his powers in battle. Fighting is interesting, with a few mechanics you will need to learn and master to win battles, like disabling enemy traits and replenishing your health at crucial moments.  Enemies can inflict damage on you which if not monitored and countered can start to multiply damage, like bleeding from gun shots and knife attacks. This is where you can use your salutor to heal you or take away these effects. There is a bar at the top of the scene which allows you to see who is next to attack, which if you can understand, as it does take a while to comprehend, can be useful in knowing when to send in your salutor. You will pick up salutors throughout the game through main quests and side quests. I collected all eight of them, and you become almost invincible with them all in your corner. There is a skill tree, where you can assign traits relating to the salutors, and also apply Thaumaturge points to learn new skills or increase your senses, because certain situations throughout the game require you meet a certain level of senses, for example, reaching level five in  to read a certain clue. The attack scenes are quite enjoyable to watch with characters running towards you slashing you or shooting you with guns whilst you stumble around in pain. The reactions to your magic attacks are good too and fighting salutors requires different tactics to win. To be honest, once you get used to removing enemy traits and watching your health carefully and reacting, I didn't have much difficulty winning the vast majority of battles on normal difficulty, so if you want to be challenged put the difficulty up.

_childDocuments_.review: A great RPG game where you are basically Sherlock Homes solving various cases and mysteries all while going on an adventure yourself....while kicking some butt along the way...... with powers. The setting is interesting, taking place in Poland back when Russia controlled a part of it. Later on in the story, you can customize the main character looks (i.e. hair, facial hair, and clothes). Great graphics, and interesting game play. A isometrically styled game to explore this semi-open world while also switching to a third person view during turn-based combat. I find that quite unique as I have personally never seen both viewpoints at the same time in a game. I love the conversations among-st characters and the action from combat that happens while you are on your adventure. I really hope for a sequel, this was wonderful! :) Wonderful game, great story, interesting choices to make that effect various outcomes. I leave you with this thought, We all have demons inside of us.....but can we control them?This game is a big yes from me. The Retail Price is justifiable for what you get. Worth the full price.

_childDocuments_.review: In this game you play as a mentally ill man who believes he is living in a fictional country named Poland, compulsively snaps his fingers, and feeds on the internalized psychoses of other lunatics. Since I've become acquainted with Wictor I've seen him start a street brawl with the police right in front of the Tsar, terrorize half the city during a bar crawl, and hang out with the most notorious Russian schizo in history. I really don't know how his life could get any more interesting, but I definitely want to find out. After eight hours I'm still rather impressed.If I had to make a comparison between this and other games it'd be a strange one: It's slavic Persona. You will become well acquainted with the Goetia and probably use them to tear someone's throat out. Warsaw is lovingly crafted and the folk that populate it are just as backward as you would expect from 1905. While the game does have a serious tone it and its protagonist are chalk full of wit and sarcasm. I often can't tell which components of the game's world are real, and I don't think Wictor can either. It's fun that way.Want to be a cool warlock that incites gunfights in the street? Don't take your meds. A++ would recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: I'll keep it short an unusual:IF YOU ARE NOT INTERESTED OR ACCUSTOMED TO SLAVIC CULTURE THEN THIS GAME WILL FEEL LIKE PLAYING AN ANIME GAME WITHOUT BEING A WEEB.It's a 6/10 if you have no clue of (or interest in) slavic/eastern european history and culture, but an 8/10 if you do. Many "jumps of logic" or paths of conversation and narratives seem... a bit off, or a bit confusing, or a bit strange to the western mind. You did read a lot of Dostojewski or are from Poland or Eastern Europe? You'll love this game. But if you didn't or are not... Well, ever played a japanese game and found yourself confused or dissatisfied with some weird reactions or conclusions to the things you did? Or weirded out by how people interact with each other? This will be the same, only the eastern european equivalent. Even the voiceacting seems strange, unless you willingly immerse yourself into the "Slavic side of things".It is a good game that brings with it the vibes of "Witcher 3 detective work", Penny Dreadful (TV show), Cthulhu-Esque-Things, Vampyr, and a visual atmosphere that reminded me a lot of RDR2, and overall... well, it's wonderfully atmospheric.The game isn't perfect. Too slow, to stumbling at points... but it is very intriguing and entertaining. A solid 7/10 for me.

_childDocuments_.review: This game delves deep into the polish/slavic mythology and culture, reminiscent of other detective type games with an interactive environment full of clues, important figures, angry spirits, and a fight is always looming around the corner. Along with branching choices that make you want to go back and try the other route.The highlight of this game is both the theme and the combat. The atmosphere is steeped with culture, while the combat breaks the information gathering monotony at just the right times. You "collect" spirits and use them against your enemies to create well orchestrated combos with a very unique fighting system featuring a timing mechanic. You alternate between using your own attacks and commanding spirits to take a chomp out of your enemies, and can even use them to influence people's minds.Some of the investigation reminds me of The Witcher series, but so far I'm really enjoying my time as a Thamaturge!P.S. If a message of inclusion at the beginning of a game bothers some that much then I can only imagine how sad and left out they must feel in their every day lives. At some point, Steam became a beacon for this ignorant behavior with a lot of racist or anti-LGBT posts and comments. They are a vocal minority that shouts because otherwise no one will pay attention to them. Thaumaturge and it's developers are much more than a few words at the beginning of their game.

_childDocuments_.review: Interesting setting and great atmosphere make this game feel unique and this alone makes it worth the cost IMO, as there is really nothing like it. Besides that, we get a solid story with solid characters and a good soundtrack. Unfortunately, there is no Polish VA which is a missed opportunity, as it would help immersion. The graphics isn't technically impressive, but the art style is great. The gameplay is pretty simple and combat is rarely challenging even on highest difficulty. It's pretty much an adventure game with RPG elements, so don't treat it as a tactical RPG or anything of the sort.My first playthrough took me about 26 hours. I did most of the side quests, but I didn't focus on collectibles and such.  Overall the game's length is pretty decent for the base price IMO. Moreover, I will probably replay the Thaumaturge in the future in order to check out other choices/endings.EDIT: Update - Polish VO has recently been added to the game and it's good :).

_childDocuments_.review: Passt game compeltion:I need a thumb that points left or right, instead of up and down. Sadly after finishing the game I have to say that it has many issues, it is buggy, the atmosphere does not get better at all, the music is bad and gets much worse over the time, since it likes to loop on itself very often and the track is quite short, in addition it also has pauses between loops which is an issue since there are only very few ambient sounds, especially indoors. Sentences get cut off at the end of recordings, echo gets worse the further you get in the game... Simply said, the sound engineer was either an amateur or phoned the whole job in. Terrible sound design, just absolutely awful, and since half of your gameplay is sound, this just drags the whole game down. They would have made a better job if they just played the whole time clown music, at least they would have had some atmosphere. Combat:And combat, My god the combat. It is not bad, do not get me wrong. It works like a puzzle. I played on challenge and it is actually very challenging.... sometimes... and sometimes if it laughably easy. The bad part is, that you can fight two groups of enemies, located 20 meters of each other in the same area, one group is pathetically easy, and the other is the most brutal combat you will ever face in any game... The issue is not that the combat is bad, the issue is that the battles are not well balanced. Character builds: The game would like you to believe that it has a talent tree, it does not. It works more like a battle pass for Talent Points. Since combat requieres you to have a certain amount of points in every "branch" you literally can not specialize, you have to progress in all branches at the same pace, especially on challenge difficulty. Since ever combat will have one trait of each type at the same level that you need to overcome that trait. So any talent choice is an illusion.All in all, it is a double A tittle with reduced price. So it passes. But not with flying colors. It passes with a scratched butt.

_childDocuments_.review: Compelling take on a choices-matter RPG with really interesting story beats and a reasonable amount of content to sink your teeth into - took about 25 hours to get to /an/ ending but I know there are more out there. A lot of the meat of the game is presented in little blurbs of info you can glean by 'reading' objects in the world so if you don't like reading this might not be the game for you.The sound design and voice acting are fun and entertaining, and do a lot of work to keep you engaged with the story.Combat was not the games strong point, with even the hard difficulty posing little problem except at certain difficulty spike points in the game. I found myself vastly outscaling a lot of the encounters just by playing the game normally, especially once you start unlocking more pieces of your powerset that can trivialize certain enemy types. But this is ultimately a minor gripe as the combat was still fun and strategic even if it wasn't particularly difficult.Some elements of the UI seemed silly to me (both the combat and the level up screen in particular) but they definitely did a lot of work to make sure even the menus fit with the games overall aesthetic, so this really is a nitpick.All in all, there's nothing bad I can really say about the game & would favorably compare it to games like BG3 and the Shadowrun series in the realm of choices/story/world design. Definitely had a bit of the TTRPG come to life in a video game vibe. So what are you waiting for, go play it!

_childDocuments_.review: Thaumaturge: On one hand, a fairly conventional game with a fun battle mechanic, and on the other, a mostly solid story told in a very interesting time period but often broken up by rather annoying side quests. For me, this is a classic 6/7 out of 10 kind of game: It is good, but not flawless nor a must-own in your collection.To keep spoilers light: You are a Polish magician (or as I kept calling him, a Stand User), who can use his magic to deduce peoples thoughts, and summon demonic companions to fight hostiles. The core combat game play remains fun and solid throughout the game. The developers did a lot with a tight and simple system, and while I thought the repeated animations was going to get stale, the fact that they are fast and the demons look universally gorgeous kept them fun and fresh. The story, when not being sidetracked, is very interesting and well presented. I would love to see more games set in this pre-WW1 world outside of the roaring 20s, and Congress/Russian Poland is a great setting. The characters are interesting and multifaceted, and great voice acting all around.Now for flaws, and there are some serious flaws: First of all, the game straight up lets you miss Salutors, and thus denying you of their power and argues the coolest part of the game. I understand why they choose to do this, but this means you have to constantly do every single side quest, many of which consists of you constantly snapping your fingers and walking to a piece of discarded cloth three times in a row, then walking to a fourth place to see a picture. This was easily the worst part of the game, especially since there were some real actual fun side quests with story implications. This is also a ‘’Choices Matter’’ game, and after reloading a certain Salutor quest, and getting the same outcome, no matter what I choose, I found that part to be somewhat lacking. So, do I recommend this game? On a sale, yes, or if you really like what you saw in the demo or in a LP. This game lives and dies by it’s Story and characters. If neither interests you, do not buy this game. The developers, despite a few hiccups, have clearly put a lot of love into this game, and that shows. Good work devs.
_childDocuments_.name: The Thaumaturge

_childDocuments_.review: A story-driven, turn-based game set in Warsaw in 1905. Still not enough? How about companions (salutors) reminiscent of Persona, in-depth dialogues, and decisions with impactful consequences similar to Disco Elysium. Add to that a soundtrack that pulls you in, alongside a stunning presentation. The game feels refreshingly different. The dialogues are captivating, constantly making you eager to learn more about the characters and the story, which helps overlook the occasional red-cloud chase. The main and side quests are convincing, though I can't say the same about the "find a viewpoint" tasks—fortunately, these are limited.At just under 30 hours, the game is the perfect length. I can only hope this won’t be the last installment in the series.See you in Albuquerque!

I cant tell if they are being sarcastic or mean and it makes no sense.The voice acting doesnt help with the situation at all either. Its a real shame.Lastly, and this is just a personal thing, not being able to move the camera around your character is frustrating. Depending on the camera to move for you is not very enjoyable...but that might just be me and the years of ARPGs that naturally allow/want you to look all around.The game has a super cool concept, I like the fight mechanics and the graphics are very pleasing. _childDocuments_.review: It's been some time since I enjoyed a game quite as much as I did with The Thaumaturge. I just finished my first playthrough and I'm about to start yet another one. All the little secret missions were fun to do, collectibles were also fun to collect. I love the character designs too, as well as the way our imaginary friends look. I loved the little easter eggs, like when there were meme references or Walter Pinkman, one of the NPC's even said the famous line of Ferdynand Kiepski from an old popular Polish TV show.And of course our schizophrenic protagonist rules. Live, laugh, love Wiktor Szulski.

_childDocuments_.review: It is a good game, but it isn't for me. Gave it an honest shot playing it for a couple of hours. Indie RPG vibes, the graphics and sound design aren't great. The combat system has interesting ideas, such as having your "companions" function as Pokemon who work alongside you to take out people.There is a mechanic to reduce focus points and stun your opponents, but it seems to be far more effective to apply the Damage Over Time effects and spam them across all opponents, as a general rule.The combat is few and far between, as most of your time should be spent on investigations. The problem is that the places you visit have a rather grey colour palette and by the end of an hour of wandering about it was positively depressing. I suppose if you're into the "gothic, war torn, old Europian town in the Victorian era" vibes then it'll still hold your interest, but it just wasn't for me.Overall it is a good game for a niche audience of gamers: Specifically turn-based RPG enjoyers who want a gothic themed game (Right, Darkest Dungeon. This thing gave me strong "Darkest Dungeon" vibes)

_childDocuments_.review: This is a kind of game that is mostly focused on its narrative (story, worldbuilding and atmosphere) rather than gameplay. Exploring the city to look for clues leading you to solving the mysteries feels great, and the characters that you come in contact with feel real and are interesting. As for the combat part - it reminds me of jRPGs, but with two "characters" in your party: the MC, and one of the monsters/ghosts he can summon, that can be changed for another every time it moves and is not targeted by enemies. It may be a bit basic, but looks cool and feels fresh thanks to the special effects the attacks can have (which can be customized in case of MC). Overall it may not be the most innovative system, but feels quite good. The game is also not long enough for it to make it feel stale (which may be an issue in case of several playthroughs) .As for bad points: minor bugs with movement and a bit abrupt wrap-up of the story in the last act (may be because of chosen path).

_childDocuments_.review: I am thoroughly enjoying this game. I have been ignoring all others in favor of this one. Despite it being "unsupported" for steam deck, that's where half of my game play comes from. It can stutter a little during loading or cut scenes. I have had it freeze if I press a button too soon after loading (like into a new area for example and immediately pressing perception). Otherwise, I don't have any issues. Anyways, the rest of my time is on PC where, of course, it runs smoother and graphics are better. The salutors are cool; I love all the supernatural bits to the game. I don't mind all the extra quests because you can follow your perception to know where to go. I'm too tired to think most things through, so I'm glad for the ease of use. _childDocuments_.review: An immersive way to lose yourself for a couple dozen hours or so if you want to read all the lore and really let yourself go into the game's environment.  My closest comparison is Vampire: The Masquerade: Bloodlines, which is high praise.  It has its flaws - combat is a bit shallow, the voice acting can be laughable, and there's some rushing towards the end including some sequence breaking flaws in the storyline resulting in plot developments coming out of nowhere - but if you are interested in a unique society and a fully realized vision of the developers, I highly recommend The Thaumaturge.  If you are more interested in game play and tend to skip plot or details, it probably isn't for you.

_childDocuments_.review: First things first: In the prologue, you're looking for a healer, and in the first like, 5 minutes of actually moving around the game you meet Rasputin in hopes of him fixing your magical ghost powers. That should be all you need to know. You get to hang out with Rasputin. Also, the way that the city of Warsaw is designed, the Thaumaturge mechanics, and the ambient story telling are all excellent. There's a morbid humor throughout the game I find very funny. I really enjoy hearing the game in Polish with English subtitles. The Polish voice acting is good from what I can tell. The only downsidez currently are that the graphics and the movement are a bit dated (no hair physics, expressions are limited, repeated models, and some clipping on models etc), but frankly I don't care. I can tell Rasputin is Rasputin. Tsar Nicholas II did indeed look like Tsar Nicholas II. I can tell the characters apart etc. Sometimes Wictor doesn't move super smoothly despite my computer being plenty high end enough. But I still sit down and play the game and am enjoying it immensely. I would *love* to see more RPGs like this! I live the historical plus magic setting, love the idea of the Thaumaturges and their powers, love the way that real life events and politics of the time are woven in. Really a great game and I look forward to finishing it!

_childDocuments_.review: If I had to describe the type of gamer who this game is for I'd go with - a Pole who likes historic fiction, who lives abroad. Anyone who has interest in Polish culture will also love this game. I'm a bit disappointed by lack of Polish voices, but I understand decisions had to be made. I hope those will be added in the future. :)I am giving this game thumbs up, because the story and the universe are really unique. They've created something truly special.I have only started exploring the city of Warsaw at the time of writing this, but I'm sure the game will get even better from this point on.There are some flaws related to the overall quality of this game, but those flaws don't get in the way of the immersion and having great experience with the game.

_childDocuments_.review: The Thaumaturge is a wonderful experience full of mystery and intrigue, I've enjoyed soaking it all in as well as getting to learn more about the Salutors and places the game is based on.Pros:- A nice take on turn based combat, Wictor has 4 separate attack "types"; Quick, Planned, Damage Over Time and Influences. Each Salutor gives you access to a new attack in one of each category and they cycle with each round so to use the strongest Quick Attack would require using the Quick Attack for 3 consecutive rounds.- Being able to customise Wictors appearance/clothing is a nice touch, clothing is tied behind a fashion magazine collectible which isn't the most obvious thing to find.- Story is very interesting with how the Salutors tie into everything with being drawn to a persons flaw.- Taking your time to explore is rewarding as everything you interact with gives exp.- Visual designs of the Salutors are unique and based off of folklore and mythology.Cons:- Poor performance in prologue cutscenes, especially so when using standard proton.- Voice acting can be hit or miss which is a little jarring.

_childDocuments_.review: Nice story- and character-focused RPG. Because of this, the narrative and plot for this character are like a novel in which you determine key directions the novel will take. Note: this is unlike shallower, less-deep RPGs where you design a character, pretend it's you (unlike any novel, ever), and experience a narrative that is necessarily vague and all-things-to-all-dress-up-dollies. If you're looking for that, this isn't it.The combat is a card-based, debuff stacking and damage system that ties in well with the ~summonings you will collect. I haven't played a lot of card-based games like this, perhaps only Deep Sky Derelicts, and am a little wary of them. However, I enjoyed the combat in this game. The abilities of the ~summoned creatures reflect their natures and make for some interesting combat.The setting, both historically inspired and novel elements, are interesting and a refreshing change; both in time period and world region. There's a lot of voice acting--although the English acting quality varies--and the "rpg text" is relegated to exploration clues you discover, which can even be skipped over although you lose out on your purchase value because you didn't learn to read. Anyway, it seems like a reasonable balance for various player types.Graphics are quite nice for this class of game. As is the music and other audio.My playthrough took 28 hours and I'm a sort of casual completionist so no side quests, activities, I think all the collectible bits or so (not all the achievements, I don't go for those, just note which ones come up). So it could be several hours less if you don't care to complete little side stories, collect the PoVs, etc.However, that length together with the strong narrative around a centrai, focused main character and overall game quality means it's a decent buy IMO.

_childDocuments_.review: The Thaumaturge is the prime example of a cool concept failing in its execution. You live the game through the eyes of Wiktor, a thaumaturge - a magician able to tame otherwordly beings called Salutors, and blessed with the gift of psychometry - helped by Rasputin in order to get his powers back, then coming back to Poland to elucidate his father's demise.While the beginning is convincing, the game falls short quickly after.Here are the main reasons why :1 - The Snappin'turgePsychometry allows you to learn many informations by touching objects - memories, feelings and so on. In order to know wich objects can be interacted with, you right click your mouse : a snapping sound occurs and the items will be highlighted, as well as your path to the next objective.And honestly a good chunk of the game is spent snapping fingers and clicking on dozens of items in order to advance the story.You may think it could make for a great investigating tool - and you'd be quite mistaken. Because of the sacrosaint snapping, exploration is a moot point and unlike, say, a game like the Ace Attorneys, you don't have to present the right evidence or come up with a sound theory.Once you have clicked on all the required items for your current objective, Wiktor will automatically put all the threads together and get the "good" answer.There is zero thought process in this, it's just busywork and after a while, one can get easily tired of both the process and the items's descriptions. This alone could make someone quit : the main selling point of the game just gets boring after a while...And it's definetely NOT a detective RPG when you almost never have to deduce anything. 2- Story and dialogsThe premise for the game is great, its development is not. The store page talks about ambiguous choices but there aren't that many or not so impactful.Most of the time you are railroaded into the main quest and while Wiktor's father's death could hint at bigger schemes, once revealed, the mystery falls flat quite a bit, the story then rushing to the last act without much narrative meat, eager to offer you three main ending questlines. I, for one, didn't feel it was "my" story so much. As for the dialogs, quite often the description of what your character can say ends up different from what he actually says, akin to what happens in Dragon Age II.Plus sometimes when you want to nudge the conversation in some way, Wiktor gets back the other way. The most blatant example was when I didn't want to disclose the existence of his twin sister, then Wiktor awkwardly says " oh by the way, I have a twin sister, Ligia ". To be fair, dialogs can often be robust, but there are alos many instances of faux-pas to make the experience jarring at times. I regularly wondered if my dialog choices were really meaningful.Thaumaturges attract Salutors with flaws, Wiktor's is pride- I tried not to choose prideful options too often, fearing it could lead to dire consequences, but in fact, as I was not proud enough, it locked me out of many dialog options ! 3 - Let's get brawling ?The studio must have thought that they needed to vary its gameplay, thus the combat system. And oh God, The Thaumaturge loves its combats. You know it because the game ensnares you in a conflict every chance it gets, most of the time the dialog options are useless and you'll fight anyways.It seriously gets absurd over time, like getting assaulted in the street because you look like a bourgeois- not that it would be unrealistic, but it's jut not needed. Why so harsh ? Because the combat, like the finger snapping, gets old rather quickly. It's turn-based with status effects and different moves you acquire, which can be upgraded with switchable boni (damage boost, a chance to interrupt the enemy's turn, protection etc.)Your Salutors attache too with various techniques, and are required to disable enemy's "traits", like a 80% damage reduction.Winning combats, completing quests and touching items all grant experience, which can be used to upgrade each of the four lines of thaumaturge powers.The thing is you mainly fight humans, the combat system is not complex or deep, not a challenge either, so it becomes a routine. Quite a pity because one could easily imagine monsters from the folklore being the results of Salutors wrongdoings, giving more practical utility for a thaumaturge's powers and thus more quest possibilities.As it stands I'm still perplexed as to why the thaumaturges are not more sought after, they could make for ace investigators, spies or military assets, a topic barely touched upon by the game.One could find more gripes (like a solid number of quests being rather bland) and while I don't wholly regret playing this game, I wouldn't encourage you to play it either. The studio claims they adore RPG but it doesn't seem to be their forte...I'll never come back to it, that's for sure.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a review originally written for . The full article can be found . Feel free to take a look at the Opium Pulse Steam Curation page  as well.Taking place in 1905- pre World War I Warsaw, Poland, The Thaumaturge thrusts you into the role of Wiktor Szulski- a man battling his own inner demons, as well as the demons of others. In a beautiful marriage of history and fantasy, Fools Theory has brought a unique Isometric RPGs to the table, full of physical, emotional and mental conflict. While far from perfect, The Thaumaturge brings detective work, difficult moral choices, and gorgeous storytelling together, making for some ultimately creative and rewarding game play. Our main protagonist Wiktor Szulski is gifted with the powers of Thaumaturgy- granting him the use of otherworldly powers and abilities. These range from the use of Salutors (entities that give Wiktor his abilities, aide him in combat, and bind themselves to him through Flaws) and their powers, to influencing friends and foes alike to manipulate certain situations. Using his mysterious and often misunderstood powers, Wiktor strives to come to grips with his relationship with his father, Stanisław, who shares the gift of Thaumaturgy with his son- as well as his family history that is steeped in mystery. Part of that family history revolves around the ability to use Salutors, if the gift of Thaumaturgy has been passed along- as is the case with Wiktor. Salutors are paranormal being- some may even call them demons, who enter into a pact of sorts with a Thaumaturge. This gift, however, is not free- as you will soon come to find out. To bond with a Salutor, you must first offer a Flaw in return. Wiktors default Flaw, is PRIDE- and this allowed him to bond with Upyr 15 years prior to the star of the game. Through leveling your character, you will be able to increase the skills he, and others, provide. In combat, they are indispensable, allowing you to pinpoint enemy weakness, and strike with precision. Navigate Warsaw using your wit and deductive abilities- unraveling the events surrounding you, and your family. Unleash the powers of your Salutors as you uncover them- each boasting it’s own strengths in both combat and in the field. Engage in a unique combat system that prioritizes forethought and strategy, equipping gained abilities to attacks to make the most of your skills, while using the enemies weaknesses against them. Make decisions that shape your story, and impact the future of yourself, and those around you- and ultimately be the master of your own fate.The core driving force in this title is, unquestionably, its story. In a wild mix of historical fiction with a sprinkling of the supernatural and occult, you will find yourself coming face to face with characters of the past, in ways you may have never thought possible. This sincerely provides some of the most compelling and, at times, wildly amusing storytelling that is, undoubtedly, the greatest strength The Thaumaturge boasts. However, it can also be viewed as a potential weakness and deterrent for players not inclined t’words dialogue heavy and reading intensive world building, relying on numerous articles found scatted about Warsaw. In short, if heavy reading and a more flourished style of writing and dialogue is not quite to taste, this may be a pass for you. While the sheer amount of reading required to build up a full profile of the world you’re in can be daunting, it ultimately feels rewarding, giving you context and subtle clues to the world around you. The amount of historical figures thrown into the mix is delightful, giving you a glimpse into the struggles of pre World War I Poland, as well as struggles of existing day to day during that time.  That, however, may not be enough to keep players interested if they lack being open to a historical fiction.  While combat is interesting, and initially entertaining, it lack any real thrill or excitement. The semi “rock paper scissors” formula is useful, in conjunction with the skill effects you can equip- but ultimately it feels repetitive (regardless of what Salutors you may have acquired), further driving home the fact that this is NOT where The Thaumaturges bread and butter are. Overall, the combat is passable. It’s not unpleasant, but it leaves you wanting something more. Exploration, unfortunately, also faces the same thought of wishing there was more- as there are far more “invisible”” and visible walls than one can imagine. Don’t look to explore Warsaw TOO thoroughly, as you be met with cleverly placed ropes, barricades, and debris piles. The world was so wonderfully engaging that I did want to see more- if only I was allowed to. That aside, the maps are beautiful with vast attention to detail; the hustle and bustle of carriages along the cobblestone streets, as well as very early trollys occasionally pass by along with plenty of foot traffic. You will ALWAYS find something happening in Warsaw. Even where you may least expect it. Overall, The Thaumaturge boasts beautiful storytelling with a great since of wit and humor that will drive game play forward. While it has some weaknesses in it's combat and exploration, it more than makes up for it in substance- it's story being meticulously well crafted. While not all players will find a historical fiction game appealing, I'd at least give it a chance- as I found myself pleasantly surprised at the attention to detail and sincere desire for historical accuracy, while providing their own their own unique twist. It's been nothing short of a sheer joy to play, and I would highly recommend give it a shot, especially if you are a fan of Isometric RPGs, and lore heavy worlds. You won’t be disappointed.

_childDocuments_.review: Ah, where to begin? Story: The story takes place around the period of Russian Revolution in the Kingdom of Poland in alternate universe. In amidst of the worker strikes, spies, industrial revolution, there in lies demons/apparitions called salutors where only thaumaturges (people with sixth sense basically) can see and yield its powers. Premise: You assist Wiktor solving his father's mysterious death and decide Warsaw's fate by finding clues and connect the dots. Sometimes you'll be in a fight. Sometimes you decide whether you should be deciding with the socialist or with the government. Sometimes you will search for new outfits and sometimes you just stand at the pavement watching people interacts with the environment.Environment: Gritty, the colours suits the vibe the game is aiming for. Also the buildings are so charming to look at. Also everything looks crispy.Core mechanics: You will right-click until you find every clues. Is this really a detective game if you only needed to right-click the areas until you find every clues? Yes. Voice acting: It sounded stiff in some areas. Most of the voices are feel like in a big hall/echoes a lot. If you're easily bothered with how the voice actors act/say their lines, then maybe you'll have some trouble adjusting with it for the whole game.Leveling up/EXP farming: If you want to level up and max out Wiktor's dimensions, you basically have to do all the side quests; from collecting all the clothes, the sketches, photographs, and side quests. At one point you'll barely feel you're making a progress as the EXP yield in these side quests are so small. This will get tedious; I think this is the part where it feels grindy and filler-ish.Ending: You'll get one main ending and several mini endings/closure, depending on you choices, what quests you completed, the level of pride you have. I only got one ending and it shooketh me to my core lol All in all, is this game for everyone? I'd say if you have extra cash and you wanted to have a good/bad time living in alternate universe of Warsaw 1905, then you can buy this game and enjoy every morsel of details being put in the game and leave it at that.I'm going to keep playing the game for at least 20 more hours. Also, please Fool's Theory; let me pet the cats, buy the jam doughnuts, have a toggle between running and walking, and have a camera mode. Thank you.

_childDocuments_.review: The game is an enjoyable experience, but I imagine that some connection to Poland or Eastern Europe is necessary to truly immerse yourself and understand the dialogues and the plot. The majority of voice actors have a polish or eastern european accent, which makes it the more important to immerse yourself in the setting. The game is mostly dialogue, walking and reading, and it's not really a rpg in the traditional sense.Apart from some clunky animations (that make this game even more charming) the visuals are stunning and atmospheric. The designs of the salutors are all unique and creative, and the combination of a supernatural and historical setting is both refreshing and compelling. The game is well written with meaningful choices that affect the ending.The weakest aspect of this game is definitely the combat. It's slow, and not always necessary. I often found myself wondering if the people I defeat in combat are dead. I didn't want to role play as a murderer of innocent civilians, but the people I defeated in combat were laying face down in the mud each time I revisited the location.

_childDocuments_.review: This game was pretty good. I enjoyed the story and setting a lot.  It's fairly fast to beat, but based on the story choices, it may be worth a second play through making other choices. The choices in this game really do matter. I made some choices and still feel bad for some of them. That's the type of impact they may have.The voice acting is excellent.  Also, the combat is pretty entertaining. I'm not a big fan of turn based combat, but there was a decent amount of strategy in the fights.  Graphically, it's nice to look at. Most the game is played via a top down diablo-style view. But the conversations and such are more third person - and there are a lot of conversations.  The idea that you are doing detective work is interesting, but in reality you're just button mashing R2 until something turns red and looking at it. There's not any strategy in the detective part, but it does fill in lore and story.I played the game in VR using UEVR. It ran well and was a lot of fun in VR.I'd recommend this as a buy if you enjoy RPG games and good story.  It took my 23 hours to beat on normal difficulty and I did as many side quests as I could find.
_childDocuments_.name: The Thaumaturge

_childDocuments_.review: An alternate history fantasy RPG.  The graphics and character designs do a great job bringing the game's historical setting to life. Design of salutors, the only supernatural element in the game, is appropriately mythical and otherwordly. Voice acting is great and the music fits the setting well.  The gameplay is a mix of dialogues, simple investigation and turn-based combat. The RPG system plays into all of these mechanics, as do captured salutors. There is a plenty of interesting side-quests, some with impact on the endings of the game. Generally the whole gameplay is well polished and fun.  The story mixes bits of fantasy into real historical setting of russian part of partitioned Polad few years before World War One. There is a lot of political, social and ethnic tensions and the quests are often touching on some of these. A lot of quest involve investigation and a sort of social engineering. There are multiple endings and they are further affected by resolution of some side-quests. Sadly I had not triggered the last part of one of these, so I missed a more positive resolution of this side story (underground university).  Overall a very interesting and engaging RPG.
_childDocuments_.name: The Thaumaturge

_childDocuments_.review: Exceptionally fun game, though more Salutor's and more fighting opportunities would be great. The only nitpick I have is that almost every Salutor is slow to very slow towards the endgame, which is horrid considering most enemies attack in one turn. Add on to the fact that most encounters have an enemy of one shield, meaning you can't even use your preferred Salutor's straight away, and combat can get a bit, boring. That being said I wish there was an arena or option to fight random people, because there is NOT enough combat for how fun it can be. This is basically depressing persona if the persona's were all badas as hell. Great game, worth the money. Another perfect example of how a double A (AA) game does the best of both worlds. The core vision is here, but the details weren't skimped on either. Also this game reminded me so much of Vampyr in style and aesthetic, but nope, happy accident, no relation.

_childDocuments_.review: This game has one of the better stories I have played in years, and that is the reason I'm recommending this game.  There is a fair bit of reactivity to your choices in the game and you have the option to, "feed your flaw," which opens up new dialog choices and closes off others.  Unfortunately, the game doesn't let you feed the additional flaws you pick up during the game, but your initial flaw and branching dialog does encourage subsequent playthroughs to see how events might play out if you picked a different path. The game is based in a magic infused version of a historic location.  I can't speak to historical accuracy,  I don't really know too much about Poland during the reign of Tsar Nicholas the second, and a fair amount of my knowledge about Rasputin comes from a Boney M song (although I do recall Rasputin being described as a rather large fellow and the Rasputin in this game was slight).  However, I did feel transported to a different place and time.  Unfortunately, the gameplay is a little simple.  I played on the highest difficulty level and only the Morana fight forced me to reload.  There's a pretty nice battle system in the game, but it's not really utilised in a dynamic way.  The problem might be that the game gives you too many ways to fight (breaking an opponents focus to activate finishers, dealing damage or employing DoTs and status effects), while the enemies tend to be quite simple.  It's kind of playing chess with all the pieces against an opponent who is only using pawns.  There are some synergies to employ like using Lelek's abilities with Bukovac's, but, other than the fight I mentioned, picking one approach to battle and occasionally healing is all that's required for success.  It took me 26 hours to beat the game, and I wasted a few of them completing the Tailor's sidequest, so, for an RPG, it isn't very long.  Still, I enjoyed my time in the game.
_childDocuments_.name: The Thaumaturge

_childDocuments_.review: tl;dr: Solid 9/10, most of my complaints are minor.Pros: + Fascinating setting+ Excellent writing in most places+ Solid soundtrack+ Graphics are (mostly) good+ Combat is simple, but satisfying+ Art direction on the Salutors is super coolCons:- Awful voice acting most of the time, only characters with decent VAs are the main cast.- Lots of reused assets and contrived ways to reuse previous areas. It is a AA game after all, but it is one of the primary ways the budget of the game rears its ugly head in the end product.- Detective segments are for flavor more than anything else. Whether it's a contrivance or a solid mechanical inclusion depends on your personal opinion. - Dialogue writing specifically sucks. The dialogue writing is worse than the writing you'll find in all of the pieces of writing and item descriptions you'll find. Don't know why. Really interesting setting, you can tell the devs have a certain affection for Poland and an interest in the time period. It tackles some social issues of the time, but often in ways that you may not notice unless you're already familiar with the history of the setting. If you are familiar, though, it will be pretty hamfisted. The flavor text is always very good. The dark and seedy tone of the game resonates throughout. Only a few cons I can think of, and none of them are serious. If you're not interested in the history of the geographic area and/or time period you may not like this game as much as I do, but even if you're disinterested in the historical aspect of the setting, I think there's plenty to enjoy. My biggest complaint so far is the dialogue writing, but it's relatively minor.

_childDocuments_.review: I've enjoyed this game more than I'd anticipated, it was quite a surprise from a title that had so little publicity or word of mouth after it.The setting of the The Thaumaturge is one of its best qualities, unique in the sea of fantasy and sci-fi themed CRPGs; I don't think I'll find another game set in early 20th century Poland any time soon.At its core it's a story about political intrigue and family issues, shrouded in occultism and slavic folklore. It's a more down to earth and personal affair compared to the world-ending scenarios that mire the genre.The graphics are better than most top-down RPGs, and there was a good amout of care put into translating this version of Poland faithfully.It plays like your standard turn-based JRPGs, think a streamlined and westernised version of SMT, and while the system isn't complex several fights kept me on my toes before I eventually mastered the quirks of its rules. Thankfully, no random encounters this time.The game, surprisingly enough, is fully voice-acted. I didn't think it would be at first, even so I still can't quite grasp if Wiktor is meant to sound tired or simply detached from his surroundings most of the time.The rest of the cast is mostly adequate, I especially liked the bombastic theatrics of his childhood friend; a stark contrast to the mostly dour and belligerent common folk and police of Warsaw.Recommended if you're looking for an RPG that is willing to explore a different setting and cast than your usual RPGs do, I will also add that it feels replayable and reactive to your choices, at least on a surface level.I hope for more from this universe now, even outside of a direct sequel.
_childDocuments_.name: The Thaumaturge

_childDocuments_.review: An absolute joy to play, the gameplay is delightful, I love running around and solving mysteries. I really like the story as well, it's intriguing and sucked me right in. My favourite part is absolutely the setting. It genuinely feels like I'm transported to early 20th century Warsaw every time I boot up this game, showing its beauty as well as its grimness and grittiness. The realities of the time period are excellently presented. I've wanted a game to dive into the city of Warsaw for ages, and The Thaumaturge delivers that in style.The only negative thing I could say about the game is the lack of a Polish voice-over option, but according to the developers' answers to similar questions, it may be an option in the future, so I will gladly look forward to that possibility .

_childDocuments_.review: This easily becomes one of my GOTY contenders. Very atmospherically set in the turmoil of Russian and Polish history, in a rather sinister re-model of Warsaw city in 1905, The Thaumaturge scratches many itches for me. I like the tingling remembrance of reading Kafka or E.A. Poe's short stories, or even Proust and E.T.A Hoffmann of that era, when diving into this game’s version of central European age of industrial revolution. What the Thaumaturge maybe lacks in character models, animation and maybe some AAA deluxe treatment, it generously makes up with its superb overall art Style, its interiors and overall atmosphere. I really enjoyed the writing, the story and side missions and the great characters. There is some stellar monster design to be found here and a really deep and enjoyable mythological horror rpg experience.I also want to recommend the playful and surreal Soundtrack from Agnieszka Wlazły and Sebastian Syczyński. It's marvellous.

_childDocuments_.review: This year started off like this - games I had high hopes for disappointed me, while those I approached with caution turned out to be pleasant surprises. From the latter category emerged "The Thaumaturge," created by just five people.To explain what the game is about... um...Imagine Poland in 1905. Pressured by the Russian Empire, torn apart by socialist uprisings, and plagued by thriving criminal gangs. Poverty, misery, violence, corruption.Now, add a dash of magic in the form of thaumaturges - people with the ability to read the thoughts and emotions of others, and to control spiritual beings called "salutors," whose powers they can influence others with through tricks, quite reminiscent of Jedi. And of course, these thaumaturges don't live in peace with each other. Oh, and there's also a proto-Nazi organization that wants to exterminate them.So in this world, you seek your place under the sun - Victor (with a double W) Zshulski, heir to a financial empire, a man with a dark past and an unclear future, and yes - a thaumaturge from a family with centuries-old traditions in magic.Your job (aside from, well, surviving) is... um... complicated.Overall, the fate of Warsaw, all of Poland, and perhaps the entire world depend on you, but while you deal with global problems, you still have time for smaller ones. Like catching a serial killer, stopping a sadistic usurer, saving the lover of the Russian czar fleeing from authorities, and finding out where exactly they sell that notorious American drink, Coca-Cola.Seriously though, the game is cool. The mix of criminal investigations, "choices matter" storytelling, and (don't laugh) Pokémon is entertaining. For at least 30 hours, which is how long it took me to reach one of the few possible endings.It's not perfect.The graphics are slightly rough, some of the voice actors sound like they've had 1-2 extra shots of vodka before recording, and besides, even on the highest difficulty, the battles are too easy.But it's worth it. Definitely a chance to play it again, as well as to buy the (very likely) sequel.Rating: 8/10

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR; Good game, not perfect, doesn't need to be. I am having a great time, but I would like to see a little bit more done with it.While only about 12 hours in, and not sure how far into the main story I am, I do want to say that I think this game is great. Making a new IP is difficult, especially in our current age of sequelitis and reboots out the ass, and making something like this is no small feat. Games are hard, who knew?Fool's Theory have done a really solid job making this city feel lived in. It's no Night City, but maybe that's for the best. All the little Points of Interest, the sketches and fashion magazines and incidental moments (like being ogled by women on the street), framed against this deeply intriguing story that blends history with fantasy, makes The Thaumaturge's depiction of Warsaw feel very much alive.The detective mechanics, while simple and not exactly rewarding for the exceptional snoop (all the clues and conclusions being drawn for you), do provide meaningful interaction and the simple fact the game TELLS YOU when you have locked yourself out of certain choices makes it narratively satisfying, even if it's a little repetitive in execution. On that point, one thing I would've loved to see is more use of the Visions Upyr bestows upon you, perhaps featuring the other wild Salutors; giving us greater immersive context into the people we are investigating. Someone like Abaurycy or Vesna would have been perfectly used for this.I think Rasputin's presence in the game, while entertaining and welcome, is a little shoehorned in. If he was a persistent accompaniment to Wiktor, instead of another location on the map of Warsaw, with more input on the story, i think I would buy his presence in the game much more. But again, I'm only 12 hours in and I've been distractedly running around looking for fashion magazines and laughing that the game has no clean-shaven options at the barber.As far as combat, it's perfectly serviceable. I do think, however, that the thaumaturgy points are awarded MUCH too freely; even reading repeated advertisements or articles that do not provide anything for quest objectives give experience; I have maxed out my Heart and Deed trees (up until the second Salutor) and I only just acquired the third Salutor in the entire game. Given that there appears to only be a total of 8 Salutors, and I still feel rather early in the story, I find myself rather worried I will max out my skill tree and have nothing to try out next time I play this game. Plus, playing on the hardest difficulty I still find myself steamrolling most enemies simply through abusing Suffering and interruptions; enemies simply don't deal enough damage to be threatening enough, and certain combinations of attacks are simply far too powerful. I would like a future update that expands combat a little more, especially since the majority of the actual fight seems-- unwieldy. Mostly fisticuffs with the occasional revolver shot against people with knives, guns, and even full-ass swords.Most of the music also feels relatively unremarkable as well; not that it doesn't serve it's purpose, it's very immersive, but even the main menu theme doesn't have anything that makes me want to whistle or hum with it. It's rather tragic because I think a game like this could really shine with a strong soundtrack. You have things like the Hurdy-Gurdy, the Balalaika, the fiddle, all featured in the game, I think using instruments like that more prominently for the music would do wonders.
_childDocuments_.name: The Thaumaturge

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR A capitvating take on creature-capture games in a wonderful setting.Since I'm both Polish and a Warsaw enthusiast this game sprang onto my wishlist immediately after playing the demo last fall. Got it a couple of days after release to see how the launch went and hopped in. The setting is wonderful. 1905* Warsaw in all it's glory. Despite liberties and abstractions made for gameplay every single district is recognizable. There's also some tasty lore and easter eggs for those in-the-know which I appreciated greatly. The setting is wonderful and dips heavily into beasts from folklore not unlike the Witcher. The only thing I can complain about is that Warsaw wouldn't get electric trams until 1908 in the real world but since everyone loves trams I'll let it slide. The setting literally made me buy this game and I got my money's worth.Gameplay is solid though nothing to write home about. The main char uses his powers to unveil secrets and solve mysteries thugh the player is being led by hand too much. Wiktor always draws conclusions himself and only a couple of quests allow you to interpret things your way.I played on normal and combat has this weird curve where I enjoyed in the beginning and end but had a lull in the midgame where you're not that powerful nor do you have many options among your salutors to torment your enemies and it boggles down to doing the exact same sequence in every encounter. Encounters are also, unfortunately, very repeatable outside of boss fights.Main storyline is interesting but a lot of the side-content fell flat. Two "freeroam" chapters include about 2-3 real sidequests of varying but never exceptional quality and the most interesting part are the salutor captures.I finished the game at close to 30h of usually good fun. Probably did too much collectibles unitl I realized getting sketches boils down to a boring right-click spam for clues and then going to a locations where the screen turns black and you see a sketch. This I felt was unnecessary and leaned heavily on my enjoyment of the game until the end of chapter 2. All in all a solid 8/10 for me. Would recommend even without a sale as the game is fairly priced for what you get out of it.
_childDocuments_.name: The Thaumaturge

_childDocuments_.review: This is clearly a story-telling game with a rather slow pace. If you are into these, you can experience an interesting, mildly scary story in a "historicized" setting. You even may learn a thing or two about the time, i.e. early 20th century, and Poland.Dialogues are really good and the music perfectly supports all the scenes. The turn-based fights are mostly easy, once you get the hang of it. Overall, a cool concept.As a welcome distraction from other, more flashy (action) games, I very much enjoyed playing it.
_childDocuments_.name: The Thaumaturge

_childDocuments_.review: Interesting game-design, story set in Warsaw 1905. Narrative, plot, and setting are so well done that it actually made me interested in the political and cultural history of this period. Somewhat buggy, for me the sound of speech disappeared a few times. Had to restart the game to get it back. Eventually, it worked just fine. I definitely recommend following a guide for collectibles achievement wise, because two play-throughs are more than enough. Otherwise, you’ll get pretty tired of endlessly clicking on objects and all the reoccurring fights (learned this the hard way). Nevertheless, I did appreciate the originality of the game-design. Recommended to buy and play but as always it’s not for everyone; some patience is needed.
_childDocuments_.name: The Thaumaturge

_childDocuments_.review: I wish I could give this game a positive review : I love the setting and the core idea, but the pacing is a disaster. It's definitily one of the most boring experience I ever had in a RPG.The gameplay loop is awful : you run around, spamming the button to snap your fingers, reading an absurdingly high amount of random boring documents to get XP. Then, to resolve quests and investigations, you run around snaping your fingers looking for clues, then the investigation is automatically solved and that's it.Here is another shining example of a game that thinks that gathering clues is the fun part of an investigation. It's not. At all. Deduction is.Story may be interesting but it is drowned under thousands and thousands of useless lore documents. After 1 hour in the game, all the excitement is gone when you find something. After 2 hours, all the excitement is gone. Period.I didn't like the combat as well, it's pretty dull for turn based combat... The add-ons management is also really annoying... So many useless work for so little...
_childDocuments_.name: The Thaumaturge

_childDocuments_.review: Game has it's flaws. It crashes, has graphical artifacts and issues. May seem confined at times. But it is incredible atmospheric and unique. You are drowned in early XX century Poland, at the edge of incredible political and historical changes (Prior to WW I and partitioned between Russia, Austo-Hungarian empire and Germany). Beautiful work was done to depict the time, social complexity, many cultures and nationalities in one spot fighting for their influence, and Warsaw in its unique style specific for that time period. You can believe this was "The Paris of the eastern Europe". Nicely rooted in Slavic mythology and spirituality which makes it unique gem among other games of this kind. To be fair it is a detective story with magical arch and mechanic comparable to games like Disco Elysium in game play mechanics. I pity that there is no Polish audio in the game as this would add to the game style and feel especially that dialog written in Polish use specific for 1900's Warsaw street slang called 'gwara'. Story is very nice and engaging. Based on family secrets in historical perspective. For interested parties (Works well on SteamDeck - could be optimized better. Around solid 30 FPS) + Incredible feel of the period+ Storytelling that is complex and not dumbed down.+ Good mechanic+ Rooted in Slavic mythos+ Great choice of historic period which is not often depicted+ Price to content ratio+ Good flow with focus on story. Not too difficult making it easy to immerse yourself.+ No woke BS overflowing even though respectful for all kinds of views and perspectives. - Graphical glitches- Crashes (3 in 6 hours of gameplay, hope to be solved after patches)- Pity you have fixed camera angle and can't turn it around (it is 3D space after all)- Graphic is nice but not stunning. - May be too historically complex for people used to simple stories and good-bad narratives.Not a masterpiece, but a nice little gem of a game.
_childDocuments_.name: The Thaumaturge

_childDocuments_.review: A very solid 7/10. Really loved the unique setting, both in the historical sense with pre-war Poland with all of its players and the magic system. I also loved the monster designs and the idea of the protag being a demonhunting detective. The game is very pretty even tho the animations can be a bit janky.I was a bit stressed by the timegating the quests, its very frustrating to see I just missed a quest (even tho the game says when a quest is about to run out). The side quests, esp the Warsaw stories were a bit eh, I really wished there were more of real side quests like the "Real Fireworks" one.Plus the detective stuff is very hand-holdy, pls let me figure it out by myself maybe with the help of the salutors, but that would be a very cool core for the next iteration of this game!I would really love to see a sequel were the devs can improve on the game and push the 7 to a 9:)

They basically end with you going to the end of the quest and looking at a sketch......Art work is good though so if you can plow through the quests and make it to the end great.
