_childDocuments_.review: Four years after , Capcom followed up with , a compilation of fighting games that aren’t in the  franchise. Well, except for …and they also threw in  and , both of which are -dominant crossover titles. Huh, did Capcom include them to get people pay attention to this somewhat insubstantial compilation?This “fighting collection” doesn’t even have classic fighting games from the  franchise, or any  fighting games! I wouldn’t be surprised if Capcom’s current licensing agreement with Marvel is limiting their ability to release these old titles; but, I also wouldn’t be shocked to see Capcom releasing a  at some point.This compilation might as well be called  because that’s what it feels like. It is made up of games that are fun and creative, but ended up being not very popular and/or lucrative like  or early  titles. These are games that actually could have been developed into their own franchises if they were branded and marketed better globally.The biggest non- draw of this collection are the  games. This franchise is arguably more popular in Japan (where it’s known as ) than in other parts of the world. This is likely in part due to the comparatively more consistent titling for the Japanese releases. If you thought  games’ naming conventions are convoluted, consider the following:If you weren’t already a  fan, it’d be hard to make sense of this list of English titles for . As someone whose exposure to  were from Capcom’s crossover titles, I thought there were only 3  games at first. It’s only from playing through this collection that I learned more about the messiness of the  series. is not a true sequel to , but more like  to . This makes  (i.e.,  on PlayStation) the true sequel. Yet,  is actually an update of , but with  roster;  – also an update of , but not a sequel – has the  roster, but replaces 3 series mainstays with 3 characters from . Confusing, right?I’m annoyed that these 5  titles amount to maybe 2.5, at most 3, games’ worth of material. The series never got the chance to have its gameplay refined to the degree that  had. Now,  – being creatively weird, stunning and noticeably different – merely stands in the shadow of . What this series could have been if it had better global branding and thus better exposure!Other games in this collection also have major titling differences that affected their recognition globally. I used to play  on my cousins’ Sega Saturn, and that’s what I’ve been calling it all these years. Yet, none of my friends had heard of it. It turns out  is the name of the Asian release, and the game is called  everywhere else. At least  is similarly titled  in Asia, but there has never been a  or non- variation. Plus, this game is actually not a fighting game, but a gem stacking/matching puzzle game. What is it doing in a fighting game collection?Then there is , known as  in Japan. Mildly boring title aside,  is unique in that it’s a story-focused hybrid of fighting game and action RPG. Regardless of which character you choose, you fight the same enemies in single-round matches. You level up as you play, unlocking new special moves. Your actions and decisions can also open up paths to different endings, making the game quite replayable should you wish to explore all narrative possibilities. It is a very visually appealing game, but can be a brief experience if you’re not into leveling up characters. A few tweaks to its gameplay and title could have made  a more recognizable brand, though not necessarily in the 1v1 fighting game field.Finally, there’s . Although simply titled  in Japan, it’s actually a spin-off of  (a.k.a. ), which is a beat ’em up that is included in . This, too, is a story-focused fighting game. Although it features 5 playable characters with loosely intertwining stories, it’s your selection of Variant Armor that determines your movesets. Sadly, many of the 12 V.A.s aren’t very memorable. On the other hand, the human characters look more unique. Making the V.A.s have more visual personality and be more instantly recognizable (like in ) could have meant different fortunes for the // brand.I actually bought  for  and -…sorry, “”. What surprised me was how much I ended up enjoying , , and  as well. I thought  could have been a great chance for Capcom to re-energize these brands, but this collection is rather insubstantial – not just in games, but also in archival materials – that it shows Capcom doesn’t really care about them anymore.’s museum of concept, production and commissioned artwork, and music library are nice, but merely adequate. Capcom didn’t even bother including information about the games’ histories, inspirations for their designs, or any value-added materials that would excite fans and generate more interest among players new to these games. Even the inelegantly packaged  talked about the franchise’s history and featured an interview with the franchise producer!It’s clear that Capcom didn’t see  as being important enough to invest more resources into. So while I did enjoy the featured games, it’s not an easy recommendation from me. If you are a fan of, or are curious about, any of the games in this collection, by all means . If not, then you may want to skip this one because the merely adequate archive of artwork and music tracks add little value to this compilation.

_childDocuments_.review: Throughout the years, Capcom's reputation has fluctuated with regards to fighting games, releasing some of the most popular series, and at times, botching the Hell out of them. When I saw Capcom Fighting Collection (CFC), I wanted it for the simple fact it includes a few popular fighters I don't have, in a convenient place. I don't really want to dig out a handful of consoles just to occasionally play a couple of games, if I could have them all on my PC instead.A decent amount of my interest stemmed from getting a solid copy of the Darkstalkers series, but I don't think it was necessary to put in five iterations. Additionally, what I'd consider to be a better version of the last release, is the PS1 Darkstalkers 3, since it included every character from the available roster. Neither Vampire Hunter 2, nor Vampire Savior 2 manages that, making this list feel both bloated, and lacking, in Darkstalkers content. Two games I haven't played before, but I've been curious about for a few years, were the chibi-style Street Fighter II games. Those would be Super Puzzle Fighter II Turbo and Super Gem Fighter Mini Mix. The first game is a gem style puzzler, outright defying that this compilation was for fighters only. It has no fighting mechanics or content, except for the roster of characters being taken from Capcom fighting games. Despite not fitting, I'm glad to have it, since it offers a different style of gameplay. Switching to the second title, it has fairly unique features for a fighting game. Each character has three special moves, and three colors of gems will spray out as you whale on the enemy. These strengthen your special moves, and is something I've rarely encountered. Red Earth is a game I've occasionally seen footage of, but because it was an arcade exclusive, I never bothered to get that invested in it. Why torture myself? Having the chance to play it was at least part of the reason for my interest. Frankly, I knew nothing about Cyberbots before seeing it in the list, so its inclusion didn't make much impact for me. I do find it odd that with 6 characters and 12 robots to choose from, none of them are pre-set choices. You're free to mix and match however you want. I think most players will have a personal preference on their optimal controller for titles like this, but I've no idea how they'd compensate for the directional inputs with a keyboard. Regardless, whether you'd prefer an arcade joystick, or a responsive d-pad, I wouldn't recommend picking this compilation up without having a capable controller first. It'd make performing all the special moves too difficult and frustrating otherwise. Theoretically, many of those moves can be input with an easier alternative, but they don't cover every move out of all the characters arsenal, so relying on this would create some gaps.Even if I were to summarize the basic premise for each game, it wouldn't amount to all that much, as most fighters don't have a lot of plot to them. For the most part, the fighters are coming together for the sake of winning a tournament, whether their own motivation is focused on glory, or the prize money. At most, you watch a short cutscene play out after you beat the game with them. It's sufficient, but anymore, I want fighting games to incorporate more story into the action. Cyberbots was an interesting exception, as you'd have at least some reason for each battle you got into.Since these are games from an older era, there is a degree of aging with the looks, but I don't think they've soured through the years. Because Capcom was a large game studio, they had the budget to produce higher-end visuals for the hardware at the time. How you judge the look of these games will depend on personal taste, and whether you have any nostalgic influence or not, yet I think only graphics fanatics would snub these titles' visuals. Having grown up with some of these games, there's a familiarity to them that I enjoy, and due to competent design, many of the characters still look pretty good, if not a bit pixelated. Another area of game design where Capcom has a good reputation is with catchy tunes. I don't think any of the songs quite reach the heights of their library, such as some Mega Man bangers, yet there's still quality jams amongst all these games. A few that stand out for me come from the Darkstalkers series, such as Jon Talbain's, or Felicia's themes. Despite its age, Street Fighter II has catchy songs like Balrog's stage. For those who know their memes, you'd recognize Guile's tune. The sound effects from super and special moves are impactful, giving the action you witness more oomph. 🌟 Due to Capcom's popularity, several of the characters from this collection are iconic. It's nice to go back to the early days when they first became huge, and experience the gameplay again.🌟 The potential playtime across all these games is pretty significant, as there's so many characters you can play as.🌟 Each game offers online play. Unfortunately, there's not many people online at any given time. ❌ CFC doesn't have features many older game compilations like these include. For example, you can't fast forward or rewind the action at will. You also can only have a single save active for the entire game, unable to have one per title. That's dumb.❌ The AI can be utterly busted and brutal, unless you reduce the difficulty. Street Fighter II is notorious for this. Of course, you can easy mode every title though, so it's entirely up to you how badly you want the AI to wreck you.❌ These games don't have a title screen when you select them, making for an odd way to bring up their options. You basically do it in advance before choosing what game to play.🔍 If you're trying to go for particular achievements, the quick save feature is useful. It'd be the most efficient way to get all of the 20 continue endings for Red Earth.🔍 Unless you plan on mastering these specific fighting games, abuse the easy special and super moves. Make the AI pay for all the pain it's caused.There were obviously some downsides to this compilation, some of which I was aware of before buying it in the first place. I don't think 50% of a mixed bag should come from the same franchise, as they start acting like peanuts in a bowl of mixed nuts. Regardless, I bought CFC for a reason, and I can't say I'm unhappy to have these fighting titles available on my PC. It was enjoyable, playing through the entire roster of a title, and seeing which characters I favored over the rest. This game compilation is one I'd recommend, but primarily for people who are already fans of some of the titles, and don't have easily accessible set-ups for them.

_childDocuments_.review: Where to even begin with this? There's a lot to unpack with this Capcom Collection, not only because it is a Collection of some of Capcom's Greatest Classic Fighting Games but also because of how much of an impact many of these Titles included were a part of the Pillars of The Arcade Era of Gaming with them FINALLY being Released Officially on Modern Gaming Platforms and with Online Features included.To start The Darkstalkers Series really ramped up what to expect from a Capcom 2D Fighter after many iterations of Street Fighter II came before it in both it's Gameplay, Speed, and how to handle Super Moves!Looking for what many consider The Best Version of Street Fighter II? Then look no further than Hyper Street Fighter II which let's you play as EVERY Playable Iteration of a Street Fighter II Character and have them fight each other as well!If you're looking for some Goofy but still challenging fun this Collection also has Super Puzzle Fighter & Super Gem Fighter added to the Mix! Hilarious Fighting Action and Competitive Puzzle Pummeling!We also got some Anime Mecha Combat with the Arcade hit Cyberbots included which has the first appearance of Jin Saotome which many would recognize from Marvel VS. Capcom!And Last but Least we even have the first home release of Red Earth! One of the few RARE Titles Capcom made for the CPS3 outside of the Street Fighter III Games!There's PLENTY of Capcom History to uncover with this Collection, a Variety of Different Gameplay, not to mention the Art Gallery & other Behind The Scenes Features like being able to listen to a ton of the Music for each Game too which gives you a sense of the Old-School Arcade Era as well.Would HIGHLY RECOMMEND This Game Collection for not only Fighting Game enthusiasts but those who genuinely like Classic Retro Titles! 👍
_childDocuments_.name: Capcom Fighting Collection

_childDocuments_.review: Conditional Reccomendation, only really buy this if you are interested in playing the games offered here, that is some quirky, High quality (By 90's Arcade standards) fighting games.DO NOT BUY FOR THESE REASONS1) Begging Capcom to make a new Darkstalkers (Yes I want this to happen too, With Anita as the Protag, but Capcom already said this isnt a "Capcom test" game, that is for those unfamiliar a game Capcom fishes out to tease/test the waters for a new game but we get baited in the end. They were upfront about it).2) Online Play: Rollback is good but there's nobody online on steam, Blame Fightcade drawing away the existing niche crowd.3) Expecting polished modern Fighters that explain everything and have UX's with Consoles/PC's in mind:Remember these games were designed to munch quarters and to be played multiple times until mastered, and are thus more frustrating when you play them casually in their single player forms, its going to be an uphill battle by design. If you play these with other players roughly around your skill level (say your friends), that's no longer an issue. You might also need to google some mechanics since the cabinent doesnt exist and doesnt tell you your main mechanics anymore.That said I think the games however all generally feel good despite this. (Disclaimer: Discussing from a casual perspective, not nessecarily a high-level one)-I fell in love with Darkstalker's Characters and game feel (All my homies main Jon Taibain! The Goku-lookin Kung-Fu Werewolf!), It honestly feels like a less convoluted and more to the point Guilty Gear with a Tex Avery/Universal Pictures Monsters Inspiration instead of Metal/Anime (In fact I'm fairly certain Daisuke stole 80% of his ideas from this and other 90's Capcom games after playing these, esepcially considering a lot of these came out BEFORE the first GG).I did pick up ressurection about a month before the collection was announced on the 360, so I played a bit of this already and didnt spend a whole lot of time here, However I'm happy its finally on Steam and modern consoles and I'm happy to pick it up for a more Resilient library.-Red Earth, despite its Password system making more sense in the context of the arcade does some neat things with its RPG mechanics and boss monster designs-Gem Fighter's Level Up system is awesome, balancing greed and opportunity with the gem and item systems, nevermind the adorable stage details and animations. It also combines a lot of the best mechanics of the previous series (DS's Air combat and Love of Meter, Red Earth items). I also think the costume changes are neat as it telegraphs when you can punish moves more clearly.-Puzzle fighter is a more sane Puyo puyo with Gem Fighter sprites-Cyberbots has a neat amount of customization (Bots which all have different properties, characters that affect the story but are otherwise not tied to the bots), as well as some pretty satisfying abilities and damage statesI didnt have any interest in street fighter so no comments thereI'm Happy with this purchase, Mind the 90's arcade jank and you'll have a good time!

_childDocuments_.review: On one hand, these are straight up arcade roms. On the other, that's not necessarily a bad thing! It's great to finally have an official release for Vampire Savior on Steam, and Warzard making its home console debut for the first time is honestly something I never thought I would see, and is probably worth the price of admission alone.Super Puzzle Fighter is also a really fun time and while it's not a fighting game, it's definitely fun to throw down with people on their ability to combo gems.Now there are concerns about the censorship of this release, but they are as follows:- The Rising Sun in E. Honda's bath house in SFII (it's been a thing for ages now, so it's weird for it to be brought up now)- One of the secret endings in one of the Vampire games (it's a bummer, but I imagine it would probably get an M rating for the nudity nowadays, so if I have to choose between less people playing this game and having access to a secret ending in arcade mode, I think I'll pick the former).All-in-all, while it's kind of a weird hodgepodge of titles, I still highly recommend it just for being able to play Vampire Savior and PC and finally being able to play Warzard.

_childDocuments_.review: Capcom Fighting Collection is out and more importantly, the entire Darkstalkers arcade collection is included and available in the West for the first time. That series specifically is one I have always wanted to try, but the others included here are not bad either.It is a little bit misleading for the Collection to say “ten games” because technically Darkstalkers 3 is split into three separate games here: Vampire Savior, Vampire Hunter 2, and Vampire Savior 2. Vampire Savior is the main game and Hunter 2 and Savior 2 are updated versions of it that split the character roster Pokémon-style and introduced some gameplay changes that remain controversial within the Darkstalkers community.Regardless, the other three Darkstalkers games are solid and Vampire Savior was easily my favorite of the bunch. Very fast gameplay, fluid animations and movement, unique characters and movesets - It just feels good to play and I can see why it is considered one of the greatest in the genre. Considering that this was the main reason I wanted the collection, it’s already proven itself worthwhile there, but there’s more than just that.This is the only game in the pack that does not play like a traditional fighter. Rather, it plays like Puyo Puyo or Tetris, where you drop blocks onto your side of the screen in an effort to match them up by color and then send waves of garbage blocks to your opponent’s side. Bigger chain combos lead to bigger attacks and it’s honestly a lot more fun than I thought it would be. It’s never not satisfying to get a massive dump of garbage blocks on your screen and then ignite this mega combo to send it right back at your opponent.This one uses the same character assets from Puzzle Fighter II and has some dumbed down gameplay to match the chibi designs. It’s got this cool mechanic where you can upgrade your moves by picking up gems mid-match, but it’s not as fun to play as others in the pack and was a bit too casual for my tastes. It’s fun for a little bit - it just doesn’t have the depth to really carry it beyond that, ending up as my least favorite game in the collection.This one basically takes all of the previous Street Fighter II releases and cobbles them together into one, allowing you to pick not only characters from any of those releases, but their specific variation based on that release. You can end up with something like base Ryu from the original Street Fighter II against Turbo E. Honda from Street Fighter II: Hyper Fighting. I’ve never really been into the arcade Street Fighter games, but even I can appreciate the sheer magnitude of options here.Cyberbots is a 2D fighter like the rest, but played with very large and clunky mechs - which sounds awful, but was actually some of the most fun I had with the collection. Something about swinging around these giant limbs, shooting off rockets and grenades, and tearing off your opponent’s limbs to limit their attacks is just so satisfying and while the game may not be as “competitive” as the rest, it is definitely fun.Red Earth is more of a singleplayer-focused boss rush game with some light RPG elements than a traditional fighter. You run through a gauntlet of bosses, leveling up your character with new skills, and there’s even a password feature so you can bring your leveled-up character into the next session and so on. It’s definitely not the greatest for a versus experience - there are only four characters after all - but it’s a cool twist on the genre norm regardless.All of these are ported faithfully to PC with a few bonus quality of life features, such as different graphic filters, screen sizes, and some insanely advanced control customization. You can literally bind individual moves to certain buttons and any number of button combinations.There’s also practice mode, a museum mode where you can view artwork, and online mode too. While the collection does have rollback netcode, the online mode does not have any crossplay, so I honestly do not expect it to maintain that big a playerbase. It’s a shame, because if you go into this collection without someone to play it with, there really isn’t that much to do outside of just back-to-back arcade modes, so that is definitely something to keep in mind before picking it up.Capcom Fighting Collection is a solid collection of games and a great way for new players to get into some classics - such as me and Darkstalkers. There are a couple iffy games here, but the rest more than make up for it and are a lot of fun to mess around with in multiplayer. If you’re looking for singleplayer stuff, it probably isn’t worth it, but if you have friends to play it with then it is easily worth a look.Follow my  for more reviews + videos!

And surprisingly I've put a lot of time into Red Earth. I've been saving my codes for each character and going back in many times to unlock new abilities. _childDocuments_.review: Capcom Fighting Collection, unlike the Street Fighter Collection, doesn't suffer from a feeling of input lag. Every game in the collection has a training mode. I've found this to be an invaluable addition, as Cyberbots and Red Earth in particular felt very odd to me until I tinkered with both in Training. Every game in the collection can be played online with rollback netcode, and you can even queue up to play every single game in the collection at the same time! Of the games I've played so far, mostly SF2 and Cyberbots, I can say the connections have felt great.Will this game be worth full price for everyone? Probably not. There are ROM-based alternatives requiring a minimum of technical knowledge to setup. Additionally, I'm sure I'm not the only one who wasn't attracted by the number of Darkstalkers games on offer. I'm still exploring that side of the collection. However, for me, the Training modes, art, integrated rollback, and getting to enjoy Red Earth/Warzard, Pocket Fighter/Gem Fighter, Cyberbots, and Hyper SF2 for the first time have already made this a worthwhile purchase.Should you get this collection over buying the games as part of Capcom's weird Arcade Stadium thing? Yes.
_childDocuments_.name: Capcom Fighting Collection

_childDocuments_.review: This is a superb package of arcade gems with a robust suite of additional features and optional extras, but that's not why I bought this. That's not why you're reading this review. We're here because Capcom is holding Yoshinori Ono's baby hostage. Darkstalkers (simply known as "Vampire" in Japan) is a cultural icon. Even if you don't know their names, you've seen Morrigan, Felicia and Hsien-Ko. Regardless of how much I suck at it, Vampire Saviour is wedged deep within the veins of my bleeding heart for its camp gothic style and razor sharp violence. Street Fighter may have elegance, Marvel Vs. Capcom spectacle. Neither made me fall disgustingly, head-over-heels-in-love to the point where every new person I meet runs the risk of receiving a three hour lecture on the subject. It's been a quarter of a century since the last major instalment. The night is still young. The moon is full. All the stars are aligned. Say it with me now...

_childDocuments_.review: A strong collection filled with gothic Darkstalkers games, eclectic titles such as Cyberbots and Red Earth (a mecha and RPG-styled fighting game respectively) and crossover titles like Gem and Puzzle Fighter. Each with a surprising number of endings, artwork, and secret characters. Oh, and a Street Fighter game if that's the only thing you actually recognize. All with QOL features and intricate training options that aren't offered elsewhere. Definitely pick it up on sale and give some love to a collection filled with succubi and monsters.

_childDocuments_.review: This collects arcade ports of all of the Darkstalkers/Night Warriors games (albeit without the improvements present in the PS3 release for Darkstalkers Resurrection), a well-loved version of the classic Street Fighter II, plus several more niche titles that offer something even for those that are not fans of traditional fighting games. I bought this entirely for Super Puzzle Fighter II Turbo but greatly enjoyed my time with the Darkstalkers games, Red Earth and Cyberbots. There are a variety of customization options and a full art and music gallery present in the collection, along with some great trading card and Steam Community items. Overall, I would highly recommend this if you are a casual fan of fighters like myself and want to get a little taste of everything Capcom has to offer. Now if only they would allow items to be purchased in the Points Shop...

_childDocuments_.name: Capcom Fighting Collection

_childDocuments_.review: Before I get too rant heavy in this I wanna state that what made pushed me over the edge to buy this collection is music from Mndsgn and Knxwledge. Two artists who I absolutely love and have been following for a long time, and some of their tunes go hard. Don't get me wrong, I am a fighting game fiend.There is a lot of love put into this collection. Lots of concept art and illustrations that have never seen the light of day are available. There are also a good amount of games that have NEVER gotten a home consoles release like Red Earth and some that have been notoriously hard to get without a Japanese console and expensive physical media like Vampire Hunter 2: Darkstalkers' Revenge and Vampire Savior 2: The Lord of Vampire. If you are a fan of Darkstalkers this collection is a must. Regardless of that the definitive version of Street Fighter 2 "Hyper Street Fighter II - The Anniversary Edition" is also in here where you can select and character from all prior versions as well. Even if you don't like those Pocket Fighter (Super Gem Fighter Mini Mix) is here as well. Which isn't the deepest game, but certainly one that people who are into fighting games and not can get into. Puzzle Fighter is also an a super good time and probably what I'll play the most if I'm being honest. I also really like Cyberbots: Full Metal Madness which is a game I've played on fightcade a ton but now have a way to play people my level and not people who have been practicing for 25+ years. This is easily the most love put into a Capcom collection maybe ever. Menus and navigation is quick and intuitive. Hated how previous collections lacked features and content? Get this one, show your opinion with a buy and maybe one day we'll get another Darkstalkers game.Edit: I almost forgot that every game in this collection has rollback netcode, making them all run VERY well online. As well as full soundtracks for every game in the collection. The only one negative I can say about this game is that it doesn't have crossplay and that it doesn't have Third Strike. Other than that, this collection does not miss.
_childDocuments_.name: Capcom Fighting Collection

_childDocuments_.review: With the number of games, the quality of them, the variety (puzzle fighter, sf2 and dark stalkers all being pretty different), the fantastic presentation, ability to choose different versions of the games with ease, amazing netcode, bonus music and art, a decent variety of display modes - this is an easy recommendation with great value for money. It's a no brainer if you like fighting games
_childDocuments_.name: Capcom Fighting Collection

_childDocuments_.review: A bit pricey, get it on sale like I did. I may not have been around to experience these FG classics in their heydays, but I picked this collection up specifically for the Darkstalkers franchise. No other Capcom fighter has been even close to how Darkstalkers/Vampire plays it cards, from almost inventing airdashing, immediate round starts, and absolutely unabashed, wacky, and lovable character designs. I can't tell you about Street Fighter, Cyberbots, or Red Earth (all featured here), but if you have any interest in creative movesets, classic arcade controls, and ridiculously fast combat for the '90s, then Darkstalkers delivers. Yes, its definitely outclassed by contemporary heavyweights like Guilty Gear and Blazblue, but there's charm and a delicate craft in the animations that are just chock-full of details. Darkstalkers was at the cutting edge of videogames as art, with smear frames and fluid motions.
_childDocuments_.name: Capcom Fighting Collection

_childDocuments_.review: Not a fan at all of Hyper Street Fighter 2 (no dashes of any kind? This is truly hellish) but am LOVING almost every other game in the collection. Puzzle Fighter is classic, Gem Fighter is a ton of fun, definitely too many Darkstalker games (but the animations for this series are top-notch!), Cyberbots is a surprisingly awesome addition. And don't even get me started on Red Earth, which crosses Fighting games with RPG leveling -- hell, I practically bought this collection just to play Red Earth. Online is spread across quite a few games of the collection, but you can thankfully queue up for more than one title, then just spend your time in the Museum or in a game of your choice. So queuing up for a match isn't so bad, since I'm getting time to play the offline mode.Only thing I don't understand is why so many Darkstalkers, really -- seems like three of them are variations of the same game, which is an annoying thing to have to pick and choose, but if the character I want to play is a mainstay like Demetri or Morrigan, it's not a big deal. If it's an unfortunate addition that is excluded from one of the variations, then that's one less game I'd want to queue for in online...Waiting to see ANYONE else play Red Earth online!
_childDocuments_.name: Capcom Fighting Collection

_childDocuments_.review: The Good: The leftovers of Capcom's glorious 2D fighting game golden age, including super obscure unknown yet mega quality stuff like Warzard and Cyberbots. The Bad: Has the un-smart controller configuration style that is has been obsolete for ages instead of the good "Hit button to do this action" type configuration that essentially every fighting game released in the last decade has embraced and made standard.The Ugly: Capcom will continue making half-assed collections for Street Fighter games that the playerbase will never embrace - See SF 30th Collection, everybody still on crap like Fightcade. Also censorship+removal of content is never welcome, like the secret endings in Darkstalkers.

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely brilliant collection packed with some very obvious love to some lesser known Capcom titles. Personal favourites in here are definitely Puzzle Fighter and Red Earth on top of Vampire Saviour and they're all playable online with really, really solid netcode. _childDocuments_.name: Capcom Fighting Collection

_childDocuments_.review: I was very eager to try pretty much the entire collection from watching Maximillian Dood playing these games with friends, and by interacting with certain characters through playing the old Marvel Vs. Capcom games and I am pleasantly satisfied with them, as they are all very fun and unique in their own ways, and despite half of this collection being Darkstalkers games, they all feel very different from one another. This collection also marks the first home release of Red Earth and Cyberbots in the west. With that out of the way, let us get to collection specific criticism.The game uses the same basic UI seen in Capcom Beat 'em Up Bundle, just with a different theme and menu music, which is very neat and tidy, even if certain options are rather easy to miss (like the progress marker in the Awards section). It's visually appealing and in my opinion was just on the edge of being excessive, so I am glad that what's on the background is in black and white and only the surrounded rectangles and the game logos are in colour to make them stand out and not hurt the player's eyes with an explosion of colours and images.The Gallery is immense, featuring a plethora of artworks from each game to check and zoom in to obscene detail wihout pixelization, and both japanese and english versions of promotional material are available. All the music is in good quality, and features nearly the entirety of each game's soundtracks (with only a few specific songs missing for some Darkstalkers games, namely secret character victory themes outside of Shadow's) which can also be set to be repeated like an MP4 player, as usual.Online Play is silky smooth, and so far I have detected no issues whatsoever, it's essentially simulating couch versus, which is a big step up from previous Capcom collections. It must be said however, that it is advisable that you hit Steam Discussions or elsewhere to gather people to play with you as it is rather difficult to find players online, specially since this release, as of this writing, does not support cross platform. Every single game (excluding Super Puzzle Fighter II Turbo for obvious reasons) has a training mode with the features one has come to expect which is very much appreciated, as well as a difficulty slider and several options to customize your experience, like adding or removing different borders, filter options including, naturally a no filter option, ability to choose if you'd rather select secret characters the original way, with button combinations, or through an  option, integrated into the games that has you use shortcuts instead (specified in the character progression within the awards section, and also in some guides I've addded). This collection's big draw that Capcom made sure to emphasize was the addition of Vampire Hunter 2 and Vampire Savior 2, previously Japan only updated versions of the original Vampire Savior, featuring gameplay changes, roster changes (most notably, adding back Donovan, Huitzil/Phobos and Pyron), updated music and a rework of the Dark Force mechanic. Sadly however, the two possess no english version.But because nothing is perfect, I must highlight the negatives as well.Picking up from the last paragraph, despite both Vampire Hunter 2 and Vampire Savior 2 having english ports that were available in a collection called Darkstalkers 3, said versions are not available here, as aren't the secret endings, which were outright removed, due to it's mild nudity. Which is hypocritical considering the games themselves are fine with blood, mild gore and nudity similar to what is seen in said secret endings and Demitri even has a super move dedicated to demonstrating his varied tastes in women. Country flags were also removed from Vampire Savior. It is also very bizarre considered there's a Graphic Content slider in the game settings.The censorship continues in Street Fighter II, with missing elements from stages and country flags being replaced. Though the stages weren't as heavily edited as Ultra Street Fighter II, it is still important to highlight that such changes took place once more.The games could really use a Reset button, which is something so basic one has to wonder why it's absent. This is something to note specially considering you not only have the options to unlock hidden characters the original way with the aforementioned button combinations, but the game outright tells them to you, so one would think Capcom would add such a feature to make it easier to redo them if failed. Similarly, in the case of Red Earth/Warzard specifically, one can input passwords to access their characters at a higher level or with certain things unlocked, as well as being able to access other extras through them, so it becomes even more annoying to have to quit the game and re-open it every time, specially since the narration and the game logo showing up are unskippable. Moreover, the game does not have a dedicated Versus button for offline play like the Street Fighter 30th Anniversary Collection did, forcing players to press Start every time they play a match and forcing Player 1 to continue using the same character until he or she loses. The game also does not support 2 keyboard players simultaneously or 1 controller and 1 keyboard player simultaneously in offline play which is a very strange and specific ommission.Unlike the previously mentioned Street Fighter collection, there is no menu dedicated to character lore, which I personally find odd given that the purpose of this collection was to bring attention to the Darkstalkers series and other more obscure or otherwise forgotten titles like Cyberbots and Red Earth, which were also highlights of this release. The Speed Selection in Super Gem Fighter specifically seems to be broken, as in my experience, nothing noticeable changes, and I had to manually set the speed to Turbo 3 on the settings outside of the game itself to apply the changes.While the Quick Save option is very useful and appreciated, specially for Red Earth, it is bizarrely shared accross all 10 games, as opposed to having a slot (preferably more than one) for each one. Again, this was not an issue in the Street Fighter Collection, which had a similar volume of games (12).The games could have used better upscaling, since in bigger screens the sprite work gets really stretched out and one must rely on the filters to mask the ugly look.Finally, I believe these games could have used more content, and in this regard, would have benefited greatly from being console ports as opposed to arcade ports. Games like Super Gem Fighter contained a Survival Mode for example, and Hyper Street Fighter II (which had a console port first and an arcade port second, ironically) had multiple soundtrack options, from CPS1 and 2 versions (for clarity, sound quality and instruments from the first few SFII versions and the later Super versions) and even including a brand new remastered version, just to name a few. Other things could have been added onto the games as well, like the minigames in Street Fighter II (possibly with the option to play them seperately like in Street Fighter IV), which are strangely absent, and other goodies like the still Japan only Dee in Vampire Savior and Zero-Akuma in Cyberbots, which given that Huitzil and Pyron were hacked onto Darkstalkers 1 to be playable, I don't think it to be unreasonable to want these characters to show up as well, given that, once more, those games were highlit in this release.Finally, and despite the fact that I pre-ordered this to get the bonus content, I feel like 40€ is a tall asking price for the reasons specified above.In conclusion, this collection is worth it for casual and hardcore players alike, if you're willing to look past the grievances I mentioned. Although, in all honesty, I'd recommend waiting for a price drop.

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly a better package than I thought it was going to be. It might seem like a bad buy due to Fightcade for PC players, but effort was really put into the game. Sometimes it looks like the devs looked at Fightcade and attempted to replicate the ROMs to success. Everything from the presentation to the netcode (which is rollback) is nothing short of great. This is also a great way for some game in this collection like Red Earth and the Japan-only Darkstalkers games to finally get an official release outside of Japan AND game platforms. In terms of gameplay, everything feels snappy and responsive. It truly feels like you're playing the actual arcade versions of these games.Some downsides though. I feel like training mode could be fleshed out a little more. Simple things like recording dummy actions feel awkward due to not having control of when the recording plays and have to wait for recording. It isn't the worst thing, but after the Street Fighter 30th Anniversary Collection came packaged with the feature, it seems like an oversight that this collection doesn't have that. In the case of Red Earth/Warzard, you can't control what level you start out with. You can adjust the levels, but ONLY in the game settings in the main menu; meaning if you want to adjust them, you have to leave the game every time do it. It isn't a deal breaker, but it seems like depending on which game you're playing, you don't have control over a few things in the training menu.A pet-peeve of mine. Not at all a detriment to the game, but I wished a trials mode existed. It would give people new to fighting games an idea of how to play these games without have to result to creating a tutorial for each one.Despite my criticism of the training mode, I must stress that the training mode itself is still very good and the UI as a whole is great and east-to-navigate. I highly recommend this game. The netcode itself should be more of a reason to get this game.

Or they like a particular version. Or trying out everything day 1. =numerous filters which may or may not suit your tastes. I think the default filter was fine.-no opponent connection indicator indicating if they're wired/wifi. No rollback indicator like in Strive or MBTL-barebones PC settings. resolution, window/borderless/full is about all you get-Default aspect ratio is a bit stretched, but easily changed-Slowdown in HSF2, not sure if native to the arcade version as I haven't played it, but it's there.-censored Honda Stage -no crossplay with consoles-no replaysFrom the games I played, the ports and online are solid. _childDocuments_.review: I've been waiting for a game like this for years. This is for the FightCade freaks. The Capcom obsessed. If you're new to fighting games, you'll be in for a shock. This is a collection of misfit games for eccentric people and you should build fundamentals elsewhere. This is for the advanced player.I'm mainly focusing on Darkstalkers in this review because it's what I am most familiar with.The Darkstalkers games were foundational for the "anime" subgenre of fighters, and make up the majority of games in this collection. Each arcade release in the series is present in this collection. They're rough. They're unbalanced. They're experimental. I love them so, so much. The amount of soul they contain is unmatched by any fighter that Capcom has made before or since. But they are best experienced with the context of being familiar with 90s Street Fighter games and similar titles, because they turn the ideas from those games on their head, and were some of the first to do so. As Street Fighter II ventured into the unknown territory of making games with competitive balance in mind, Darkstalkers ventured into the unknown territory by making more abstract, non-human characters with unique powers and movement options fit into a similar competitive context. Each game adds more and more, and makes the combat more complicated, adding more mechanics, making the game faster, adding more counterplay to each strategy you might come across, until it reaches a crescendo with Vampire Savior, a game that has still seen competitive play at fighting game majors and supermajors to this day. This game is so fast, with so much to understand, demanding so much of the player, it overwhelms with adrenaline. This is the game most people competitively play on ranked. Rushdown is everything in this game, but defensive options are powerful enough for a good player to combat it. Matches (not rounds) often end in less than a minute. Top 8s at major tournaments for Savior can be as short as a Grand Finals bracket for another game. The community is also very inviting and dedicated to helping new players build the skills to compete. This game sells the whole collection on it's back, in my opinion.This collection also contains the unfortunate mistakes that led to the downfall of the franchise. Vampire Savior 2 and Vampire Hunter 2 are concurrently released versions of the same game with different rosters. They didn't have the secret sauce the original Savior had, were seen as inferior by most arcadegoers at the time, and competed with each other. The colossal failure of these two games killed the franchise (they're fun to mess around with, though! I main Pyron in these games). The spirit of the gameplay of Darkstalkers lives on in the Versus Series (Marvel vs Capcom, Capcom vs SNK, Tatsunoko vs Capcom), as well as some of their characters, but there hasn't been a new game outside of rereleases for Darkstalkers since, and the last rerelease for Darkstalkers was on PS3/360.Speaking of rereleases, how is the performance of the collection itself? Not bad. The presentation is phenomenal, I love the new music and aesthetics of the menus. The online matchmaking is the best part: the netcode is competent, you can select multiple games to be in queue for at once, and the ranking system seems fine. The emulation can have some glitches, however. Thankfully nothing impacting gameplay so far, just occasional audio issues that end up fixing themselves by the end of a match. Nowhere near as bad as the Street Fighter 30th Anniversary collection, but I still hope they patch the few problems. The achievements and fighter awards seem like nice long-term goals for completionists, and the museum and soundtracks are very nice and contain tons of cool stuff for nerds like me. I'm enjoying it a lot so far.Puzzle Fighter, Gem Fighter, Cyberbots, and Red Earth are all also working without problems, and are a lot of fun as well. Most of these games are acquired tastes that are either parodies of other franchises (in the best possible way) or highly unorthodox experiments in what /makes/ a fighting game... or both, depending on how you look at it! I haven't played much of these games, but I know that they all have their own dedicated fanbases that have been chomping at the bit for a collection like this to finally be able to play with friends and support their favorites.The true odd one out in the collection of odd ones out is Hyper Street Fighter II. It's the final arcade release for Street Fighter II, and it lets you play as any character from any revision of the game from World Warrior to Super Turbo. It's wacky and broken, but doesn't feel as weird as the other stuff. Also, online is filled with ST players who just wanna use this game as a vehicle to play ST. It's funny to mess around with, but definitely not the main draw.Overall this game is worth buying and is very enjoyable. If you're not really into fighting games, maybe wait for a sale. If you are the type who would fall in love with this game, chances are you've already bought it. But if you're on the fence, just do it!Darkstalkers 4 would be cool to release someday, Capcom. Just an idea haha

_childDocuments_.review: Maybe a 2 out of 5 if you're into fighting games. Honestly, this is just a pretty transparent market test to see if there's still interest in Darkstalkers (the series that comprises half of this collection). There's less than 500 people playing it on the Saturday night after release, so it's not looking great.Thumbs down is just due to game selection. There's no reason for there to be more than one or two games from each series, but FIVE Darkstalkers games in this seems pretty overkill. If you're into old arcade games you might get a kick out of Red Earth and Cyberbots, but the fact that there's no Street Fighter 3 or Marvel vs. Capcom representation here at all is kind of a drag. I know there's legal problems with getting stuff from Marvel right now, but I can't help but want to play those games again. Everyone who knows the scene knows that the Darkstalkers community pretty much sticks exclusively to Vampire Savoir 1 anyway, so the rest of the games in the series are kind of a needless addition. They didn't even bother to translate all the text, even in the "English" versions of the game.It's cool that these games are here, but honestly, even with the quality online experience (thanks for rollback) it's not worth 40 bucks unless you're really, really into old fighting games. Because there's so few people playing, you're going to get either total noobies or absolute monsters in most of the games, but maybe matchmaking just needs more time to separate the elite from the rest of us. I'd wait until it's 15-20 bucks and throw the money at it then, hopefully it's still got some life in it later on.Extra points off for barely any concept art for most of the games. If you're gonna include a "museum" in the content, why not provide more than I could find with a 2-minute google search?

_childDocuments_.review: What a MESS!How, how do you **** up something as simple as this Capcom? In all honesty, I bought this predominantly as a fan of the Darkstalkers franchise in hopes that maybe the sales figure could result in a new entry for a franchise that has long been dead and deserved a sequel for well over TWO decades. That was wishful thinking at best, I know that now, because they can't even port their original arcade titles from the early 90s - which on modern hardware should be effortless - in a working fashion.There are countless bugs in this game (I work as a video game tester, so I know exactly what I'm talking about). The latter three Darkstalkers games contain numerous characters that all share the same iniquities. The mid-air block doesn't work properly, a persistent (or should I say, consistent) glitch found in SF2, and at least 3 of the Darkstalkers games in which the character either halts, freezes completely in place before conjuring some random input, or even worse completely jumps to the opposite side of the screen, as opposed to whichever you intended to direct them. It's unbelievable. Not only do you pay £30+ for a collection of old video games that could easily be emulated by somebody with  the same intelligent quotient of an infantile chimp, nor does it have the crucial cross-play feature, but when the games that you created nearly 30 years ago don't even function correctly, then, well, I'm flabbergasted, There;s nothing else to say but avoid this compilation, at least until Capcom decide to start thinking of the consumer rather than what they consume from them. Appalling. It's a shame Steam reviews don't allow for profanity, because believe me, what I've written here does not accentuate the disappointment felt. I pre-ordered this 4 months in advance, you money-hungry, greedy ******* capitalist bastards. Hang your heads in shame.

_childDocuments_.review: Capcom got almost everything right with this collection: low input lag, training modes with hit and hurtboxes, museum, original soundtracks... The first of three flaws I´ve noticed is that as with any other Capcom classics collection there´s literally NO ONE playing online, so the effort put into adding rollback netcode to all titles has been useless. Besides there´s no lobby creation to invite friends and no spectator mode, details that will come with the second Fighting Collection (the Marvel one).The second flaw is that Capcom has managed to "offer" 8 different screen filters but 6 of them are horrible. Any MAME scanline filter looks 1000 times better than most of the 8 filters added in this collection. Some of them are a lazy pixel net like the one added to SFV in its latest iteration and that looked like  s h i t.The worst of all three flaws IMO is the f...ing DRM.So is this one a good classics collection? Indeed. Is it worth the full launch price: No. I got it for $13 USD and I don´t regret it, but I´d never pay more than that for a game from a company like Capcom who has literally been spitting on fans faces by adding DRM to games that were 1, 2 and even more than 3 years old, breaking the contract rules since the DRM WASN´T INCLUDED ON LAUNCH. The filters are super lazy, and last but not least we´ll never know whether Capcom has recompiled its own ROMs (highly unlikely), or like Nintendo with the mini NES and mini SNES, Capcom has sold us the ROMs that the MAME scene has compiled and improved through decades of hard work FOR FREE.
_childDocuments_.name: Capcom Fighting Collection

_childDocuments_.review: It's a collection of 5 Darkstalkers games, the funniest version of Street Fighter 2 in Hyper SF2, and some proper hidden gems in Cyberbots and Red Earth. The shortcuts for special moves are a nice option for newcomers, and the art gallery is top-notch.If this had crossplay and better netcode overall I'd keep playing, but if you don't care about that it still might be worth picking up.

_childDocuments_.review: Interesting collection of fighting games from Capcom's more niche franchises.  Although there maybe better options in playing these games, I feel like this is also a test to see what franchises could get revived or be integrated into others simlar of that of SF2turbo HD on the console back in the day did for SF4 release. This is definitely a collection for those who are fond of these games but new players should not be shy in trying this since there's a lot of games to appreciate here. Overall it's a solid gameplay experience based off the arcade versions of the game with solid emulation, rollback netcode, it's a decent way to play these games but again there are other options as well, especially if you are playing online. I'd recommend this game only on a sale but it is a solid experience for some timeless classic that deserve some notoriety.

_childDocuments_.review: Any attempt by me to review the individual games in this collection will end badly.So all I will say is there's rollback netcode, and the training modes have hitbox/hurtbox displays. The latter of which is both insane and highly useful for ancient games like these, and shows the developers put in more effort than just bundling emulators and wrapping it in a fancy frontend kinda like the Street Fighter 30th Anniversary Collection here on Steam.Just 5 mins spent there messing around with the hitbox/hurtboxes in training mode with your preferred character will give you a good feel for your character's attacks, because in these old games it's not always intuitive what their attacks' priorities will be.Ye, buy it. And not just because I need more people to play with.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a nice collection of some classic fighting games (mainly the Darkstalkers series) along with some forgotten favorites (Puzzle and Gem Fighter). Unlike the bare bones Street Fighter anniversary collection, all of the titles come with training mode, quick save/load, online play (with rollback), settings customization, and a polished interface. There's a lot to like here, especially if you haven't played some of those titles lately...or ever. That said, it's still an arcade emulator + roms with some bells and whistles. All of these titles are readily available within Fightcade and have been playable online for years. Graphically, there are plenty of emulators that can make things look/run better than this, too. Plus, Cyberbots and Red Earth aren't particularly good games. Adding Hyper SF2 feels a little tacked on considering how many versions of SF2 there are with online play already. Why not Capcom Fighting Evolution/Jam? It seems like a good fit with Red Earth. Why not one of the Alpha 3 ports with dozens of characters that are missing from the SF Anniversary Collection?Considering things are just emulated older titles, they're probably going to crank out more of these that include those other games eventually.Still, it's a good package for what it is. It's not amazing, but it's good.

_childDocuments_.review: Great collection with really good online. Unfortunately not many people picked it up at launch, thankfully it does have background matchmaking with multiple games and a big gallery so it's easy to kill time between matches. I think this collection has tons of potential but the playerbase needs to grow a bit or Capcom needs to add crossplay. For people just getting into fighting games, there's also a 1 button special move mode, but honestly for the games I've played, they aren't too important. Dark Stalkers mostly relies on chaining normals and universal mechanics and Pocket Fighter is mostly based around strings. The inputs are mostly just tools for neutral in these games, though they do have some ability to combo, it just doesn't seem as important for damage as they are in other fighting games.Like I said, it's a good collection just it needs a bigger player base. I know the price might be a bit daunting for some but I think it's a good value for the games and the online. You could pick it up on sale some time, I recommend getting your friends to get it especially if they have been wanting to get into the genre but the z motions and quarter circles have been a bit daunting to them, might be a good way to learn and like I said the player base could use some growth.
_childDocuments_.name: Capcom Fighting Collection

_childDocuments_.review: The Capcom Fighting Collection is finally here and it's simply beautiful. Capcom has been killing it lately and this collection has a lot of love poured into it. Seeing all these classics from the golden era of arcades and fighting games returning in a very accessible way just makes me feel beyond grateful. Darkstalkers, Red Earth, Cyberbots, Pocket Fighter and Puzzle Fighter? Heck yes. Thank you so much, Capcom. Let me talk about some of the positives:-Rollback Netcode: every fighting game should have it these days and the games in here are no different.-Simple controls: if your desire is just really to have a go through the single player of these classics and have some simple fun, not having to memorize command inputs (you know how frustrating fighting the ai of these oldies can be) is a blessing. Capcom already revealed that they're working on a simple control scheme for SF6 and the fact that they also implemented something similar here shows that they're looking into making fighting games more accessible and I really appreciate that. People can check out fighting games in a casual manner and switch to classic controls if they really wanna learn a character and get more involved with the game.-It's a work of art! I love the new artwork they did for this and the OST is a banger.I honestly can't think of anything wrong with this collection, at least from a more casual point of view. The only nitpick I have is I wish the Alpha games were in here, I personally think they would have been a better fit than SFII. I don't mind SFII at all, but there are just so many more ways to get it than the Alpha games...Anyway, that's all I have to say, really. Plenty of nostalgia for everyone who wants to relive these gems while also appealing to the new generation who wants to experience an important era of fighting game history!
_childDocuments_.name: Capcom Fighting Collection

_childDocuments_.review: This is a well made collection with a great art gallery and fun music. The games play great as ever and the optional "one button supers and specials" is a great addition for new players or anyone looking to have some casual fun with friends. There's a lot to like in this collection: the sprite art in Red Earth/Warzard is beautiful, Cyberbots remains one of the most unique and underrated fighting games of all time, and the inclusion of Puzzle and Gem fighter means you have something to turn to when you want to relax after busting a blood vein from getting rushed down to death in five seconds flat in Darkstalkers. ;)Good games, good collection.
_childDocuments_.name: Capcom Fighting Collection

_childDocuments_.review: This game absolutely oozes love and nostalgia for the Golden Years of the Arcade. I come at this game from a modern perspective having missed the era personally, but with a strong desire to hammer down fundamentals and footsies. While the controls may be frustrating at first for those used to modern buffer systems, there's nothing near as rewarding as learning those perfect combo timings in these old classics. Literally Hundreds of hours worth of potential grinding in online ranked thanks to the games beautifully executed netcode. Well worth 40 dollars if you are intending to really make an effort to get into the genre.
_childDocuments_.name: Capcom Fighting Collection

_childDocuments_.review: The sheer amount of games here is worth it. I bought this for the Darkstalkers/Vampire Savior games but oh my lord am I losing myself in everything else along the way.Red Earth is an absolute romp. With 4 playable characters you play through a series of boss battles, all of which are insanely strong and level up you character getting new moves and resistances along the way. Never before has a fighting game felt more like a Soulslike title.Puzzle Fighter is one of the funnest versus puzzle games ever, it's my first time playing and I actually think it will be one of my most played titles on this list.Gem Fighter is a fun little game where you fight an opponent while racing to level up your moves each match. Each move has 3 levels, changing the move's properties, reach and duration. The roster is interesting and the animations and move sets are absolutely adorable.If you have literally any inkling to try these games out, please do it. Sales for this game are paramount for the futures of some of these titles. They are masterpieces on their own and deserve the love they have been put into them. I have experienced no errors, crashes or lag on any of these games and the bulk amount of features and loading times for these games is stupendous.Capcom deserves a round of applause for this release. Buy this collection, it is absolutely stunning.
_childDocuments_.name: Capcom Fighting Collection

I've played a good bit of online and so far have had no issues so the rollback is quite good!It's nice to have an official release to play these 10 games on even if you can play them by other means. Hopefully we can get more collections in the future to bring these amazing classics back cause they're great games. Good job, Capcom!

_childDocuments_.review: It's great to have some of these games available for the first time like this. Having options for training modes is a really excellent add in. The art and promotional material archives are worth the price alone if you're into that sort of thing. High res scans of old arcade promotional materials and even some animated key frame work for attacks in the design phase. Really an astoundingly cool collection of materials. If you're just here for the games, they work, they're fun, and you're getting a solid bunch of them.Even if you shave it down to:The one Darkstalkers you will playPuzzle FighterGem FighterSF IICyberbotsRed EarthThat's still 6 solid games with more features than they've ever had in one package, with good online play.
_childDocuments_.name: Capcom Fighting Collection

_childDocuments_.review: Capcom really knocked one out of the park here, and it puts both Sonic Origins and Pac-Man Museum+ to shame.. They went out of their way to make one of the best retro compilations of the year, and is everything I wished for ever since Capcom Arcade Stadium (and for that matter, Darkstalkers Resurrection) first released. "All" of the Darkstalkers games, Puzzle Fighter, Pocket Fighter, and even a port of Red Earth. Hyper Street Fighter II was a bonus. Basically, if you like the Street Fighter series, you'll definitely love the games in this collection.Aside from slight copyright and censorship edits (No more QSound logos, for example), the games look and play exactly as they did in the arcades. The online mode is pretty good as long as you're playing against someone with a good connection, and you can further enhance the experience with specialized CRT-like filters. You can play through with original difficulty settings or practice with an option that makes the games easier and lower in difficulty than the original arcade releases. Also, Huitzil and Pyron are now bonus characters in the original Darkstalkers game. Please, show your support and buy this collection. Now, I can't wait for the Capcom Arcade 2nd Stadium releases! (If you aren't willing to pay full price for the few games in this collection that are going over to that one, at least consider picking the games up from there).
_childDocuments_.name: Capcom Fighting Collection

_childDocuments_.review: Games are as close to arcade perfect as you can hope for in an official release.  The main draw for me was the entire Darkstalkers arcade games, but having Red Earth for the first time on home consoles, not to mention the criminally underrated Puzzle Fighter, Super Gem Fighter, Cyberbots, and even Hyper Street Fighter II makes this a fantastic collection of some of the best fighters Capcom put out in the 90s.  I appreciate what Capcom has put into this, and hopefully this will lead to more collections as well as possible new games for these classics in the future.  At the very least, new fans can find some new favorite games.Online is fantastic, although a few quality-of-life fixes could make it even better.   In addition to the much-needed crossplay, the ability to drop in and out of online search would be appreciated.  Otherwise, as an online casual, I really do appreciate the effort they've put forth for the online infrastructure, and hopefully things will continue to stay strong for this and future games.

name: Fading Afternoon
detailed_description: You play as Seiji Maruyama, a middle-aged yakuza recently released from prison. Old tropes are here but you can choose to not follow them. The question is — does anything really matter that much now? The game features: - Multi-endings; - Complex beat'em up action; - Mini-games; - City to explore.

short_description: Seiji Maruyama is a middle-aged yakuza recently released from prison. Known as 'Gozuki' (one of the demon generals from Buddhist mythology) he is the power that his oyabun counts on. But there is one thing his aniki is not taking into account: Maruyama is getting old.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: Great game. It’s vibes. 9/10Have you ever experienced being alone in a world that has moved on without you? Being in a city where you fill your time with the ghosts of the past? Unsure of what your next step in your journey is so you continue on with the dueling nature of who you are against who you were?Developer Yeo does a phenomenal job capturing this exact feeling and theme in all of his work with Fading Afternoon being no exception. I’ve played all of his previous work and was eagerly awaiting his third installment in what I deem -  reflection core. His theming in all of his games capture a sense of solitude and quietness I haven’t discovered in any other games I’ve played to date. It is incredibly relatable, and I’m always surprised at how someone can evoke such an abstract and personal feeling. The moments where you look out at the bay and sit alone with yourself, reflecting on your life and the steps you took to land you in the place where you are now.Fading Afternoon is exactly this. You are an aging Yakuza and must return from a place of isolation and rebuild your former families glory while also navigating an uncertain future. This game has you live vicariously through your characters life and provides you with moments to ponder and reflect. Everything from Yeo’s previous games work in tandem, so if you’re unfamiliar with Yeo’s style of game design, allow me to provide you a quick rundown:His first game –  focused on a coming of age story about a young man who lives alone and leads a school gang. He trains in various disciplines and grows skills while balancing his school work and personal relationships. All the while looking ahead to the bleak future of himself and his peers. The combat was tight and evoked River City Ransom mechanics with the use of increasing your stats and maintaining your satiety by consuming food bought at convenience stores.His second game –  dives deeper into the solitude of man, following an individual who’s only true joy and skillset lies in his assassination contracts. The dichotomy between the protagonists every day mundanity and his contract killing is stark. The gameplay evokes the boring and unfulfilling nature of the time spent between the action filled shootouts and gunplay. In this game, Yeo introduced some of the coolest shooting mechanics that evoke homage’s from Wong Kar Wai’s Fallen Angels and John Woo’s The Killer. The bulk majority of the game and narrative is spent wandering 1970’s Paris, smoking cigarettes, drinking alcohol, and watching movies by your lonesome.His third game –  is a culmination of the previously mentioned themes and gameplay mechanics tightly wrapped up in a focused narrative package where the intersection of action, story, and theming meet.You play as Seiji Maruyama who is recently released from prison. You meet with your old aniki- Azuma san and begin your life again as an aged Yakuza enforcer. From what I’ve gathered, you don’t learn new tricks as you did in The Friends of Ringo Ishikawa. Seiji is an aged man who has seen his fare share of gang wars, so his arsenal of combat is vast. The two main buttons you focus on is your punch and kick button. (I’m using a steam deck for reference) that being X and A.The main combat loop consists of positioning, punching, kicking, blocking strikes, and most importantly encourages you to perform catch strikes. Catch strikes immediately kill your opponent and you preform them by holding down the X button to guard and time your A button as a strike lands to reverse and immediately preform a kill. You can catch weapons to use against your opponents this way as well The satisfying crunch of their ripped elbow kills the individual. Your arsenal overall is fluid and a mix of martial arts of Judo, Karate, and Boxing. Yeo has trained in martial arts and his animations are surprisingly accurate.The gunplay takes cues from Arrest of a Stone Buddah. Every shot you inflict on your opponent is an instant kill and you can retrieve firearms during larger gang fights by performing the same catch strike mechanic, while also pulling back on the directional pad.Fighting rival gangs is your main way to progress the story and earn income. With every foe you defeat you earn a noticeable amount of yen. Yen is used for various activities in the world such hostess clubs, drinking beer, and most importantly buying cigarettes.The gameplay loop has you travelling to different locations, engaging in gang fights, going home to heal, and repeating this loop until the gang boss is available for assassination in that region. You receive Polaroid's of potential hangout spots of the opposing gang leader, and you must hunt them down by visiting the various haunts located throughout the city.I can’t forget to mention the music in this piece of art. Each location has a certain lofi jazz song attached, but the clubs bring a Japanese city pop spin to it, vocals and all. The best soundtrack with The Friends of Ringo Ishikawa at a very close second.To conclude this piece of fellating prose, for those who are unsure of whether or not to start with this game. I recommend any of Yeo’s games, and this is a great place to start.9/10Tips•	You can heal in a few ways – Sleeping in your hotel, eating at the restaurant, or going to the bath house. I recommend going to the bathhouse located in the Mahjong district. You heal a lot faster this way.•	Begin combat with a rival family as soon as possible to start earning money and progressing the story. •	Make sure you buy additional days at your hotel. You can end up homeless. You lose respect with each passing day you’re homeless.•	If you drop your coat on the floor, you can re-equip it by heading to the clothing store and choosing the same outfit.•	For those of you who like yakuza cinema, you can pull a Takeshi Kitano and take your own gun and end your life. A nice touch with call backs to Outrage and Sonatine.
