_childDocuments_.review: I must truthfully admit that I’m not an avid fan of JRPGs; and my first introduction into the Persona series through P4G was mediocre at best because at the time I thought of Persona as a glorified dating sim/visual novel. Thankfully, P5R has proved me to be dead wrong with its charming style, enthralling story and the most amazing soundtrack I’ve heard in a while.Now that I’ve finally finished the game with all achievements, the whole experience felt like an extremely emotional roller coaster. After getting off this ride, I felt both immense joy and bittersweetness: Happy because I was able to acompany the Phantom Thieves to the end of their journey, watching the characters grow and develop as a proud parent watching their children; Bittersweet because the ride is finally over and I would never be able to experience it for the first time again.Now it sounds pretty weird to begin a review about an RPG with its OST but the music in this game is truly phenomenal. The game has a track for pretty much every activity you do and all of them are bangers. From strolling around the city and socializing with people, to ambushing and beating up your enemies; from working hard on your final exams, to going all out on the final bosses; all of the tracks in this game is truly unique, catchy and memorable. So much so that I will definitely continue to listen to the OST long after finishing this game. I would even consider recommending people try this game out for its music alone; and after the music has drawn you in:I find this aspect hard to review without risking major spoilers, so I will try to keep it to a minimum. You take on the role of a typical anime/manga high school protagonist nicknamed Joker, transfering to a new town after a false accusation. He awakens to a power that allows him to tap into the subconscious minds of other people in a place dubbed the Metaverse. Over the course of one year in-game, he forms bonds with various characters as well as made new teammates who accompanied him as the Phantom Thieves – using their special powers to steal malicious intents from the hearts of evil adults. Now as for the rest of the story and its intricacies in character development, I wholeheartedly believe that it will be much more enjoyable for you to discover as you play the game.P5R’s gameplay is essentially broken into 2 main parts: The socialization/life simulation part and the actual combat RPG stuffs. For the life sim part, you get to hang around time, discover a surprising amount of activities to do and socialize with an ensemble of endearing cast (most of them at least ahem). It’s tough to list all of the activities available but just to name a few: going to the movie theater, training at the gym, reading books, going on dates and hangouts, etc.; all of which will ultimately help boost your power in the combat part of the game. Since time is limited throughout the entire game, you’d have to learn to balance these activities in an optimal way, or just go wild and have fun enjoying the city.On the other hand, the combat part mostly takes place in the metaverse where the Phantom Thieves will go on heists to steal people’s hearts and deal with evil shadows and Personas along the way. In a traditional turn-based JRPG fashion, you, your teammates and the enemies will take turns duking it out. Also similar to typical turn-based JRPGs, you will have access to normal attacks, ranged attacks, special skills and items to defeat your foes. Honestly the combat in this game is so stylish that even though it is a bit grindy, I still enjoy the flashy moves after hours into the game. On occasion you can also negotiate and convince the enemies’ Personas into joining your crew, adding new skills to your arsenal. People also draw comparision between the Persona-collecting in this game to that of a Pokemon game.Now, being a JRPG, it also has its fair share of cheesy and cliché moments. But ultimately, it didn’t bother me one bit; and I think it even added to the charm. The game also provides fan service in the form of allowing a highschooler to date adults, including a teacher, which is questionable at best. Good old Japanese fan service I guess.Persona 5 is truly a masterpiece in my opinion and it easily made my personal top 5 games of all time. I’m so glad I listened to the memes and gave this game a chance. Came for the music and memes, stayed for pretty much everything the game offered.

_childDocuments_.review: Playing and beating this game felt like the anime equivalent of picking up One Piece. Did Luffy find the One Piece yet?GAMEPLAY: 4.5/5The gameplay of Persona 5 Royal encompasses... quite a lot, actually. The game is a mix of a slice of life simulator (playing through almost every calendar date of an entire year), a visual novel where all you have to do is focus on the story, and classic jrpg action where you raid palaces in the metaverse, stylishly fighting enemies in turn based combat. As most of the game is story-driven, there's not too much to say about the gameplay apart from free time, and entering palaces/Mementos. One quip I had with free time was hanging out with confidants - the occasional extra filler hangout required to bond further with someone and get a new cut-scene felt largely unnecessary given the abundance of activities you could do elsewhere in the game. Apart from that, spending time with confidants was definitely a highlight of free time, with how real and developed most of the Persona cast feel.The palaces in the game felt great. Kamoshida's castle admittedly gives the game a bit of a slow start with the introduction of the Metaverse, but the game only goes up from there. By the time you get to Madarame's flashy and golden museum, you really feel like as the player, you're on a HEIST and it's going down in style. The palaces following the theme of the seven deadly sins was a cute touch, especially considering that the game was all about stealing evil hearts. The ambience and atmosphere of the palaces also drastically differed (in a good way!), from cyber city outer space, pyramids, and a casino. The puzzles typically reflected the theme of the palace as well, keeping the raids feeling different and fun throughout the game. Combat felt moreorless like your typical jrpg, with default attacks, guarding, and special skills. The gun being a secondary option to a default swing made for some interesting management decisions in terms of palace raids and SP spent, and physical attack skills taking away your HP instead of SP was a fun mechanic to juggle with as well. Similar to how turn based combats tend to have "ultimate" abiltiies, P5R has "showtimes" and "all out attacks," featuring special cinematic attack animations. They're silly, cool, and leave you with a smile on your face. Balancing in the game felt just about right (I played on hard mode), and if I ever felt underleveled, I never had to grind for long to make up for it. Before I move on from palaces though - Okumura's boss fight was NOT it. The gimmicks were annoying, and felt punishing to the player for simply not being leveled up enough instead of encouraging strategy, given the time limit of wiping out mobs in one turn. Also, I wanted to square up with Okumura himself, not his goons. Grrrr. Every other boss fight gets a pass, though! Finally, the movement in the game felt a bit awkward at times. Like, you try to walk up to an npc to talk to them and overshoot a little, and have to re-adjust kind of awkward. It wasn't rough enough to take away from the gameplay, but making it a bit smoother would definitely make the game feel even better!NARRATIVE: 5/5For a game that's 100+ hours and largely story driven, I'm sure glad that Persona 5's story is TOP TIER. Woo! Honestly, all I have to say about this section is 'congrats to Persona 5 Royal for being the only video game to have Futaba Sakura.' Jokes aside, the character writing in this game is amazing. Some characters just feel so real and relatable, making any down time in the game to spend time with the cast a treat, instead of a chore. Even the less interesting characters like Ryuji, as forgettable as he is, is undeniably a bro. I found it so funny how Yusuke would claim he's not a pervert, and yet all the perverted dialogue options in his hangouts boosted your friendship the most. Futaba is undeniably best girl, and the game spoils you by including her in Sojiro's hangout storyline too (which is downright touching). I need to throw in that Goro Akechi is a hilarious character. No I will not be giving context. Just trust me on this one (source: dude trust me). Persona 5 manages to tackle a lot of serious and heartfelt issues in a wholesome and satisfactory way, instead of being overly clichéd and cringe. Having a likeable cast in a game like this is so important, and the end result is a game that feels like it's spoiling you for being as long as it is. Considering the sizeable number of confidants and party members as well, there's bound to be someone you like or connect with to some extent. The plot has a clear beginning and end, and has its fair shares of twists and turns. While some plot twists are all but expected (I won't be going into spoilers here), how exactly everything unfolds and plays out is usually where the story line delivers when it gets predictable. My favourite antagonist is easily the last one in the game (in the true ending). The complexity of the final villain in terms of their motivations and what their stance was on justice and the "greater good" felt refreshing and set apart from everyone else that came before them, and actually makes you want to pause and think for a moment if they really are the bad guy. Brilliant. I've heard before from people that have played P5R that they got depressed after beating the game, because it felt like they were leaving behind the friends that they made along the way. High praise that's honestly deserved, and speaks volumes of the world building and likeability of the character writing.GRAPHICS: 5/5It's one of those games that make you feel cool just for playing the game. The animation you get for ambushing an opponent? Getting behind them  on their shoulders, ripping off their mask? Kinda hot, if you ask me. HAHA. Character design and art are amazing, and the proof is that Futaba has glasses. The general aesthetic of the game is clean and pleasing, and a lot of touches to the art (including the white/black squares in the font) matches the theme of the Phantom Thieves. Plus points for creativity! The game always looks great to look at, minus that one enemy that looks like. Um. Anyways. P5R also adds animated anime-style story cutscenes, and they were all amazing as well! The game art design also pays attention to the personalities of the cast. One of my favourite examples is when the gang is sitting around together. Ryuji would be manspreading (LOL), Ann sitting up on the table, Makoto sitting like the prim and proper lady that she is, Yusuke standing around, Futaba lying down on her stomach... all these subtle touches to the art really shows how much care and thought has been put into this game, outside of the plot and gameplay.SOUNDTRACK: 5/5Chances are, you've heard Persona music before, even if you've never heard of or played the game series before. The music is iconic, catchy, and good. The music always gets the atmosphere juuust right, while being fun and engaging. About to re-enter someone's palace to steal their heart? You're about to feel real cool for it. Something sad is happening? Prepare for the music to make you depressed. The Persona soundtrack has surprisingly good diversity as well, flexibly allowing the music to enhance the game experience. What more could you ask for in a game soundtrack? As well, the voice acting for the entire cast is great, and suits the characters they represent. I can only imagine that the voice actor for Goro Akechi must've had a lot of fun ;)OVERALL: 5/5Persona 5 Royal is a phenomenal JRPG that sets a high standard for future games to come. Sure, the game is long, but considering how good the game is across the entirety of its length... it's a gift. You get over 100 hours of an immersive world with a diverse cast, in an emotional and cool rollercoaster of a game. If that doesn't sound fun to you, I recommend going on a merry-go-round instead. I'm sure you'll come around!

_childDocuments_.review: The game as a a whole is just as much of a masterpiece as the perfect soundtrack.Most fun and engrossing game I've played in many, many years, possibly ever.Edit: I really keep coming back to and thinking about my time with Persona 5, it really achieves perfection in so many areas:Premise:The idea of stealing someone's dark desires away is already a very interesting premise, and in the context of the settings chosen is all the better. I think everyone knows about the castle being the first palace, but even after that every heist location fits perfectly with this core idea of being Phantom Thieves.Soundtrack:The total number of osts is above 100, and I have about 35 of them downloaded to my spotify, which should say a lot. It's incredible how instantly catchy most of the recurring themes are, and the perfection of the soundtrack really makes every moment in the game memorable and enjoyable, no matter the pace you set. I found myself intentionally slow walking through the sixth palace because I could not get over how great the payoff of all the story telling and character building up to this point was.Game Design:The core game mechanics (turn-based combat with some light puzzle solving) was just engaging enough to be a challenge and rewarding, while never being so difficult or so time-consuming to become stale. Controls are smooth and responsive (I played with a controller) and level design is smartly focused to integrate permanent progression without ever being jarring. Again, it's just a perfect balance (Aside from the twins and Lavenza optional fights).Voice Acting/Dialogue:I played with English voice acting and could not recommend it more. All the main cast have a great level of consistency between the way the characters are written and the emotions intimated by the VAs. Add in the always tone-appropriate dialogue and perfect delivery (Yusuke: "Ann, are you all right? Is yours cracked as well?")Graphics/Art Style:Again, it's just remarkable how well the art style lines up with the atmosphere of the game, and especially for all the palaces it becomes a joy just to see what new and over-the-top setting you'll be pulling a heist in next. The large range of character sprites and animations as well are all just so, so good.So yeah, just overall, I can not think of another game in the past 5 years that I've sunk so much time into, played through entirely twice, and still wanted to experience all over again to get even a fraction of the enjoyment I got playing through the first time.

_childDocuments_.review: What a journey this game has been. It'll always have a place in my heart, and the characters you meet. This game sucked me in so much that I forgot there's real life stuff and obligation that I have to deal with. You just need to master the way combat and turn-based battle works in this game and you're all set (which can get real hard as it goes). Might need to grind pretty hard if you want to get really strong, especially at higher difficulty. And then there's the other half of the game where you hangout with friends and strangers you meet along the way, increasing your bond. Love this part of the game, it is pretty much the 'break time', the 'slice of life' you need after getting through the combat.To me, both part of the game are balanced pretty well that I'm able to 100% my way through it on my first playthrough with barely any guides. That won't stop me to go for another playthrough though, sometime in the future. I need that feeling of reliving this game for the first time to replay it. The story made me sit around waiting for more, and I really like that feeling. It might get cringy at times (which is not a crime) but it really is worth sticking around.Oh and the music. Best part of the game. I can't stop listening to it after playing the game, basically half of my playlist now. They slap so damn hard man... (looking at you, Life Will Change.)Anyway, recommended, get it if you can, I'm just ranting. Off to real life now.

_childDocuments_.review: Persona is peerless in the "Pokemon meets Final Fantasy meets Visual Novel meets High School Sim" sub-sub-sub genre of game, and Persona 5 Royal is the most stylistic, addictive, and immediately engaging game of the bunch.  Certain characters and their plotlines are archetypical, or somewhat thin variations on past characters (Ryuji from P5R and Yosuke from P4G might as well be brothers), and the difficulty may be rather easy, but if you haven't been bitten by the Persona bug yet, this may be the easiest way to do so.  It's a long game, so some perserverance is a must to make it to the end (especially if you get the bonus third semester in Royal - max out Maruki's confident!!), but I guarantee you'll be fiending with the rest of us for more.

_childDocuments_.review: Persona 5 Royal reminds me of an expensive lunch I once had in Seoul. There were nine courses in total—tiny, cupcake-sized creations that looked almost too beautiful to eat. When each dish was laid in front of me, my server would spend a long time describing its flavor and mouthfeel. I listened to the lectures attentively, but I honestly just wanted to try each dish for myself. The whole ordeal took much longer than it really should have. It also failed to be an actual meal, because I exited the restaurant hungrier than when I came in. I literally paid money to become hungrier. I still consider that meal to be worth its price, however, because each dish was something that I had never tasted before and have never tasted again since. Like my lunch, Persona 5 is uniquely beautiful on the surface. The visuals, the music, and the themes of the story connect together artistically, and the general vibe of Persona 5 is immaculately well-defined: indignant, self-righteous, and unflappable. These exterior aspects have a unified style that elevates the overall experience more than I thought was possible.Unfortunately, everything below the surface leaves me dissatisfied. The main character’s schedule gets interrupted frequently and in inconsistent ways, making it hard to trust any sense of regularity. Major plot points are repeated over and over, often in the same scene, drawing out an otherwise compelling story to excessive lengths. The dungeons (or “Palaces”) hold your hand through every puzzle, unnecessarily tutorializing basic gameplay mechanics. And the Pokemon-style turn-based combat never develops beyond debuffs and elemental weaknesses, making battles feel simplistic. Based on the game’s lack of faith in the player, I would have expected its target audience to be young children, but the adult themes clearly indicate otherwise. During most sessions of playing Persona 5, I feel like my intelligence is being insulted, and I often walk away hungry for something more fulfilling.To me, Persona 5 is a terrible game and a wonderful experience at the same time. It is both exquisite and frustrating, delicious yet hollow. Unlike that lunch I ate in Seoul, though, this game will not break your bank account. I think it is worth playing if you are prepared to put up with its condescending nonsense.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a really, really small game in many ways. The places you can travel to are limited and small, the music is lacking compared to other Shin Megami Tensei soundtracks, the actual plot is basic and even cringy. However, the presentation is one of a kind, this game manages to draw you in with it's intimate settings, lifelike characters, conversations and interactions that direct where the story will unfold. Sometimes it feels a bit railroaded, but even then, it's quite a freeform RPG. If you enjoy this, try playing NEO The World Ends With You for a more interesting approach to the urban sprawl or Yakuza 7, which is basically Persona 5 with worse but more entertaining combat, way better sidequests and an infinitely better story.

_childDocuments_.review: + fantastic story driven by nuanced characters+ flashy aesthetic makes even minor things stand out+ presentation is the best in JRPGs to date+ combat is the most refined seen in RPGs more broadly+ great performance on DeckPersona 5 is a JRPG in the broader Shin Megami Tensei franchise, and it's much closer to more traditional SMT titles than other Persona games in my experience. It felt like a slightly darker story than Persona 4, although less so than Persona 3. The tone is definitely more mature than Persona 4, and this is shown with the dialog, level design, and general atmosphere.Talking about the story is tricky because it's quite a good narrative and it can lead to spoilers. You play as a Phantom Thief poised to steal the hearts of criminals and other morally bankrupt characters in order to change society for the better. You recruit many along your journey and continue this process of finding a new person to change their hearts, setting up an invasion of their dungeon (here called palaces), and securing a route to perform your heist.It features an interesting cast of diverse characters, each with their own personalities which you explore through social links, or little dialogs you have to increase your effectiveness both in and out of battle. This aspect of the game closely resembles a visual novel and comprises about half of the game's content. The other half, like more traditional JRPGs, is dungeon exploring with a side of turn-based battles.Battles themselves utilize the One More system as found in Persona 3 and 4, a somewhat simplified version of the Press Turn system used in some other SMT titles. You can gain an additional turn by exploiting weaknesses or landing critical blows, turning combat into an abstracted form of rock-paper-scissors. Enemies can likewise exploit the system to their advantage in the same way.Another major improvement is the ability to baton pass, or to give your extra turn to another character in your party, meanwhile imparting some boon like a damage buff. As well are additional elements like gun and nuke which makes this rock-paper-scissors more multifaceted and complex. There are other mechanic improvements to battles but this is the one that fundamentally changes the flow of battle.The level design is a lot better than prior Persona titles and even more broadly most SMT games. They each have distinctive styles, are often labyrinthine yet laid out in a logical way. Compared to something like P3 or P4 with randomly generated corridors with zero landmarks or features, Persona 5 is miles more interesting.The Royal content is mostly nice. There's a lot of mechanic additions that fundamentally change the way the game is played, for example you have disaster enemies which explode when killed, and combination attacks that pair characters to deal a hefty blow. I would say it borders on mechanic bloat, as there's a lot more ways to opportunistically turn battles in your favor over the original. These additions only make the game even easier.There's also the new social links and entire new semester. The new social links, at times, felt shoehorned into the original game's plot, never really influencing events until the third semester content. The new story content is quite nice, though, adding more nuance to the story beyond what the original release did. It felt natural enough and it's essentially just more Persona 5, which is appreciated.A common complaint of the original release was Morgana stopping you from going out at night, so much so this became a sort of meme in the Persona community. Thankfully this was all but removed in Royal, making evening social links much easier to complete. Even without a social link guide, I had maxed out almost all of the social links by games end, when with the original release, I maybe only maxed half of them. Take from this what you will, but I found it a positive change that I could more completely experience the game.I play JRPGs in a way where I never run from battles and instead try to fight everything I come across. I never go out of my way for a battle (unless it's a special boss), and I felt the game was adequately difficult by doing so. I never felt underpowered; in fact, I sometimes felt a little overpowered. The third semester posed no challenge, however, because I had already approached level cap for all of the characters by then.There is no granularity to difficulty options like there were in Persona 4 Golden, there's just a selection of easy, normal, hard, etc. I think this was a missed opportunity because customizable multipliers for experience, money, and damage would have allowed players to more customize their experience. On normal, I would say it's fair or maybe a little too easy. The difficulty, in lieu of more granular options, could have been balanced a lot better, but it's a minor gripe.Persona 5 oozes style and atmosphere in a way that was groundbreaking at the time and still holds up. The art design and direction are unmatched even beyond the JRPG genre and, in my opinion, one of the major selling points of the game. Even something as banal as navigating menues is so flashy and energetic. It never feels like a typical "four-guys-in-a-row" RPG, everything is stylized to an exceedingly high degree.Likewise the soundtrack is absolutely stellar, with a lot of upbeat acid jazzy tunes and rock, every track is a banger, especially the battle and boss themes. It's one of the few games I'd suggest the soundtrack to even non-gamers. It's masterfully created and one of the defining features of the game.The game is very long, I clocked just under 100 hours. It takes place over the span of about a year, with each day varying from a few minutes to possibly hours depending if you are in the middle of a palace. It's also extremely dense, although as you finish more social links, your available options per day does diminish. Near the end, with most social links completed, often I did menial things like go to the gym for stat bonuses rather than any meaningful content. I would say of my 100 hours, 4-5 of them were bloat for this reason.It's just such a blast to play, it's the perfect coming together of aesthetics and design, coupled with spruced up JRPG gameplay with much more involved mechanics than traditional. As well, the story and characters are memorable and intriguing, keeping your attention well after you see the credits roll. A fantastic JRPG, something I'd highly recommend to even those who don't tend to like RPGs.At high settings, it can keep 60fps for most of the game. Some areas, like Shibuya central street and a couple of the palaces do have drops to low 50s and sometimes high 40s, but it was rare. The third semester palace had more pronounced drops, even as low as 30s. You can drop max TDP to 10w and it will keep more or less the same performance, but keeping TDP control off, it still kept those drops.For some reason, at 60fps, frametiming can be all over the place. At many instances it will say 60fps but frametime graph will seldom be locked to 16.7ms. In palaces, you'll notice when running around that it feels slightly jittery. Changing ingame settings does nothing to abate this jitteriness, unfortunately.Incidentally, setting max refreshrate to 59hz seems to be a much, much smoother experience. In fact, I played the game at 59fps after the first palace because it lead to a better experience as the frametiming is much more consistently around 17ms.

_childDocuments_.review: A year on from finishing Persona 4 Golden, here I am with about 90 hours logged into Persona 5 Royal as the ending credits roll. Much like the previous review, I’m a little perplexed as to how to even begin this review. Simply put, Persona 5 Royal is a stone cold classic JRPG, and easily ranks amongst the best that’s out there. I do have a few misgivings, but it’s been phenomenal.For the uninitiated, Persona 5 Royal as an RPG mixes several elements together: turn-based battles that rely on elemental weaknesses, monster summoning/collecting (the titular Personas), dungeon crawling and a social link system with the in-game characters. The core game play wont be unfamiliar to anyone who has played a JRPG before, but the focus on elemental weaknesses and the role of social links are central features in this game. Most of your party has set elemental affinities, but you are able to switch between an ever-increasing range of Personas to adapt to this spell element-driven system. As the game progresses, mastery of this system, which allows you or enemies to get '1 more' attack by using with the right spell becomes a crucial component. Building further upon the foundation of Persona 4 Golden, social links are a key component of P5R and are a significant chunk of the game. In between story events, you have the option each day to interact with members of your party and other major NPCs of the world. There's also a fairly faithful recreation of a wide range of areas in Tokyo as a backdrop to this, some of it freely explorable. Each party member and major NPC has a sub-story that ultimately enriches the overall plot and has extra gameplay-related bonuses for completing all ten ranks for each character. This additional layer adds depth to the plot and ends with giving access to the strongest Persona summons as compensation. In the process of my run (including Royal’s extra ending), I completed all but a handful of these, even if some were due to the skin of my teeth due to time limits. The game also rewards players for these links by giving passive bonuses that enhance any future new game plus attempts.The narrative of Persona 5 Royal focuses on the seedy underbelly of Tokyo society and a series of increasingly high stakes heists. Your character awakens to the use of Personas, which sets off a string of events that leads to the creation of the Phantom Thieves, a supernaturally powerful group that can change hearts. Part slice of life, part science fiction, part crime drama and part social commentary, it’s an interesting mix in many ways. I’d argue that this leans more on a philosophical and sociopolitical angle than its predecessor, and a range of social issues in modern Japanese society, ranging from structured hierarchical harassment, dog-eat-dog mentalities, corruption, mob mentalities and even populism are addressed as part of this. Each major villain has an arc that features a specific dungeon with a theme, and it’s a little like watching a season of anime each time – which of course also gives you the ability to take a break and come back to the game when you’re ready. It’s a broader mix than Persona 4 Golden, but an intriguing one. Again, I recommend looking up a spoiler-free guide for the True Ending requirements, for your best possible first-time experience.New to this entry is Mementos, a secondary and evolving randomised dungeon that serves as both a means to gain more battle experience and Personas, and explore smaller stories as part of this. Mementos eventually ties into the main storyline, but for a lengthy game, it also presents a very important feature: cutting down on grinding. As you progress through this special dungeon (which can be accessed for most the game), you gain the ability to add passive buffs that improve the amount of experience points, money and items you gain from items. Better still, the cat-bus-based (yes, I said cat-bus) navigation of the area also allows you to run down lower-level enemies, skipping the need for a battle. By the end of the game, Mementos was giving me a 200% EXP boost and helped greatly in preparing me for the late game challenges. As someone who can be starved for time, this was a welcome and gameplay-based addition.Much like its predecessor, the soundtrack and aesthetic look of Persona 5 Royal are absolutely fantastic. Who’d have thought that a JRPG soundtrack using jazz, blues, R&B, and even disco elements would be so memorable and effective. The UI and transitional screens of the game have also been heavily stylised, which is absolutely gorgeous. My only major criticisms of Persona 5 Royal is that it’s beginning to test the limits of some of the features of this franchise by overdoing and overdelivering. It’s a fairly reasonable criticism that Persona 5 Royal has a bit too much dialogue, and can become like playing a high-end visual novel for an hour or more at some points. Likewise, some of the puzzles in dungeons… get a bit grating by the end. There are some really neat and inventive ones, but some, like the colour-mixing puzzle in the game’s final area, grew to be tedious and kind of frustrating. These are only small marks on an otherwise fantastic game.I played Persona 5 Royal in about four blocks, correlating with some quieter times, breaks and holidays, and in many ways, it’s a game where you can binge an arc and set it down for a while, only to return later. The game also offers a handy story recap, should you need it.If you’re into JRPGs and Persona 5 Royal is on your radar, it’s a must-play. Just be ready for the time investment.

_childDocuments_.review: Persona 5 is my first Persona game and it's probably the best JRPG game I've played in a long time and has an enormous replay value. I spent my whole winter and spring holiday to finish this game and wow I loved it. It certainly made me realize I missed something during my high school time. Like the rest of us.Persona 5 Royal is not for everyone. It's heavily narrative driven and has a lot of dialogue which can be a dealbreaker for some people who wants non-stop gameplay.You go by almost every single day in a year, living the student life but also trying to change the society for the better when you awaken your Persona powers. There is so much you can do when you're not at school preparing for exams, playing with friends or clearing palaces. You can self improve your social skills by studying, watching movies, books or exercising which is crucial if you wanna improve your relationship with your crush or your friends. Which is highly recommendable as strong relationships will also make your palace clearing and boss fights go more easier.With Royal you have a few new characters. A new party member and a new teacher at your school who's also one of my favorite characters.I was surprised how very well written the story and the characters is. There are times when I feel like I wanna skip dialogue because it's either just boring talk or fillers. But it makes me want to learn more about the characters, their backstory and motivations. Without going into spoilers I found it really entertaining how some of the characters grows as the story progresses. Oh right, they call it for character development! Your party members are of course the type of friends you can never get irl, which makes them so great and the time you spend together are really fun and there's always something new with them going on.The voices in both languages are really good, although I personally preferred Japanese voices. A tip though, time is limited and not everyone is available every day so you might feel some time pressure at the end of the game, but don't worry. Focus on improving your social stats as you gonna need to max out all of them if you wanna max out your relationship with various characters. Be prepared that by the end of the game you won't have time to max out all characters as there are plenty of other stuff you need to do. So pick your favorites on who you wanna be a best friend with or go on a date with. I recommend getting high levels with the Shogi girl and your blonde short tempered friend as you will get some abilities that makes fights go slightly easier. It really is up to you on who you wanna focus on.It is turn-based combat which throws some people off. But the way it's designed is really fun. Every character, friend, foe have weaknesses and strong points such as Ice, Fire, Wind, Holy, etc and knowing your enemies weak points makes battles more fun and smooth. I liked the baton pass system when you attack one enemy with their weakness, you pass your action to your next party member to do the same thing until all enemies are stunned and you go can go for a All-Out-Attack.The music is a real banger. Which is probably one of the most praised things about Persona 5. You're gonna hear the same combat music again and again. Oddly I never once became tired of it and it's very weird but the more I listened and the further I progressed it just got better and better until the point I started to listen to some of the tracks on the train when I'm off to school myself. I live in Tokyo irl and whoa it was immersive!? Anyway, the music and vocals are pretty good and they fit so well with game's atmosphere. I started to really appreciate the music when I was running up to defeat the first boss and just turned the volume up because damn!!For those who played the base game.Just to say this, the new Royal content starts reaaallly late. Right after December which can be a bummer for people who are interested the new red haired character and gotta spend around  hours to get to the new story. I really liked having her in my party and her Showtime with  was really really cool which is such a shame she doesn't  But I also wanna recommend this to players who also have only finished the base game. If you thought the base game ending was cool, you haven't seen the new ending with the new palace. And the new palace and it's story is my number one favorite out of all of them.For those who like JRPG's I really really recommend this game. It's a very long game which makes the money worth it and even if you might have spent over 100 hours, you might feel like you want 100 more hours.There's no shame in looking into guides if you need guidance or want to be more proficient with your time. But refrain from reading about characters until you finished the game as you might face some spoilers.Enjoy

_childDocuments_.review: A Masterpiece Worth Every SecondWith over 300 hours spent on Persona 5 and its Royal edition on my PS4, buying the PC version was the perfect excuse to dive back into this masterpiece once again. Because Persona 5 Royal isn’t just a game; it’s a complete experience. The way gameplay, story, and battle mechanics intertwine so smoothly and seamlessly is unique, setting a new standard for the genre.One of the game's biggest triumphs is its ability to blend various gameplay mechanics harmoniously, keeping an experience that spans over 50 hours from ever feeling monotonous. There's always something to improve, a goal to pursue. Whether it's enhancing relationships, leveling up skills, or managing time, the game creates an environment where every choice has real weight on the story and the bonds you create. And those bonds are truly special: each character has a unique, deeply crafted story. There are no unnecessary characters; each one has an impact on the narrative.Relationships and the romance system fit perfectly into the game’s universe. Everything feels so natural that, along the journey, you end up forming real connections with the characters. And the battle structure? The difficulty is masterfully balanced, providing an engaging challenge curve. The ability to customize builds and exploit weaknesses makes combat strategic and dynamic, adding even more replayability. For those seeking a greater challenge, simply increasing the difficulty is enough—the game rises to the occasion.Persona 5 Royal is, without a doubt, an experience that deserves to be lived multiple times. The freedom of choice and the richness of different routes make every new playthrough as exciting as the first. It's more than a game; it's art.

_childDocuments_.review: Persona 5 Royal is a very special game to me, I first played the original Persona 5 at the start of the covid 19 pandemic, and let me tell you, it helped me through it quite a bit. I cant stress enough how in depth, and beautiful the story of this game is, the characters are so real and all have their own qualities that make them unique. The main story is insanely interesting and will keep you wondering what will happen next at any given moment. The dungeons are amazing and each have their own gimmicks that stop them from being repetitive. The combat system is the best in the series, although a bit too easy at times, i think this game has the best rendition of the one more system so far. There's no way i could put my love for this game into one review, so go play it, you owe it to yourself to play what i think is one of the best JRPGS to come out in the past 20 years.

_childDocuments_.review: I have bought this game 5 times. I have played over 100 hours, and I have found the game to be overwhelmingly terrible. Not terrible in a fun, funny way, terrible in such mundanity that you'll certainly see reviews positing the game is the greatest of all time.Persona 5 decided to take a brave step and remove several series traditions for "style", like shuffle time (a borderline perfect mechanic in P4G that makes even low-level fights engaging, and eliminates the time of grinding whilst not overpowering the character) for Hold-Ups - a watered-down Shin Megami Tensei mechanic that gets annoying by hour 2.The dungeons too are customized, Atlus recognizing what fans really wanted was 50x more pointless text and puzzles (not good ones, mind you, every single one is horrid in a way that actively makes your day worse thinking of them), whilst making every single enemy encounter entirely pointless as you cannot leave cover ever and actually ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ explore the dungeon. Every movement you make will be quick-swapping from one cover to the next (that's not how stealth works, Atlus), and every encounter will be a sneak attack. What's the fun in this you ask?Anyways in P4 they actually made encountering shadows fun too, you had to sneak up on them and hit their back, a challenging task as they'd chase you if they saw you. That's all it was in P3, but they actually updated that in the sequel to give half a second of stun when they saw you. This meant you were no longer screwed by being seen at all (which was too finicky to be reliable), but if you didn't do it right you would get caught. It also meant that running past enemies wasn't a headache, but again, taking still to do so. Remember when Atlus improved their games? In P5 Atlus added the fantastic feature wherein being caught makes the entire dungeon harder (alert meter), keeping the disadvantage of losing the first turn too. Why would they want to disincentive more an already disadvantaged position? Why will it still disadvantage you even if you don't get caught? Why did Atlus make exploring a dungeon more of an overall annoying experience?The alert meter never actually came into play, ironically, but that's cause I was always in stealth. In every ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ dungeon there will be hiding spots, and you don't have to leave one to go to another. I will repeat. You *do not* have to leave cover in a stealth sequence. This is the exact same as having no stealth whatsoever, because you will never have to worry about enemies. But., it does make the dungeon more annoying! And the dungeons are customized! Every theme is just annoying, there's significantly more there but it doesn't add anything to the ambiance, to the aesthetic, to anything really it's just like a regular building. A building you have to backtrack all the time for no good reason, making this annoying game much more so. People say it's good in the first dungeon and gets subsequently worse with each addition, which it does, but the first dungeon was alright at best.The combat is also bad, ♥♥♥♥ everyone who says this game has the best gameplay quite honestly. Gameplay, obviously, isn't just combat, the previous stuff alone makes that distinction. But the combat is also just boring. They added nuke and psychic to the elements list, something so unpopular SMT V removed it. They're pointless, and add to bloat as you can never cover all elements without constant persona switching, which is annoying (or having an overpowered one, which isn't fun). They also got rid of every weapon but guns, and made them worse, weapons were a way of making sure you could still attack without any SP, but now they're inaccurate and weak making them honestly never used. No reason for doing this, really. There's also no reason to remove the fox from P4, they refilled your SP for money making dungeoneering less annoying (for, again, a very high cost, you could only use it like once maybe). Nobody likes multi-day dungeon exploring and effectively forcing that isn't great design. You could say that this is them pushing certain styles of play, but that style isn't that different from the other yet significantly more grating on one's mental. If the stealth and puzzles were better, the dungeons being lockboxes to carefully disassemble this could have worked. They're not.It's also quite brainless, every enemy never really posing a challenge if you exploit weaknesses. This has always been the case though, in every game. But you have so little SP that every encounter you want to avoid.  if your players are actively avoiding encounters constantly, your combat is bad. But the foundations are there. Baton pass is fun, although the upgrade system should be tied to confidant progression not stupid-ass darts/pool. Darts is kinda fun, pool isn't at all, it's not that big of a deal. The bosses suck more ass than I've seen in any game, Okumura was the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ catalyst for my dislike. They are all damage sponges but none of them have interesting mechanics you have to play with. It's always one thing: add multiple targets that you have to destroy before they do something bad. That's interesting for 1 boss, not every single one. The only differentiation is the types of attacks they do, but only status changes never something interesting like Fortune, Chariot/Justice, Shadow Rise, or Shadow Mitsuo. Some of those are annoying, but so are P5 bosses and at least these are diverse. Okumura is the exception here, but he is terrible. Also eat ♥♥♥♥ for making a fakeout boss you can't beat.The story is bad. Straight up. The buildup is through cutscenes going 'hehehe the evil bad guys are plotting!' which is childish writing. It also makes every potentially shocking moment feel dulled cause you've been explicitly told it was going to happen 10 times already. _childDocuments_.review: Just as good as I remembered, and an excellent PC Port. I first played P5R 3 years ago, shortly after it was released in the West. That being said, I am happy to say that in my 170-hour playthrough, I never experienced a single bug, glitch, or crash. This port seems to be very well optimized. As for the game: There isn't much to say about it that hasn't been said already. The soundtrack, voice acting, and character development are all of an insanely high caliber. So too is the gameplay, and unique visual style. This was my first JRPG and also the first game with Turn Based Combat that I've played. It's quite a large leap outside my usual comfort zone of gaming, which should tell you just how good of a game ATLUS has created. That being said, I do have a few complaints about the game. While it is true that ATLUS has made a game that can truly be enjoyed by all ages (at least for like 13+), the pacing can be extremely slow during certain story sequences. I understand this is done so players of all ages can follow the plot, but at times it almost feels like the game think's we're stupid, by hammering in the same point multiple times over. Another thing I've realized during this playthrough is the dialogue can be a bit cringe/ cheesy at times.  This annoyed me at first, but as I continued to play, I realized there was a certain charm about it, and it added to the experience towards the end. In conclusion, I highly recommend P5R. It is easily worth every penny, even at full price. If you manage to grab this gem while it's on sale, that's even better. The amount of quality content you can enjoy is crazy, and adds a tremendous bang for buck. Overall, I feel like this is a great stepping stone for people new to the Persona and SMT Franchises. I will absolultey play Stikers, Persona 4 Golden, and Persona 3 now. It's also a great game to help get into JRPG's and Turned Based Combat. If I were to give a rating, it would be 9.5

_childDocuments_.review: Persona 5 continues the tradition of the modern Persona series (post-3) in delivering an additive, story-heavy JRPG in a novel time-based social connection format. It's officially the longest game I've ever beaten. There's not a lot here to set the game apart from the games in the series before it, but the staggering quality at which its all delivered is admirable and the formula is addictive as ever.The game is so slick, so well presented, any question of technical competence is thrown out the window. The game plays well on a variety of devices including the Steam Deck (1080p at a very uneven 60fps) and the PS3 roots of the game have aged very well. Some of the environments are sparse but it just doesn't matter when everything is so well done and it makes such a cool look seem effortless, much like the characters themselves.The story is fine, not as strong as Persona 3 but better than 4. But where all three games really shine is in the quality and maturity of the writing, the moment to moment dialogue and the three dimensionality of every character. Many JRPG's are quick to throw characters into lazy cliched buckets comprised of simplistic bullet points, but here it's all done with a keen eye and careful layering. There are also some plot beats that are so satisfying it's hard to put into words - small details pay off dozens of hours later in extremely fulfilling ways (including one for series veterans).I don't think the Royal add on content is very good. It's obviously bolted onto the existing game, with interjected scenes obviously stitched into the the original. Knowing how to get the extra content is arcane and expecting players to just figure it out is asinine, and the actual reward after the original ending of Persona 5 feels incredibly tacked on. The game basically loses all momentum at this point and while there is some good story content and the characters/writing remain as good as ever, it really just feels like a superfluous bonus rather than a continuation of a story that needed further development.Overall, there are no deal breakers here. It's a good PC port of one of the best JRPG's of all time. Series newcomers will find a lot to like, and fans of Persona will feel right at home with a new cast and scenario. Recommended to all.

_childDocuments_.review: I first played Persona 5 many years ago on PS4, enjoyed it very much and came close to finishing it, but unfortunately I had a lot of things going on at the time, so I had to put it aside. Alas, the console broke down before I could return to it, and I had moved away from PlayStation hardware in favor of PC gaming. Fortunately, the improved Persona 5 Royal version eventually went multiplatform, thus enabling me to play the very best version on the most powerful hardware available.Being originally developed for the PlayStation 3 hardware, Persona 5 was never a game which featured cutting-edge visuals, but nevertheless the game's stylized artistic direction manages to make Persona 5 a visually interesting game. Persona 5 features colorful graphics set in the distinctive style of Japanese Anime with a combination of fully animated 3D models as well as 2D animated portraits for each of the major characters, complete with both in-game rendered 3D and 2D anime cutscenes. As a result, P5R looks like a combination of a Visual Novel and a 3D Japanese Role-playing Game, which is likewise reflected in the gameplay, but we'll get more into that later.Persona 5 Royal features multiple musical tracks, consisting of both orchestral melodies as well as complete songs, each with English language lyrics. The music sounds good and the songs are extremely catchy, provided that you can appreciate Jazzy tunes, lounge music, and Japanese Pop. The in-game dialog is available in your choice of either Japanese or English, with all critical, plot-significant dialog and story sequences featuring full voice acting. The English Dub is best described as adequate, the performances aren't outstanding, but they suit the characters well and the lines are well spoken. I haven't sampled the Japanese Dub, but I'm unqualified to comment on it regardless because I don't speak the language.Persona 5 Royal is a combination of a traditional Turn-based JRPG, Dungeon Crawler, and a Life Sim/Visual Novel in which you must balance a daily schedule of attending High School, spending time speaking with friends to strengthen your bonds with them, exploring dungeons and engaging in traditional turn based combat with enemies. As you would expect from the aforementioned combination of genres, the game is extremely dialog heavy, including sequences in which you must answer questions in class, engage in conversation with friends, and carefully choose your responses from a multiple choice dialog tree in order to answer questions correctly as well as get closer to your friends. You also have a variety of stats directly associated with social interaction — Knowledge, Guts, Proficiency, Kindness, Charm — which directly effect your ability to express yourself. These stats are increased by engaging in various daily activities as well as interacting with particular individuals, and are fortunately in most cases gained passively from average everyday activities, so you don't have to invest too much time into increasing them. Interacting with your friends increases the Rank of your bond with them granting various perks in combat and allows you to fuse more powerful Personas to equip yourself with.The JRPG portion of the game is likewise exactly what you would expect from the genre. You explore dungeons, (Palaces) engage in turn-based combat with enemies (Shadows) with a variety of techniques at your disposal, earn Experience Points to Level Up along with money to buy equipment, and open treasure chests to gain loot in the form of various items. The only variation to the standard JRPG formula lies in the eponymous Personas, Mythological Entities which are equipped to you and your party similarly to weapons, granting magical abilities. Personas level up passively along with you when equipped, but have their own separate stats. Those who have played various Monster Taming RPGs will be familiar with the basics here, but it isn't difficult for newcomers to learn through progression.Altogether, the combination of genres compliment each other and makes for an engaging, multifaceted gameplay experience which can seem deceptively overwhelming at first but quickly becomes second nature in practice.In Persona 5 Royal you take on the role of a teenage boy who has been moved away from his home out in the country to live with a family friend in the city after he became involved in a confrontation with a drunken man who was attempting to force a young woman into his car, with the man injuring himself in the process and the boy arrested then charged with assault. The boy arrives in the city only to find that his undeserved reputation as a juvenile delinquent has followed him there, with his new guardian addressing him as an unwelcome guest, his teachers at school likewise dismissing him as a delinquent, and his classmates avoiding him while exchanging rumors regarding the details of his arrest.Shortly after his arrival, he discovers a mysterious App has appeared on his Phone which seems to restore itself no matter how many times he deletes it. One day on his way to school the App is inadvertently activated during a conversation with another ostracized student, transporting them into another world in which the School has been replaced by a Palace ruled by the School's abusive P.E. Instructor, with the two being locked up in the dungeon by the guards. They escape their cells with the help of a mysterious feline creature named Morgana, but are quickly caught by the guards on their way out of the palace, leading to the boy awakening to his Persona — his "other self" — granting him the power to defeat the palace guards and escape. The next day they return to the Palace where they are informed by Morgana that it exists within the mind of its ruler as a cognitive manifestation of his distorted desires, and that by stealing his treasure they can change his heart, thus putting an end to his abusive behavior. From there the trio forms a team known as The Phantom Thieves of Hearts, setting out to use their powers to reform society by changing the hearts of various corrupt authority figures, recruiting new allies along the way as they are drawn ever deeper into an insidious plot to seize control of Japan by manipulating the masses.Being a port of a game which was originally developed for the PlayStation 3, Persona 5 Royal doesn't require a particularly powerful PC to run. I encountered no performance issues whatsoever over the course of my 171 hour long playthrough and the game ran flawlessly at Max Settings on my PC. Your experience may vary based on the specs of your PC, but I can safely say that there are no bugs, glitches, or performance issues to speak of regardless.Persona 5 Royal is an excellent game featuring many hours of content between the deep, engrossing story and entertaining assortment of gameplay mechanics. I came just short of a 100% run, missing only a single Confidant, yet completing the story and side quests in their entirety, closing out the game by earning 100% of the Achievements. My playthrough lasted 171 hours, thus making it by far the longest of any single player game I have ever played in 35 years of gaming. I enjoyed the game thoroughly and am left with nothing bad to say about it whatsoever. I highly recommend it to anyone seeking an immersive JRPG to occupy their time.

_childDocuments_.review: Persona 5 Royal is by far the game with the best catharsis in its combat mechanics and presentation out of all others in the main series. In the sense that it's a monster collector with great music, it's hard to beat. That's why it earns a recommendation.Where it falls flat, however, is the narrative. While P5R doesn't hesitate to point out the ills of a degrading, aging Japan getting its comeuppance, it chooses to show it through Atlus' very own myopic lens. As with many Japanese games, the criticisms of society are abstracted through their familiar urban fantasy setting. Hypothetically, this would allow these story beats and oppositions to take on multiple different themes. In practice, the complete lack of self-awareness on display only feeds into the juvenility of attacking a system through the behaviour of its actors rather than its incentives. Never once would P5R stop to reflect on whether or not the way it chooses to tell it story may contribute to the very same attitude it so proudly, and shallowly, demonises.P5R's most memorable aspect is its characters, who has about as much depth and growth as one could surmise from a paragraph of their wiki character profile. This is especially damning considering Atlus has been doing the same character archetypes for decades, but are never able to really take any bold steps in fear of negatively affecting their appeal to weebs (and the Japanese national equivalent).Persona 6, whenever it comes out, will be yet another iterative version of this same formula: same cast of characters, same mind-numbingly dull inability to introduce any meaningful choices, same thin plot that the game will be too cowardly to actually interrogate. If I'm lucky, they'll learn to leave out the annoying mascot. At least the game play will probably be good.EDIT: When I first wrote this review, I was coming in with my memories of playing P5 on the PS4 years prior. Now that I've completed the extra royal content, I have to say the standards of quality is more dire than I remember. The addition of Will Seeds just piles on more unemergent gameplay onto an already terrible streak of bad dungeon designs, giving hand-holdy backtracking to every palace there was. Even the extra story content was disappointing. It's nothing more than the coming to life of bad fanfiction for an already aggressively mediocre light novel-esque narrative. The post-new year "twist" was marginally interesting, but the entire DLC felt like we were being led by the nose by a group of writers who think they're too clever for their own good. There're good things about the DLCs. Jose was a decent addition, so were the various hangouts and activities where you can spend time with your confidants, and the overall Persona management. I do believe it makes the game overall better, but the dogpiling of an already lengthy campaign makes me dread the thought of consequent playthroughs.

_childDocuments_.review: One of the best games I've ever played, bar none.  It knocks it out of the park in so many ways.  The art and graphic design is eclectic and bombastic, the soundtrack is engaging and unique, the story is interesting with great and memorable characters, and the gameplay is nicely split between the varied dungeons (palaces) and slice-of-life gameplay.I don't think I've played a RPG in the past decade that has this level of quality and it easily sits among the best RPG's of all time.  I can't recommend this game enough.

_childDocuments_.review: Love it, subjectively. I had played the vanilla version of the game previously and waited for Royal to release for PC. The gameplay, music, and visuals make Persona 5 an amazing game to play through when you are in the mood for a comfy singleplayer game and Royal mostly just adds to this experience overall.That being said, I do wish they did more to make the game easier to get into for newcomers. From the start of the game, there is a grueling, several hour long, "tutorial section" that lasts basically until the end of the first palace. This section is mostly railroaded where the game slowly gives you access to different aspects of the game, but the sheer amount of time this takes can make you feel very bored very quickly and very likely to drop the game.Royal adds numerous quality of life upgrades to the game that I honestly think are good additions for the most part. However, some of Royal's quality of life changes seems like they may have also inadvertently affected difficulty, which would be my biggest issue with the game. While it is a single player game and you can "make your own difficulty" to an extent, it is extremely easy to forego any challenge. I played through the whole game on Hard (the most "grindy" difficulty setting). I only passively gained money and XP while collecting stamps in Mementos (no grinding sessions), but still ended up so rich and overlevelled that I was able to complete most of the game with little to no effort after about the second palace. Before that, the DLC accessories and personas made the early game a breeze. If you would like a challenge of any kind from the main game (not counting secret boss fights and challenge battles), I would recommend avoiding using the DLC personas at any cost. Even if you fuse them at appropriate levels instead of using the feature to summon them all for free, they are extremely strong compared to any similarly leveled personas.Also, the extra Royal story content was mostly pretty predictable and, while it was nice to have the extra time in the third semester, it honestly didn't feel like it added much to the overall narrative. To the point where I do not feel that I had missed out by not playing Royal until this point. Of note, I wasn't the biggest fan of the true final boss fight music and, in a game like Persona, this is very detrimental to the experience.However, I only focus on these negative points because I feel like it does so much right elsewhere. Overall, I would highly recommend this game as long as you're willing to put in the time before they take off the training wheels and let you experience the game.

_childDocuments_.review: One of the best games ever. Hard to put into words how it feels, but even after 3 playthroughs it still hits a spot in the heart. Finishing a persona game is always a pretty sad experience and 5R is no different. The final message of the game is about moving on to new beginnings and starting a new journey. That sadness has a true purpose and can allow someone to finally break out and see the world. Even if it from a video game, book, movie, or a video on youtube, someone can always find inspiration from whatever they consume. The medium doesn't invalidate the feelings you felt or the experiences you gained from it. Use those feelings, memories, and strength gained from the experience and grow from it.

_childDocuments_.review: This was my first entry into the Persona series, and to turn based RPG's as a whole. Despite having watched someone play through the ENTIRE game already, I still wanted to play it for myself.At the time of writing I have just completed the game, yes it really did take 152 hours. Everything from the presentation, the characters, the story, exploration, combat, music and just living day to day is unlike anything I have experienced before. You do NOT need to have any prior experience, or even any knowledge of the franchise to get seriously sucked into this experience and to really enjoy it. In my whole 150 hour playthrough there were but a handful moments that I was ever frustrated, and those were some of the bosses you come across at the end of some of the chapters. However, where there's a will there's a way, and finally figuring out the trick and beating those bosses was admittedly immensely satisfying.If you are a tentative newcomer to the franchise then worry not, this game has so much to offer not just in combat, but also in the way you live every-day life and grow closer to the people around you. I'd probably go as far as to say that the "daily life" aspect was my favorite, but when the time came to fight, it didn't feel like a detractor to the rest of the experience. The combat is easy to learn, but not so simple that it gets boring.An absolutely incredible experience. 9/10

_childDocuments_.review: Little needs to be said, it's a simple and mostly standard RPG but the quality of those building blocks are shining. _childDocuments_.review: I started playing this game because my little brother told me about it and initially i could not get past the tutorial it was just way to long but a few months ago my friend got persona on pc and i have been loving it. I still think the tutorial is a little to long and tedious but once i got past it i had so much fun. For me personally i think the battle in the game is really fun and the personas can be really cool even if it take a really long time to get any good personas, But I think this game really gets good when it comes to its story and characters. I think all of the members of the phantom thieves have such an awesome personality and story to them and i love the confidont system i think its really fun to go through there coinfidontes. I also think that the main story while it can progress at a snails pass sometimes having such a slow pass makes it so the story really comes out nice and i really enjoy how its been going. I think this game could have come up with a more fluent way of starting the tutorial but its not something im really mad about its more so i wouldn't have been able to get through the game if it wasn't for the second copy and i wouldn't have been able to get to the good parts of the game i really like. All in all i think this game is really really good and i understand that it has some flaws but that hasn't stopped it from being one of my favorite games that i have played recently i really think if you like rpg games with good characters and a good story and you have a lot of time thins game is really good and is worth the time.Over all id give this game a solid 8 out of 10

_childDocuments_.review: It is a nice game with great story, round-based battles and decent monster catching gameplay. However, it is very long - I am currently around the 120 hour mark on my very first playthrough - and some stretches of the game feel overly drawn out and tedious.My main issue with the game is Denuvo, which will try to do an "activation" seemingly at every single launch, when running the game in Linux. Not only has it blocked me from playing the game on the go several times, this means that you can easily run into the 5 launches per day limit, if you play the game on the go or do small sessions throughout the day. Unfortunately, this issue persists to this day and I have just run into a strange error message that states "An error has occured" and points you to a support-page using code 88500006 - which merely states "Currently your game purchase cannot be re-validated successfully, please wait 24 hours and try again.". I am being blocked from continuing a game that I have bought via Steam, because of Denuvo still not being able to work decently under Linux?!

_childDocuments_.review: Well, shoot, I got way too attached to the game. I spent about 65 hours over the duration of 2.5 weeks for a single play through and couldn't be happier with the time spent.Pros:-character immersion is nearly endless. You can connect with anyone at different levels and build special relationships.-turn-based battling has always been a favorite of mine and this game nails it. Almost brings me back to pokemon games.-graphics are great, and I didn't even play it on my PC. I played it strictly on the Steam Deck and it played flawlessly. I almost want to do another play through to see the comparison to my 3090 build.-apparently there's multiple endings which is always a plus. Something a game like cyberpunk could've greatly utilized.Cons:-you can't get deep DEEP in any intimate relationships. Being bf/gf is more of a title than anything.-not all dialogue options have a HUGE impact, and sometimes it's tough to say when it matters. Stick to your gut responses for the first play through to know what I mean.-I almost felt like too much of each day was skipped or wasted. I feel like I could've achieved more if I could use each part of each day properly and skip when I wanted.(These cons are not really cons, but could've really added to my game experience)Overall:Get this game. Don't sleep on it. It was gifted for me, and after playing it, I will not hesitate to buy the 6th persona. The story will captivate you and steal your heart if you let it ;)

_childDocuments_.review: A must play game in the genre. Even if you aren't a fan of JRPGs there's still a lot in this game for you to enjoy. The game is an amazing interactive movie dripping with style, a well written story with multiple endings, amazing music with what I would consider the best OST of all time, and of course it's all coupled with with the usual Persona combat system that feels more like solving a puzzle than just mashing attack every turn. The combat in no way feels like your typical turn based JRPG.On the note of combat. If you just want the story and life sim stuff, you can select the easiest difficulty and breeze through all the dungeons with relative ease. Late game even offers a mechanic that allows you to insta kill enemies if you are a high enough level, to further make it easy to ignore combat if you aren't into it. As for people who want the combat, if you crank it up to the harder difficulties it turns every fight into a complex puzzle where every action matters. My only complaint about the combat is that for veteran Shin Megami fans the later game fights can become a bit repetitive as we know of all the optimal strategies, so the fights begin to feel like a forgone conclusion as we blast through them. The early and mid game still feels deeply satisfying combat wise as you get your perfect team together though, so don't let that dissuade you. Though I imagine most Shin Megami Veterans don't need this elevator pitch.  To sum up even at full price this game is an absolute steal.  I played it for 142 hours, and could easily see myself playing the game again in a few years. Atlus did a great job with the port, and I really really hope that we can continue to see Atlus giving some love to the PC market going forward.

_childDocuments_.review: At its core, P5 is a game of two halves. The first, is a fairly standard JRPG where you go through dungeons, engaging in turn-based battles as you grind your way to the boss to claim the MacGuffin. This is enhanced by some clever twist such a simplified stealth mechanic that allows you ambush enemies to gain an advantage in battles and a complex system of elemental attacks and weaknesses/resistances. That last part may sound pretty standard, but even that was given some added tactical depth since hitting an enemy's weakness doesn't just do extra damage, it knocks them down, and if you manage to knock down all of the enemies on the field, that opens up other options. This leads to a combat system where you're encouraged to use every tool available and think tactically about how to make the best use of your limited resources rather than simply mindlessly mashing your default attack and only busting out the big guns for boss fights. (Final Fantasy, I'm looking at you!)The other half is a life sim that plays out more like a visual novel. While not as immediately engaging, this is where you get to really know the people around you, both your party members and others who cross your path over the course of the game. Every one of them has their own stories as you follow along and grow closer to them. This isn't purely for lore purposes, though. The closer you grow to your confidants, the more benefits you receive. Some will help in the dungeons, while others will help you make more efficient use of your time in your day-to-day life, but all of them are useful. Yes, more efficient use of your time... as that's the core pressure in this half of the game. You only have so many slots available each day, and every major action uses one up. Invariably, you find yourself having to weigh the pros and cons of spending time with one person to grow closer to them, working a part-time job to earn some quick cash, or studying so you can pass your midterms. There are almost always a half-dozen things you could be doing that would all help in some way, but you can only do one of them before time marches on and you need to move on to the next slot (or get swept up in the next bit of the story).The two halves aren't quite as tightly interwoven as something like XCOM (where you'd go on battles to retrieve equipment that could then be studied back at your base to better equip your troops for the next battle, and so on). The dungeons, for example, are far and away your best source of income, but while there are definitely places where it can help in your everyday affairs, most of it will likely be sent on upgraded equipment and supplies to assist in your next dungeon run. The personas you can acquire in the dungeons (the source of your more mystical abilities) can provide a slight boost to your relationships if they happen to match up with the person you're trying to grow closer to, but otherwise the dungeon delving  does precious little to help as you go about the daily routines of a high school student. Even so, there is enough interplay between the two (in addition to simply breaking up the gameplay so no, one style overstays its welcome), so that the overall experience of each would be greatly diminished without the other. In short: it may have taken forever to come to PC, but it was totally worth the wait! P5 is easily one of the best JRPGs. It still borrows from many of the same tropes (teenage protagonists banding together to save the world), even if the high school setting is somewhat unique (though typical for the franchise). If you can't deal with those quirks, this may not turn everything around for you, but if you've ever enjoyed a game in the genre, this is a must-own!

_childDocuments_.review: Persona 5 Royal is an outstanding turn-based J-RPG with exceptional characters, a compelling story, and enjoyable gameplay. The game also includes a unique aspect where the more rizz you have, the more power-ups you can earn. These power up are equal to time spent with your teammate and other confidants (NPC which have unique stories). While the story progresses nicely, players should be aware that they may miss certain elements if they do not engage in certain activities or talk to certain characters. My main issue with the game is with Mementos, as it can be tedious and repetitive. The requests you receive, such as "change the bully's heart," are often located in remote areas of the dungeon, requiring a significant amount of time to reach. However, the story is captivating and the characters are likable, making the journey well worth it. Additionally, the main character, Joker, has several romance options, all of which are enjoyable, except for the adult ones. Overall, Persona 5 Royal is a fantastic game that will keep players engaged with the story and characters. I highly recommend it.

It's a visual novel, which I know is one of the many misleading tags this game has but it should be the only one- with only forced dialogue choices, you can try to click what the game doesn't brute-force you to choose in dialogues and they have voice-lines for it, but said voice-line will only repeat and nothing will progress until you click what it forces you to click. Hours upon hours of time-wasting with pointless dialogue. Walking around in "the open world" is basically just a cutscene because you have no choice where to go, you can only go to the one place the game forces you to, so there's no point in making you walk around in the first place. Devs probably know how dogwater the combat is since there's a mobile-game auto-combat function for every match. The music is nice though, but it's not enough for the price of admission, go listen to it on youtube or something instead. There is absolutely no good reason for why this visual novel masked as a game has such high ratings. If you're on the fence for buying this: please save your money. Might as well listen in the background to someone else click through all this pointless dialogue in a let's play because there's nothing here but needless yapping anyway- though calling it a let's "play" is an overstatement for this garbage. I would refund if I could but I had no idea it would take me HALF OF MY WEEKEND to get to any small semblence of what COULD be gameplay though I was wrong there too because there IS NO GAMEPLAY, and then I realized I had wasted 3 hours just getting to that point already. What a piece of trash.
