_childDocuments_.review: The Stanley Parable: Ultra Deluxe, a game that initially beckoned me with its tantalizing array of branching paths, unfortunately succumbs to the inevitable shortcomings that plague many meta-game experiences. As I delved deeper into its intricate web of choices and narratives, the illusion began to unravel, revealing the stark reality of its underlying code. The once formidable narrator, now reduced to a predictable set of phrases triggered by my calculated path selection, relinquished its power and left me yearning for a more immersive and dynamic experience.Initially, the allure of The Stanley Parable: Ultra Deluxe was captivating, like discovering a rare fossil of branching narratives in the vast Paleozoic expanse. The sense of agency and exploration was palpable, igniting my curiosity to chart new paths and unearth hidden depths. However, as I continued my journey, the cracks in its immersive facade became increasingly evident, exposing the underlying framework that dictated each narrative twist.Regrettably, this revelation transformed the game into a mechanical chore, akin to the repetitive movement of an Apatosaurus grazing upon monotonous foliage. It no longer felt like an engaging dance with a powerful narrator but rather a predetermined flowchart, devoid of the unpredictability and spontaneity that makes such experiences enthralling. The shallow puddles of its design became glaringly apparent, leaving a hollow impression where once potential depths beckoned.Furthermore, the absence of any meaningful chore mechanics only exacerbated the sense of shallowness within The Stanley Parable: Ultra Deluxe. Like a Triceratops lacking its iconic horns, the gameplay failed to deliver satisfying interactions or engaging challenges. The absence of engaging puzzles or intricately designed mechanics left me longing for a deeper, more immersive experience, akin to a thrilling chase with a velociraptor or the delicate balance of a Tyrannosaurus rex's predatory instincts.In conclusion, The Stanley Parable: Ultra Deluxe, while initially promising with its branching narratives, falls prey to the pitfalls of predictability and shallow immersion. The apparent coding, diminishing the impact of the narrator's once commanding presence, and the lack of satisfying chore mechanics erode the game's potential for a truly captivating experience. It is like stumbling upon a rich fossil bed only to find a dearth of unique and compelling specimens. While it may hold intrigue for those seeking a surface-level meta-game, I longed for a more profound and immersive adventure, akin to the awe-inspiring majesty of the Mesozoic era.

_childDocuments_.review: Stanley arrived at his office building as usual, but to his surprise, the doors were unlocked, and no one was inside. He wandered through the empty cubicles and offices, looking for any sign of his co-workers, but it seemed that he was completely alone.At first, Stanley was confused and a bit worried. He wondered if there was a memo or email that he had missed, announcing a company holiday or closure. But as he searched through his emails and checked his phone, he found no messages or notifications.Feeling a bit lonely and uncertain, Stanley decided to take a break and grab a cup of coffee from the break room. As he entered the room, he saw his best friend waiting for him on the counter - the bucket he used for cleaning coffee he spilled on his desk.Stanley smiled, feeling a bit relieved to have some company, even if it was just a shiny metal bucket. He sat down at the table, sipping his coffee and chatting with the bucket about the strange situation."I don't know what's going on," Stanley said, shaking his head. "It's like everyone disappeared."The bucket remained silent, but Stanley felt comforted by its presence nonetheless. He decided to make the best of the situation and explore the empty office building, with the bucket as his trusty sidekick.Together, they wandered through the hallways and explored the various floors of the building. They found some interesting things - a stash of office supplies in a storage closet, a collection of funny photos on a co-worker's desk, and even an old dartboard in the break room.As the day wore on, Stanley began to feel more and more at ease with his new situation. He realized that he was enjoying the peace and quiet, and the chance to explore the office building without any interruptions or distractions.And through it all, the bucket remained by his side, a constant companion in an otherwise strange and empty world. In the end, Stanley decided that he and the bucket could handle anything, as long as they had each other.

_childDocuments_.review: This is the story of a game named The Stanley Parable.It had everything a game needed: a well written story, great visuals, simple controls and good audio and music; however, it only had 2 characters: YOU, playing as Stanley, and the Narrator, the one responsible to guide you until the end with his majestic voice and beautifully written dialogue. So, you played it until the end and got everything it offered... what now?Suddenly, you discovered that a sequel had been released, so, looking for a way to defeat boredom once again, you bought it and started playing. It was the same game? No new content? Just an switch of the game engine and graphical changes? Unbelievable! Infuriating even! That was, after getting some endings, hoping to find something new, that you found the door that would change Stanley Parable forever.You got it! New endings, new achievements, new Narrator voicelines! So you buckled your seatbelt, hugged thightly your new companion for the ride and finished it all. At the end, having done everything, you ask yourself again: "Was it worth it?"; but you already knew the answer to that question, it was at the tip of your tongue all along!Yes, it was. For you have beaten The Stanley Parable 2.Now, for the achivements:Even sillier achievements. Most acquirable in no time at all!COMMITMENT actually works thanks to the engine change from Source to Unity;UNACHIEVABLE was replaced by an actually doable achievement, the TEST ACHIEVEMENT PLEASE IGNORE;However, GO OUTSIDE was buffed. Now you need to not play the game for 10 YEARS! Also, good luck cheating this one. The game will know.To all of you that are doing this the legitimate way, I'll see you all in 203X.

_childDocuments_.review: Minor spoiler warning.Everything added to The Stanley Parable in this edition fits perfectly within the theme and context of the original game. It sets up an expectation of a minor refurbishing with a few added jokes, and instead delivers self-referential, self-aware running gags that play off that very expectation, deconstructing the nature of game sequels, game designs and the process of game reviews. The bucket given in the game automatically doubles the number of endings, as every ending with the bucket is unique from every other ending. That being said, the bucket endings have a downside to detract from the original philosophy of the game. While the bucket endings are hilarious and unique by themselves, they do not deconstruct the nature of choice and freewill like the original Stanley Parable does. Rather, the bucket endings as a whole are a single running gag on the nature of added content to games. Some bucket endings are also less unique than others, and can be just a re-imagining of an OG ending with an added bucket. While the original Stanley Parable works as a dual dynamic between the player and narrator, the bucket adds a third party that becomes a triad of personalities: Stanley, the Narrator, and the Bucket. This again complicates the original philosophy of the Stanley Parable. But at the same time, it is impressive how the bucket is given so much personality without actually doing anything in the game, akin to Wilson in Castaway or the Companion Cube in Portal. In addition, there appears to be some added depth to the game that suggests actual hidden lore instead of a straight-forward philosophical statement, which certainly appeals to the younger generation of post-FNAF fans.

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly, as someone who played and loved the original, This review was on point. Overwhelmingly Positive is for those who haven't played it yet."Back when this was announced at The Game Awards in 2018, I was hyped.The game experienced a lot of delays since then, but recently it finally released in 2022.And I am severely disappointed.The original game is almost unchanged besides graphical tweaks and new effects here and there.The original game now has two new endings and one that has been changed, presumably for copyright reasons.I assume the door that leads to the actual new content unlocks after doing some of the original endings.And this is where it goes downhill. The game tries to be self-aware and ironic about itself, jokes about it being a expansion or even jokes about a sequel!But here's the thing: That's the only gag. That the game got new content. It grows stale after a while, and are probably more true to the actual experience than the writers might have intended.The new content of Stanley Parable Ultra Deluxe is lacking, and it doesn't help that the game was joking about it early in the path of the new content.After going through some areas that can't be accessed again until "completing" the game, the narrator makes some tweaks to the original game and we are send to: Stanley Parable 2!Except it's just the regular office with some balloons and figurines you can find here and there. But what about the new endings? As already mentioned, there are two new endings to the main route of the game. After being send back to the office in Stanley Parable 2, you will see a bucket on a pedestal on your way through.And that's how you get the new endings. You pick up this bucket, and go about the original game's endings with almost the exact same condition. Every mian game ending has a bucket-variant, except for two, which in turn have been replaced with one bucket centered one.Yes, the glorious new endings revolve around a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ bucket. It was funny at first, I'll admit, but it grew stale after the second Bucket-ending.But at least the whole Stanley Parable being recreated is correct, right? Well, yes and no. It's complicated:As also mentioned before, the original game is barely changed. It doesn't look any better than it did in my memory. But it was recreated: In Unity, which might explain the fact this is a standalone title and it took so long to come out.Wait, standalone title? That's right!For the cheap price of 21,99€ (10€ more than the original) or the bargain price of... 14,66€, if you already own the original game.What?The majority of this game is just the original game from 2013, except you have to rebuy it + increased price if you already ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ owned it.This should've been either a free update or a 5€ to 10€ DLC for the original title, not this lackluster 15 bucks expansion pack.Conclusion:Buy the original. A large part of it is identical to the fancy new Ultra Deluxe version, and it sure is a whole lot cheaper and more worth the price.If you already own the original, don't buy it either. Pass it up. If you really wanna experience Stanley Parable again, just download the OG-version and play that." - MissCassidy

_childDocuments_.review: There are games, and then there are art pieces.If "The Stanley Parable: Ultra Deluxe" was a movie, it'd get a bunch of Oscars.If it was a book, it would get a Pulitzer prize.It is a game, so all it gets is this review.I am a big fan of the original game, so I was hoping for the best, but fearing the worst when launching the Ultra Deluxe edition.I was hoping to find the same humor and playfulness of the first part, but discovered a postmodern masterpiece, which uses the same old engine of humor to achieve transcendence.Take the bucket gag for example! I first took it for one of the many stupid jokes, but quickly realized: this is actually a profound philosophical concept. Is a bucket  just a bucket? Well, maybe  bucket is. But THE bucket most definitely is not. THE bucket really deserves all the praise it is given. It might  like a bucket, but it is nothing else but the life force itself!

_childDocuments_.review: This review will contain spoilers!! I played the original Stanley Parable shortly after it came out on steam, and I loved it. I had high hopes for the Stanley Parable: Ultra Deluxe, and I would say it mostly delivers, but i do have a few issues.The main appeal for me in the original game was the feeling of everywhere you go, there's a new ending to discover. You always want to revisit areas to make sure you hadn't missed anything, this is the one thing that I think Ultra Deluxe fails in. All the new areas only have one ending to them (if you ignore the bucket- I'll get to that later) and I didn't feel that sense of exploration that I did in the original, and didn't feel like I was missing anything in any of the new areas I walked through. Even if you wanted to go through the endings again to see if you've missed anything, you might just not be able to. The new content door is a one time area, and as far as i know, you cant revisit it, which is really disappointing because I would've loved to go through it again. My second main issue, the bucket. Now don't get me wrong, I  the bucket. It has to be one of the comedic highlights of the game, but did it  need to take up 90% of the new endings?? After the first few runs and after doing the Stanley Parable 2 ending, the entire gameplay loop was pick up the bucket, then do the 20 endings you've already done before. There was no sense of exploration or discovery. Pick up bucket, do ending. Pick up bucket, do ending. It just wasn't all that engaging and when I heard that it had over double the amount of endings the original had, I was worried they would all be tied to one mechanic. I was right.Okay enough negatives. This game is funny as ♥♥♥♥. It has made me burst out in laughter more times than i can count, and the charm and wit of the original is cranked up to 10. The narrator is hilarious as always, but the visual comedy takes front and centre in some of the endings, particularly ones focusing on the bucket and Stanley (the escape pod ending comes to mind). One of my favourite jokes in the original is when you unplug the phone and the narrator plays an old timey instructional video, and I'm very glad to have seen a couple more of those in UD. The really good endings are at the same level or above that of the originals best, my personal favourite is the skip button ending, it's just so eerie and really captures exactly what I wanted in this game (its unfortunate it was played so early and was followed up with all the bucket endings- which are far less engaging), I felt myself wanting to exhaust all of the dialogue before pressing the button again, partly to hear all that I can, and partly to postpone the inevitable pressing of the button again. Hearing the narrator get more and more desperate for us to stop, and then eventually accept that there is nothing he can do to stop us, is chilling to hear him say, for him to beg us to not press it again. Both him and you know that its only a matter of time before you put your own enjoyment over his sanity. It is very similar to the red door ending in the first. You'll do  to get a new ending, be it jump off a catwalk to your death, with the narrator begging for you to stop in the back, or putting the narrator through centuries of torture, just so you don't have to suffer the same fate he does.In conclusion, The Stanley Parable: Ultra Deluxe is a great addition to the original, but sadly has too many faults for me to not be at least a bit disappointed. The comedy is just as good if not better than the original, but unfortunately it comes at the expense of the mystery and engagement that some of the endings the original would provide.

_childDocuments_.review: The Stanley Parable has always been a beautiful, witty, and profound experience- and one of my favorite gaming experiences of all time.  The Ultra Deluxe Edition has so much more to add, so much of what I loved in the original Stanley that I am not disappointed after waiting three long years for this.  This game will have you laughing, and then dead quiet in somber pondering of what it displays to you.  You can play the game, the game can play you.  You have many choices, you have no choices.  This is The Stanley Parable.
_childDocuments_.name: The Stanley Parable: Ultra Deluxe

_childDocuments_.review: Wreden, I love you. Truly.Pugh, ♥♥♥♥ off. Crows Crows Crows has tried to be Galactic Cafe ever since it disappeared. Adding the writing/improv talent of Justin Roiland in Dr. Langeskov did no favours to the lacklustre story. However, I might just be a fickle prick.I'm not sure what happened between Pugh and Wreden, or if anything happened, I wish they could make something great again. Wreden's The Beginners Guide had heart and was a touching story about artistry. Ultra Deluxe is the true embodiment of the soulless corporate nightmare the original story line portrayed. Taking the original concept that defied linear game play and creating a vacuous extension. The Stanley Parable opened my heart to great story telling in Indie Games, Ultra Deluxe drowned it in fake nacho cheese.
_childDocuments_.name: The Stanley Parable: Ultra Deluxe

_childDocuments_.review: Yes I do recommend this game simply because you most likely have never played a game like this. It's hilarious. It's worth every cent and big kudos to the man behind the voice of the Narrator. The only issue I have is that I have technically finished the game after 8.1 hours. I've achieved all endings except the World Settings ending. So how can some people have more than 50 hours of gameplay? What more are they doing? I've been everywhere, with and without the bucket. Had fun though, so that's what counts. 10/10 Bucket.
_childDocuments_.name: The Stanley Parable: Ultra Deluxe

_childDocuments_.review: From the ashes of depravity rises the phoenix of quality. How else to describe the Stanley Parable: Ultra Deluxe? Such a revolutionary step forward in the lineage of one of the most beloved video game properties of all time! The additions and changes made to this expansion will surely resonate in the annuls of history of all media ever made. It is perhaps true to say that no mistakes are forever etched in stone for the stone into which the Stanley Parable was carved has itself been transmuted offering a message of hope to those who have ever erred in their judgment. You are not beyond redemption. You may change, and you may become more so much more than you were before. If there is any message to be taken from the Stanley Parable: Ultra Deluxe it is this... What a fortune, a privilege, a joy it is to have had such an experience it leaves me hopeful that as a community - as a world there is time for us to become our greatest selves as great as we ever could dream of in out wildest, most ambitious visions for a brighter future.
_childDocuments_.name: The Stanley Parable: Ultra Deluxe

_childDocuments_.review: This is the story of how I experienced the greatest experience of all experiences of all time. When I booted up the game, I wonder where the new content is, I found one new thing and that's it. Then I did some of the endings I was familiar with, and after that I found a new door called "New Content". I was excited to see what was the new content. then I laughed as the new content was just the "Jumping Circle" because it disappointed the Narrator. Then the Narrator showed me the memory zone, which was cool to look at with the Narrator, also seeing the Serious Ending filled with sad and happiness. Then we saw the Steam Reviews of The Stanley Parable, how ironic that I am making one right now. then The Narrator made the skip button. which I continued pressing until the end of time, also hearing the Narrator being desperate to keep me away from the skip button made me feel bad, but it was the only choice I had. Seeing that the world ended and I was the only one there, was lonely sad. Then The Narrator made the Stanley Parable 2 and the BUCKET. Seeing the new title screen was so cool and nice. I did the escape pod ending with the bucket and seeing it being different was surprising as I saw Stanley gently put the bucket in the pod. I had so much fun seeing the different endings with the bucket. But then came the epilogue, It was the true ending to the Stanley Parable, as I met Settings Guy one more time. He told me that the true ending to the game that there was no ending. That's why the end is never. and it's why I can't beat the Stanley Parable. This is the story that I have come to love.
_childDocuments_.name: The Stanley Parable: Ultra Deluxe

_childDocuments_.review: I mainly bought it to support the creators for such a creative and an amazing game that they've added new content onto. I was very much playing it to interact with the narrator, hearing new dialogue, enjoying the storyline that leads up to the ending. Everything was interesting to me, and somehow, I spent roughly 8 hours on this game even though it never felt like it. I enjoyed everything about it, and I didn't really care how much I paid for it if it meant that the quality is still there even after waiting for 9 years. Kudos to Crows Crows Crows for elevating an already fantastic game, you deserve my money <3

_childDocuments_.review: I very liked the original, I think its a milestone in surreal narrative gaming.I was excited for this (of course not as a sequel), so I bought it at launch day.But I was disappointed.The positives:- Nostalgic feelings, references to community content- Well done optimizationFor the other side:- The extra content is short overall (got all endings in ~8 hours)- Has some parts that are stretched to frustration/boredom and don't have any additional meaning- A bit pricey considering the wait time- Almost no difference in graphics qualityIn summary:If you haven't played the original and this is in sale, get it.Otherwise forget it.

_childDocuments_.review: If you somehow don't know what this is: It's a meta-narrative focused walking sim with a funny narrator. Only you know if that kind of thing sounds like a good time to you.Subtract about 26 hours from my playtime because I'm a lunatic who left the game running for a whole day to get a silly achievement.I loved the HD remix (never played the og mod), and I really liked this one too, but I will say that a lot of the commentary the original offered doesn't hit as hard or hold up as well almost a decade later, just because the narrative structure and how narrative is tied to gameplay of many story-driven games has changed in that time (because of course it has), as well as the mindset of a lot of players being different. So I think that it's worth keeping in mind the cultural moment the original was made during... if you're the thinky type who likes to overthink things. You massive nerd.Still, it felt nice to jump back in and spend a little more time with the narrator, and there were some legitimately striking moments in the new content that I found to be quite powerful and engaging. Overall, though, having played the original, getting all the new stuff (and revisiting the old) felt a lot more like checking off a to-do list than active exploration teasing at the boundaries of the game and it's layout than the first one.
_childDocuments_.name: The Stanley Parable: Ultra Deluxe

_childDocuments_.review: Like so many, I enjoyed my time with the original Stanley Parable, which underscores how truly disappointed I am with its sequel. Where the first game teemed with originality, The Stanley Parable 2 is dull, uninspired, and often insulting to its fan base.Rather than expand on what made the first game enjoyable, the sequel veers off into territory nobody asked for. An infinitely deep hole? Who cares? Where are the new endings? What about enjoyable bits from The Stanley Parable 1, like the Adventure Line? Instead, we get an uninspired sidequest collecting figurines. Even this diversion feel is incomplete: collecting all the figurines gives you nothing! I must say, though, I found the bucket to be quite comforting, a welcome reprieve from the reckless and insulting creative visions.
_childDocuments_.name: The Stanley Parable: Ultra Deluxe

_childDocuments_.review: I'm feeling conflicted. I understand that the game devs wanted us to understand what it means to not want to disappoint people. There's a very deep uncertainty in remaking the same game to cater to the same audience almost a decade in advance. And I was really charmed by the little things they added in. All the uh... bucket content. And side areas that gave you a bit more time to connect with the narrator. Honestly, I'm not too sure I'm all done with the new content. I hope I'm not! It all went by so quick, and was just kinda a bummer. I'm familiar with CrowCrowsCrows using their games as a storytelling device rather than an engaging plaything, but I was hoping maybe it'd tickle my brain in ways the first time seeing it did. Of course, they understood this was going to be the case with some returning people. It's funny, I'm the exact person they envisioned. After all these years they spent on this new version, I thought maybe they were going to completely flip it. But things like this take time, all the environments and such. Especially since development started taking place during COVID season. However, even with how seemingly minor some things were, it was still a trip down memory lane. For having spent this much time, the amount this is priced at is reasonable.
_childDocuments_.name: The Stanley Parable: Ultra Deluxe

_childDocuments_.review: I love The Stanley Parable, but waiting 9 years and paying $25 for a version with only 2-3 hours of new content (a lot of which is only slightly altered endings from the original) does not sit well with me. I honestly expected after so much time in development and with the price tag discrepancy that this would be a Frog Fractions-esque surprise game that was something completely new.TL:DR If you own the original, there's simply not enough new content to justify the $25 price tag.

_childDocuments_.review: This is the story of a man named Stanley.Stanley worked for a company in a big building where he was Employee #427.Employee #427's job was simple: he sat at his desk in Room 427 and he pushed buttons on a keyboard.Orders came to him through a monitor on his desk telling him what buttons to push, how long to push them, and in what order.This is what Employee #427 did every day of every month of every year, and although others may have considered it soul rending,Stanley relished every moment that the orders came in, as though he had been made exactly for this job.And Stanley was happy.And then one day, something very peculiar happened.Something that would forever change Stanley;Something he would never quite forget.He had been at his desk for nearly an hour when he had realized not one single order had arrived on the monitor for him to follow.No one had shown up to give him instructions, call a meeting, or even say 'hi'. Never in all his years at the company had this happened, this complete isolation.Something was very clearly wrong. Shocked, frozen solid, Stanley found himself unable to move for the longest time.But as he came to his wits and regained his senses, he got up from his desk and stepped out of his office.

_childDocuments_.review: I found this game through a handful of YouTubers a couple of months ago and then it began popping up on my feed on social media platforms. I thought the characters seemed interesting, that the fact you could screw with the Narrator was a fun idea so I played some of it on a friend's account. I immediately fell in love. Not only did the Narrator's voice work to soothe most of my anxieties, even when yelling, but the very idea of the game caught my core. I've watched many playthroughs, I think I'm currently on my eleventh, and I've played the game over three times. I even went and played the original, working to get all the achievements. To say this game took over my life is an understatement but I'm so glad it did. The Endings, the Narrator and even Stanley himself are always welcome in my home. (I wouldn't have 15 tiny buckets if I didn't want the game in my brain, now would I?) I highly recommend this game to anyone who's looking for a meta and sometimes dark game.

_childDocuments_.review: This is the story of a man named Stanley.Stanley worked for a company in a big building where he was Employee #427.Employee #427's job was simple: he sat at his desk in Room 427 and he pushed buttons on a keyboard.Orders came to him through a monitor on his desk telling him what buttons to push, how long to push them, and in what order.This is what Employee #427 did every day of every month of every year, and although others may have considered it soul rending,Stanley relished every moment that the orders came in, as though he had been made exactly for this job.And Stanley was happy.And then one day, something very peculiar happened.Something that would forever change Stanley;Something he would never quite forget.He had been at his desk for nearly an hour when he had realized not one single order had arrived on the monitor for him to follow.No one had shown up to give him instructions, call a meeting, or even say 'hi'. Never in all his years at the company had this happened, this complete isolation.Something was very clearly wrong. Shocked, frozen solid, Stanley found himself unable to move for the longest time.But as he came to his wits and regained his senses, he got up from his desk and stepped out of his office.

_childDocuments_.review: The original Stanley Parable was a lovely piece of art and a really fun game. It was short but left an immense impression. Its incredibly memorable and did a lot of unique and fun things for its time. It did have its issues but those could be overlooked because what it was trying to do was so incredibly interesting. I even remember it started many debates on what video games really are and how choices matter in a video game. The original was and still is a master piece. Its a game that could evoke genuine emotions out of you with the most basic of mechanics and with some of the most iconic voice acting out there.Now nearly 10 years later the Ultra Deluxe edition came out and if you are going in blind you are probably wondering what this is. Is it a sequel? Is it a remake? What new content is there?The best way I would describe it is that its a truly unique take on a follow up game. I wouldn't use the terms sequel or remake or anything like that. If you enjoyed the original then this is a must buy, there is new content and its all incredible. If you haven't heard of the Stanley parable before then I also can safely say this is the best way to experience the original game nowadays and I highly recommend you try it. The Stanley Parable has done it again and created another absolute masterpiece.The only thing I will say is that Jack Black becoming the Elden lord really shocked me.

_childDocuments_.review: The Stanley Parable is a work of art. The Stanley Parable Ultra Deluxe expands upon that. _childDocuments_.review: Honestly I was unsure about this game when I was playing through it. I started out going through all of the original routes that I knew and slowly making it to new content. But once I completed all the original content I felt like I could move on to the new. And I found so much enjoyment in this new content. It felt like there was so much to explore and see. The game kept dragging me in with its gags and had me laughing from each one. I felt fear when I experienced something unsettling. I felt a wide array of emotions playing this game and I recommend everyone to play this experience.Pros:- The game is more than twice the size of the original- updates to the original content (with little to no loss)- The story feels more enjoyable to play through- so many easter eggs and things to findCons:- there isn't even more to enjoy (it is still a good amount of content)- some feelings of motion sickness when playing the new content (hopefully they add a setting for bobbing)- Some of the graphics feel old (may be intentional)When exploring some of the new content it felt like I was comparing it to the old content (which may be intentional). With this it made me examine the new content and made me compare how much I enjoyed it to the original. For example I felt that the length of the new content was sometimes shorter than the original.Suggestions:- Would love to purchase a soundtrack for the game as there are some new banger tracks- Ability to stop bobbing so that motion sickness is minimal- I'd love to

_childDocuments_.review: This is the story of a man named Stanley. Stanley worked for a company in a big building where he was employee number 427. Employee number 427’s job was simple: he sat at his desk in room 427 and he pushed buttons on a keyboard. Orders came to him through a monitor on his desk, telling him what buttons to push, how long to push them, and in what order. This is what employee 427 did every day of every month of every year, and although others might have considered it soul rending, Stanley relished every moment that the orders came in, as though he had been made exactly for this job. And Stanley was happy. And then one day, something very peculiar happened, something that would forever change Stanley, something he would never quite forget. He had been at his desk for nearly an hour when he realized that not one, single order had arrived on the monitor for him to follow. No one had shown up to give him instructions, call a meeting, or even say hi. Never in all his years at the company had this happened, this complete isolation. Something was very clearly wrong. Shocked, frozen solid, Stanley found himself unable to move for the longest time, but as he came to his wits and regained his senses, he got up from his desk and stepped out of his office.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm kinda disappointed, ngl. The game starts off good, at first seeming "normal", only to show a door to "new content", that's just a joke to get the narrator pissed off enough to show off "The Stanley Parable 2", which at first, I thought was the big twist of the game: you go into it expecting an expansion, but get a full-on sequel. Oh, how I underestimated the writer's level of irony. The features exhibit has some nice gags to it, but then, when the narrator decides to implement them into the game, it's just... The Stanley Parable 1. But now there's balloons in the office, and you can pick up a bucket that changes the endings. The new endings all have new voice acting, and new jokes, with varying levels of changed visuals, but it's just... not very funny? Or insightful? Instead of commenting on the nature of choice and player agency in videogames, or anything else meta about game design, it's all just... bucket jokes. The bucket is your friend. The bucket is the villain. The bucket isn't real. The bucket is the universe. You want to fornicate with the bucket. That's about it. According to "The Beginner's Guide", one of Wreden's previous works, he doesn't seem to like the thought of video essayists psychoanalyzing game devs and writers through their games all that much. So I guess in this game, he just decided to give them nothing interesting to talk about, so they couldn't comment on it anymore? Would've been meta if it was acknowledged in-game, but it wasn't, so I can't really give him credit for that, and even if it was, the price tag still stings, even with the 33% discount for owning the first game.I can't say I recommend this. I'm aware that "expansions and sequels are derivative trash meant to scam players through their nostalgia" is a big talking point in the pre-bucket portion of the game, and this game is kind of an intentional demonstration of that, and I'm not even against charging money for it, since it obviously took some extra effort to make, but charging THIS much? Did they really need to scam players in real life just to tell them about how bad scams and cash grabs are?
_childDocuments_.name: The Stanley Parable: Ultra Deluxe

_childDocuments_.review: Holy smokes, this game is genius as all get out.The game is very humourous and also provide a subtle yet snarky commentary on video game choices and culture. Kevin Brighting nails his role as the Narrator once again. And the new stuff? On par with the original game. The Bucket was my favourite new character. They are the key to unlocking what I call a "Side B" to the story. (Or a "Side Bucket" if you wanna be more clever about it.) Overall, this game is fantastic. I highly recommend it and this game earns my Pixeling Seal of Approval!

_childDocuments_.review: Finally finished the game and I'm really glad I decided to return to it. I played initially the game 90 minutes and left it sitting it for a year. The biggest problem of the Ultra Deluxe is that the new content takes time to catch on. Most of the negative reviews are people that (like me) decided to stop playing the game after hour or two, but they never returned. For their consolation there is achievement for returning after 10 years.Ultra deluxe is a very weird kind of animal. It very much plays with player's expectations on it being additional contented slapped on the original game. If you don't want to revisit Stanley Parable, this isn't game for you. At the beginning Ultra Deluxe plays exactly like the original game. Then it starts shouting with neon signs "The new content!". Those players that didn't spent time trying to find more obscure endings of the original Stanley Parable might get fooled believing "THIS IS THE NEW CONTENT" is the new content and then stop playing. "The new content path" however deviates and takes very unexpected directions in really over the top Stanley Parable ways and has over the top progression. The original portion of the game has also been changed in some surprising ways and some of things that would have been cool to work in original game, now actually work. What I'm trying to say that the Ultra Deluxe branches wildly in the true Stanley Parable fashion. I spent playing 8 hours Ultra deluxe and maybe 3 hours actually playing the original game (additional 2 hours of original game were failed macroing of a notorious minigame). The new content is there, it just at the same time isn't where you'd expect it being and at the same time it is exactly where you'd expect it being.

_childDocuments_.review: Never in my entire life have I ever felt as much love and compassion for anything, or anyone, as I do for the Bucket full of pure love, joy, and happiness, that this game provides me with. _childDocuments_.review: This game builds on and improves the original Stanley Parable.While I thought it was witty and had something to say, I didn't really care that much about the original game. I found it hard to follow along with the authorial intent. I responded to it, paradoxically, as another piece of "content "-- I closed the game after reaching the "credits" and moved on with my life. The Stanley Parable Ultra Deluxe, on the other hand, has me actively engaged and discussing its messages. It's a delightful croissant of self-critique, reflection on the video game art form and the role of narrative in general, as well as a piece of art itself.I recommend playing this game.

_childDocuments_.review: I was a huge fan of the original game.  It was innovative, interesting, and had a great sense of humour.  The meta-narrative was interesting and unlike anything I'd seen in gaming before.  It was truly something different.The "Ultra Deluxe" version is... more of the same.  The same game with a handful of extra stuff tacked on.  Which itself wouldn't necessarily be so bad, but the extra content really doesn't break any new ground.  Where the original Stanley Parable was cleverly self-aware, Ultra Deluxe is irritatingly self-indulgent at times.  Where the original was short, quick, and never worse out its welcome (except maybe for the baby game); the update is uneven and at times even tedious.  It's telling that the overwhelming majority of the positive comments so far are essentially just memes and quotes, not saying anything of substance about the game itself.The bulk of the "New Content" part of the game purports to comment on the changing world of gaming, criticisms of the original game, and the predictable nature and desires of gamers -- as exemplified by its new collection quest.  But rather than providing any real insightful commentary, it comes off as merely encouraging and exploiting them.The absolute worst part is the interminable diatribe against the previous games' critics.  Rather than addressing the criticism in good faith, it ends up merely creating a straw-man version of said criticism, and then going on an interminable tirade, utterly lacking in humour and bordering on on mean-spirited at times.  I nearly quit the game at that point, but wanted to give it a fair shake and evaluate everything available, so I could ensure that I didn't miss something that really set the new version apart from the original.  So I completed every pathway and got every ending (again, except the baby game, because I was not about to sit through it for four hours, and didn't feel like looking up the cheats), including all the new versions of the original endings (not going to say what these are or how to get them, to avoid spoilers).Aside from the protracted whinging about fans and fan-demands, there wasn't anything here that stood out as significantly different, thematically or philosophically, from the original game.  It felt less like an extended exploration of the themes and topics of the first game, and more like a cynical cash-grab pandering to the sorts of gamers who want to play the same game over and over and over, instead of exploring anything truly new and innovative.If you haven't played the original Stanley Parable, then a lot of the "new content" in this one isn't going to make much sense, since it's mostly meta-references to the original game; but it's still worth playing if you can sit through (or skip through, since that option is now available) the tirade in the middle.  If you have played the original, then you're not really going to find anything particularly ground-breaking here.  If you're the sort of person who enjoys games that are little more than re-hashes of games you've already played... well this is the game for you, I guess.  Either way, if you do plan on playing it, do yourself a favour and wait for it to go on sale at a deep discount.

_childDocuments_.review: From the ashes of depravity rises the phoenix of quality. How else to describe The Stanley Parable: Ultra Deluxe? Such a revolutionary step forward in the lineage of one of the most beloved video game properties of all time! The additions and changes made to this expansion will surely resonate in the annals of the history of all media ever made. It is perhaps true to say that no mistakes are forever etched in stone for the stone into which The Stanley Parable was carved has itself been transmuted offering a message of hope to those who have ever erred in their judgement. You are not beyond redemption. You may change, and you may become more so much more than you were before. If there is any message to be taken from The Stanley Parable: Ultra Deluxe it is this... What a fortune, a privilege, a joy it is to have had such an experience it leaves me hopeful that as a community - as a world there is time for us to become our greatest selves as great as we ever could dream of in our wildest, most ambitious visions for a brighter future.

_childDocuments_.review: As a person who first consumed it when I was a child, seeing this game come back in any way shape or form is amazing. I, even knowing that I'll never get the years-long achievements, will replay every few years just to go back to familiar territory. Now after years of the same dialogue, I finally get berated by my favorite narrator! I also loved the environments in the game, I feel it's easy to notice the larger tricks and fun voice-over lines but it's obvious that over the years these creators have grown. The humor for many might be much, but I grew attached as it felt like a natural place for this story to go. I know I am missing things but I have my favorite endings already! Don't be afraid to invest if you're a long-time fan, and try to go in as blind as possible! Thank you so much for bringing the world so much love back to life!

_childDocuments_.review: This is the story of a man named Stanley. Stanley worked for a company in a big building where he was employee # 427. Employee # 427’s job was simple: he sat at his desk in room 427 and he pushed buttons on a keyboard. Orders came to him through a monitor on his desk, telling him what buttons to push, how long to push them, and in what order. This is what employee 427 did every day of every month of every year, and although others might have considered it soul rending, Stanley relished every moment that the orders came in, as though he had been made exactly for this job. And Stanley was happy. And then one day, something very peculiar happened, something that would forever change Stanley, something he would never quite forget. He had been at his desk for nearly an hour when he realized that not one, single order had arrived on the monitor for him to follow. No one had shown up to give him instructions, call a meeting, or even say hi. Never in all his years at the company had this happened, this complete isolation. Something was very clearly wrong. Shocked, frozen solid, Stanley found himself unable to move for the longest time, but as he came to his wits and regained his senses, he got up from his desk and stepped out of his office.

_childDocuments_.review: ..What exactly is The Stanley Parable: Ultra Deluxe? This game, if it is a game, is both nothing and everything I could have wanted from a re-release of The Stanley Parable. Playing this game, I had no idea what to expect, and by the time I finished playing the game I had no idea what I had done. Is there a goal here? Is there an ending? Who is Stanley really? Was this here before? This game will make you ask all of these questions, and answer every single one of them with another question. This game never ends, much like this review which has already far outstayed it's welcome. Play this game, experience it, really take it all in and maybe you will find happiness through it. I know I did...But I realise that this review still hasn't answered the question - why would I recommend this game to others? The answer is simple really - it's a piece of art, it's humour shines through as bright as the shine of a finely polished bucket, it's craftsmanship comparable to that of only the most durable bucket, it's very existence is in fact comparable to a very well constructed bucket! "That makes no sense!" you think, "Why are so many of these reviews talking about buckets?! Have these people gone mad?!"The answer to that question lies within the game itself, for who are we if not the beings through which the game can tell its narrative? This game is the game that plays you, and by the time you are finished with it, you too will tell others of your experience with it, your opinions, your thoughts and feelings, and maybe even write a review of your own. There is no choice, this is the cycle that will repeat endlessly until the heat death of the universe.But in the end, there is still that question, the question of..

_childDocuments_.review: This is the first time I played any version of the Stanley Parable. This game is pretty fun, but it gets far too meta. It's mediocre, after awhile it feels like just another drop in the bucket. At first there are all these different things to do, then the number of things start to shrink, then there is less to do, and finding the stuff to do new things gets much harder and more tedious. This is not a game I would put on my bucket list. Sometimes the game play gets so tedious it's like going back and forth filling and carrying buckets of water.  There should be a run button but there isn't, the normal speed is pretty fast, still there should be a button to go faster. Also the game is unfinished there was this feature that involves a button, and it didn't work the way it was supposed to, considering they had all this time to work on it, I was deeply disappointed, deep as a very large bucket. All in all, it's a pretty good experience (not a great game though). I would wait for a sale, I wouldn't spend a bucket load of money on this. It's not like it's a bucket of dung, the game has some good things going for it. I will say it's overrated, so lower your expectations and view the bucket as half full (of something good, not dung).

_childDocuments_.review: The Stanley Parable was a landmark of 2013- it lambasted and parodied the gaming landscape of the day. Without giving too much away (as I am sure some people reading this have still not played the original), The Stanley Parable was, at it's core, about challenging the illusions of choice in game design. To that end- and, because the original game still exists in a mostly untouched capacity (with a few minor updates), The Stanley Parable still contains everything it once did, even if the message no longer hits as well- because, unlike in 2013, there is some meaningful choice in video games of the 2022 era. That is where the Ultra Deluxe version comes in. It once again has a statement to say about the games industry (which I think you can probably guess from the trailer), and it does so in a way that, if you enjoyed the 2013 release of The Stanley Parable, will probably be meaningful to you. Plus, I think you get a discount on this version anyway.If you never played The Stanley Parable, buy this version. If you have played The Stanley Parable, buy this version.

_childDocuments_.review: Let me be clear: This is not a cash-grab re-release of the original game with just a few more endings, it really is a re-imagining. I own the original game, and I am very happy with my purchase of this one.Like the original, this is a game best played with no spoilers, so I won't give any here. I just invite you to remember how you felt the first time you played the original - unable to fully grasp the game's fleeting narrative structure, trying to find footing within the story, surprised and delighted by the subversion of expectation. If you're anything like me, this version of the game will reignite the same sense of wonder that captured you nearly a decade ago.They really explored every possible narrative theme in this, so I couldn't imagine them making another follow-up. With this version, the series now feels satisfyingly complete.The Stanley Parable: Ultra Deluxe manages to take the original Stanley Parable, a game about nothing, and flesh it out into a much richer, much more ambitious game about nothing. And the Narrator is with you for every step of this terrible, beautiful, dumb, excellent non-journey.

_childDocuments_.review: The Stanley Parable is like an episode of Black Mirror. It's basically the "phone bad" message constantly beaten into your mushy brain. The entire point of the game is that video games are a waste of time. Almost as much of a waste of time as it was for me to write a review of this pointless game and how much of a waste of time it was for you to read my review while you could be doing literally anything else that would be considered semi-productive. But the narrator will tell you that over and over again while you keep restarting, effectively just pissing away your life in front of a computer in a futile attempt to "beat" the game or something while you actual life moves on around you absently.So, yes, I recommend playing it.

Now I mentioned that the game wouldn't be completely worth the price it is at and the reason for that is... the old endings are still very much there and still quite a big part in most of the game. The new content that was made for the game was honestly mind blowing and a super fun experience (blew 3.5h away when I first booted the game). I will still say that the old endings sure did bring some smiles back to the face and some very nice memories happened during play time. I do wish there could be a bit more for the price it is at and therefor is another reason I cannot recommend the game at the current price. although the price is high the game is still very much enjoyable, makes someone like myself laugh (I can be quite hard to make laugh) and spend bunch of time on the game without even realizing how long that i've been playing. If you never played the original give this one a shot. If you did play the original playing this would still be amazing though if you can get it for a bit cheaper price than what it is at I would definitely do that.

_childDocuments_.review: It may seem weird and even greedy of the developers to try and sell you The Stanley Parable again. But let me assure you - well, okay, they kind of are. But! Not only are you getting The Stanley Parable, AGAIN - because let's face it, the original game is a classic that deserves to be bought twice - but there's all new, ULTRA DELUXE stuff! What kind of stuff? Well, I mean, it's pretty ultra, and deluxe, too. But what if I told you, this game is also The Stanley Parable 2? Well, I mean, it's not... But what if it was? Wouldn't you want to play that yourself?
_childDocuments_.name: The Stanley Parable: Ultra Deluxe

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a lot of fun and very funny. I needed a break from shooter type video games and this game was perfect. I could replay it and had so many choices and fun things to do and see, to me this game is truly amazing, and I would say even a master piece game. I want to make a video game and this game has truly inspired me and shown me a lot about choice and action.  10/10 do recommend.
_childDocuments_.name: The Stanley Parable: Ultra Deluxe

_childDocuments_.review: Listen, if you like this game, that's fine. Don't let my dumb opinion ruin your day.For me, I thought this game would have way more content. new places, routes, and just other fun things. But instead, I was given 1 big message about how "sequel bad". Games can be more about messages then being a game. Example, Undertale, while the gameplay is pretty crap, the message it sends is really good. What makes it different then TSPUD, It's not $25. Stanely Parable was a really good analysis on giving the player freedom. While the idea of looking at why sequels can ruin games is cool. I felt that they just took TSP, and made it have a bucket, and a new message.I get that it's the "point" That the narrator is just ruining his own work trying to make it better.  But I felt like this idea could've been expanded on. Since the game now runs on Unity, (please do correct me if I'm wrong!) it could've been the narrator turning TSP into other genres of games. Trying to appease different audiences, only to push away the people who loved his work. But instead, it's just TSP, but better graphics, and you have a bucket.For me, the biggest problem is the price. I know that making a game is hard. Adding all the new lines, and endings for the bucket was not easy to make. But as a player, I felt like I was just playing a joke. They advertised it as this big expansion to the game. Then make fun of the idea, and just reskin the base game.Like I said, if you love this game, keeping doing it! I can't stop you! But for me, this game was really disappointing.
_childDocuments_.name: The Stanley Parable: Ultra Deluxe

_childDocuments_.review: Incredibly funny, creative, satirical and overpriced. The first game was already a little gem but this deluxe edition includes more to see and find while having a lot to add to it’s original themes. People who played the original should wait for a sale as I don’t think it’s ENOUGH to justify it, but for newcomers it’s absolutely worth.
_childDocuments_.name: The Stanley Parable: Ultra Deluxe

_childDocuments_.review: My honest review of Stanley Parable: Ultra DeluxeFrom the ashes of depravity rises the phoenix of quality. How else to describe The Stanley Parable: Ultra Deluxe? Such a revolutionary step forward in the lineage of one of the most beloved video game properties of all time! The additions and changes made to this expansion will surely resonate in the annals of the history of all media ever made.It is perhaps true to say that no mistakes are forever etched in stone, for the stone into which The Stanley Parable was carved has itself been transmuted, offering a message of hope to those who have ever erred in their judgement. You are not beyond redemption. You may change, and you may become more, so much more than you were before.If there is any message to be taken from The Stanley Parable: Ultra Deluxe, it is this: What a fortune, a privilege, a joy it is to have had such an experience. It leaves me hopeful that as a community - as a world - There is time for us to become our greatest selves, as great as we ever could dream of in our wildest, most ambitious visions for a brighter future.
_childDocuments_.name: The Stanley Parable: Ultra Deluxe

_childDocuments_.review: The Stanley Parable: Ultra Deluxe is a mysterious, ominous, multiplex of conundrums that really make you think about the perspectives of the reality around us. The intrinsic desire to find every ending, toggle every button and door knob, while our beloved narrator guides Stanley to a higher plane of existence. It also questions our profound understanding of inanimate objects and their importance to society. Thus, we must evolve to be at peace and harmony with said inanimate object and accept our dismal fates in whatever this short, quaint and mysterious life we live. For the affordable price of 35 dollars from Hobbington, one can experience not just a game, but a work of art.

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly wish there was a "Neutral" option when reviewing a game.If you haven't played the 2013 The Stanley Parable this is definitely worth $25 buy it and play it!If you have played the original game, it is not worth the $25 and you should wait for a sale.The game itself is basically a Copy-Paste of the original with a couple of extra endings that I honestly had to Google to find all of them.  It does add extra twists to the original endings witch is neat, but it seemed like (for the price if you've played the original) kinda lazy when it comes to "New Endings", witch explains the "Not a Sequel" title that it was given.  However the game kinda treats itself like a Sequel, and kinda parodies the idea of Shameless cash grab Unoriginal Sequels (Witch was probably the point).This game almost seems like a Re-release for Console players with added content to make it worth while.NOT saying this is a bad game, quite the contrary.  I'm saying is that this game isn't a Sequel, and is not worth $25 if you have the original.  It is a nice touch to the original game that rewards all those Console dedicated players that were waiting for a console release.As a sequel, it would have benefited with endings that go along with the original ones.  More or less "extra branches", like that "Third Door" idea from the original.TLDR; Good game, definitely recommend... But NOT for $25 if you have the original.  This game is not a Sequel, but a twist on the original.Edit; Spelling

_childDocuments_.review: I am very disappointed with this game, there is very little new content, there is 20 new endings, is what is marketed. But about 15 of them are just the same endings that are in the original game but you pick the bucket up at the beginning, this felt honestly more like DLC for the original game rather than a sequel. And the progression is weird and most of the new endings were bad or incomplete. They either were too similar to other endings or, you could only get them once, the way that they are originally played. The game feels like you are progressing towards something like a bigger ending. Also they gags were all terrible except the bucket but that got old quick. If you haven’t played the originally game I would recommend this. Honestly the game is great. But there is just not enough to make it worth it if you have the original game.TL:DR if you have the original don’t buy this but I recommend if you don’t have the original

But despite this major downside, the game is still totally worth your money. Also buckets now included.

_childDocuments_.review: My name is Walter Hartwell White. I live at 308 Negra Arroyo Lane, Albuquerque, New Mexico, 87104. This is my confession. If you're watching this tape, I'm probably dead– murdered by my brother-in-law, Hank Schrader. Hank has been building a meth empire for over a year now, and using me as his chemist. Shortly after my 50th birthday, he asked that I use my chemistry knowledge to cook methamphetamine, which he would then sell using connections that he made through his career with the DEA. I was... astounded. I... I always thought Hank was a very moral man, and I was particularly vulnerable at the time – something he knew and took advantage of. I was reeling from a cancer diagnosis that was poised to bankrupt my family. Hank took me in on a ride-along and showed me just how much money even a small meth operation could make. And I was weak. I didn't want my family to go into financial ruin, so I agreed. Hank had a partner, a businessman named Gustavo Fring. Hank sold me into servitude to this man. And when I tried to quit, Fring threatened my family. I didn't know where to turn. Eventually, Hank and Fring had a falling-out. Things escalated. Fring was able to arrange – uh, I guess... I guess you call it a "hit" – on Hank, and failed, but Hank was seriously injured. And I wound up paying his medical bills, which amounted to a little over $177,000. Upon recovery, Hank was bent on revenge. Working with a man named Hector Salamanca, he plotted to kill Fring. The bomb that he used was built by me, and he gave me no option in it. I have often contemplated suicide, but I'm a coward. I wanted to go to the police, but I was frightened. Hank had risen to become the head of the Albuquerque DEA. To keep me in line, he took my children. For three months, he kept them. My wife had no idea of my criminal activities, and was horrified to learn what I had done. I was in hell. I hated myself for what I had brought upon my family. Recently, I tried once again to quit, and in response, he gave me this. [Walt points to the bruise on his face left by Hank in "Blood Money."] I can't take this anymore. I live in fear every day that Hank will kill me, or worse, hurt my family. All I could think to do was to make this video and hope that the world will finally see this man for what he really is.

_childDocuments_.review: What can I say about The Stanley Parable: Ultra Deluxe edition that hasn't already been said? It is a genuine delight to see a game so lovingly crafted, so self-aware and showing respect of its audience within what is otherwise a sea of mediocrity. Kevan Brighting's sublime narration is as rich as ever and the writing has stayed just as fresh. I lost count of the number of times I laughed out loud in this game which reminds you that a) things are never as they seem and b) you never really had much choice at all.Well you'll have to play it yourself to find out more as the less you know about it, the better the experience. If you have never even heard of Stanley or Narrator before, you will love it. And if you have played the original, you will love it just a little bit more.

_childDocuments_.review: My name is Phantasmagoria. P-h-a-n-t-a-s-m-a-g-o-r-i-a.Brief synopsis of the joke:This is a joke about the game "Stanley Parable: Ultra Deluxe. The very first choice of Stanley Parable is between two doors. The narrator clearly states "When Stanley came to a set of open doors, he entered the door on his left." If Stanley goes through the right door despite that, plus knowing it wasn't the correct way, he would be subverting expectations. The joke is Stanley reviewing the game on Steam, in which he presses "no" on the question "Do you recommend this game?", even thought he would, indeed, recommend it, since he enjoyed it and played it for hours; thus subverting the expectations once again. He thinks, "Just like the time I went through the right door!", this thought pointing out the similarity. You are supposed to laugh after the thought is delivered.P-h-a-n-t-a-s-m-a-g-o-r-i-aStanley opened Steam to review the game Stanley Parable: Ultra Deluxe. _childDocuments_.review: The Stanley Parable: Ultra Deluxe is a game whose joke is upon the player. By buying the game-- you have already fulfilled the punchline, but you won't  realize that at first. The Meta fictional Ruminations on the idea of Choice, our sense of Individualism against a cold, claustrophobic-- even frightening environment, and the intrinsic impossibilities to make a truly open game as a video game is, by it's nature, undeniably a linear experience: are set to the side in favor of satirizing the Human Desire to hang onto the past as long as possible, to add as much as you can to your dearest memories in the hope of extending those as long as you possibly can. To franchise your dearest creation in the hopes of seeing it flourish forever. But the ultimate message is that the past cannot live forever. The present always comes. And with the present? The future follows. You can't flourish in the past forever, no matter how hard you try. And the Stanley Parable: Ultra Deluxe brings that home in a subtle, nuanced sort of fashion. The New Content added is frivolous and satirical of trends that plague the modern gaming industry incessantly-- from Collectibles with no reward to them to mechanics that, at best, slightly alter the already existent game in basic, parodist ways.And in the end? The only way to win is to quit. The end is never the end, after-all.But that's the ultimate joke. A joke on both the player, as well as the entire industry. And I cannot recommend it highly enough.

_childDocuments_.review: Well... I did enjoy most of the time I spent on this game, but I don't see a single reason to play it again. Ever.So why the negative review then?Because you're basically just buying a ticket to see what all these strangely intriguing inside jokes and 5-star reviews saying "don't read any reviews" are about.Here's a "SPOILER" for you who (like me) never played the original before:It's one of those "artsy" games, which usually rely on beautiful scenes and captivating storytelling (via a narrator or written text) to fill up the void left by the minimal amount of possible interactions implemented withing the game for the player to actually "play" the game. As such, TSB can only be considered somewhat unique in it's way of relying on jokes and the silliness of the game itself instead of deep, immersive storytelling....Now, I'm not saying that you shouldn't do that. It's just another genre, of which some people like and some people don't.It's just that I've been a gamer for over 30 years now, and I still remember the times when spending 20$ on a video game was such a big investment, that I could realistically expect to have a new game twice a year (birthday and Christmas).And the main reason I always preferred games over movies, was that in video games my interactions had an impact within the game world. In TSB, you're interactions are basically reduced to which doorway you walk through, and only thing you can do besides that, is to hunt hidden monologues from the narrator by pressing the "interact" key on everything you see.In the end, TSB's game loop is no more than going through all the possible options in an interactive movie.Like I said, I did enjoy it while it was interesting. But as far as I'm concerned, you ain't paying for (or actually playing) a video game.

_childDocuments_.review: For previous Stanley Parable players: (Without spoilers) There's certainly a fair amount more to discover that warrants some more time with Stanley, with some changes to the original routes as well as new pathways to explore.As I was revisiting Stanley after a long absence, I felt this was worth the full purchase (with limited time discount for owning the previous iteration).However, if you've recently been through the 2013 version, you may want to hold on for a sale as there will be some repetition. ---------For those that have NOT previously experience the Stanley Parable:You're unlikely to feel like you have missed anything by "skipping" to this version.The beauty of the Stanley Parable is in the exploration of possible outcomes and seeing where your choices take you: "What would have happened if I had done this, or Not done that?". Stick with it and it can be quite the hellish rollercoaster; going around and around, each time a little different ("Was that Desk always there?"... "Was that phone always ringing?"). Alongside excellent dark humour that would be well at home in the Portal series, it also manages to be quite a poignant experience; with moments of philosophical introspection and some interesting commentary of gaming as a medium thrown in alongside odd and disturbing outcomes in the many possible "endings". I've found this difficult to stop playing...This Sequel of sorts is very self aware and leans into the fourth wall breaking with gusto for those that enjoy that style of humour.Great for those who enjoy exploration, mystery and puzzle solving.

_childDocuments_.review: I have always been someone who wants to go the "wrong" way first in games. When I sense that a game is trying to usher me down a particular path, to get me to run from left to right or maybe to charge straight ahead, I need to satisfy my instinct to go against the grain, to explore, to see what the designers have put back the other way. Sometimes I find a 1-up or a collectible stashed away to reward me for my intrepid behavior. At other times, my explorations are rewarded only by the crushing disappointment of running up against an invisible wall. Whatever I find or don't find, my action is a manifestation of my desire to exert some independence, to make my own choices within a system that severely limits my options and encourages certain, specific behaviors.I think of The Stanley Parable as a sort of video game analogue for Charlie Kaufman and Spike Jonze's brilliant film Adaptation, which gently mocked the ways in which so many films manipulate audiences with formulaic plot twists and situations in which characters learn huge life lessons, while simultaneously moving me with its formulaic plot twists and situations in which characters learned huge life lessons. The Stanley Parable is both a richly stimulating commentary on the nature of choice in games (and in other systems, too, like our workplaces and our families) and a game that offers some of the most enjoyable, surprising, and rewarding choices I've ever been confronted with in a game. Going the wrong way has never felt so right.(Joke implied.)

_childDocuments_.review: Context: A friend of mine gave this to me as a Christmas gift and ask for an in-depth review and analysis to be complete 2 days from when I received it. This is the byproduct of that request and I thought I would also post it here.The Stanley Parable: Ultra Deluxe In Review.An Analysis & ReviewOpening up this document I would like to state that I received as a gift from a dear friend. However, I will be taking this fact into consideration when assessing the game in question. This is also NOT a spoiler free review. Additionally, I am judging this game by itself and not in comparison to the original as I have not played The Stanley Parable.The Stanley Parable: Ultra Deluxe is one of the greatest pieces of media I have ever had the opportunity to consume. From the gameplay to the story, the way it’s presented and the way it functions is absolutely unique and I have played next to nothing like it. Even the games I have to compare it to fall flat compared to The Stanley Parable: Ultra Deluxe. It is, in my eyes, a one-of-a-kind game that I believe almost everyone should have the pleasure of playing blind.Gameplay.The gameplay of The Stanley Parable: Ultra Deluxe involves two major characters; the titular Stanley and the Narrator that both narrates Stanley’s (the players) actions and also instructs him on where to go. at heart is a walking simulator in which you walk through a repeating environment that changes as you play through the game. On a first time playthrough, the player is told the story of Stanley. Stanley is an office worker who is given instructions on a monitor of buttons to press on a keyboard, how long to push each button and in what order the buttons should be pressed. However, one day Stanley notices something and the Narrator points this out to the player, noticing that all of Stanley’s coworkers are gone. After an hour not experienced by the player, Stanley gets up from his desk and begins to investigate.The office that Stanley works in changes randomly through resets of the game and completion of endings, with random rooms appearing, corridors being shaped differently, scattered papers could be everywhere. It’s all something that a player could easily not pay any mind to if strictly focussed on the gameplay. Games often have easter eggs that can only appear due to random or luck based circumstances. The whole of The Stanley Parable: Ultra Deluxe however is essentially altered by random aspects and in some parts of the game, procedural generation. Simply leaving the office each time can lend a different experience to the beginning of each repeat of the story. Let’s say a group of people were to play this game, each person completing the game once. Each player could have a different beginning office, could make different choices and could very possibly each complete the game in a different way. However most players will reach the same point at least once.The player will very likely come to a room with two open doors, in which the Narrator guides Stanley to go through the left door. This scenario is what inspired the game as a whole, where the developers thought about a game in which the player had the option to defy the game’s narration. Almost everything that happens in the game stems off of a choice that involves picking one of these two doors. To listen, or to defy.The game does have a canonical ending, in which Stanley leaves his office, goes to speak to his boss who is also missing, finds a hidden passage, discovers that he is being mind controlled and the mind control facility using him as a subject is built under the office he works in, shuts the facility down and becomes a free man. However, upon leaving the facility, Stanley is then placed back in his office as if he just started the game fresh. This is where the bulk of the game happens. The player is given free reign to test what they want, from defying the Narrator's actions to glitching out of bounds, to even killing themselves in game. This aspect is where the story and the game intertwine incredibly well.Story.To be blunt, I cannot explain the story of The Stanley Parable: Ultra Deluxe. It’s a meta commentary, an argument, a comedic routine, a tragedy and a story of becoming your own self, all wrapped into a Groundhog Day-esque repeating scene that changes through gameplay. The story is influenced by small things, such as Stanley entering the boss’s office and entering in a code for a secret passage before the Narrator has given it to him. Do this enough times and the Narrator will open the secret passage automatically, sigh and disappointedly say to Stanley to hurry up with it. However, much larger aspects affect the story as well. Doing a specific achievement gives access to the New Content section of the game, which shows sarcastically small changes that have been added to The Stanley Parable: Ultra Deluxe. However after beating the game, when coming back to this area it will be missing and will be replaced by the New New Content area, where the Narrator, fed up with the “lack of content” in the Ultra Deluxe edition of the game, chooses to create a sequel to the original game. From that point on, The Stanley Parable: Ultra Deluxe is then referred to in game as “The Stanley Parable 2”. As well as some new content will be available to the player from then on in Stanley’s office, with balloons in the office and the game changing Reassurance Bucket being added.The story is different depending on which ending the player follows. In some cases the Narrator is Stanley’s Enemy, in others he wishes to be Stanley’s Friend. The whole game can be a delusion in the crazy mind of Stanley, or it could be a game entirely made up by the Narrator for Stanley. As far as I’m aware, there is no way to form a coherent story that incorporates each ending. But this is not a bad thing. I personally really enjoy the fact that the game can tell so many different stories in one title, without needing to find a convoluted loophole for the stories to all align. Conclusion.The Stanley Parable: Ultra Deluxe is an incredible piece of content that is unlike any other in its class. So reviewing this game compared to its peers is difficult for me. A game with a similar story that I could compare it to is Twelve Minutes. However, I found that game confusing, uninteresting and overall disappointing. So by comparison I would regard The Stanley Parable: Ultra Deluxe a lot higher. As well as I mentioned in my disclaimer, I can’t rate this game based on a remaster as I never played the original. However while researching the original game, I found out that an ending was made inaccessible from the transition from the Source Engine to Unity. The Serious Ending originally could be obtained by using the Source Engine console and enabling cheats. Since Unity doesn’t have a console, this ending is unobtainable. Personally, I would’ve liked to see this ending still put in place in some way. Perhaps altering the game files while playing could trigger this ending as a failsafe. However this is a nitpick at most.Overall I would recommend The Stanley Parable: Ultra Deluxe strongly. I personally found it to be one of the best gameplay experiences I have ever played and I absolutely think it is well worth the money the developers ask for. Although this review may have taken away some of the surprises the game holds, I would still recommend it as even if you know what each ending is and how to achieve it, I almost guarantee you’ll still find something unexpected.

I recommend it, for nothing else than the fantastic 10 minute rant from the Narrator about the Ultra Deluxe being a cheap scam made to get a quick buck off of a beloved masterpiece.
