_childDocuments_.review: I kinda can't believe how people made a big deal about the mangled baby resulting from a freaky threesome between CoD, Half Life and Halo back in the day. Cry Engine was and is still impressive to look at yes, but without decent boss and level design all you end up with is some semi-enjoyable moments in a sandbox-ish island at the first half and just unprecedented and almost completely un-enjoyable chaotic warfare at the latter half of the game. Like, I couldn't even enjoy the supersuit abilities because of weirdly unresponsive controls. Additionally, couldn't even use most of the cool abilities because the game does a rather terrible job of explaining them anyways and sometimes they outright don't work for some reason, albeit excluding some very basic ones. Then I also think the game fails to deliver the whole supersuit aspect as well since you frequently go from feeling like you are the single most feeble being on earth at one moment to feeling like the indestructable super soldier the next, depending on what the game decides at any given moment. While I inititally thought there would be certain upgrades that could fix that uneven dynamic at the early stages of the game, it turned out that that wasn't the case unfortunately. So yeah, I am still surprised about how this (or at least the original) is considered a  according to many people and critics alike because I think it is way too scuffed be put on any all-timers lists.To summerize, when I decided to play this the main thing that worried me was the optimization but the game was supposed to be a grade-a classic so it'd worth the hassle in theory, yet after some minor tweakings to get the game running smoothly on my medium level system I just ended up getting frustrated with the game itself instead. I did encounter some glitches here and there but nothing game breaking; catching some dude t-posing out of the corner of my eye was the worst it got honestly and sadly I learned to tolerate stuff like that thanks to the state of modern gaming. At the end of the day even though I don't really recommend it, I know there can be certain people who can overlook its issues and enjoy it and with that I'll just say that while you won't lose anything particular by passing on it, if you got it as a part of the Remastered Trilogy bundle as I did, you can safely give it a chance.

_childDocuments_.review: Dumb, action packed fun in a similar vein to Command and Conqueror: Renegades, after never really playing the original past the first couple levels, I went into the game relatively blind and after people had hyped it up so much in the past, I was underwhelmed in some ways. The game has problems in that, you don't necessarily feel like a super soldier, you feel like a normal squishy soldier with the odd buff here or there for a couple seconds at most.The Nano Suit is at its worst here, it has next to no energy, meaning you take 4-5 shots and your armour depletes, you sprint for 5~ seconds and your energy depletes, you do anything but crouch whilst using invisibility cloak, your energy depletes after a couple seconds.The game suffers in my opinion with a lacklustre second half since the aliens that show up are much less fun to fight than the North Koreans and there is lots of jank from 2007 you have come to expect. In saying that though, I enjoyed the majority of my time with this game and beating up conscripted soldiers in a super suit is really, really fun. I really feel like the game would have been better if it expanded upon the power trip and made you near unstoppable on normal difficulties whilst throwing more enemies at you. Another thing, that some people might like and some people might not, it's got a very open level design, this translates into sprinting past entire objectives the majority of the time since the sandbox isn't enjoyable enough that you should take every single fight. This game would have worked better in a much more linear hallway shooter style and thats what the rest of the trilogy turns into for the most part.The story and dialogue is pretty damn corny, like Transformers (2007) levels of corny but if you embrace that, it's all the more enjoyable, overall I would recommend it but I suspect Crysis 2 and 3 are the better of the bunch.You want guarantees, buy a toaster - Admiral R. Morrison (2020)

_childDocuments_.review: Crysis was a cornerstone in 2007, with stunning graphics, huge freedom on how to tackle objectives and a lot of possibilities with modding. 16 years later, this remaster has actually not remastered a thing when it comes to AI, gameplay, gunplay or even graphics. It's the same game, and to be honest you can have better through modding the original game. Definetely a pass!It's clunky, it feels heavy, the commands are not reactive (like sprinting and jumping) and overall, the change to the nanosuit was for the worst (changing from armor mode by default to Power mode. Sprinting activating the speed mode, etc). They didn't even try to modernize the commands or the gunplay. Still the same as back in 2007.The game is OKish in 2023, but honestly, you don't need this remaster. The modded 2007 original version will do better, with lot more possibilities (textures, Time of day, lightning, effects, etc).Super basic scenario. I actually preferred the first part (with the koreans) then it goes into a more sci-fi vibe. Nothing fancy. Nothing engaging.For the hunters only. this is a very straightforward 100%, all in 1 playthrough and no collectibles. Most linked to campaign progression and a few linked to actions.

_childDocuments_.review: Normally, I don't write a lot of reviews for games anymore. I've played and tried so many different games that new games rarely make a big impact. However, Crysis Remastered, which I decided to try during this period when I tried games that I could not find the opportunity to try at the time, really blew my mind. Besides, I'm not that much of an FPS fan. The game that I started playing so that I would give it a try, with its colours, texture, Turkish voice-over, missions and story, magnificent mechanics and sense of hitting, officially captured me in the very first hours. A true classic that everyone should try... It will probably be the first FPS game that I will finish after a long period of time.

_childDocuments_.review: Even if you've never played it, as a PC gamer you've undoubtedly heard the phrase "Can It Run Crysis". The first installment in the trilogy is a great shooter but it lacks the refinement and polish of the 2nd and 3rd titles. Playing all 3 back to back, you'll notice an inherent clunky aspect to the original. Not that it doesn't have it's charm and appeal but it lacks the smooth power solider power fantasy the sequels provide. The narrative leaves a bit to be desired, often times a bit generic and campy. It's also a bit painful that games and movies around this time always have the "we're gonna nuke it" moment. That being said, if you're in the mood for a solid sci-fi shooter, Crysis is a great pick. The remastered version performs excellent on modern hardware.

_childDocuments_.review: Get this in the bundle for all three. At a discount when it is offered. I played this game quite a lot back in '07/'08. The remastered is good. This game was the beginning of a generation from late 2007 until 2016, when the new generation of games began.

_childDocuments_.review: Realising that you aren't supposed to ghost your way through levels like Metal Gear but instead use the cloak to hunt your enemies like the predator turned this game from one I could never enjoy as a kid to one of the best FPS experiences I've ever had in my life. everything just improves once you figure out the intended uses for the mechanics.It's also so fantastic that the levels essentially just give you a semi-open world, an objective, and lets you loose to figure things out however YOU want. after properly playing through this game multiple times and 100%-ing it I came to the awful realisation that there's nothing else like it out there. of course there is the third act to talk about but I didn't really find it all that bad, sure it's nothing in comparison to Act 1's predator game play or Act 2's Halo-like vehicle segment power trip but it isn't garbage like I've seen some people say about it; It can be a bit of fun to doom marine your way through a bunch of alien scum.Anyways play this game please.

_childDocuments_.review: I bought this knowing ahead of time about the game's imperfections and shortcomings – even visually in some cases – compared to the 2007 release, and I set my expectations accordingly.It is way worse than I thought it would be.In the half-hour or so that I spent playing, I encountered numerous bugs and deficits that made the game too frustrating to play given that I can play the original any time without dealing with those issues.A few examples:I know that in areas that are indirectly lit (interior spaces, shaded areas) the lighting is massively ahead of the original, and transparent and reflective surfaces must look better too. But I didn't get to see any of that before I quit, so I can't give my impression. All I know is it doesn't make up for the cost of buying the game, especially in light of all the bugs and other frustrating elements that dragged the game down considerably from the original.If after watching the Digital Foundry videos on this game you're not bothered by the shortcomings they list, nor bothered by any of the ones I shared above, then sure, it might be worth getting if it's on sale for 50% off or more. But I personally wouldn't recommend spending any more than $5 unless they significantly improve the game via patches, which seems unlikely at this point.

_childDocuments_.review: Good game. This reminds me of the old FPS I used to play when I was in my mid 20s. Its still playable and an enjoyable shooter. Nice graphics, sound effects and music. Story is good for a video game. I did encounter multiple bugs and crashes towards the end of the game. Also vsync does not work properly atm. The most annoying bugs were the ones that stop progression. Enemy AI would stop moving then I would kill them and game would not continue with cutscene. The way I fix this was to restart checkpoint or reload an earlier save. The last boss was also problematic but I manage to finish the fight. I reach the end of game by hour 8. I recommend this game for 20 bucks or less if you dont mind the bugs.

So I really wished to like the first game.- When I tried to use the grenade button, the game blocked all my actions unless I got some weapon from the ground.- No quicksaves, so depending on the checkpoint system to save, was a very bad experience (playing on delta difficulty and dying really fast).- VTOL for some reason after clicking the boost button, stopped from flying and I couldn't control it unless realoading checkpoint.- Almost at the ending, my character started to stuttering when walking, so i needed to constantly sprint in order to stop the bug.- The "endboss arena" kept killing me in some strange ways: not on fire, not receiving enemy damage (no visual queues), but having my HP sucked constantly and dying (had to keep walking far from the boss itself).I've been forced to download a mod to have the first 2 gameplay problems that I listed solved.Can't say much about the graphics since I can't compare the original from remastered.+ My PC is not beefy and I didn't have FPS drop.I don't have much positive to say since I was constantly annoyed by the bugs.I'll definitely try the other 2 games, but I WON'T return to this one and will never recommend it with mechanic breaking problems.

_childDocuments_.review: It looks worse than the original - the graphics in the water are marginally better but some textures which used to look ok are now worse and the god rays flicker horribly through whatever is filtering it be it a tree or antenna or whatever, the explosions look worse, the bullet hits look worse, the physics aren't as good - less objects can be picked up and thrown seemingly and the houses have bits disappear when they collapse rather than all the parts being present post-destruction, ragdoll physics has been all but disabled especially on the animal corpses, picking things up is janky af - it's impossible to actually pick up ammo unless you're aligned with the gun and <0.0001mm away from it which never used to be an issue, the menus are seemingly worse - the gun edit menu you can't change things by clicking on the circle, only the tags, the sounds is utterly stuffed - if they've remastered that they wasted their money because it's more janky and less immersive than the original with sounds getting flat out cut off halfway through playing and maybe i'm misremembering but the shotgun used to have two choke settings - that's gone? _childDocuments_.review: Ever want to feel like the Predator without the name? This is that game; Crysis is an open-sandbox stealth game where you play as a high-tech supersoldier that uses a nanosuit to accomplish objectives on the map to progress the story. The first playthrough is slow getting used to the abilities and stealth mechanics, but as you get better at abusing the abilities and AI, the game kind of opens up to a playground of sorts. Almost 8 hours in and I feel spec ops elite solider put on a island to bully some north Korean soilders until the aliens showup so fun ride so far.I'm just going to put it out there since it's kind of important. It's a CONSOLE PORT, meaning its a port of a PC game ported to consoles and then ported back to PC again with that console port in mind (xbox 360). It isn't a direct remaster of the OG PC Crysis, so you lose a bit of PC polish that the OG PC Crysis had, like quick saves, but it isn't enough that it kills the experience, at least for me. Also the game itself doesnt look that impressive with the all the modern graphic effects shoved into it to get it to todays standards,maybe it's the lighting and color saturation but it doesn't look photorealistic as it did back in 2007 maybe it's and I don't know what a island enviorment looks like in realtime during the day but it looks weird.Get the game on sale.9/11/2024 Edit: Finished the game and by god does it end with a mixed bag,the first half of the game is hunting north Korean soilders in the jungle taking objectives, which is probably the best half of the game,the 2nd half is a mixed bag of Alien things,literally, boring Alien zero grav level,Alien snow level,Aircraft flying with bad controls level and the final Aircraft Carrier level with a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ finall boss. Crytek just sort of fumbles with the campaign when aliens are introduced into the gameplay at some parts. If Crytek would have kept it going with the island map sanbox concept for the whole game, I would have love this game to death, but the 2nd half of the game killed  me. Get it on sale and experience the best first half of the game, and just stop playing it when you get to the core level, because at that point its just a genertic sci-fi FPS onward.6/10 will probably only play it on Delta mode on certain levels for fun, but not the whole game again.

_childDocuments_.review: The classic first person shooter from Crytek is back with the action-packed gameplay, sandbox world, and thrilling epic battles you loved the first time around. Suit up: Your Nanosuit’s speed, strength, armor, and cloaking allow creative solutions for every kind of fight. Adapt: In an ever-changing environment, adapt your tactics to dominate on battlefields ranging from frozen jungle to alien environments. Customize: A huge arsenal of modular weaponry provides unprecedented control over play style, with options ranging from the experimental to the alien. Conquer: Life-like enemy AI require a strategic and flexible playstyle, as new challenges – including a zero-g battlefield– require players to take the offensive and be proactive. Explore: Choose your own path through the open world of Crysis, destroying obstacles, driving vehicles, and using the environment itself against your enemies. What begins as a simple rescue mission becomes the battleground of a new war as alien invaders swarm over a North Korean island chain. Armed with a powerful Nanosuit, players can become invisible to stalk enemy patrols, or boost strength to lay waste to vehicles. The Nanosuit’s speed, strength, armor, and cloaking allow creative solutions for every kind of fight, while a huge arsenal of modular weaponry provides unprecedented control over play style. In the ever-changing environment, adapt tactics and gear to dominate your enemies, in an enormous sandbox world.

_childDocuments_.review: By now, this game has been data mined like crazy, and there are plenty of guides and strategies to min-max your monsters, and play in the most "efficient" way possible.  But for me, the most fun I had playing this game, was as a 13 year old kid, going in to it blind with no help from the internet, and figuring things out on my own.  I spent a good chunk of my summer after 8th grade trying to unlock the Dragon and Henger monsters in MR1, and the sense of accomplishment and joy I had when I finally spawned them remains unequaled in my gaming life.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Rancher 1 & 2 DX

_childDocuments_.review: MR2 is literally my favourite Psone game of all time.But does it hold up to modern scrutiny?Kind of.The story is essentially non-existent. You are a rancher of monsters, you raise them, fight them, breed them, and (if you see fit to) sell them.The human characters are equally lacklustre, but they are not why you play this game.Music is passable as is sound design in general(although some of the remastered sounds actually seem worse?). The battle sounds have some satisfying moments (Zuums “Millionbites” attack is so crunchy, I never get tired of hearing it). Graphically its middling. The monsters themselves look good even though many lost some extra features from MR1 (Pinkeyes “wings” for example). The backgrounds are basic and often low res. The battle stages are equally simple.But this is a game about battling monsters not exploring rich detailed worlds so…First up the star of the show, the monsters. From telekinetic eyeballs to farting baboons, all the way through to good old fashioned dragons. There's something here for everyone and if you cant find a species you like then seriously what's wrong with you?They are well animated, full of personality, and each offer subtly differing training obstacles for the player (what works for a Dragon may not necessarily work for a Hare).Unlocking them all is a pain but save scumming is nothing to ashamed of in a game like this.(There's only so many times a monster can miss the turn-off in an expedition or die right before a special tournament a person can stand before losing their mind)Oh yeah...Monsters have perma death. Once its dead its dead, no phoenix downs or revives here. The best you can do is reload and cryogenically freeze your charge before they snuff it thus allowing you time to try and decide the best course of action (Combine it? Defrost it for important fights? Send it on a suicidal expedition to acquire a rare item?)Second the meat and potatoes of the gameplay Breeding and Battling. As this game is closer to a horse breeding simulator than it is to Pokemon, you can forget about camping out in the tall grass fighting pigeons, raising monsters is all about optimising training, diet, and battle schedules. At first you’ll struggle to have a monster capable of living out even half of its lifespan, as you stumble through semi-hidden mechanics like stress and fatigue, desperately trying to squeeze that last training session you need to stand a chance in the next tournament…But stick with it, experiment, learn and soon you’ll be running a boxing boot camp for velociraptors. You’ll forget what a stressed monster even looks like.Battling is an odd but compelling affair. Fights occur in real time and monsters can attack from 4 different ranges depending on their learnt techniques and costing “Guts” as a resource, meaning it often feels more like a beat em up than an RPG. The majority of traditional RPG strategies will work for these battles (Tanking, glass cannons, resource control etc etc) but they are limited to the capabilities of the monster species and the individual attributes of each monster itself (Some species are much easier to train as glass cannons and other species lack the techniques to starve the opponent of resources).Breeding is also a bit of a misleading term. Monsters in MR2 are not bred in any physical sense but are in fact combined magically in a lab to produce offspring at the cost of both parents existence.The combining system is a rabbit hole itself with pages and pages of guides and forums breaking down parental compatibility, combination item use, and selective breeding through generations. Its overwhelmingly in depth stuff but well worth a browse if you’re planning on raising the perfect beast.Overall this game is and will likely always be my favourite Psone game.Its core gameplay loop is easy to learn difficult to master.Its premise is casual but its depths are hardcore.Its understandable why it doesn’t (And didn’t ) appeal to either crowd when one balks at challenge and the other loses interest in ease. Still awesome. Still ranching. 8/10

_childDocuments_.review: I picked a cool monster. It looked awesome. I gave it the best treatment. It beat the A-Rank leagues. I tried to beat S-Rank but it grew old after 3 years. It was about to die. I froze it. I will combine it later to create the best. monster. ever. period.I picked another monster that complimented the stats of the first monster for combining, but It looked like a pervert in a gimp suit. It drank. It smoked. It constantly spat at the floor when I told it off. I told myself it would make good cannon fodder for the next monster, but my hatred grew in time. The amount of care I gave it was slowly slipping. Letting it get old faster would mean a new monster sooner I told myself. But it just wouldn't grow old. It made it to 6 years and it was still going strong. It developed amazing stats. It learned an absurd move that never missed and always laid down the hurt. And then it demolished the end game leagues without breaking a sweat. And before I realised what was happening, there it was. The credits screen rolling. and my fat gimp monster immortalised on the end game content congratulations screen. This is my legacy now. Just a trainer who dreamed big and ended up as a fat alcoholic gimp's ♥♥♥♥♥.No I said. This won't be the end. I'll freeze this gimp and make that cool monster. I'll combine them and make a new monster. Better. Faster. Stronger. And then, there it was. Reborn. Gimp Jr. I wanted to reload the game. But his stats were undeniable. And it remembered that insane move. And then, I accepted my place. We're going back to the ranch. Welcome home, master gimp...

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: If you where a fan of the game back on the PSX and PS2, then this game is for you. It has everything you loved and some quality of life improvements that make it quick to jump in and have fun.Value: A+ To do everything there is to do in each games takes about 20 hours each. SO it will beat the $1/hour value of entertainment and then some.Game Play: Get a monster, raise it, train it and become the greatest trainer in the world. The Fusion system allows you to fuse your older monsters together and give them a new life and raise them again.Updates: Ability to raise any monster, CDs no longer required. _childDocuments_.review: Monster Rancher was a quite memorable game for me back in my childhood. Seeing MR 1&2 DX comes back again brings me a good rush of nostalgia, and with it also a sense of duty to "finish" the game that my child-self failed to do. The game is mainly about training and raising a monster with the goal of achieving better ranks than before. Each monster is unique, and there are many different kinds of monster for you to see and experience. Back then, the unique appeal of monster rancher is that you can pop your CDs into PSX and the game will generate a monster based on your CDs. Now it changed into you choosing a song from the in-game database list which consist of approximately 664,909 titles that you can choose. However, don't expect the monster variety level to reach pokemon and digimon since this is a 25 years old PSX game. To note, MR2DX also support "slating" your MR1DX monsters, which is using your MR1DX frozen monsters to "import" them into MR2DX (this does not delete the monster used to slate in MR1DX).After you have yourself a monster, the only things left is to train, care, and bond with your monster. On the surface this sounds easy enough, but monster have "fatigue" and "stress" that you have to watch out for that the game only scarcely gives you info about it. Too much stress and fatigue can makes your monster run away from you and it also makes them grow old faster. Hence, we need to care our monster. You can combine your monster with other monster to create a new breed of monster which will inherit the parent stats, which completes the cycle of breeding and raising monster. Training your monster increase their status, and sending your monster into training (MR1DX) or Errantry (MR2DX) can help them acquire new techniques to use in the arena. With your monster trained and grown up, you can battle other monsters to win gold and reach higher ranks. In a battle, you can give your monster "advice" which is essentially you controlling your monster, or you can just sit back and watch as your monster battle by itself through AI. You can also battle others through Vs match but sadly Player vs Player is limited to the switch version, the steam version only has CPU vs CPU or Player vs CPU. MR 1&2 DX is a polished version of the PSX version of the game with bugfixes and hidden easter eggs for you to see. However, that is also the negatives about the game, as this is only a "remaster" of the old PSX games. So you can see that the graphics are of an ancient PSX as well as the content itself is limited to the era itself. Other notable things: - The game has a fast forward feature that is only accesible from the menu, which can be accessed whenever you are.- The game does not have a volume dial, there is only ON and OFF for the sound, and the music volume is crancked on to the MAX so take care of your volume and ear when playing the game (Edit: use  to tune down the volume, but still this doesn't bring volume dial to the game)- As a port, Keyboard-mouse support is kinda off but the controller support is betterAll in all, MR 1&2 DX is a good monster raising sim. Although to be honest this game feels like Koei Tecmo testing waters if the market for monster rancher is still here or not. if Koei Tecmo ever read this, please make a new monster rancher game.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Rancher 1 & 2 DX

_childDocuments_.review: At long last, the classic niche monster raising games return, for a new generation (and old generation) to enjoy!I've long considered this series one of the "Big 3" of Monster Raising Games (i.e. Pokemon, Digimon, and Monster Rancher).So...for those who've never heard of these game(s), in the original PS1 game, you would insert your own music or game CDs, the game would read them, and generate a monster to raise.At your ranch, you feed the monster, train it, battle with it, and enter it in tournaments.That said, I will warn you -- These games are famed for their difficulty. Monsters have a limited lifespan, and your actions can shorten that if you push the monster too hard. They can get stressed and fatigued (both of which are semi-hidden stats).If totally outmatched in a battle, to the point of getting one-hit KO'ed, they can be injured or even outright die.But, these games are charming in their own way, it's always a treat to see what a CD will generate.Now, for this DX remaster, since most PCs (and the Switch) don't have CD drives, Koei-Tecmo have instead included a database of metadata for over 600,000 CDs (including a few important PS1 games).Search for an artist and album you want, and see what comes of it.Sure the graphics are from the PS1-era, but honestly, they hold up surprisingly well in this day and age, especially the monsters themselves.If you want fun games, two games that won't hold your hand and actually will give you a challenge, then this game bundle is for you.-----Q: "I've played Pokemon. How does this compare to that?"A: "I like Pokemon, too. So... imagine a Pokemon game where you own a ranch. Instead of walking around and catching what you find, you go to a shrine and pick a CD, and are handed the monster inside.You train the monster through drills, and have unlimited tournaments/battles for money and items.Oh, and the monster will eventually grow old and die, leading to you generating a new one. (Assuming you don't combine two monsters into a new hybrid).And instead of a gym challenge, there's no hard endgoal.This will be somewhat easy in some regards...but that disguises the true difficulty. It's not hard to get to a meager C rank. But to get to the world-class S Rank (where the endgoals are)... that's gonna take true skill from you. So imagine a Pokemon game where beating the first few gyms is fairly simple... and then the kid gloves come off and the game gets brutal, to the point facing the champion requires tons of effort and tears, after dozens of hours of work.And lastly, instead of separately buying two versions of the same game...here, you instead are buying the game, and its sequel, in one neat package."-------As I said, these two games are difficult, but fun, and rather unique, in my opinion.Very important to remember: This includes TWO GAMES in one.So for $30, that effectively makes both games $15. And each game has dozens of hours of things to do. Well worth their price tags, even for these older games.So, do you like a game that you definitely are not going to blast through in a week (or even a month)?Do you like getting two long games for a mere $15 a piece?Do you like a game that's not afraid to kick your rear and punish you for making bad choices?Do you just want to enjoy a fine slice of monster-raising history, maybe even raise an adorable Moochi?If you said yes to any of these, then yes, I definitely recommend this game.

_childDocuments_.review: Been having a spectacular time with this game. I had a blast making an int based monster line and a Mock made it all the way to the hall of fame. _childDocuments_.review: I appreciate this childhood favourite being made available on modern hardware but it's too clunky a port for me to enjoy.The good:- It loads quickly and runs smoothly.- Although you can't generate monsters from your physical CD collection anymore, the in-game CD database is a nice way to replicate the experience of popping in your favourite album and seeing what monster comes out of it.The so-so:- As far as I can tell, the visual assets are exactly as they were presented in the original games and have not been rebuilt or remastered in any way. This isn't a bad thing in and of itself, but they were designed to be viewed on a CRT at lower resolutions and to be honest they don't look great on a modern display.- The remastered soundtrack is pretty cool, though I'm not sure what the need for it was - you can turn the original back on in the options menu and it sounds great.The bad:- The game doesn't control very well on mouse and keyboard at all. You can technically do everything with just the mouse but nothing about this feels intuitive and battles are downright clumsy.- The new UI elements were clearly designed for touch controls, which makes this PC version feel a bit like a mobile port.- You can turn the sound master ON of OFF but you can't adjust the volume of individual aspects and you can't turn music off while leaving SFX on. Either you have the music on full blast or you play the game on mute.All in all, a bit disappointing. They've made it run on PC but they haven't made it click. I wonder if it feels any better on Nintendo Switch?

_childDocuments_.review: So, first things first, we have to address the elephant in the room - this is pretty clearly designed as a mobile port of the first two Monster Rancher games. The title screen says "tap to start", the border has virtual buttons that you're expected to use to control the game (using a controller or keyboard just seems to map keys to trigger the virtual buttons), and the new way of summoning monsters is is definitely meant to work with streaming. The virtual buttons would actually be phenomenal with a phone or table screen, but they're really cumbersome to trigger with a mouse - I highly recommend using a controller or spending some time mapping keyboard buttons instead.The change to the summoning system is also a little disappointing, but understandable when you keep in mind that this is effectively a mobile game. The way it works is that the game has a big database of music; you just enter either the artist or album title and it searches it for you. It also has a random option, so you can always fall back to just hitting that and seeing what you get. It's a little sad that you're not actually scanning anything, but makes sense as fewer and fewer files are stored on physical media or even devices themselves these days.The music it has in the database is, admittedly, a little weirdly hit-or-miss. Some of the music I consider a little more obscure in my playlist was found with no issue, including Mal Blum, Math the Band, SALES, and even some rare EPs from the some of the less obscure artists... But then there are some bigger names that just don't appear at all: Mice Parade, Neko Case, and even Juno and Polaris award winning artist Caribou are mysteriously completely absent. It also has an odd habit of sometimes mistaking tracks for albums. This is especially obvious among the works I tried with Justice, whose entries are filled to the brim with track names from the album Cross, but somehow don't include the album Cross.All of that said, if you can get past that weirdness (and it's not that hard to get past, honestly), it's basically straight ports of Monster Rancher 1 &2. They're still some of the most clever and unique monster raiser/battler games out there, they're still very charming and enjoyable - and for that reason I wholly recommend this game if you want to play these games again, or experience the series for the first time.

_childDocuments_.review: These two may not be full-on remasters, but an enhanced port available on modern platforms is more than we have already.While I may have been familiar with this series, this would be my first crack at it. And I gotta say, I went in expecting something like Digimon or Pokémon (two games this franchise gets compared to A LOT), but got something completely different. It’s much less a full-on adventure RPG and more so a life simulator RPG.The vast majority of the gameplay is done through menus, where you will be directing training for your monsters, managing a small inventory of goods, and coming up with more monsters. Coming up with a new monster at the shrine is perhaps what this game is best known for. Back in the day, you would have to physically insert music CDs into your PlayStation and hope that the game’s mystery algorithm would spawn a powerful monster from it.The new method is simply looking up an album by name and artist, which I think this is a good workaround to maintain what made the original games unique. It’s always fun to go through your favorite albums and see what monsters spawn from them - my first monster, for example, was a small pixie spawned from Rick Astley’s piano rendition of “Never Gonna GIve You Up”.Anyways, each in-game week acts as a “turn” of sorts, where you give your monster one instruction and pray that it succeeds in doing so - because each monster has its own personality and will sometimes fail or shortcut training. Each time it does succeed though, its stats go up - and that’s basically what these two games revolve around.You will spend hours clicking through training menus and getting these monsters ready for battle, oftentimes repeating the same set of inputs over and over while you wait for your monster to reach a certain stat level. There is stuff to break up this monotony, but I would be lying if I said that the core loop wasn’t tedious.The point of all of this is to win battles, which are NOT menu-based and actually take place in real-time. They’re simple mechanically, but play out VERY fast and you’ll need to know what you’re doing to clear them. Again, there’s a lot of repetition involved because you will be going through a lot of these battles, but seeing training pay off and having your monster one-shot another with a single slap is always satisfying.Despite these seemingly simple training exercises and battles, there is a lot going on under the hood here. Stress levels, loyalty, stat gain modifiers, monster type combinations, lifespans, unique techniques - I could go on. For example, I spent several hours hunting down a specific monster: the stone ape. This required me to reach certain training goals, find a specific item on an expedition map that only opens once per year, and hope for the small chance that combining my ape with my golem would result in the monster I wanted.This process was both a pain and a testament to what makes this game unique - it’s not all just menus, training, and battles. And honestly, I kinda liked it. It is repetitive for sure, but it’s charming in its own way and the hours flew by while I was playing. It is definitely not something I can see myself powering through to the end, but spread out over some months and yeah - I’ll probably end up completing both of these provided I don’t get distracted and spend hours chasing a specific monster like my Stone Ape - but I guess that’s just part of the fun.The PC version comes with a launcher where you can adjust a grand total of three settings: fullscreen toggle, window resolution, and controls. It’s a bare-minimum port, but that’s par for the course from Koei Tecmo. It at least works though - in my many hours of playing, all I had was one crash (there is an auto-save though).Controls are also surprisingly good. I didn’t change any of the defaults and had no issues swapping between controller and keyboard/mouse, depending on what I was feeling at the time. The game has full mouse support and can actually be played entirely using just that - no keyboard necessary.For someone that has never played the series before, Monster Rancher 1 & 2 DX is a nice package to have. It ports both titles to modern platforms, enhances their visuals and playability a bit, and stays true to the disc-swapping mechanic of the original with its own unique interpretation. It’s not an easy recommendation to make, but it’s one I might throw out there if you like monster collecting games.Follow my  for more reviews + videos!

_childDocuments_.review: I have been waiting for a hint of life from this series since Monster Rancher 4. Sure it had some iterations on Nintendo DS and Advance but I only ever played the core games in the series. This port is okay, though since it has been around in ROM format for ages for use in emulators it was not exactly a tough ask. Do not let the lack of disc use push you away. Sure it was a part of the game and part of the fun of it but the database system is pretty good. You can search for albums or songs and games as well and if you are lazy about it just hit random and it will just pick one of the 600,000+ items from the database to get you a generated monster, assuming you have unlocked that monster through game play. I have already sunk 11 hours and it has all its charm in the "just one more week, just one more battle" area. This is not a graphic over haul and yes it is a port from a more mobile version of the game though it plays well. Controls can be clunky but can be remapped. I don't like that I cannot skip training scenes (except errantry can still skip those scenes) but since there is a fast forward option that you can toggle in options it does at least blow through the animations quickly. The graphics are not upscaled much if at all. Maybe some smoothing out at best but nothing else. There is the addition of a job game that was only released in the Japanese version but I saw no real point to using it though I did mess with it once. Sound is pretty good, at least in MR2 as it has a remastered soundtrack. I have not hopped into the original game as I have always preferred MR2 over the original. I still like the first one I just prefer 2.Over all I would say that if you are a first time player the graphics are PSOne so don't expect much there. The game play loop is satisfying and there are a ton of guides out there to help learn about the game. I usually just roll with whatever I feel when I train but there are guides out there that can help you create epic monsters in short periods of time, but keep in mind the first go around with a monster you will need to really make money for some of the  techniques to work. For my old heads who have played the game on and off over the years like myself. It has all the charm still, the addicting play loop and the challenge. I have played Monster rancher since the first one released in 1997 here in the states and I always come back. This just makes it easier rather then pulling out the old PSOne or 2 and swapping discs and dealing with long load times. I have the games still and until this released I would often boot them up and play them or at least use an emulator and ROM it. Now that I have it on Steam here and with my Steamdeck eventually arriving I will be able to play this on a whim whenever and not worry about if my memory cards have gone bad or if I lost my save on an emulator. If you are on the fence I feel the hours you can sink into this game are absolutely worth $29.99 and I am sure there will be some future polishing that happens with the game. Who knows, maybe Tecmo will see merit in releasing a new game in the series.TL;DR versionit makes it much easier for me to hop in and out of monster training and the database is actually not bad to use. Graphics are PSOne and audio is remastered in at least MR2, not sure about original. Gameplay loop is still as fun as ever.

_childDocuments_.review: Nostalgia is the greatest component with this release, and boy the nostalgia is real with this one. This game takes me back to being 8 on Christmas morning and i love every minute of it. It really makes me wish i would have kept up with the series after 2. This is basically a port, so what you remember is what you get. Altho, they have made it possible to play it discless. In the old ones, you could pop music CD's into your Playstation and get new monsters. This is a problem in modern day as most of us don't even have diskdrives. The rest of the game is the standard Tamagatchi/Digimon pet sim with battle mechanics. In this, however, you don't always get to use the move you want. The moves you use all depends in how close or far away the monster is from yours. There's more strategy to these games. You also have to sent your monsters out on adventures to get new moves, which severely cuts their life expectancy, so you need to plan out what you want before hand. Yes, this is an old school spreadsheet game of yore. Each monster has their own hidden stat raises like Pokemon, but with the added twist that they die, like Digimon, so combining them is necessary to get max stats. All in all, this is a great game that holds up today. If you like this series please consider buying this instead of emulating. Money is the only way we're getting another one.

_childDocuments_.review: Pretty quick and easy review, this is pretty much MONSTER RANCHER 1 & 2 essentially updated to work on PC // soon to be Switch. If you liked Monster Rancher back in the day and still want to play it, this is def. an easy pickup.The only major change is that instead of disc-swapping for the monsters (which is really fun), you now instead use a virtual catalog and look up different discs that exist in real life, it's much faster and responsive, and there is even a Random button to press and just see what you get which is actually really fun. You can even use a mouse instead of a controller now, and it is quite nice in certain situations.The only other minor change I noticed was that item stacking was a thing, which is nicer visually, but the item limit is still pretty low. Otherwise this game is pretty much exactly as it was when it came out 22 years ago.If you're new to the series, its basically a monster life simulation game, you train up your monster, enter it in tournaments, try to unlock new types of monsters to train and become the master rank. People always compare this game to Pokemon, but other than the fact that you 'collect' monsters its not even close. You primarily focus on one monster at a time, and its a very laid back and relaxing experience most of the time. Train up monsters, fight them in tournaments, send them off on adventures and eventually even combine them together to make more unique monsters and find cool (hidden) combinations or entirely new types of monsters.Highly recommended, classic game.

_childDocuments_.review: Bad port of a beloved title, I sunk a ridiculous amount of time into this game back on the original Playstation, so the issues with this port were glaringly obvious.First off, the audio cannot be adjusted to your liking. I'd love to have the in-game sounds with no music, but this isn't possible, apparently. Keyboard support is also weird. Why can we not just type in names? Controls for the most part are pretty much what you'd expect, it's a menu game everywhere except for battles. As for visuals, they're good enough, the game keeps the original look and style, so it's good for nostalgia.One of the most unique aspects of Monster Rancher was always the ability to create new monsters through reading other discs. In this game, you just look up the artist and track, and hope the game can find what you're looking for. This is fundamentally flawed, as it does not allow you to look up other old games, which did give new monsters in the original, and the system also seems to have trouble even finding artists/tracks that were proven to provide specific breeds. Of the dozen searches I performed of some old favorites, I found two. The others turned up no results. This is unacceptable, as it's literally the cornerstone of this entire franchise. How did they screw this up?The biggest issue for me was the removal of the ability to skip individual training exercises, which was possible in the original. You just start the training, press a button, and boom: you've got your result, whether it's a success or failure. For some reason that I cannot fathom, this was removed, and it's the final nail in the coffin for me. That one little button press saved SO MUCH time during the monotony of training up a fresh monster, as the little video that plays during a training session gets extremely repetitive, very quickly.I loved the original, so much that this port was an instabuy for me purely for the nostalgia, but less than half an hour was more than enough for me to demand a refund. The original was great, even with its various flaws, and this port (while mostly faithful) feels like a huge step backwards. Damn shame, because this could have been great. Instead it just sucks.

_childDocuments_.review: First off, the main real reason this has a negative is purely a lack of a mediocre rating, and it's main thing dragging it down is purely the price. On sale for 10 or maybe 15 it's probably worth it, even if not that great.The main downside listed and stated, are the controls. The key binding menu is horribly clunky and nigh nonsensical, forcing you to use a dropdown menu without letter or input hotkeys and tiny scroll bar so unless you arrow up or down, it can be a huge pain to adjust. Controller keybindings are changed from the PS1 and un-changable, annoying but not deal breaking. Touch screen functionality is a distinct sign this is a mobile port, but it isn't that bad to have it, it doesn't detract from much. This all could be handled better, and hopefully if they bother to do any updates this is one of the first they do.The gameplay seems about normal for vanilla monster rancher, with a small few tweaks like AI attacking under 45 guts but nothing seems broken either. However it is very clunky regardless, there is a "part time job" minigame based on a VMU-like minigame, that pays awfully low amounts and only is accessable on the title screen. Music sometimes cuts out and won't come back. Overall it seems fine, but woefully unpolished and anything added in was an afterthought to say they added more, instead of actual additions and fixes.The new features that I can tell, are as follows: More save slots(But actually less if you factor having multiple/swappable memory cards), listing your total stats, a remastered copy of the soundtrack (toggleable for the classic as well), graphics are a little clearer (but still has that low-render quality wobble), a disc library to search from, a bit easier updated online fighting, faster loading screens, a fast forward mode... and you cannot skip training animations anymore. All said and done, it is not bad, because the games themselves weren't bad. But, ultimately the only thing this game can sell itself on is if you don't have access to this game in any other way, as what is out there is at worst on par, and in some cases superior to this poor port. Nothing was ruined, but nothing to gain unless they start adding more updates. If you get this, get it on sale or if/when they lower the price.

_childDocuments_.review: I bought Monster Rancher 1 when it first came out, I think I was 8. I stumbled upon it randomly and thought the game's cover looked cool. I bought it with money I saved up that summer. I didn't know all the ins and outs of proper breeding and training, but I could hold my own in battles. I spent hours upon hours going through every single CD in our music collection (anyone else remember the myths at school about doubling up CD's in the PS1? Like they'd somehow make even better monsters, damn... kids are dumb).Anyways... I had my favourite Monster, a plain ole green Dino, I took such good care of it, tried my best to spoil it, give it the best digital life I could, as a dumb kid, thought it was just the tops. And then Goregon came. We had made it to Rank C, we were winning, we were finally going to make REAL money... Next up is that yellow pile of rubble, Goregon, and with one lucky chop, my Dino was no more. We were pulled from the tournament due to injury... we made it back to the ranch, it looked like Dino had made it home safe, I was so relieved, everything was going to be ok... and then there was a white flash, and Dino collapsed - dead on the green ranch grass. I was heart broken, I was a kid, I don't think I ever got over it. This is Monster Rancher, and there is no mercy for weak monsters. I'm coming for you, Goregon. Buy this game.

_childDocuments_.review: Monster Rancher 1 & 2 are classic epics, from a time when games were actually art.This is the director’s cut of the original PS1 titles from the late 90s. Both of these games put you into the shoes of a newly licensed rancher and your job is to raise and train monsters with the goal of becoming the best monster rancher in the world. Unlike in Pokémon, here you focus primarily on a single monster at a time - it’s more about carefully raising your monster, bonding with it, and the choices you make that ultimately determine their success.All in all, Monster Rancher 1 & 2 DX are games that will mostly appeal to fans of the originals, but it’s also the most complete version of these games that we’ve ever had. There’s so much depth and complexity here, that if you’re into the concept, there’s a solid chance that you’ll become completely hooked for hundreds of hours. Some slight clunkiness and definite signs of age aside, it’s still clear why so many of us fell in love with these games when they first came out.

_childDocuments_.review: For those who don't know Monster Rancher is a Monster Battling game at heart, more closer to Digimon than Pokemon. The game tasks the player to breed, raise then fight other monsters in arena battles using their monster. Monster Rancher is a long winded game in that your first monster won't be good enough to get to S Rank, no where near close in fact. However that monster will earn you money and can be used to breed better monsters. The ultimate goal of the game is to get S Rank on all four continents. To achieve this you must build up your ranch and your quality of monsters till you can start unlocking better monsters and breeding better monsters by combining powerful monsters together.So how is the port?While there are a few baffling decisions in this port like not being able to skip the drills and the omission of local Vs and Online Vs. and the lack of graphics options other than resolution change, this is a pretty well done port.However on the other side of the coin I would also argue that this is the definitive way to play this game. The in game Disc Database (which replaces using physical CD's in this version) and being able to upload your monster online to compete against other people in Ai vs AI Tourneys is super fun. Also other smaller quality of life changes like being able to freeze more monsters and buy multiple items at the same time as well as now finally being able to unlock the region locked ??? Monsters make this a must have for any die hard Monster Rancher fan.While I hope the developers continue to smooth out some of the small issues I have with this port, all in all as it stands I would currently recommend this port of the  game to anyone who owns a controller as the keyboard controlls are scuffed.

_childDocuments_.review: Of note: This is a port of Monster Farm 1 & 2 with "Rancher DX" tagged onto it.  It is not a port of 1997 & '99 NTSC/PAL Monster Rancher.  That being said...The Good:There are some Quality of life features introduced to the game that have made this quote an enjoyable experience.  Load times are virtually Zero, bulk item purchases, a Fast Forward (FF) mode that speeds the game up 2x across the board, and some upscaling that smooths it out a bit from the original. The game still holds up after so many years, albeit easier since so much time has gone by to learn how the game works, but if you're new to the games, it will still prove just as challenging.  The traditional CD/Shrine system is replaced with an elegant solution that uses a CDDB/List lookup to choose from instead of requiring physical media, and Shrining monsters has never been faster. Overall, the improvements with Load times, play speed have made this a treat to replay, and playing at normal speeds is difficult to revert back to.The OK:There were some bug fixes applied to the game to correct things that were present in the originals, but there are also new bugs introduced.  The Translation was redone, but still contains many errors.  For those unaware, the western games received an additional 100 weeks of lifespan for all monsters, but as this is based on Monster Farm, the original Japanese lifespans are what is used in the game; Not a big deal for experienced players, but could be punishing for brand new players.  Monster Names are pluralized in their "Main" and "Sub" sections for some odd reason, it's weird to look at when it's never been done this way before.The Bad:There are several game-crashing bugs present, a SPD Gains bug (which is arguably fantastic, but still a bug), that as of this writing still have not been fixed nearly a month after the game's release.  Monster Farm 2 had no option to Skip Drill animations, which unfortunately also does not exist in DX either since this was added in the actual NTSC MR2 game and not MF2.  The Online battle menu and user friendliness is clunky and leaves a lot to be desired for a good user experience.The Verdict:Buy the game, Support the franchise, have fun with it.  It has been an absolute joy replaying a commercially supported product again, and seeing so many new players popping up with new or renewed interest.The re-release/port isn't without issue, but For a single player game, this is still great fun and likely a much better experience than on the original console.  For online battles, it allows people to do what used to require a DexDrive or mailing physical memory cards. Even with the clunky online interface, at least it is still an option and can be quite entertaining, and opens the door for people outside of the emulation/modding community to participate in tournaments.

_childDocuments_.review: Favourite part about it is that you actually raise your monster and have to take care of it- managing fatigue and stress and the like. It's gotten some nice improvements (more special monsters) and important bugfixes (no double lifespan hit for learning new moves) with this new version.Some make or break bits about the game:- Monsters have a lifespan. If you like the challenge of raising a monster to the best of your ability within a time limit this is fine, but I get that it's not very fun to deal with- Lots of important mechanics aren't explained particularly thoroughly, the usual thing when it comes to older games. Major ones that I'll mention now are that there's items that will reduce fatigue and stress, but they'll never mention that you should use them even though they make training so much easier, and loyalty caps out at 50 if you spoil your monster. I personally don't like that you gotta be a bit mean to get higher loyalty, but despite that I love the game to bits, enough to buy it again and dive back into all the guides and old sites I used to peruse to calculate a perfect combination of monsters.10/10 would ranch again

_childDocuments_.review: One of my all time favorites finally gets a PC port!! I've only played the MF2 port since that is the one I grew up with !I have been itching to play MF2 again for quite awhile, so much that I had made a back up of my original game to try and play it on my computer, only to find out the brilliant disc swapping technology doesn't really work. Since I do 99% of my gaming on my PC I was hoping to avoid having to hook up my PS1 with an adapter just to play and I found this!So far I'm having a great time in scratching that itch but there are some things that bother me. As people have noted the controls are definitely made with the intention of touch screen, so using a mouse to navigate training / errantry, then swapping to KB for battles using Q and E to move and K and L to push / attack is quite annoying.Not being able to skip training or errantry cinematics is quite frustrating, so to speed it up I open the menu and enable FF while doing drills, but having to switch off for battles. Speaking of battles...It seems the input during battles can lag severely, I'll get stun locked even while spamming the button to use a skill by a monster due to game ticks I assume. Can be quite frustrating especially going up against the Golem/Golem in C rank that can OHKO your monster.Having no volume control for BGM and SFX is especially frustrating. You either have sound off or on and there's no in between. I enjoy the remastered audio but it's just waaaay too loud.All in all, I do like how they just created a library to pick from when doing disc stones, although it does kind of take the magic away of putting in Spyro the dragon or a Tomba! 2 CD in and finding out what monster it gets. I am enjoying the game besides a few control and system changes. Definitely recommend at least getting on a sale if you enjoy the franchise.

_childDocuments_.review: If you're not familiar, Monster Rancher 1 and 2 are Playstation 1 era monster breeding games. Their gimmick was that you could use CDs (DVDs or words in later games) to create monsters. So it encouraged trading and word of mouth really well. This series is a favorite of mine and is near and dear to my heart. As for the ports? Pretty solid. A touch screen UI hovers in the borders, but it's not horribly intrusive. I haven't yet encountered any bugs, but I'll update this if I hit any gamebreaking ones. The additional features and tweaks are really nice, and breathe some fresh air into old favorites.Overall? I recommend these, and I'm glad that Koei Tecmo ported them. I'd love to see the others in the main series (3, 4, Evo, Advance 1 and 2, DS) or even the side games brought over. But mainly the core series.

_childDocuments_.review: I always hop back to  and  on the  every couple of years ever since these games were first released back in . The nostalgia factor is very high for me and many of my friends, so to finally be able to play it wherever I go on my computer is so exciting, especially since I move across the country a lot. _childDocuments_.review: Both Monster Rancher games are even better than I remembered, granted there’s tons of internet resources nowadays so you can learn about all the things the game never tells you to help you get started. Looking at a guide or two on how to raise your monsters right feels necessary to be able to get them in shape for higher rank tournaments, but knowing what to do is only the tip of the iceberg and applying this knowledge through how you train, feed, rest, and battle with your monster is the hard part.Each monster has its own specialties and personality, so raising different monsters requires slightly different approaches. One monster will make you proud by doing its best every step of the way, while another is a little twerp that will cheat on its training drills, but you can’t really complain because it gets results in tournament. Your relationship with each monster is unique, making every monster you raise special.The port itself is… questionably designed. It’s basically a direct port of the japanese mobile release of the games, so it’s not really designed to be played on computer. For the best controls, use a controller during battles, as these games were originally designed for controllers, and use your mouse everything else, because they apparently forgot to rebind some of the menu items to controller inputs.The port’s addition of a fast forward button is quite welcome, and how they dealt with generating monsters through CDs in the original PS1 versions of the games was quite smart. They simply added a search engine into the game so you can look up any album or PS1 game to create a monster from. The search engine is fairly picky as you have to put in the title or artist name in order if there are multiple words. For example, if you want to look up Perturbator’s “Night Driving Avenger” and you put in “Driving Avenger” it won’t show up, but if you put in “Night”, “Night Driving”, or “Night Driving Avenger” it will be in the results. Some artists and games don’t show up in the search engine for some reason, but most of the time if it doesn’t show up, the engine is being picky about what you were trying to search.If you want a monster raising/battling game and don’t mind PS1 level graphics, Monster Rancher 1 is quite good, but Monster Rancher 2 is amazing. I may be biased by nostalgia, but I can't recommend these games enough.

_childDocuments_.review: Gather round kids, it's story time.Years ago, I played Monster Rancher for the first time. I know, common story so far. I bought this game for nostalgia sake mostly, but I also knew I'd actually have fun with this game for a long while at least. So I played and noticed something different. The game was cleaner, everything is smooth and concise, and the game is just as cute and entertaining as it ever was. Now here's the thing. When I started this game through Steam, I was expecting the same story line as I've played before. Type stuff, get a monster, go a few weeks in and suddenly face and op monster that belongs in the strongest division before you even get to fight a proper tournament. But missing that story line in this game, I looked it up and realized what I used to play was actually Monster Rancher Advance 2 on the Gameboy Advanced.So far, I love the classic game for what it is. While relatively minimal, it's still relaxing and calming to play, Reluctant to play pvp any time soon though since there's people making saves with fully maxed out stats just to never use that monster outside of pvp, otherwise i'd love to try it if i knew there were some way to monitor and balance out the matches (such as only being able to use monsters within certain parameters, such as not allowing a monster to have above a certain level for any stat).Would I recommend this game to newcomers? If you're a fan of pet and resource management games where combat is involved, I would encourage you to at least look into the game and try it out yourself. I will say that it's not for everyone, but keep in mind that you have up to 10 save files. you can save before making crucial or risky decisions, then load back if you get easily frustrated by mistakes or anticipated failures. While it's not photo-realistic or high-end like many new games are, keep in mind that this bundle contains 2 games from the 90s. It is polished, refined, and outstanding in comparison to the respective games of their original system.Keep in mind, you can change the keyboard inputs through the game selection screen. The game works best with either a controller or touch screen inputs, but you can make it convenient on keyboard as well. The default keyboard setting is fairly awkward and annoying to navigate, especially since there is no tutorial or mention of what keys are what once the game is initiated. I think it's unfair to downvote this game when it allows you to customize the controls.

_childDocuments_.review: If you've played the game before, there's some new stuff. Online player vs player, mouse-only and keyboard options (some complain about controller options, I've had no issues with my Xbox controller personally), a Remastered Soundtrack for Monster Rancher 2 (you can switch to the original if you want), and the CD Database which allows you to just type in a Title or Artist of ANY CD (Music, Shows, Video Games, Etc.) and if it was one of the CDs that worked with these two games, its in there and you can just select it and pop a monster out of it. No physical CDs required to play this. Honestly that was the main reason I got it cause while I have the physical copy, it got tiresome swapping CDs in and out. So I switched to the emulator, which limited the types of CDs I could use to PS1 games.There's also a Fast Forward button you can use to double speed the entire game, but apparently they took out the option of being able to skip Training cutscenes for this button. Its not the worst thing but its still a thing.For anyone whose never played and curious about this: this is basically Princess Maker, but instead of raising a girl, you're raising monsters. You can only raise one monster at a time and the goal is to raise a monster so strong that its able to beat all the Ranked Tournaments and become the strongest Monster out there. Train it, battle it, feed it, give it praise and scold it. Also if you're not careful your Monster might get sick, injured, run away, get lost or even die. If it survives all that, it will still eventually need to be retired (basically go to the lab and Freeze it) or just let it die of natural causes.Frozen monsters can be combined and that's how you're expected to get the really "strong" monsters. Combined monsters earn the stats of their parents and can continue to grow stronger. Its not the same as Pokemon; any monster can combine with any other monster. A single combination of monsters can result in one of several different types of monsters.You can also go on Adventures if you get enough Fame through winning battles. You won't get much from Adventures (you'll be lucky to even find 1 item) until you have a certain few stats really high up. Really high. I'm talking 300+. That's the SMALLEST one.This game can be grindy. Some people can beat the game with their first monster. There's tricks and strategies out there. I'm not one of those people. You can control just about every aspect of it. Pretty much everything in the game has some sort of purpose from your training Style to Stress to Weight and even the week of the year you decided to combine your monsters! You can literally manipulate everything into creating the perfect weapon. Or you can treat it like a Tamagotchi and try to raise it as lovingly as possible. Or forcefeed it tablets and torture it until you game over because you ran out of money!Obviously 1 and 2 are different games with 1 being more simplistic: only 3 food options, you earn money during regular training sessions and training animations are 2d pixel graphics. 2 has more overall Quality of Life fixes, like your monster not getting lost while Adventuring or doing Special Training, likes and dislikes become a thing and your monsters earn more points overall during training. It also introduced attacking monsters during Special Training and minigames, which I despise, but at least I can watch my monster wander around a small 3d environment when I'm at the ranch and pretend its my screen background while I take a break.

_childDocuments_.review: If you like monster raising games, this is the one for you! A true classic from the late 90s comes back today and I couldn't be happier!Graphics: Keep in mind this is still a PS1 game and not a full-on remaster, so going by the graphical standards of then, this game looks great! Many bright colors and everything just pops out at you. The monsters you raise all have various striking designs and even many combined sub-breeds (more on that later) stand out on their own while incorporating elements from the two monsters that made it, while having unique features of their own. For example, a Pixie (think a mini succubus) and a Suezo (The yellow eyeball guy)) combine to make a Vanity, which is a yellow Pixie who lost the wings and tail in favor of a mirror-like thing that floats in front of her. It should be noted of course that this is especially true of Monster Rancher 2, as the first game while not ugly by any means, is a lot more simplistic in its aesthetic. However it does get a point for its little sprite cartoons for when your monster works, trains, and rests. All of which are unique to each main breed across any task. In both games (especially 2) you can also simply wait in the main screen and watch your monster do its own thing and just be itself. And these are always full of charm and personalitySound: The music and sound design is top notch and every moment feels like it should, from the entering of a small tournament sounding tense but not necessarily dangerous, to the S-rank top tier tournaments sounding like a major event, to the monster getting sick and feeling incredibly tense in MR1 and unnerving in 2, right down to the actual death sounding depressing as a funeral dirge plays through the process. And the sound effects are equally perfect, as every monster has its own sound bank, as well as a sound bank for general sounds, which allows the game to add to the aforementioned personalities. Dinos/Zuums sound like mini raptors, Suezos sound like comical little guys, and Monols sound mysterious and foreboding while the evil Jokers have all sorts of unnerving laughs and noises as they swing those scythes around. If a hit lands or misses in a tournament, you will hear the audience react to it. There's tons of little details that make the whole experience feel that much more alive. Remember, these are games made back in the late 1990s. This much detail was not a common thing.Gameplay: Hoo boy, these games are DEEP! Not so much the first one (though its certainly got plenty of depth) but ESPPECIALLY the second one. Actually, it might be a little too deep, as there are many mechanics that are hidden from the player that determine a lot of factors. For example, you never really have any helpful indication of how stressed your monster is until its too late. You generally want to focus on a few key stats throughout its life, or if you're going the full competitive experience (Yup, there's actually a competitive scene for this game too!) then you're gonna need to make full use of your money and items to maximize training and minimize rest. Each monster has its own personality. For example, Apes are lazy SOBs who will fight you at every turn to be able to sleep instead of train while Tigers (definitely not a tiger by the way!) are loyal good doggos who always try to perform at their best. Combinations can have aspects of the breeds that make them up influence their personality, there's training courses for new skills, there are many unlockable breeds, the list goes on and on. There's certainly no shortage of things to do in either Monster Rancher game, and while the game gives you a clear goal of win your way up the ranks and clear the major 4 tournaments, the game doesn't really end until you decide it ends. Maybe you want to try raising a new breed or shuffle through the Shrine to see who pops out, or whatnot. You decide where your game ends.Speaking of the Shrine, in the 90s, the game used your actual CDs at home to produce monsters. We're talking ANY CD so this includes those old AOL discs they used to send in the mail every week, your parents' music collection, and even those collector's edition soundtracks you get nowadays! Due to the CD becoming obsolete in favor of digital music, that method is also obsolete, so to compensate we have a music database built into the game itself. This does two great things for the game: First, you won't need to be online in order to use the shrine and reproduce a monster, so no worries of the database being pulled and the game being unplayable. Secondly, it allows anyone access to any monster, which was not possible in the older games since monsters had a sort of rarity system. For example, the Disk breed in MR1 was completely unobtainable for many players as it was not available in any form save unique sub-breeds in two very specific CDs you probably didn't even have. Now you can raise one here!When your monster gets old, you can combine it with another monster to generate a new monster with attributes of the previous games. This uses a system that quite frankly is way too complex for me, but from what I can understand, if you can figure out how exactly it works, you can create some truly broken juggernauts right out of the box with extensive and careful lab combining. They will inherit moves, stats, and even personality traits! There's a lot you can do here and you will always have something you can do.In battle is where things both shine and falter however. The battle system is pretty straightforward: You and your opponent will have one minute to dole out attacks to each other, and whoever has the most hp at the end wins. Different monsters have different guts rates. Guts are spent to use attacks, and recharge over time, with the speed depending on the breed. Bigger, stronger, and flashier attacks consume more guts which can be a killer if it doesn't work out, so you need to be strategic in your use. Of course the fight really begins before the battle, as there is no real protection from fighting an overpowering enemy you can't hope to beat, save for forfeiting before they get to kill (emphasis on KILL) your monster. Good judgment will allow you to pick and choose your fights and clear through tournaments effectively while poor judgment may lead you to a funeral procession. Inversely however, enemies will also use their judgment on you, and may forfeit the match before it begins if your monster is simply too strong for them. The problem with the battle system is the AI simply put is random. Some battles it sluggishly reacts and gives you a free win, while other times it can spam attacks instantly and not give you a chance to breathe. This isn't much a problem in earlier tiers where you can usually weather the storm, but in the lategame where battles tend to be one-hit kill fests, it can kill you before you even got to play the game.Finally, are expeditions. When you get far enough into the game with a monster, you can be invited to partake in an expedition which has you explore desert/volcanic ruins, a jungle, or a tundra. These use your stats differently than battles and are usually a good way to get money, rare items, and even entirely new monster breeds you can't get anywhere else! However your monster needs to be strong, skillful, and intelligent in order to do these well or else the cost in fatigue, stress, and lifespan will simply not be worth it and you won't get far in them. Additionally they need to be strong enough to rank high enough to be invited in the first place. These are however quite fun (when your monster isn't getting lost in MR1) if you need money, making a monster  specialized for these is an excellent way to generate a great burst of cash on hand.Final Verdict: Due to Steam review text limit I can only say this with no further elaboration: Great game. Buy it. 9/10!

_childDocuments_.review: I've seen people say this is a 'Pokemon-like' game and I'm going to say right out; if you go in with that expectation, you'll be disappointed. Monster Rancher is more of a Sim than an RPG where you play as a monster breeder. You raise a monster recruited from a disc, sending it to work jobs so you can pay for items, ranch upgrades and expensive training routines so you can fight in ranked tournament battles to win money and prizes. Your monster can get spoiled, fat, stressed out, injured and even lost. It can even die eventually, either through old age or injury. Eventually you'll also be sending your monster out on expeditions, exploring ruins and even combining them into stronger monsters with the help of items you find out in the world.These are older games and time hasn't been especially kind to the graphics, UI or controls but there's a ton of charm here and seeing DX get a US release gives me hope for the future of a fun and unique series, even if it's just re-releases of the other games.
