_childDocuments_.review: Completely blown away by this game. Utterly enraptured. I didn't want it to end. Combat was always an absolute blast. Well-tuned difficulty aligned perfectly with an expected and gratifying grind. Constant twists in the story to match equally compelling character growth systems. I want to call this _THE_ sidescroller RPG experience. Thank you KEIZO for a game I'll never forget. ---Getting into this game was so fascinating for me. ASTLIBRA evokes an air of nostalgia surrounding perhaps a respected sleeper PC-98 game, one that you've only ever seen on the periphery of game lists. A game always just out of reach but always lauded whenever mentioned... a remake of a game for another day, maybe. The art, animation, and overall design experience lend themselves  well to this feeling, as if you're playing something utterly classic and uncannily familiar. This makes ASTLIBRA feel like a triumphal love-letter to the genre, obfuscating itself as a hidden lodestone. As you play you'll learn it sets a new mark, surpassing expectations set by its forebears.  Gameplay was consistently engaging and rewarding. Always new techniques to try out after grinding for mastery and equips through each new zone, culminating in zany, creative abilities and combos that allow for a surprising range of builds. I recommend playing on at least Hard, since the grind makes itself worthwhile without becoming overbearing. There are some difficulty spikes around bosses-- some early ones being absolute HP sponges-- but as you experiment with your various options and find patterns you start to see how the game is really played. Hint: Possession skills give i-frames. I said earlier that the story is compelling- and it is, if you have a ounce of soul- but take this with a grain of salt... as seasoning, rather than skepticism. The translation  pretty hard, yeah, especially at first. The vast majority of the game is extremely well translated at this point, but there are still some moments with typos, syntax, or strange idioms that stand out. Personally, this is a pinch of that aforementioned salt: just part of the experience of doujin/fan translated media, lending strongly to ASTLIBRA's authentic feeling. The charming episodic openers make it clear that this game was formed chapter by chapter in its original doujin publishing online and make for excellent stylistic bookends. ASTLIBRA retains a lot of sentiment this same way through its storytelling: narratives and plot spectacle shenanigans that wouldn't be out of place in a LN or anime, moments of sudden levity that strike from nowhere, and an ambient level of horniness (providing much of said levity) that matches any given classic shounen. "Forgivably horny" is the term I've been throwing around. Wrap your expectations within this package and you'll be a very happy camper. The music selection and placement throughout the story are top-tier, and it makes me wince that we probably won't get a compilation for easy direct access. "Wintering Ezo Red Fox," "Go When," "Black Tears and Lives to Protect," and especially "Relic of Agunamonita" are all living rent-free between my ears now and forever.The heart, dedication, and compassion put into this game by its developer are entirely evident, and he deserves every last ounce of praise we can give. KEIZO, you can have my "Love," specifically the one Porin found on the ground for me. That one was cool.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm not sure I'll ever forget a game like this. This was an experience, perhaps one of the best modern RPGs I've played. It's a master piece that I'm sad is over.What's so striking about this game is that none of it should really work. The art constantly shifts between beautiful and ugly. The controls feel clunky, the combat stiff. The story is very anime and translated stiffly. Yet, I was hooked minutes into the demo. However, there's just something about this game that even with it's flaws, it just works together. Learning that this was in development for 14 years is no shock. It's very polished, with all the systems being fleshed out and having a lot of thought put into them. The more you put time into this, the more you get engrossed into it. _childDocuments_.review: I'd give it a 6/10. Still worth playing if you like this Metroidvanias. But not a particularly good one. The fighting mechanics has that thing where the game pauses for a split second whenever your attack connects. This is a combo-heavy game. In addition, one attack hitting multiple enemies freezes the screen for each enemy hit. Really annoying. You do get used to it.The magic system is interesting. You can equip 8 different magic attacks/summons and you have use them through a button combination. It's quick and easy to use. The magic/summons have situational uses, so you still use different ones every now and then, even if one of them is overwhelmingly the best for enemy swarms. To build up magic meter, you need to do physical attacks. It goes down over time if you are not attacking.The passive bonus system is a little too much. Leveling up grants you stat points that you can allocate and respec whenever you want. A "growth" screen has a skill-tree looking thing that lets you buy stat points and sometimes new magic skills. The amount of stat points you get from this screen overshadows anything you get from leveling up.Lastly, you get to pick items that give passive bonuses. This part is cool. You get scales that need an equal amount of "karma" from items on the left and right sides. You mix and match items (consumables, crafting ingredients) of different karma values and different passive bonuses to get the two sides as equal as possible. If they are not equal, you still get the bonuses, but the values are diminished. Again, the "growth" screen provides so many stat points that the bonuses from the scales are not as big a deal.The weapons aren't very varied. You have a few magic staves that give mostly useless magic attacks. Can't really aim them right. 1-handed swords / hammers and some two handed weapons. The attacks though are pretty much identical. Spear and rapier are different, but everything else has the same animations/attacks.There is also the passive magic bonus system. You equip magic passives such as double jump, swing heavy weapons faster, auto-guard, etc. Utility skills mainly. So far the gameplay is:1. Start in town. Arena in town has challenges where you can win extra items. Some shops, but you have everything after the first visit.2. Go to the guild to get a new mission. You get transported to a new area.3. You leave town and can't come back until you finish the mission. Every mission so far has had a shop in the mission area itself so this isn't a big deal. It does mean that you can't just go to the arena whenever you want. The new area contains all of the ingredients for the new items you can buy from the new shop.  Each area is only a few different screens. No real exploration.4. Back in town. You can go back to old areas through a portal once in town again.It's a pretty grindy game. I am playing on Hard and it takes forever to master the weapons you get. Mastering equipment through use grants you new magic passives I mentioned earlier, so you want to master all of them in case you get a good utility skill.But the biggest problem is there is nothing to discover. Metroidvanias are about exploration and getting skills that allow you to explore old areas you couldn't reach before. None of that here.  There is ONE area so far in Chapter 4 (I think) that has a secret entrance to some secret area with super strong enemies. One-hit kills at the time you first get there. Maybe later the game has more of this stuff, but I'm a solid 16 hours in the game and that's the only thing so far.So yeah, the issues are that it's a bit too straightforward, too many mechanics that have overlapping effects (leveling up, growth screen, and scale system all add passive stat bonuses), and the fighting is a bit clunky, though not as bad as Salt and Sanctuary or Blasphemous.
_childDocuments_.name: ASTLIBRA Revision

_childDocuments_.review: After 100% finishing Astlibra, the only thing I can say is that is painfully Japanese. A game trapped in his retro inspirations. But I would say is kind of a worthwhile ARPG experience. Super long, with a convoluted plot about time travel, magic and other sci-fi tropes. It is the quintessential power fantasy adventure. You literally start swinging a stick and end more powerful than gods  (Flying all over the screen swinging epic magic swords). In the end it is a hard game to recommend for a couple of reasons, some anime tropes that are used as "fan service" are a detriment to the experience, the other big reason, is that it is loooong. This game is a good example of a niche game, that is going to be liked by a bunch o people, but not others, in that regard the game has a demo, and I feel that is the best way to see if you could like the game, the gameplay is fun, but it's also a little simplistic and monotonous by the end. The game have multiple difficulties, and on the hardest difficulties the start of the game is pretty slow until you understand all the mechanics. I feel this game is like a 3.5/5 game for me, with a better translation and a little less fan service this game could be a 4/5. There is a new translation and DLC in the works. So I feel this game can improve, it has a solid foundation.

_childDocuments_.review: PLEASE PLEASE PLEASE BUY THIS GAME!!!!!!!! ALSO PROBABLY DON'T PLAY THE DEMO MODE IN THE DEMO BECAUSE I DID AT FIRST AND DIDN'T THINK I'D LIKE IT!!!!!!!!!!!! IF YOU PLAY THE DEMO START A NEW GAME!!!!!!!!!Now with the formalities out of the way, Astlibra Revision is one of the absolute greatest games I have ever had the pleasure of playing in my entire life. I will admit, it probably isn't for everyone, but I highly recommend buying it if it seems even a little bit up your alley, since if you don't care for it you'll still be helping to support an incredible developer. This game excels extraordinarily on every front imaginable. So lets go through those fronts, shall we?VISUALSThis is definitely the most debatable point. From an objective perspective, I'd say the visuals in this game aren't great. There are various mismatched artstyles all over the place, and a lot of things seem to just be stock assets. However, this strange artstyle gives the game such a unique feeling that very few other games capture. It makes the game stand out among all its contemporaries for being so unusual. For me, the visuals evoke a very strong sense of nostalgia. As to whether it's the early 2000s, late 2000s, or early 2010s, I have no clue. It just captures that vibe, whatever it may be, and just makes me feel at home, reminding me of the good old days, whatever days those were. Plus, when this game wants to do spectacle, it definitely does some great spectacle.SOUNDTRACKThis game's soundtrack is mostly, if not entirely, made up of stock and copyright free music. However, the song choices that were included go so unbelievably hard. The very first level theme is one of the most motivating and awesome songs I have ever heard for a first level, and all you're doing it hitting slimes with a stick. If you want good examples of tracks from this game, listen to Enter Velocity by Shimajiro and Lava Belt by TAZ. Both are absolutely amazing. Also there are even a few songs in here by Sakuzyo (for my fellow rhythm game fans), who always makes excellent songs.STORYNow we get into the really incredible stuff. Astlibra's story is completely unhunged, utterly nonsensical, and frankly deranged. It is also one of the best stories I have ever seen in a video game. It isn't quite to the level of the NieR games or Omori, but I'd place it as a solid 3rd place. Nothing ever makes any sense, every twist is insane, and the game outright lies to you on multiple occasions. And yet, it's told beautifully, everything is foreshadowed very well without being predictable, and the feels hit so hard so many times they'd be convicted of murder. This story is one-of-a-kind, and I wouldn't wish spoilers for it upon my worst enemy. If the game itself isn't to your liking, at least watch a playthrough just so you can experience the incredible narrative it has to tell.GAMEPLAYOh yes. This game is pure and utter chaos in the absolute best way possible. Early on it plays fairly basically while managing to not feel boring or like a slog. However, as the game goes on, it slowly becomes more and more apparent that battles are not just enemies to fight. The combat system in this game is a lock, and you have been given a keyring so full you could never manage to count all the keys it holds. By the endgame, battles feel less like planned and crafted encounters and more like "how much insanity can we theoretically throw at the player? Oh that much? Ok cool do three times that." And somehow, it never feels unfair. Except Beatrice, she's kinda annoying. But one slightly annoying boss out of a 50+ hour game is such a small issue I wouldn't even bother saying it is one. And on top of all of that, there are the system mechanics and upgrades.Karon skills are a very neat addition. Every single weapon, shield, and piece of armor in the game can be leveled up, and will give you either a new ability or an extra resource for assigning those abilities when mastered. This sounds like it would involve a lot of grinding to get everything, but I spent very little time overall grinding for anything, and I never felt particularly bored while I did so. I say this as someone who hates grinding in games with every fiber of my being. The abilities you can get are also all very interesting and fun, leading to all sorts of potential builds and shenanigans.The Grow system, however, is where things get insane. From the outside it seems like a basic skill tree. Gather different colored Force from enemies and spend it to unlock stat boosts. However, this skill tree is essentially its own entire dungeon. There are chests to find, special items, locked doors and keys, all sorts of crazy things. And the sheer size of it is unbelievable. It is likely the largest skill tree in any game ever made. And yet, you'll likely fill out almost the entire thing by the time you beat the game, and likely not feel any real need to finish it unless you really, really want to. There are more very cool and interesting mechanics on top of those, but I think I've gone on for long enough.CONCLUSIONPlease play Astlibra. It is one of the greatest pieces of media I have ever experienced and the fact that it was mostly made by a single person is utterly insane. The fact that this game is so obscure is devastating to me, because I want as many people as possible to experience this game's perfection of its craft. Play it. Tell your friends to play it. Tell random strangers on the street to play it. Because with the massive amount of work that went into this game over its 15 year development, it's earned it.

_childDocuments_.review: Easily one of my favorite games of all time.  It reminds me of both Bloodstained: Ritual of the Night (though no necessary backtracking typical of Metroidvanias) and the couple Ys games I've played.The game's story is compelling and the English localization is really good.  Every time I asked myself about some implication of an event - how or why did this happen? what will result from it? - the game dev proceeds to answer or at least acknowledge it.  It shows a lot of thought went into the story which tackles a topic that so often creates plot holes.The gameplay is very fun and is what mostly reminds me of Bloodstained.  Each "chapter" provides opportunities to grind - there are a multitude of progression elements to grind for - and I was always excited to do so.  This was helped by the fact that there is a pretty clear-cut way to determine if you're done grinding for a given chapter - it made it feel like an optional goal to hit each time.  And no problem if you don't hit that goal, you don't have to backtrack but you certainly can!I'll stop myself from going on and wrap up with a testament:  Every time I turned the game off late at night, I always literally said out loud "my god this is such a good game".  The fact that it was largely created by a single individual, KEIZO, over the course of 15 years is an inspiring display of the capacity of a person to produce something incredible.

_childDocuments_.review: Well, I finished ASTLIBRA Revision. On the timer 16.5 hours (Proton does not count playing time offline). In-game time is as follows: about 70 hours on "Normal" difficulty, and about 17 hours on "Hard" difficulty. Had to go through the game twice, as I wanted to collect all the achievements. It was two completely different experiences. On the subject of time, to confirm my words left only one word: . If you know, you know.So, review. Saw a lot of good reviews of the game, decided to try it. I can say with confidence - it was one of the best gaming experiences.What I liked:-The story is strong, and it really is very good. The story leaves a nice aftertaste, it is completely finished and leaves no blank spots behind;-Music accompaniment fits the game perfectly, the combination of multiple genres sets the pace of the game. It's a subjective feeling, but through the music you can somewhat predict which way the story might move;-Various bosses, especially it feels that way on difficulty "Hard" and above;-Was pleasantly surprised that some bosses can make a real bullet hell, it was a very pleasant experience since the days when I played Rabi-Ribi. It's not often you see a 2d side-scroller project with bullet hell mechanics;-One of the best endgame content, with new mechanics and a big part of the story (no spoilers, it's just worth it);-The game is well balanced on "Normal" difficulty, and some will find it challenging on "Hard". I can't speak for the other difficulties.-Responsive controls, the character always does what you want to do;-A lot of RPG mechanics, some mechanics show themselves very well in the endgame;-Many options for enhancing a character's power, their combination makes the game very entertaining;-Well-hidden secrets and puzzles that are fun to solve;-The ability to quickly skip dialogues, which saved a lot of time on a second quick playthrough.Neutral points:-Although the secrets are hidden very well, there are some secrets that can be found either by accident or by digging every stone. Although I only had a few of these moments, -Maybe not everyone may like the graphics, but the game manages to pleasantly surprise with stunning views, especially in the second half of the game.Controversial points:-If you properly level up your character, the endgame part may be too easy for both "Normal" and "Hard". On the other hand, the balance of the endgame will depend entirely on the player.I could not identify obvious disadvantages in the game. It completely fulfills its functions.Bottom line: a great game, with good mechanics, bosses and a good story. ASTLIBRA Revision deserves to go into my box of awesome unique projects.

_childDocuments_.review: Astlibra's odd, but I'll say that it never once bored me.Its controls are pretty nice, its music is great, its progression is surprisingly fantastic with all the systems it uses, it has a large amount of content that only get better the further in I got, and despite a bit of messiness I think a lot of people can find worth in the narrative.All of these things alone are enough for me to recommend the game but let's get a bit more detailed.The combat's pretty simple but man is it fun, there's a real nice amount of enemy variety, a lot of the larger bosses are pretty fun to get through, and honestly my biggest complaints would be that you can become too powerful for your own good.On top of this is the magic system, full of legitimately useful and powerful spells for all kinds of occasions, and the way magic works is great.MP or as it's known as ST, builds up as you hit targets, so it promotes aggression instead of just sitting in the backline.There's tons of spells to unlock as you go through the game, and while I may have been basic with what I actually used, there's a lot of really cool ones to use.There's tons of worthwhile progression, from a basic level up system where you individually increase your stats, equipment to provide new passives that you can learn and use permanently so long as you have the resource to equip it.A MASSIVE growth tree that lets you get loot, character upgrades and additional permenant stats via a secondary form of EXP, and even more progression in the post-game, which lets you become stupidly overpowered.The best part about these systems is that it's all very easy to respec into whatever you want, as the game will allow you to mix and match whatever passives you want, when you want, and also change your level up stat allocations at several points, including when you level up.It also incentivises grabbing every single piece of equipment you can get your hands on, to learn even more abilities that'll make you even more busted, it's just a brilliantly crafted system.The game also never lets you miss out on content, while this isn't a metroidvania, it is possible to gloss over nice pieces of equipment/upgrades here and there, not to mention superbosses, so being given to option to go back to prior areas in-between chapters is legitimately appreciated.Let me be clear and say that the game will NEVER, let you miss out of items, with there being a few exceptions to gain an item that'll help stop a certain optional grind much, MUCH later into the game.To be a bit more negative, the quality of the game is a bit, "uneven", not bad, just off.Graphically I think it's apparent that Astlibra is probably a tier below most games you'll play, and to go along with that its art can be a bit inconsistent, using a mix of custom artwork of varying artstyles and slightly animated jpegs.It's iffy, and when it comes to enemy design I feel it can be problematic, as some telegraphs can feel a bit cheap with how poorly animated/displayed things can get.To its credit though, I feel the game despite how graphically poor it might be, never wanted to be a bore, as the backgrounds are decently layered, bigger entities are given the graphical quality they should receive and there is genuine effort put into trying to make the background/world feel less still than it could've been.Regarding the level design, it's kinda bad.It feels very "game-y", with tons of wall clipping, tiny blocks for platforms, weird scrolling for some areas, I wouldn't call it too well designed.What really doesn't help is how backtracky the game can become at points in the main story, as sometimes it just feels like it's wasting your time.But it's also not the biggest selling point here, as for the most part you're just going to be mowing down enemies as you get from point A to point B.Commenting further on these negative aspects, I will say that it feels like KEIZO did a better job designing the later areas in the game instead of the early ones, maybe it's just due to a lack of experience at the time of developing some of these levels, but it's most notable during the early parts of the game, which I feel can help sour expectations.One thing I won't necessarily defend though is an optional grind at the end of the game, as while there are methods to skip it throughout the game, if you miss these items, you may just find yourself mindlessly grinding enemies until you get the drops you need for some additional content, just a very odd choice.As advertised, it's a sidestory. While it does hint at more content to come, its story is pretty basic and non-essential, and it's gameplay is still as good as it ever was.The new progression systems work well, death has some fun consequences instead of just sending you back to your last save, but its biggest problem is that as a roguelite, it just doesn't have enough variety. You see all there is to see on the first layer and from there you just kinda go through the motions. The new bosses aren't interesting enough, especially with how strong you can get, and there's no new enemies at all.Perfectly harmless if you really want more once you finish the game but easily skipped if you're satisfied with what you got or didn't like the few rogue parts the game had in the base game.I think a second pair of eyes during development could've fixed a lot of my issues, but man this was still so much fun to play through, it feels nice playing something that feels like someone knew what players actually wanted.Very easy to recommend, with or without a sale.

_childDocuments_.review: While this game has many issues, it is far more than the sum of its parts. I was absolutely entranced by it; the story is fascinating, the gameplay is phenomenal, the various systems that unlock as you go are mostly well thought out and very fun, and the sense of growth is almost unmatched. There are just SO MANY things to do and ways to power up your character, and you'll need all of them to succeed. I'm afraid to say much more without spoiling things, almost everything is tied to the story so well that describing most of them in detail would rob you of the moment of discovery.A relatively minor, lategame-only system is actually one of my favorites, and non-spoilerey, so I can talk about it a bit: Boards. They serve many purposes, but chief among them is the ability to make ANY weapon or armor good with enough work. Just getting a board takes all equipment up to *rough* parity, but with enough work you can almost completely customize them. Want your claws to deal all 6 elements of damage? Sure, go grind for a few hours. Want your starting wooden branch to be better than most postgame weapons? Not even that hard tbh, just get the board and toss on the accessory that focuses Board drops on equipped gear and it'll catch up in no time. Between Boards and skills, you can make basically any playstyle work by the end, regardless of how good or bad they are baseline.I will, however, note that there are many, many, *many* issues with the game that may lessen the experience. There are a few absolutely awful bosses (ex. chapter 3) and two chapters (7 and 8) that have genuinely some of the worst video game design I have ever experienced in 30 years of gaming. There's also a *lot* of 2000s Japanese flavor, both for good and bad - I hope you like puerile jokes about boobs, cross-dressing, and some absolutely nonsensical puzzles without even a single meaningful hint. Consider using a spoiler-free guide if desired.The overall experience was absolutely worth it in my eyes, and unless the above is a total dealbreaker for you I highly recommend giving it a shot. This game is really something special. It won't change your life, but it's an experience that you won't soon forget.Just don't get the DLC, lol.

_childDocuments_.review: Astlibra is a fantastic 2D action RPG. It may look like it's a Metroidvania, but there are little to no powers or unlocks that provide access to new areas. Each area is mostly self-contained per chapter of the game's story. And this game's story...I wish I could play this game again blind.The main character starts out as a young boy who befriends a girl about his age. Their village is attacked by demons and he attempts to save her only to be killed. Or does he?This game has so many twists and turns, and every time you think you know what's going on, you're wrong. It seems like it's going to be formulaic and follow established tropes, but then pulls the rug out from underneath you. Straight up to the very end, I could never have guessed where the story was going, and it was all excellent.If I had to make any complaint, it's that the when the story switches to moments of levity, they are usually a bit on the pervy side, such as borrowing one of the girls outfits to masquerade the main character as a woman and having the aforementioned girl follow behind in provocative attire, or having a main plot point kick out with one of the male characters leading the player character to watch the female characters in a hot spring. Additionally, a few of the bosses are women with huge breasts that range is level of provocative appearance. While I didn't have any problems with these things, and they didn't happen too often, I'd be remiss in not mentioning them.Finally, regarding the depth of game mechanics:There's a plethora of weapons, with different stats, swing speeds, etc., but they also unlock different abilities once you max out their proficiency meter, so you'll want to seek out, buy and craft all that you can to unlock them.There's a huge grid of stat-ups, spells, and other goodies that you can unlock with elemental crystals you get from killing different types of enemies. And if you can't find the exact color you need, you can buy it with a different one, albeit at 3x the cost.There's a system where you put different items on a set of scales. Each item has it's own passive effects, and the closer you can balance the scales the bigger percentage of the effect you can get.I can talk about how great the game is forever, but if you dig 2d combat, like what you'd find in a Metroidvania, but not necessarily the exploration aspect, this game should not be missed.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is great and its gameplay loop scratches a lot of itches for me. I won't discuss the story as part of this review, but suffice to say it's compelling enough and has a number of interesting twists to it.The bulk of the game is a side-scrolling action RPG, with the combat and enemies giving me strong Castlevania: Symphony of the Night vibes. You're going to amass an arsenal of weaponry, and at a surface level combat is going to devolve into running at the enemies and spamming your attack button while occasionally busting out a special move. That said, there's nuance in the details and in the optimizations, and boss fights will also require at least some adjustment to your strategy if only because of the sheer numbers behind their attacks.The game encourages and rewards exploration. Some very powerful equipment and upgrades are hidden behind a gacha machine that requires "small metals" hidden in chests throughout the game world in order to access. Despite the name, the machine is not random at all, however it always dispenses items in the same order. Your fifth metal will always get you the same item whether that was the fifth metal it was possible to get, or whether it was the 20th you could have possibly gotten. So getting the rewards from it on-pace requires careful exploration of each area. Fortunately, the game is organized into chapters, and between chapters there will be a point where you can backtrack to previously explored areas to find what you missed, so you can always just breeze through the story and come back later if you'd prefer.The game also encourages and rewards grinding, on several fronts. Each chapter has a blacksmith with an assortment of weapons, armor, and shields you can forge. Forging these requires money, but it also requires items that are dropped by enemies in that chapter. So you're encouraged to grind on the associated enemies, get their item drops, come back, and forge the equipment. What do you gain from this aside from stats? Well every weapon has an EXP bar that gradually fills up as you kill enemies with it equipped. Once it fills, you will either unlock a Karon Skill, a special ability that modifies the gameplay in some fashion, or a Magic Crystal, a currency that allows you to equip Karon Skills. Additionally, if the equipment granted a skill, you can equip that skill for free while the item is equipped, and if it gave a crystal, its stats will be enhanced going forward.So you're encouraged to get into this loop of forging equipment, grinding on enemies to master that equipment, going back with your new loot to forge more items, and repeat the cycle until you've mastered all of the available equipment. While doing this you'll also gain EXP for your character which earns level ups which allow you to buff your base stats, as well as "Force", another currency that can be spent on the Growth Board, a system reminiscent of the FFX Sphere Grid where you can spend force to unlock nodes which grant stat boosts and unlock further nodes, with some special nodes even giving you bonus equipment and new special moves to use in combat.Overall, the combat feels satisfying to execute, especially at the endgame, and the gameplay loop and progression systems kept me very engaged for the entire play time. If any of the above sounds fun, you should grab this game.

_childDocuments_.review: This has been one of the most enjoyable Action/RPG I think I've ever played; almost up there with Nier:Automata. 2D side-scroller combat with tons of gear to craft. A lot of the weapons are basic stat upgrades with a choice between preferring Range, Speed, or sheer Power. Good range of evasive/defensive options (an evade/dash with invincibility frames, a shield to block with its own health bar; can unlock abilities for "perfect block" that if timed correctly can restore health or prevent shield HP from going down). Plenty of "special attacks" (summons) that continue to unlock throughout the game, and even into the "post-game". Combat always felt fun, unlike some other action RPGs where the combat gets old after a few hours.  Replaying in 2024 with the new English translation - it's much better now, very good overall. Only noticed some rare minor issues. A few puzzles mid-game were a bit confusing, and I had to resort to using Google Translate on the Japanese Wiki to get solutions. This may have been partially due to the rough translation, or with not understanding an expected mechanic. [spoiiler](I couldn't knock the "Green Orb" lose with a sword or club; why would a Bow + Arrow work???). [/spoiler]  - game is well worth full price, I have no regrets and I'm a cheap bastard. :)

_childDocuments_.review: If you like Hack and Slash games, and JRPGS, please stop reading reviews and actually play the game. It's shockingly good. This game plays more linearly than a few other Metroidvanias, but I never felt like this detracted from the game at all. Combat is relatively simple but the content the game has allows you to create a few cool strategies that can give the game a lot more depth. I did initially play the game as a "just keep whacking the enemy before they die" sort of playstyle, as I did for most Metroidvanias, but this game genuinely allowed the option for a fun playstyle where I had to think about when to utilize i-frames while performing magic that took HP away to stay net neutral with costs while outputting significant damage. Honestly? Not many games tend to have that sort of freedom which is really cool.Also, I have to say that I also thought that both the OST and the story kicks ass. The story can be a bit zany so for people looking for a more grounded and realistic story for one setting, it's sort of understandable, but even then, I still think it's really cool. The fact that the game's able to introduce details, and somehow make them all relevant at some point of the story is really admirable.I really enjoyed this game, the 74.4 hours of playtime are all part of one save file, with me playing on the "Hard" or "Difficult" setting. It's just that particularly long of a game, with it never really feeling like it falters, and even delivering during post-game, which is fantastic. Please play the game, especially if you're into Hack and Slash or JRPG's.

_childDocuments_.review: Global Achievements don't lie: Over a quarter of all players have reached the true end.  Even absolutely top tier games rarely boast more than 10% finishing the game - let alone massive long RPGs like this; Divinity Original Sin 2 has about 12% game completion rate, for example, and is one of the top RPGs of all time by basically every measure - and ASTLIBRA has twice the percentage of people who stuck with it all the way to the very end.  It's not just a good bit of a game - it's amazing start to finish.I didn't know if Symphony of the Night would ever be dethroned, but in spite of a little bit of map jank here and there, the weirdness with overlays and mining, and the fact that the first two boss fights in chapter five felt over tuned, this is my new top metroidvania.  The weapon mastery system ensures that you're always trying out new gear so the combat never stagnates, the magic, growth, and spell systems are very well done, and the post game equipment boards and weapon upgrade systems add everything you need to keep the game feeling fresh from the very first level to the true final boss mechanically, and the story has plenty of turns to keep you engaged the whole time.Normally I'm a bit more reserved in my reviews, but honestly?  Buy and play ASTLIBRA Revision right now.  Don't wait for a sale.  Right now.

_childDocuments_.review: EDITED REVIEW: Well, I suppose this is one instance where I have to eat crow (heh, apologies to the little buddy in this game). To use the Shaq meme, "I have to apologize, I wasn't really familiar with your game."Have I changed my mind about the critiques I mentioned? No, the translation still hurts the game and the graphics are still somewhat underwhelming. However, after finishing it and experiencing it firsthand, I can say without reservation that the story is SO good that even despite the terrible translation it carries the game and makes it a must-play. I don't want to spoil anyone but it really is the sort of thing you have to experience for yourself, just hearing about it doesn't do it justice. It's been a long time since I actually felt emotionally attached to a game's characters, but this one actually did it, and I got tears in my eyes during one of the climactic fights (you guys will know the one). So yeah, I'm turning this review from negative to positive and encouraging everyone who reads it to forget my earlier churlishness and buy this game. Just try to ignore the bad translation (so far, hopefully they'll patch it soon).A couple other reasons for a positive revision. First, when you get a wider variety of combat skills, it really does become pretty satisfying and engaging. The fact that there are so many mistranslations (for instance, the description for one crucial skill says it recovers ST when it actually recovers HP) hurts it, but like I said above, they should fix it with a new translation soon. Second, while it's still not genuine Vanillaware quality, some of the boss sprites, especially near the end, do look super cool. Third, the music is MUCH better than I gave it credit for at first. Most of it is taken from free stuff, but by the end you can tell the dev became an expert at choosing good songs, as a lot of the themes and event music are absolutely perfect and wonderful to listen to, I especially love the Belkade late-game themes.Finally, more than anything else, there's one primary reason I revised my review to a positive one: One of the devs themselves (specifically the publisher) took my concerns to heart. In general, I'll almost always support a dev if they acknowledge my suggestions and make changes even if I'm dissatisfied with a game at first. I did this with They Must Be Billions, didn't like it at first but changed my negative review to positive after they released a patch making the game less annoying and adding more content. The publisher, WhisperQ, acknowledged my complaints with the translation and has mentioned there'll be a patch to fix it soon! So I'm definitely all about supporting folks who want to improve even if they've made a mistake, and I can't wait for the revamped translation so I can enjoy the game as it was really meant to be played. I now encourage all of you to buy it, support the devs, and join me!(OLD REVIEW)First solidly negative review I've written in a while, but while I really tried to give this game a fair shot, it has too many problems for me to recommend it. Despite some extremely good points--15 years of effort, an absolutely massive, in-depth combat system and art from Shigatake, one of the Vanillaware guys--the flaws of this game make it impossible for me to recommend or even justify paying 20 dollars for. Specifically, like I said, it has one of the most in-depth combat systems you can find anywhere, but the atrocious translation hurts it severely. There's a huge amount of skills to unlock, many of which are absolutely crucial, but mistranslations or outrightly incorrect translations make it very difficult to tell which skills you actually need--you need to use some of the guides friendly people on Steam have provided, which isn't acceptable for a professionally produced game. The control mapping is also absolutely terrible. Thankfully, you can change some of the more annoying button mapping, like the dash and enter room buttons being the same, but there's a shield bash move that makes some of the platforming segments nearly impossible when it activates when you don't want it to, and you can't disable that without either not using shields at all (locking yourself out of a pretty significant number of abilities and gameplay choices) or going through a bizarrely arcane method, one again described by some good steam folks. Like I also mentioned, the art from Shigatake is very nice, but unfortunately you won't find the delightful backgrounds of Odin Sphere or 13 Sentinels in this game, because the great artist just did character portraits--the backgrounds, terrain, etc. looks like cheap freeware fare. The plot, from what I've gathered, is actually relatively compelling despite how it starts off as not a basic riff off an old-school Ys style platformer, but again, the poor translation cripples its impact. As much as I wanted to love this game I cannot in good conscience recommend it, though if my refund request doesn't go through since I've beaten the first chapter, I might play through it some more if I'm stuck with it after this. We'll see if I change this review.

_childDocuments_.review: Ignore my playtime, I played through the entire game on a friend's account, but I ended up loving it so much that I bought it to support Keizo and leave a review. I don't want to spoil anything, but the story is phenomenally good. It's a real emotional rollercoaster with lots of unpredictable twists and turns, and even a few gut punches, but there's always a light at the end of the tunnel. It reminded me a lot of Gurren Lagann, which is my most loved story of all time. Just like Gurren Lagann, it can be a little corny, silly, or bawdy at times, but that's part of its charm, and it rarely loses sight of the overarching themes of humanity, love, and hope, even when faced with overwhelming despair. It's very much a story about "the indomitable human spirit". Beyond that, the world-building is surprisingly good, and it plays around with a lot of tropes that you wouldn't initially expect. There's lots of mysteries to uncover, and the game loves to drop hints about things so you can feel smart for correctly guessing before the answer is outright revealed.As far as the gameplay goes, it's solid. It won't blow you away, but it's entertaining enough for the game's run-time. There are lots of progression systems, so you always have this sense of growing and getting stronger. Some people might be turned-off by important items being hidden, but I liked it, because it meant exploration and curiosity felt genuinely rewarding. I've seen some complaints of too much grind, to which I'd say, turn the difficulty down and ignore the progression systems. Though as a grind hater myself, I rarely was bothered by it.Lastly, while I can't credit Keizo for the soundtrack, as it's entirely freeware, I *can* commend him for his choice of songs. There's a wonderful variety here, and a lot of really energetic, catchy songs. Some of the more emotional tunes were absolutely mesmerizing when I first heard them in-game as well. They definitely amplify and enhance the impact of the story beats.In all, I ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ love this game and the story is going to hold a special place in my heart for a long time to come.

_childDocuments_.review: I've never written a review before, but I felt the need to now.  I just finished the game in a little over 72.5 hours (most of it played offline so it doesn't reflect here). When I picked it back up on release, and finished the first boss, I had a feeling it was going to be a wild ride, but not this wild.  This game is the embodiment of soul.  The story, the characters, the music, the gameplay, the graphics... you can feel the love that was poured into it.  By the time I got to what I thought was the end, I felt that this game would be among the few games that I would consider my personal favorites of all time;  and when I realized that it wasn't over, it only cemented that feeling.  When the final credits rolled, I  had a smile on my face; this game is one of those few gems that pop up every once in a while, and I'm glad I got to experience it.  Do yourself a favor and give it a shot.Update (2024/03/18): I've just finished 100%ing the DLC,  I've clocked a total of 215 hours (not all reflected due to offline play), and I still stand by my original words. _childDocuments_.review: Come for the gameplay, stay for the sweet tunes. Reminded me a lot of Wanderers from Ys (Ys III.)The Good:- Gameplay is pretty snappy and there's a ton of options to tweak things how you like. Even a few accessibility ones! (My poor thumb after not using the 'hold to continuously attack' one for most of the game.)- Most of the music is great and can live rent free in my head for a bit.- The story has a bunch of good twists and turns and it goes some interesting places with it, even if it takes a bit to get there.- The skip functionality works and is very good.The Bad:-If you don't trim some of your combat options it's pretty easy to end up fuddling about a bit. Hovering in midair instead of downstabbing a fool happened to me a lot.- Difficulty is a bit wonky. For me the toughest boss that I died the most at was the Chapter 6 mid-boss. Also some of the enemies there caused plenty of game overs for me. Very much a bell curve with dips and peaks.- The story leans a bit too much on telling rather than showing. Lots of places that could be improved with visual aids or animations instead of text boxes. (Really wish there was a world map.)- Similarly the formatting of the intro movie between each chapter like a book/episode would have been much better if it actually changed as the game went along. It does not. I guess it could be handy as a reminder? But really it mostly reminded me of the skip function.- One character has a whole extra pile of misery to go on top of the misery they already have and it's just too much misery man. You don't need to escalate with that! It's counterproductive!The Annoying:- Heavy use of already-overused tropes. Oh there's a pervert, oh there's mention of a hot springs, time until pervert peeps at the hot spring t-minus 10 minutes. It feels obligatory and low effort.- One song for an encounter in the postscript. The first time it's neat and spooky and weird and then the other five or so times it's just annoying. Much like that encounter really, so at least it's fitting! Bad earworm though.- There's one side-quest that requires you to collect every weapon, armor and shield in the game. _childDocuments_.review: Have yet to finish but am at the end of chapter 5. First RPG I've played in years that I felt was amazing. It's hard to say any one thing is the reason, it's just overall great. It has a good soundtrack, and the art is charming. Gameplay is a lot of fun, not only increasing your stats and getting equipment, but increasing your own skill as a player. It's one of those games where I can laugh at how bad I was at the beginning compared to now. Using the possession skills (basically magic) in combat and mixing it in with your regular attacks feels great.There was a couple "systems" I don't like. The Libra (one aspect of character development/gearing) system, I don't see the point of its existence, its basically set and forget unless you really want to swap stats constantly. I found the amount of semi-useless consumables in the game annoying. Like torches, lanterns, and keys. All three of those are fairly easy to get, but you constantly need more. Feels like a pointless tax, wish they just had infinite uses. Also each chapter has 5-10 (on average) hidden chests with great loot, which is nice in theory but it results in feeling obligated to scour a level before you finish it to make sure you got everything. You can come back to levels later but only at certain (regular) points.The story is enjoyable, but I wouldn't say it's groundbreaking or anything. I found it pretty depressing so far, but that's up for interpretation I suppose. Not exactly a con, but a few times a chapter (depending on the chapter) there's basically horny 13 year old humor, which feels pretty out of place with the overall somewhat serious plot. It didn't affect my enjoyment, I just pressed through and ignored it.Highly recommend playing using a controller, feels great that way and seems intended to be played that way. I personally played it on my steam deck. A lot of the combat involves repeatedly pressing the attack button, so prepare for a sore thumb if you play for extended periods of time.Overall if you're interested in a polished indie Japanese RPG. Would only not recommend if you think you wouldn't enjoy the combat. I didn't think I would at first but ended up enjoying it.EDIT: Just finished. Very enjoyable and highly recommend. Only complaint is that the append/post-game chapter felt very unnecessary, almost like filler. Enjoyable filler but still. The new systems introduced there felt awful too, but it was easy to use it at least. Game didn't need enhancing/boards. At least you have control over enhancement, but boards are so powerful and almost completely beholden to RNG that it's unfun. Fortunately those systems only affect a small part of the game. Plot overall definitely wasn't great, it's all about enjoying the journey.

_childDocuments_.review: Do you ever know from the very moment a title screen hits you're about to play an all-time great? The PC-98 music hits, the moonlit background descends, and I knew instantly Astlibra was about to become one of my favorite games.There's something to be said for the sheer freedom of expression allowed when one has absolute authority over their creative expression, especially in a culture like Japan routinely producing off-kilter ideas. Keizo is, like any good Japanese artist, ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ horny. You thought Takahashi was horny while directing Xenoblade 2? Nah, fam. Astlibra is plagued with scantily clad titty beasts. Plant monsters whose only censorship is her vines, floating bodies without appendages but no deficit of cleavage, goddesses whose battle armor is lingerie, , and a year's supply of juvenile sex humor you've seen in literally every ecchi you've ever watched. To really round off the sentiment, there's a traditionally JRPG colosseum-like arena with individual matches and one of those matches is titled "Harem" in which you have to slay every degenerate demon the game has ever thrown at you. Keizo is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ horny.Keizo is also, like any good Japanese artist, ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ . This man has read his fair share of visual novels, clearly loves time travel, and probably threw every idea he ever had over its development time at the wall and performed mad science to fuse it all together. This design philosophy extends to the gameplay for sure, but I'll come back to that later, because there's a phenomenal story here if you can make sense of it all.Time travel is fascinating; even when it's riddled with plot holes it's gotta be one of my favorite genres. There's not a lot of "meaningful" choices in Astlibra, but there are choices, you can make the wrong ones, and you will feel the weight of them. There's VN-style epilogue-like "dead ends" (not always bad endings, necessarily). But most importantly, Astlibra's central theme is its opening tagline: life is a series of choices, and every time you make a choice to help someone, to save someone, you hurt or lose someone else. You could have the literal tools of God in your hands with the ability to correct any history you saw fit, but the butterfly effect unfolds -- what will you lose in the process?Chapter 7 really struck an emotional chord with me, one that all-time greats like Fullmetal Alchemist (2003) and Mahou Shoujo Madoka Magica have, when the price of obsession was made manifest. What are you willing to sacrifice for your obsession? I watched a dry comedy-drama called Russian Doll last year, also a time travel story, and a certain character described something they termed a "Coney Island moment": your one past decision where everything went to hell. You made one catastrophic decision, however inconsequential it seemed at the time, tugging the lynchpin that kept your entire life together, and the butterfly effect surely unfolds. Astlibra's thesis is thus: if you could reverse time and undo the "Coney Island moment," sacrificing all the bonds and memories you made in the process, would you, and could you live with the consequences afterward? So many ideas are thrown into the story & lore it can be difficult to untangle, and yeah, I'm pretty sure it's riddled with plot holes (although I'll note that by the end it *felt* like every loose end was resolved), but if you can untangle the mess and bask in the distinctly Japanese zaniness, it packs some serious emotional weight.The over-the-top design philosophy is infused into the gameplay as much as the narrative. By the postgame there are four different progression systems, a wide variety of techs with near-infinite build options and the ability to respec whenever you want.  I finished the game on hard, and it was ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ hard. My final clock time -- getting 100%, including achievements -- was 61.5 hours, and Steam registers a playtime of 95 hours. There's idle time in there for sure, but that demonstrates well over a dozen hours of lost progress because there is no autosave and trash mobs can ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ rip you a new one. By chapter 5 or so, it's entirely practical to be dying within 3 hits.Combat is visceral and the gameplay loop is crack. You will be  by fields of mobs as you hack 'n' slash your way through them, manipulating your iframes, guard gauge, cleverly hidden techniques, and Karon build to steamroll them as efficiently as possible, the gamepad rumbling in your hands with every slash, the frustration of playing what often feels like a 2D soulslike where every input matters, dying, dying dying to trash. Every chapter has its own equipment section with materials dropped by mobs only found in that chapter, accompanied by a super streamlined and super rewarding crafting system, making it sinfully easy to blow 5 minutes grinding for a few more mats to purchase that next available weapon. The game rewards grinding almost  well.The game's biggest flaw is how it reeks of early-to-mid 00s development. The gameplay loop is simple. The ♥♥♥♥♥♥ ESL translation steals heavily from American idioms, like "using the John," in ways that just make zero sense within the setting's context, yet it's nonetheless nostalgic to a time of mediocre VN translations (Tohsaka's anus is defenseless), ♥♥♥♥♥♥ anime subs, and downloading new episodes on BitTorrent then burning them to your DVD while posting screenshots of your ripped DVD collections on fan forums. The puzzles and platforming are excruciatingly retro; satisfying in their own way, but to solve them you have to think about them from a design perspective of a different era. You literally walk through glitches in the scenery to solve puzzles. Secret treasures in the game are well hidden in ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ pixel-sized green arrows, in the late game behind scenery, obstacles, and other hurdles making them, frankly, impossible to find unless you have a treasure guide up, and I absolutely recommend one to the side while playing. It's borderline cozy how there are virtually zero guides available online because it's so niche and playing it draws you into a real community; but there is a treasure guide, you should use it, and expect that otherwise, you will probably have to figure ♥♥♥♥ out on your own.Everything comes into harmony to produce a grossly addictive game as I was propelled from literally the first 30 minutes to see the plot unfold, yearning to see the story's earliest and most harrowing mysteries resolved -- in most cases, far differently than I could have ever imagined.It's rare these days I can play a game and not levy a dumptruck load's complaints at it; I'm aging and I have a lot to ♥♥♥♥♥ about it. A game's worth isn't so much defined by its flaws as it is how much its draws transcend those flaws. Astlibra is a gem. It's uniquely its own, there's so much to digest, and its creative expression is something you can really only get out of a game developed by one KEIZO for 16 years. The sort of poetic beauty to it all: the slice-of-life adventure of handling a new town's dilemmas every chapter; your guild master opening each chapter with a spine-tingling, heartrending summary of whose woes you must resolve; to see a VN-style opening theme at the end of EVERY ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ CHAPTER; all in a spacetime transcending romantic epic in pursuit of your first love. It's quirky, it's convoluted in a way only a JRPG could be, and it's beautiful. Go, my minions!

_childDocuments_.review: I haven't quite played a game like this since "Death's Gambit" (now "Death's Gambit: Afterlife"), ENDER LILIES, or NieR/NieR:Automata. It seems that the "Overwhelmingly Positive" reviews and the absurdly high number (~33%) of all players that got the "True Ending" are for a reason, after all.When I first saw the game, I thought it looked ugly and that the gameplay looked boring. I could not be happier to have been wrong, as it ended up being a fantastic game. The story was great - full of twists and turns, insanely increasing stakes and comedic relief. The gameplay was surprisingly fun - fluid and responsive with lots of different abilities to master and press. There is a giant skill grid called "Grow" in addition to a traditional leveling system and an armor/weapon/shield mastery system that also unlocks various skills ("KARON"). There is blocking, and i-frame dodging ("Backstep") and i-frame magic to avoid damage or even heal.As it turns out, the reason for both the initial off-putting impression and it actually being really good is that it was made by a single developer over the course of 15 years; a mixture of extremely limited resources/budget and it apparently being something he really wanted to make; something he himself wanted to play -- a rarity in a world where games are made by a boardroom decreeing they want yet another seven Assassin's Creed games being made simultaneously.I would not really advise playing on the highest difficulty as all it really does is extend grinding periods, but you can freely change it for the duration of the first chapter so you can easily see for yourself. Hard difficulty is probably the best balance between grinding and being a completionist.An amazing one-man accomplishment, for sure. ありがとうKEIZOさま。本当に。

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a masterpiece. I've spent over a 100 hours playing this.... so this should be a good indicator of how much I like this. The combat is great and I love how every weapon gets to be useful. Some may not fit your play style, but there are plenty to choose from. Daggers, clubs, swords, shields, great swords, spears, mage staffs, bows, crossbows, etc. Some weapons have different element types, some are faster, so the weapon with the highest attack power is not always the best.There are lots of different skills to find which basically work as passives, about 10-12 different special moves, and a bunch of magic spells. Late game you unlock additional gems that can completely modify the original skills and magic spells. The game has a system which allows you to combine items into new items. The ingredients are mostly drops from monsters, which makes for a far better system than endlessly grinding for more money to get better equipment. The boss fights are large and enjoyable. Killing one of the major bosses actually feels meaningful here and serves to move the story along. If you want to find every item in the game, some back tracking will be needed but you can do so at any point in the game. Nothing that you can miss and lose out on permanently. A few minor things aren't translated too well, but its pretty much limited to the skill descriptions and it looks like the developers are patching it. You shouldn't let that stop you from enjoying an otherwise great game. I consider it to be a bargain at the $25 asking price, especially considering the amount of enjoyment I got from it.

_childDocuments_.review: Truly a great game. If you like long action JRPGs and collecting equipment you will love this game.Pros:- story- tons of equipment and skills to collect- a lot of enemy variety and plenty of bosses- music is really exceptional- long (70h+)- plenty of options for builds and variables to play with- only 1 missable achievement (play the game on hard or higher)- arena challenges (mostly normal battles but there are some dps checks and a bit of a puzzle fights too)- you can skip cutscenes- bossfight checkpoints between boss phases (with 1 exception for some unknown reason, maybe an oversight)- situational humor, no modern day politics or meme/celebrity references- over 100 save slots for your game saving needsNeutral:- if you are underleveled you will be 1 shot, if you are overfarmed you will just steamroll. I played the game on Hell difficulty which is next to last and honestly it wasn't so bad. Last difficulty makes the enemies too spongy for my taste for most of the game and Hell was perfect for me (there are like 3 or 4 lower difficulties too and you can always go lower but not higher)- ability scrolls are hidden in the world (there are some ESSENTIAL combat skills that make this game so much better, hiding them isn't the best idea imo)- a lot of cutscenes and reading (no voiceovers)- a lot of time in the menus- nostalgic feel, it plays like an "old" game so you have to think like you are playing an "old" game. For example, if you want to use an item on an object in the wold like a key on a locked gate you have to go into your inventory, select the key and use it.- backstep instead of dodge forward but on the other hand shields are very strong in this game + you can always quickly turn around and "backstep forward", it just needs getting used to (there is a skill to make it into a forward dodge but you get this skill mod in postgame so it is waaaay to late for that)- when you die you have to load your last save so you know, you lose everything you gathered up and done to the point of your demise (which is a great incentive to not die)Cons:- the further you progress the more flashy abilities you have, same goes for enemies and sometimes it is impossible to tell what the hell is going on during those massive bossfights because it's all overlapping- solutions to some problems the game presents are mostly reasonable and were in one way or another mentioned along the way but this one part where you have to fill a huge jug with water so the STONE would float up to the surface is so mind boggling I would have never guessed wth I was supposed to do- berserk skill breaks the game (3x damage but 1 hp), you can just turn skills on and off without any consequences and it seems to be a solution to many difficulty related problems people have, just turn berserk on when boss is "broken" or when  the window is open and turn it off the second you feel threatened, repeat to win ez. In other words, there is easily available cheese in the game.- when you restart a boss fight from the "bossfight checkpoint" it doesn't give you back your consumables that you have used so better stock up before bosses

_childDocuments_.review: Very great game and obviously a passion project of the developer. Lots of attention to detail and many cool small touches such as all of the equipment changing your appearance (sometimes pretty dramatically).Essentially this game is a metroidvania that leans very heavily into JRPG game-play influences (as opposed to the more "souls-like" metroidvanias that have become more popular recently). Lots of equipment, stats (all sorts of "numbers go up" to play with) but also a really neat system that lets you kit out your character with different abilities to suit how you would like to handle combat and exploration. I'm also a big fan of the magic/summon system that takes some ques from Symphony of the Night but handles it much better since you have to build up a charge, the press a button which stops the action while you input a two button combo to trigger the spell/summon you want. That probably doesn't entirely do it justice but it works very well in practice. I'm not sure I've seen an action RPG or metroidvania use quite the same system.The basic loop is that you enter an area, explore it, harvest materials from the enemies in an area and then use that to upgrade your equipment at a shop. You learn abilities from said equipment so it is worth your while to collect and use as much as possible. The equipment also lends itself to very different fighting styles depending on your kit.The game-play loop is occasionally broken up a bit by some light puzzle and problem solving that is just interesting enough to keep things fresh and keep the main game-play loop from getting monotonous.I haven't finished the story yet but so far it is extremely enjoyable with a nice balance of exposition and game-play. Also some nice comic relief thrown in. From what I can tell based on where I am in the game and what I've seen about the game it is clear that this is going to be a lot longer than the typical 15 to 20 hours that this style of game usually clocks in at. And given the great story I think the increased length is a major plus. I am at 24 hours at the time of this review and I am nowhere near done.One of the biggest standout areas of the game is the banging soundtrack. Seriously, there are some killer dungeon themes in particular. I am going to be on the lookout for the soundtrack for this one.If I must list a complaint about the game it would be that it is just a touch grindy if you want to fill out all of the available equipment for each area. It isn't anything game breaking but it wouldn't bother me if the drop rates for material were just a touch higher.Overall though this game is worth the very modest asking price and a real steal if on sale. If you at all enjoy metroidvania style games and/or JPRGs playing this one is a must.

_childDocuments_.review: So I just finished spending 57 hours being completely absorbed and compelled by a game of which I had understandably low expectations. And man was I blown away. I do not usually review games - I just play them and move on - but man this is different. The screenshots, previews, and the demo that comes with the game understandably temper your expectations. The backgrounds and environments are off-putting the first time you see them. And the combat feels stiff. And the story line in the opening few chapters feels a bit aimless and stock-standard (you have amnesia and are trying to find your hometown - this feels like it has been done quite a few times). But the strength of this game is that it grows on you and continually develops. The action gets more and more fast paced and satisfying. I can't emphasize enough how good the combat gets and feels. I had more fun with the combat in this game than other Action RPGs like Nier Automata. With a lot of those games, you just mash the dodge button over and over again. With Astlibra, you charge into the fray of battle, execute combos, and devastate your opponents with combos and magic. It's all so satisfying. And the graphics grow on you. They mesh perfectly with the combat and magic graphics. Some of the animations for the gods and mechs look surreal. The design Keizo implemented into the game encourages grinding and fighting. He wants you to battle and enjoy yourself. And you are rewarded for it!  You get crafting items, and a multitude of other types of experience to grow and power up your character - and it all feels so intuitive.  Nothing is hidden, and you always feel rewarded for your time commitment. The storyline is probably the most unique narrative I have come across in a long time. it starts our so simple, so that you (the player) are not expecting much. But layers and layers keep getting added on, and when they all come  together, you are taken aback - you simply are not expecting the plot twists. And the ending ties up all the loose ends perfectly. Others have mentioned that you can't go into the storyline much without giving too much away, and i agree. You should experience it for yourself. I will say this, though, that crow is my ultimate bro. If you are a fan of action RPGs, or RPGs in general, or if you grew up during the 90s and 2000s with RPGs like Chrono Trigger, Xenogears, or maybe even Ragnarok Online, play this game. You will have a blast. Keizo, if you are reading this, you are the man. This man spent a decade creating a game that feels so good to play - a game that looks and feels like it knows exactly what it wants to be. I definitely recommend this game.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a gift that just keeps on giving! I've got a ton to say, but all you need to do is read the header and the bold bits to know whether or not this game is worth your time.  Look, when I first saw this game, I told myself, "damn, this looks a bit dated. I haven't played a game like this in a long while, I'll probably not like it." I proceeded to try the free demo, went absolutely wild with all the fun equipment, magic, and tools you're given to play with, and got extremely interested in the brief bit of story that was teased. It was a little overwhelming at first due to how much stuff you're given to test out, but I bit the bullet, bought the game, and went on an emotional roller coaster that kept me invested every step of the way! My god, where to begin? You're an orphan who got separated from your childhood friend, and you set out on a quest to find her. A simple enough premise, but add a talking crow, some magic scales that give you the ability to travel through space and time, and you've got yourself a recipe for a plot that will keep you guessing up to the very end! You'll meet so many wonderful, memorable characters that will win your heart and make you want to do everything in your power to help them, even if that means making some very difficult decisions. In the end, you'll grow to love your companions, especially your talking crow, and you'll come to appreciate how much you've accomplished together.Time and fate are, of course, key themes of this story, and you'll leave every session thinking about how the story relates to your own life, and be inspired to take your precious time on this earth more seriously. I can not emphasize enough how much this story will stick with you as you slowly but surely make your way through every chapter.... it's a masterpiece. Did I mention that a single dude poured his heart and soul into this game? Every played Stardew Valley? That game had a similar development cycle, and it was friggen AMAZING - same holds true here - Keizo has truly perfected his vision for the experience he wants players to feel as they progress through this game, and I can 100% attest to that. I'm not ashamed to admit I wanted to cry a few times through the story. Ok, let's say you don't care much for story - that's ok, you're gonna love this game's combat. Swords, hammers, maces, axes, magic staves/wands, bows, crossbows, guns, and much, much more are available for you to use and abuse on your enemies. You've got an extremely rewarded leveling system that makes you really feel like you're growing in strength from your battles, and it's extremely fun being able to harvest materials and craft new equipment for yourself as you progress through the map. Friends, when you boot up that demo and start fighting a few demons, the very first song you hear is going to give your ears an orgasm. I kid you not, the official game has the most BADASS music to go along with you fighting beginner enemies! Keizo didn't need to go that hard, but that's just an appetizer for what you're going to be enjoying as you play. The music, like the story and combat, gets better, and better, AND BETTER, AND BETTER. Every single stage of this game kept blowing me away with how great the soundtrack is!I'm a guy who likes to exercise to kickass tunes, and I can tell you now, Astlibra Revision's soundtrack has been added to my lifting and cardio playlists. Simply put: this is the greatest JRPG music I've heard in a LONG while, and I've played a lot of fantastic JRPGs with banger soundtracks... this is in a league of its own... similar yet arguably better than the music you'd hear in the YS series. Look, I don't write reviews often. See that giant wall of text up there? It means: THIS GAME IS AMAZING! BUY IT RIGHT NOW! You could wait for a sale if you like, but I guarantee that this is one of those rare gems that's worth every single penny. You're going to remember this game for the rest of your life.Thank you, Keizo, for sharing your passion and vision with the world. Your game has truly touched my heart and I've a greater appreciation for life and the journey I've taken to reach this point. We can't go back in time IRL, but you've taught me that we can always fight for a better future. Truly, this game is a masterpiece in every sense of the word...

_childDocuments_.review: A fantastic RPG. The world is starved for side-scrolling RPGs that go beyond Metroid, Castlevania, or Dark Souls. Even with all its obvious Falcom influences, Astlibra is a unique game balancing arcadey combat, hardcore RPG grit, and abundant quality of life features without any sense of compromise.You gotta love the pick-and-mix of proven RPG mechanics here: mastering equipment to learn new abilities, use-times for healing items to keep 'em from trivializing combat, MP that regenerates quickly from melee attacks to promote a spellblade playstyle... Wonderful. There's some grind for crafting materials, but it's a joy to scan back and forth across save points, see the fireworks go off, and snag loot.And the doujin visuals! All the strange detailed textures and lumpy tilesets... Painterly paper-doll goblins fighting alongside squash-and-stretch photo manipulations of snapping turtles... *chef's kiss*Its weakest point is its story. It's not bad, exactly; it gets you from point A to point B, and it takes place in a charmingly cliche JRPG world. But there are long stretches of time where you, the player, sit with two-dimensional dramatic ironies or obviously suspicious characters while the mains blabber on and on in confused exclamations and redundant questions. It's like, "Hey guys, I figured out the whole mystery behind this town an hour and a half ago!" Few of the games' premises require extended dialogues,  yet here they are in abundance.There's also a moderate amount of pervy comedy, like sexually appraising a girl's fat ass as she's on her deathbed. I'm not a prude, but I do think it's tonally weird to sexually appraise a girl's fat ass as she's on her deathbed. Better have a tolerance for this stuff coming in.Also, the translation is bad. It's charming and you can get the gist if you're familiar with amateur Japanese-to-English translations, but woof.
