_childDocuments_.review: This is the type of bootleg/janky JRPG I would play on my jailbroken iphone on my way back from school when I was 12 because I didn't know better.  Unfortunately, I'm not playing this game as a kid trying to kill time on their commute, and even if I was, there are FAR better options now than whatever this is.  I played through until a fair bit after the intro and first boss before I couldn't take it anymore and skimmed a full game playthrough video to see if it got any better later (doesn't seem like it). The combat feels mindless and grindy.  There's basically no difficulty here beyond the raw numbers and stats, you spam your weapon attack and press a spell when you get enough ST, maybe dodge if you're fighting a boss, open the menu to heal occasionally, etc. you probably know the type of combat I'm talking about if you've played some bad side scrollers before.  From what I've seen the gameplay is like that all the way through to the end, just spam attacks and spells, let your numbers do the work.  The scale mechanic is the only somewhat interesting part of the gameplay; I obviously haven't explored it fully but from what I've read it doesn't appear to be an insanely must-play!!! level groundbreaking mechanic that changes the entire game.This game also looks pretty rough, there are probably flash games that look better than this.  The "city" is just a bunch of pictures of churches and stone buildings cropped and set against a static background.  Enemies look lifeless or like they were drawn in paint; sometimes they're also just cropped pictures.  There are only a handful of sprites that look like they were made for this game, which is fine if the art direction is strong and they're used creatively and smartly.  Plenty of games use still photos and can look fantastic, but it's painfully noticeable in ASTLIBRA that they just wanted to cut corners on their art assets.  Animations are also pretty stilted and awkward looking, particularly on larger enemies.Obviously can't speak to the quality of the story, you'll have to look at other reviews for that.  From the few hours I played it was at least interesting enough to not feel the urge to skip any cut scenes, so there's that.Anyway, this game is definitely not for me, maybe my standards are too high since the other reviews are overwhelmingly positive, but my recommendation is to steer clear unless you like low quality mindless JRPGs.

_childDocuments_.review: Simply one of the best games I've ever played. I cannot even put into words how incredible some parts were because of the music alone. Play Astlibra.

As someone with little to no experience or interest in side-scroller RPGs, I can confidently say that this is a high-quality game in that genre.The story is a little cheesy, but in an enjoyable way. However, the combat is where this game truly shines. Combos, skills, equipment—it nails all the core mechanics and enhances them with its own features, making everything even more satisfying.I thoroughly enjoyed every aspect of this game, and it genuinely surprised me with how good this was.
_childDocuments_.name: ASTLIBRA Revision

_childDocuments_.review: The gameplay is alright. It has some metroidvania elements. It has RPG elements with a big passive stat tree, different weapon types and passive bonuses, that make your build. The loop is, you getting new gear, playing with it so you unlock the passive of said gear and make a build with it. I played the game as a mage for the biggest part, as an example. If you like a challenge, this game can deliver on that on higher difficulties. The strongest point of this game is the story, in my opinion. The story made this game one of my favourite games of all time. It is quite long, it will keep you guessing and it will surprise you for sure. Even if you are not a fan of the gameplay, please stay for the great story. I would say the whole presentation, the story, the characters, the plot and the music make this game special. The opening theme has a special place in my heart now. It is by Memoria, title is “As You Wish” and it´s just magical. And a big thanks to the developer, KEIZO, for making this game.
_childDocuments_.name: ASTLIBRA Revision

_childDocuments_.review: This game is phenomenal.  It reignited a lot of what modern rpgs for me were missing, and kept me captivated throughout my time with it. At just over 100 hours I'm nearly done with all the achievements and collectibles, yet want to dive right back in for a run on impossible difficulty. It was a blast that I don't regret any second of. Thank you Keizo for your work on this masterpiece, and I look forward to the DLC and your future work!
_childDocuments_.name: ASTLIBRA Revision

_childDocuments_.review: There's a reason this game has "overwhelmingly positive" reviews!  I haven't had a game grip me like this one did in a long time... in these days of being unable to stick with a single game this one quickly became one of my new favorites, possibly top of the list!  You owe it to yourself to play this one all the way through!
_childDocuments_.name: ASTLIBRA Revision

_childDocuments_.review: it may look ugly and feel clunky at the beginning, but give it time, it takes some time to get used to the rhythm of combat and a later enemies and locations look amazing. I recommend playing it on "hard" if you usually play 2d action games, "hell" if you are confident...there is one boss that you encounter early that has some bs invulnerability 80% of the time with only a vulnerable hitbox at the center until you get it to 40% HP, use skills and a weapon with long reach...but aside from that one boss everything else is quite fair once you understand the fight.The systems and lore are a lot more complex than it looks like, the story is far better than it has any right to be, its been quite a while since I've played something expecting nothing more than "fun", yet ended up 100% the game for the story. (the previous game I went in like that was "MMQ", kudos if you know what I mean)...it was good, truly damn good. A masterpiece. just give it a chance, its money well spend.

_childDocuments_.review: Looks like clip-art and google image vomit, has a dumb story, but fantastic gameplay and progression. You farm enemies to get mats to make equipment, then level up that equipment which unlocks skills and skill points. You then do this for a few dozen hours while you enjoy the feeling of becoming ever stronger. It's an extremely satisfying game with tons of content.
_childDocuments_.name: ASTLIBRA Revision

_childDocuments_.review: I have to say this game is amazing.  I nonchalantly added it to my wishlist because it was in my discovery queue and I thought "Hey this looks like it might be pretty good when it comes out".  Pretty good hardly even begins to describe how much I enjoy this game.The combat is okay at first, then it steadily trickles in more ways of fighting and different mechanics and it just does so without it being just a massive overload of stuff.  Sure by the time you get to the end there are a lot of things but it was slowly given to you over the course of the game allowing you to learn before smacking you with another thing.I very much enjoy the story, I think it is a bit cliche in some parts but overall I have to say it is a great premise and is very well executed for the most part.  I will agree with another review that I read saying that some of the character dialogue detracts from the whole.  I do believe it is somewhat damaging to the presentation of things but it goes with the 90's jrpg vibe of things.The characters do feel quite fleshed out, the main character is a mostly silent protagonist with the characters around him sort of repeating what I assume he says.  There are some of the cliche character things happening a little pervy here a little tsundere there, not terribly overbearing but as stated above it does take away from things a little.There are some issues I ran into, mainly way towards the end of the game, which really ends up amounting to just the screen freezing and not being able to see anything, can still attack and hear though.  A fix that works for me is alt tabbing out of game and then coming back in, pausing first if I am fighting.Adding this which I forgot, the music is great.  It is really well done and it can fade into the background as you're playing really easily and then you start paying attention and think "Wait this music is really good"; lather rinse repeat.Short version, I highly recommend this game and if I see another game from Keizo I will probably just buy as soon as it is available.
_childDocuments_.name: ASTLIBRA Revision

_childDocuments_.review: Pretty good game. It starts of pretty slow but cranks up into pretty chaotic combat until you really focus in on how you build your character. Optional bosses, various endings, and numbers going up make it an enjoyable experience. Much, much longer than it looks, the story is pretty anime-y, I didn't mind the pervy jokes, they gave me a chuckle but also can be tonally jarring at times. Play the demo if you are curious, buying the game on sale would be pretty good steal.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a holiday weekend in 1998 and you're at the mall.  Your mom needed to return the dress she only wore one time to your aunt's wedding to her 3rd husband.  You ask her if you can stop by Babbage's (or whatever place it is you people in Canada shop for games and computer software, IDK) or maybe you're at a Hollywood Video because on the weekend you get pizza, a movie, and rent a video game on the two weekends a month you stay at your dad's and his 26 y/o GF's apartment.  Either way, Xenogears and Suikoden II aren't available, you see this game on the shelf and if you're at the mall with mom, you can get it for $34.99 (or whatever maple leaf money you Canadians use).  If you're with dad you can rent it and he'll burn a copy for you since his tech-savvy buddy sodded that modchip in your PS1 a few months ago.  Choose your own adventure here gamers.On the way home you read the manual and while you really wished you were able to get a copy of Suikoden II because your friend at school won't shut up about it, you weren't going to leave empty handed. You begin cautiously optimistic but become skeptical after looking at these weird backgrounds that look partly pre-rendered but digitized in a weird way.  You haven't really heard of this game or it's developer and you're beginning wonder if you're going to regret your purchase.  As the cigarette's embers from your mom/dad's gf burn your little sisters face in the backseat driving down I-10 back home, you figure that if the game isn't great, at least you were able to borrow those anime OVA's on VHS from your friend at school so the weekend isn't totally lost.You get home, throw a couple slices on a paper plate, and briskly head to your room.  You turn on your 19 inch Toshiba TV/VHS combo.  You take Astlibra throw the disc in your PS1 and flip that bad boy upside down.  Ope!  You forgot to pour yourself a very large Sprite into you're scratched up giant plastic Jurassic Park cup you've had since 1993.  It begins to rain outside on this cool, late afternoon and you're greeted by the title screen.  You start the main quest...DRUM AND BASS floods your room it melts your eardrums.  You're blown away by the soundtrack, each strike against the enemies the feels so satisfying.  It's challenging at first but as you progress, you notice you're getting good fast.  The story is ridiculous but you're a kid/teen, so you think its awesome because you think anime and video games about getting to literally KILL GOD is peak story telling.  You get stronger and there are so many weapons and custom builds you can make for you're character.  There's big breasted women and bad ass dudes with head bands and big swords.  DRUM AND BASS, Metal, Electronica, Hip-hop!  Fan service!  There is even an adorable anime pig that runs a shop floating on strings of balloons!!!THIS is a game released in late 2022 but feels it came out so long ago.  It feels like a hidden gem when hidden gems were exactly that. The kind of hidden gem you tell your friend about, let borrow and they return it to you with the jewel case cracked. The kind of hidden gem a game mag gives a middle of the road review to because it's lack of 3D polygons.  Astlibra feels like a PS1 era game from a time you may have never actually experienced, but have misplaced nostalgia for.  It feels like a memory your adjacent to but may not exactly be your own.  This is a game that if released in 1998 someone on Youtube 2023 would be write a video essay for decades later.  Astlibra is a game about changing the past, and if you're an older gamer you'll be returned to a past you hold warm memories of.  I've been meaning to write a review for this game for several months.  This game is far from perfect, but it was great and it was my favorite game 2022.
_childDocuments_.name: ASTLIBRA Revision

_childDocuments_.review: I almost dropped this game on the third chapter (volcano) but I'm glad I didn't, that's the lowest point and it really picks up after that.If you like this kind of game (closest I can think of to compare it to would be the original Ys III, kinda reminds me of that with more indepth combat and RPG elements), then this is some incredible value. My playthrough was almost 80 hours. This game is DENSE with content.PROS:- Looks and sounds excellent- Great story (reminds me in some parts of Chrono Trigger/Cross, Okami)- Great characters- Mostly stays somewhat challenging (I played on Hard) while being unbalanced enough for you to get insanely powerful and do some broken ass sh!t if you want to. Many aspects to building up the protag's strength. Combat is excessively satisfying.- Has a postgame (new story developments included) with even more ways to get stupid powerfulCONS:- The volcano area's boss is stupid. There's a couple sh!tty fights in the game but they're very much a minority.- The combat can get extremely loud at times with overlapping, repeating sound effects. This isn't necessarily a problem but it really made the game tire me out in longer sessions- The other female characters, thanks to how much time you spend with them, ended up being a lot more charming to me than the girl I was supposed to be finding/saving. The game teases them as potential love interests quite often but I don't think it's actually an option. Also, Shiro is best girl.
_childDocuments_.name: ASTLIBRA Revision

_childDocuments_.review: I still am not finished with the game, but this game has taken over 100% of my gaming time. There is not a single spoiler in this review.I am a fan of metroidvania games absolutely. That being said, I picked it up after a lot of thinking because the art direction in screenshots didn't really grab me, the story seemed maybe a bit convoluted and cliche.I am so pleased to tell you that I couldn't have been more wrong. The art can be bizzare at times, but it all fits and it all works. The story is astonishingly good, like ABSURDLY good. I cannot stop playing.Some of my favorite games are Yakuza 0 and the Persona series. I also love listening to deep dive lore videos on games like Marathon. I mean it with my whole heart that this story holds up to the best of them, just play it.I cannot tell you in any other terms other than if you aren't put off by anime, if you aren't put off by the frame work of the gameplay, just buy it. Just play it. I bounce between games constantly, I have a massive library and a massive amount of games I've dropped after an hour or so. This game is truly, truly special.

_childDocuments_.review:
ASTLIBRA Revision is a side scrolling 2D action RPG. It contains various reinforcement elements, exhilarating combat, rare equipment, battles with huge bosses, beautiful art, and long story. 

The main character is separated from his childhood friend when his village is attacked by a demon. When he comes to his senses, he finds himself in a world with talking birds and no humans.

This is a full-length story about the many adventures of a young man who is tossed about by time and fate, but faces them with true courage and kindness.

name: Aspire: Ina's Tale
detailed_description: Ina was trapped, placed in perpetual slumber inside the Tower – where she dreamed. Suddenly and unknowingly, she is woken. Ina must now explore the Tower’s inner chambers in search of a way out and a reason for her imprisonment. Along the way, she’ll traverse marvelous scenery, meet enigmatic characters, solve intuitive puzzles, and conquer platforming sequences as she comes closer to her goal - but farther from innocence. For this isn't a story about how Ina was saved. This is the story about how she discovered she could be so much more. EXPLORE A LIVING TOWER Get lost in a mystical side-scrolling adventure through beautiful sprawling levels, each with their own distinct feel. Every region presents its own peculiarities to unravel. ENGAGING STORY Ina's dreams shape reality while the Tower feeds. Hopes and imagination satiate its hunger. How are the two connected? MEET THE TOWER DWELLERS Learn about the other denizens of the Tower as you search for the truth. Uncover their pasts, their memories, and set them free. CONTROL SPIRITS Ina was trapped for a reason, and her powers resonate with the spirits that inhabit the Tower. Use them to manipulate objects, solve puzzles, reveal hidden passages, and navigate the environment to find your way out.

_childDocuments_.review: Is this game a masterpiece? Hm, no, but it is colorful. It is also a good puzzle platformer. You play Ina, a little girl able to learn magic abilities, but also trapped in a damaged magical tower. To escape, she has to repair the tower, while solving puzzles and avoiding the few monsters. And the endless pits. And the acidic pools. Most of the time, she has to solve puzzles, though, carrying around objects and placing them in the right places, often under time pressure. Pushing some crates is also required. And talking to the weird inhabitants. All in all, quite nice.A beautiful, relaxing puzzle platformer.

_childDocuments_.review: There are games that are so impactful that you’d want to remove from your memory only so you can experience them all over again. For many,  is a good example of that: playing through it left countless wanting more.  comes to fill in this exact void, and while it does have a lot of similarities with GRIS, it can hardly be regarded as a mere clone of it: it’s unique, breathtaking and heartwarming in its own specific way and will likely move you and leave a mark on you, just like GRIS did.In a nutshell,  is a stunning puzzle-platformer targeted at people who prefer to experience a game in a more casual, relaxed way rather than being confronted with a challenge. That doesn’t mean that playing it is trivial: there are bits in which your actions need to be timed at the right moment and some mild speedrun sequences towards the end of the game, but these are usually easily done after a couple of tries and after learning what one is expected to do. The game is intended to be pleasant, immersive, stress-free and thus the puzzles and the platforming aspect are designed so that even non-veteran players can enjoy them. Also, there is no combat and no boss fights.You play as Ina, a young girl who wakes up trapped inside a ruined tower, without having any knowledge about why or how she got there. Ina remembers Kamiura - her homeland, her family and that she was a priestess there, therefore she embarks on a quest to escape the tower and go back home. Her path is filled with lots of traps and puzzles, but also with mysterious characters that will guide her on the way to the exit. Her priestess training allows her to control light spirits that she then uses to fend off shadow creatures, power up various platforms or activate door pillars, and enlarge blocks in order to reach higher levels. While the first areas teach the player how each of these abilities work, the puzzles towards the end of the game are slightly more complex, often requiring Ina to combine her abilities and the different types of light spirits that she can control.The selling point of the game is clearly the astonishing art: each area is remarkable in itself, with magnificent graphics depicting a world in which the vegetation conquers the disrepair state of the tower. When Ina moves towards the upper levels, the views start to bloom with vegetation bursting out through the ruins, creating wonderful spring-like panoramas, with cherry trees and flowery vines. As beautiful to look at  is, as beautiful to listen to it is: the score is almost as outstanding as the visuals, and the two of them are perfectly in sync all the time, combining together flawlessly in order to deliver an enrapturing experience. The writing is also top-notch, at times fun and witty, other times deep and meditative. I particularly enjoyed the fact that there are always additional dialogue options that you can explore in order to gather more details about the background story of the tower or of the NPCs, together with information about what your next goal should be or about the main concepts of the game.Ina moves with elegance and grace, and her jumps feel feather-like, almost ethereal. She can grab onto ledges, although these are never placed too high, nor too far away to become a pixel-hunt challenge. The controls are very good and responsive, and the game can be played both with a controller, or with the mouse and keyboard. Personally, I played through it with a controller, since I found the default placement of the interaction keys being somewhat unintuitive; however, these can easily be changed from the settings.Another thing that I liked in  is how the collectibles are handled. It’s partially an exploration game, so collectibles are to be expected but usually in games like this one needs to frequently consult a guide, if one wants to be sure not to miss anything - this is something that I dislike to a certain degree because it breaks my immersion in the story. In  there are only four collectibles to gather, and even though all of them are placed outside the main paths, it’s quite clear how to reach them without even needing the help of a guide: there are platforms not used for progression that will instead lead to one of these collectibles.Just like GRIS,  is a game that isn’t played, but absorbed and lived through. Its three-ish hour run time is admittedly a bit short for the price (albeit much lower than GRIS which has quite the same length), yet it's satisfying in a way few games really are.

_childDocuments_.review: Rating: ★★★☆☆ (3/5)I feel a bit conflicted over whether or not I should recommend  to other players. Ultimately, I decided that I wouldn't so long as it is not heavily discounted. It pains me to say this, as the style and score are so beautiful and the puzzles are actually pretty fun to figure out. I loved these aspects of the game and I'm saddened that they alone weren't able to make this game great.I say this because aside from the eye and ear candy, there wasn't really much there for me. The game is , capable of being completed under less than two hours easy, which wouldn't be a problem in and of itself. I've played short games with a good enough story to make up for it, but that's 's problem...the story is lacking. Its presentation makes it seem like there will be some heavy themes to deal with while you're playing—at one point I even felt that it would be a potential tear-jerker—yet, when it was over, I was left completely unsatisfied. The mystery of the Tower, the War, of Ina, Joker, Thief, the Architect, and the Guiding Light (the game's only characters) remained unsolved...untapped and unfulfilled. Perhaps this is the point? Maybe it doesn't matter in the grand scheme of things, but to me that's a cop out. I can't connect with characters whose story I do not and cannot know. Sadly, though she had potential, Ina and co. fit that category.
_childDocuments_.name: Aspire: Ina's Tale

_childDocuments_.review: Ina is unexpectedly awakened from a spell like slumber, imprisoned in a tower where here dreams have motivated its inhabitants. Nevertheless, she explores the tower for a way out, encountering characters who question her motives and reason for escaping. Along the way she will need to avoid dangers and solve puzzles by using her powers to manipulate objects and traverse platforms. The start of the game is quite depressing when trying to escape those initial dreary areas, and compounded by the fact that the puzzles ramp up in difficulty, the beginning of the game was a bit disappointing. Fortunately, it’s not too long before you are out into more interesting areas and the puzzles start to become more compelling. The journey through the tower is a pleasant experience with some attractive backdrops and quirky landmarks. The different areas you traverse and the array of characters you interact with balance perfectly with the number of puzzles you have to perform so it never feels unbalanced one way or the other. It feels like an adventure game with puzzle elements rather than a disconnected puzzle game. Environments are very colourful with a whimsical feel and the characters you meet along the way are as bizarre as the story. The interaction between yourself and the characters is quite brief. There are some dialogue choices, but none of them change the narrative, they will always be exhausted, and just act as an exchange between the character to get information. Even though these exchanges are quite brief they are fascinating and do manage to build layers of intrigue. There is no voice acting but some enchanting vocal noises to mimic dialogue exchanges makes it quite endearing.The puzzles were very well crafted I thought, and they hit that sweet spot between being frustratingly difficult and too easy. I didn’t have to look at any solutions or guides, but I did spend a lot of time trying different solutions and thinking about different ways of approaching the puzzles. I got a huge amount of satisfaction solving them and there were more than a couple of “whoopee” moments when I finally worked out the solution.  I did have a few frustrating moments with the controls as it can be troublesome picking up objects if you’re not positioned correctly. This doesn’t usually result in death but it’s just a minor annoyance. The same goes with depositing your powers into blocks sometimes. It takes a while to get the hang of switching your powers when you accrue a few of them, although I think that’s more user error, but there did seem to be a bit of a lag when trying to deposit a power which did cause a bit of frustration now and again, especially when puzzles demanded quick timing. The arcade chase sequences injected some drama and adrenaline into proceedings, adding pressure whilst avoiding monsters, or trying to solve puzzles or perform platforming. The checkpoints are generously placed which keeps frustrations levels low but does make it easier to work out patterns and solutions to bosses’ movements and how to avoid them. The chase sequence starts at 17:00 minutes on my gameplay video if you want to take a look.The soundtrack can be beautiful in places, especially when complimenting dialogue interaction between characters, or entering a stunning locale, whilst action sequences tend to promote fast, loud, drum beats that get the heart pumping. Whatever is on offer sounds very professional and immersive.Gameplay is broken into ,  and  Ina can push and pull blocks, mainly to use as platforms to reach higher ground, but when Ina progresses through the tower, she meets spirits that grant her powers. These powers can be used to move the block, enlarge the block or illuminate the block, depending on the puzzle. A block will have the power symbol it can harness engraved on its face. A block can accept up to three different powers, so in theory, you could move, enlarge and illuminate the block simultaneously but in practice puzzles tend to demand that you switch in-between powers with two active at any one time. The RB switches power and the triangle button loads the power into the cube. Light plays an important part in some puzzles, especially when you are trapped in the dungeon areas. Any creatures located in the dark recesses of the tower are frightened of bright light so your illumination power can keep them at bay by lighting small lanterns. Light also opens doorways and dissipates evil black goo that blocks your path. Sometimes you can chain together light sources to extend the light range and activate doorways. Light also powers your mechanical friend you encounter later in the game that clears goo, but needs constant power top ups. Puzzles revolve around these themes of light and use of the different powers, but they are quite varied and throw in circumstances that make you think outside the box.Towards the conclusion of the game there is a long chase sequence where you have to use your powers to manipulate platforms, blocks and shields to protect yourself from a powerful enemy. You will need to run, jump, climb ladders and hide behind protective structures whilst the enemy sends out a destructive pulse every so often. If you are subjected to the pulse for too long you will be killed and sent back to the last checkpoint. There are three stages to the chase, each one getting progressively harder and each stage contains more puzzle elements whilst also trying to avoid death.There are about five different characters for you to meet in your adventure and they are all very interesting with bizarre looking features and a whimsical Presence. Dialogues don’t take long at all and usually consist of two or three questions with concise answers. Strangely enough this still manages to hold the story together quite well and enables a semblance of mystery and intrigue. It had that vibe of Alice in Wonderland.
_childDocuments_.name: Aspire: Ina's Tale

_childDocuments_.review: Aspire is a side-scrolling platform game that has a 'GRIS-like' feel but requires the precision and timing of Limbo. You guide a small character, sideways, through a series of beautifully crafted environments with a lovely sound track. You meet other characters, evade beasts, and continue your quest to escape 'The Tower.'  In each segment of the game, you receive different spirit powers that allow you to solve puzzles to continue moving forward.Puzzles are about timing and pressing keys/buttons in perfect order while running and jumping.  There are moving platforms, boxes to push/pull, ropes to climb, and chasms to leap. The game is lovely but pushes my limits on the skills needed to succeed. While others may finish the game in a few hours, I am slogging through and it is taking countless attempts to perfect various scenarios. The good news is that the game is quite generous with save points to almost no rework is required as I fail-fail-and-try again.I would recommend this to those who have the prerequisite coordination and who enjoy navigating a beautiful environment with a friendly quest. At this point I am only about half-way through and my adventure continues...
_childDocuments_.name: Aspire: Ina's Tale

_childDocuments_.review: Based on the trailers and very favourable Steam reviews I was expecting that Ina's Tale would be reminiscent of Gris, but unfortunately it wasn't. The art style is very beautiful, and the sound track is athmospheric, but the gameplay was not fun at all.Ina's Tale is advertised as a puzzle platformer, but the platforming part is kind of lacking with clunky movement and frustratingly poor responsiveness. That only leaves us with the puzzles. However, the core puzzle mechanics are poorly explained, resulting in lots of trial and error to solve certain puzzles. After 2 hours of playing I got increasingly frustrated, and because I did not have fun anymore playing I refunded.
_childDocuments_.name: Aspire: Ina's Tale

_childDocuments_.review: Bahh, in my opinion this is an incredibly overrated game. I didn't like it at all!!I just couldn't connect to the story, which is poor, unfinished, abstract. The same could be said about the shallow charachters.And neither was I compatible with the game mechanics. First of all, reading the reviews, I thought that ASPIRE is a relaxing platformer. But no, this is 100% a PUZZLE game. The platformer part is secondary. The puzzles are based on frustrating mechanics. You have to use certain colored powers to activate various mechanical contraptions or items in order to pass the obstacle/puzzle. In the beginning it was easy, but then as you progress it is more and more over stretched and I had to consult a you tube guide from time to time( which is always dissappointing to me having to do that ).  Well, I'm sure some people didn't have any problems with the puzzles, but I had. I found the puzzles nothing less then boring. I'm not saying that the game is trash, because it isn't. It is a solid game, but....do you know the feeling when you start a game and you think: "damm, this game is so different from the way I think, the way I like to play, the way I like to solve things. So, it's a problem of compatibility with the game mechanics. The game has also the issue of the main charachter beeing unresponsive or slowly responsive at times, that leads to failure of interaction with the environment and thus.....death. Let's put it plainly: this is a pretentious game created entirely on it's only strong feature: stunning graphics ( clearly inspired by GRIS ). The game authors clearly planned to create a stylish game, that will become popular because of it's style and graphics. Well, it seems that plan worked perfectly, judging on the ratings and steam reviews. I just don't understand the high ratings and the many positive Steam reviews, that only highlights the positive sides and are silent about the shortcomings, like the lack of some really fun game-play and cohesive story!!!
_childDocuments_.name: Aspire: Ina's Tale

_childDocuments_.review: Aspire is clearly inspired by Gris but it can't quite live up to it.The gameplay is mostly little puzzles of moving blocks and light platforming. The puzzles are not too bad but there could be more variation. The visual and sound design is certainly good, but /compared to Gris) a little incoherent. The dialogues I found really cringy and there isn't really a story, it's more like a collection of vague ideas and suggestions.In the end I have to give a thumbs down because I found it too short. I was really surprised when it was suddenly over.
_childDocuments_.name: Aspire: Ina's Tale

_childDocuments_.review: This game definitely has GRIS as insipiration so if you enjoyed GRIS, run for it (or run for GRIS if you like that game, what are you doing, run, buy it, it's one of the best game EVER).I streamed the whole experience and it was relaxing and not complex platformer with little puzzles and a few moment where you have to rush (or die). The story is touching and the question you might have at the beginning (where are the ones who saved her ?) will find their answer in due time. There are 4 poems to find and text to decipher all along the game, you can use the poems to find the meaning of the rest of the text such as the first text you encounter and the ones in between areas which I didn't try to decipher but I believe it's the text of the poems again, I would need to check once more but that was intersting to read as they explain why there are four other people in the Tower and how remembering your name is more precious than anything else in that word.I really enjoyed that game, it's a short one, we stopped to decipher the texts, I did a few breaks and I returned to the game to get the two missing achievements. I believe it can be finished in two hours and a half if you're in a rush and don't care about the achievements (or are really good at getting things in the first try, that's definitely not me lol).
_childDocuments_.name: Aspire: Ina's Tale

_childDocuments_.review: Full playthrough w/ all memory stones here: This is a very beautiful game the art for the environment characters etc. is extremely well done the music is on point as well. The puzzles are a bit easy unless they have to do with the movement spirit those can be the devil actually. I loved seeing the world I wish I would have got a bit more back story for the characters with the memory stones, but it was a very nice heart warming game definitely recommend.
_childDocuments_.name: Aspire: Ina's Tale

_childDocuments_.review: An absolutely gorgeous little puzzle platformer that deserves your time. Each area has a new gimmick, so things never get old. The art and music are absolutely to die for, and the game tells an interesting little story with some fun characters. If you liked Gris for example, then I would totally give this a shot. Here's hoping it gets the attention it deserves!
_childDocuments_.name: Aspire: Ina's Tale

_childDocuments_.review: A beautiful game hampered by poor responsiveness to the controls.  Most of the difficulty for me came from waiting for the game to accept keyboard input e.g. I'd be positioned correctly to pick up something but pressing the action key would do nothing for several seconds.One oversight in the game is that, if one drops an object near to a fixed environmental object (e.g. the uncharged flumyes) one won't (as far as I can tell) be able to pick up the object again.  The puzzles are mostly fairly straightforward puzzle platforming
_childDocuments_.name: Aspire: Ina's Tale

_childDocuments_.review: Short and sweet game with beautiful art style and music. There is no combat so you progress by avoiding threats, puzzle solving, and platforming. Basic combat that anyone can pick up and very generous checkpoints to avoid any frustration. The puzzles are the challenging part, as a couple of them had me stumped for a few minutes.  Aspire is a nice rewarding indie experience that you can complete in a few hours. I recommend for anyone who enjoys and appreciates an indie gem that gets you thinking and looking inward, as Ina's Tale can touch the heart.
_childDocuments_.name: Aspire: Ina's Tale

_childDocuments_.review: -beautiful visuals-relaxing gameplay-easy puzzles deliver a sense of accomplishment often-while the story doesn’t deliver any out-of-the-box message, it talks about important ideas / ideals-gameplay needs a 150% speed increase-easy puzzles wont challenge experienced puzzlersDespite the few cons, out of which probably game speed would be the biggest and most easy to fix in a whim, I can only recommend you give Aspire: Ina’s tale a shot. Think about it as a relaxing stroll in the park on a pleasant, warm early-autumn afternoon. At the end of the day what it’ll come down to is whether you find short games worth your time and money, or nay.For more detail on the above points and a look at gameplay, please join me as I elaborate on my thoughts in this video:.
_childDocuments_.name: Aspire: Ina's Tale

_childDocuments_.review: Really fun at first! Love the story and the visuals. I enjoyed it until I got to a puzzle that even though I figured out how to advance in theory, I am not a fast enough PC game player to make it happen with the timing of the elevators. I wasn't able to move forward in the game so I had to quit entirely. Sad. I'm sure more advanced gamers will enjoy this more!
_childDocuments_.name: Aspire: Ina's Tale

_childDocuments_.review: 2 hours. 6/10. Alright. Nice. Great for this genre, stunning at times. 2D simple puzzle platformer. Awesome. None.ᶠʳᵒᵐ ᵐʸ ᶠᶦʳˢᵗ ᵖˡᵃʸᵗʰʳᵒᵘᵍʰAspire: Ina's Tale is, as the name suggests, a tale about Ina. About Ina's escape from her dreams, from her confinement. The game has pleasing visuals with beautiful scenery. At times it was marvelous to look at. The story was alright, it wasn't anything fancy or mindblowing, but it was on point with the gameplay and it was nicely delivered. The movement was fluid for the most part, I managed to die because the character didn't grab a ledge once and once because they didn't grab a chain you had to climb on. Other than that it was a pleasure to play with a controller. The puzzles were simple which was a bit uninspired with just one puzzle using all the game mechanics at once, and it took about half a minute to pass. The audio was fantastic and I even got goosebumps once, although it might've been the AC but I doubt it.TLDR;Simple puzzles with enjoyable gameplay.
_childDocuments_.name: Aspire: Ina's Tale

_childDocuments_.review: Was really excited as it seemed to be like Gris, one of my all time favorite games. Here the art is beautiful in most levels, the music was ok, but the gameplay was just not very good. Movement and controls were clunky. Puzzles were just ok. I stopped on the final boss area. I just wasn't enjoying it. Gris has these huge environments which are surreal and amazingly beautiful, and the journey is really an amazing experience like Abzu. But here in this game I didn't get that wow sense.
_childDocuments_.name: Aspire: Ina's Tale

_childDocuments_.review: I usually love atmospheric puzzle platforming games. The puzzles here are so simple, and the main issue I have is that the character moves so so so slowly, and the spirit transfer/absorb mechanism is so slow that you have to retry the same timed escape challenge over and over because you cannot tell where the hitbox is for the "spirit energy" input. You can immediately figure out what you're supposed to do, but actually getting Ina to do it is painstakingly slow and very unsatisfying. If you don't mind a character that moves at a glacial pace and badly programmed controls that feel sluggish or unclear, then maybe you'd like to play this. But if any of the above is an issue for you I have to recommend you skip it. I also immediately deciphered the hidden language and was rewarded upon finding a memory crystal with the game translating it for me? So there is no point to actually thinking or working it out on your own. I think this game is intended for children maybe? But it seems a little too scary for kids.....so I don't understand who the audience of this game is supposed to be. Couldn't be me. Beautiful animations, terrible game play and story telling at the exposition. Bad enough to where I'm not interested in spending more time watching this girl take 30 seconds to push a box five feet. Hard pass.
_childDocuments_.name: Aspire: Ina's Tale

_childDocuments_.review: ✔️ The game is pretty short and self-sufficent.✔️ Some interesting game mechanics.✔️ Intriguing, though rather cryptic, narration, with some charming characters.✔️ Very beautiful environments.✔️ Nice music.❌ The platforming gameplay is very rigid - which doesn't matter much most of the game, but when the game throws actually challenging platforming at you, prepare to cry from frustration.❌ The puzzles are sometimes a bit obscure because things don't always work in a consistent and predictable way. I had to check walkthroughs twice or thrice because I didn't see enough clues in the game on how to solve a puzzle - and I recommend for anyone to do the same instead of remaining stuck on something for too long.❌ Generally speaking, I don't think it needed such rough difficulty spikes, keeping the game generally easy wouldn't have made it less enjoyable, probably even more so for quite a few people.Overall it's a small recommendation for me - the game is rather nice, especially thanks to its gorgeous art direction, but it also could have been much more if it had received more polish on the gameplay side.
_childDocuments_.name: Aspire: Ina's Tale

_childDocuments_.review: The art is amazing and the soundtrack is absolutely beautiful. The mechanics are a bit wonky and delayed in moments-just not quite polished on that front. It feels like the game is lagging but it's not, and once you 'touch' an edge the only direction you can go is up, even if you just clipped it on your way down. The game is short and the puzzles aren't too complicated but do offer some unique thinking to get through them. Many sections of the puzzles just feel finicky, though, rather than mentally challenging to work through. I'm not in love with the plot of this game.--SPOILERS BELOW--
_childDocuments_.name: Aspire: Ina's Tale

_childDocuments_.review: - The visuals are a little inconsistent. The background art is amazing and very interesting to look at with the angular crystals and shard-like architecture. The character and enemy designs are, in comparison, fairly simple-looking and generic- The animation in this game is grim. It feels sluggish and looks awkward. You don't so much mantle ledges as you clumsily flop your way up them- The score is probably the high point of this game. From the tinkling, austere keys in the game's main theme to the booming percussion of its boss themes, there's almost always something for your ears to latch onto, at least- The overt narrative follows Nina, a magical priestess of some sort who finds herself waking up following an attack on the tower she's imprisoned in. You're trying to escape even though the tower itself is sorta opposed to that idea- It appears to be a metaphorical, infer-your-own-meaning sort of tale about growth and awakening. There's even a dialogue option for you to choose what sort of figurative issue you're trying to run from. That decision unfortunately felt a little trite- Overall, this game doesn't have a strong Identity or message. It couldn't even hone in on a central theme. When the game's answer take-home message is, "lol I dunno, what do YOU think I'm trying to say?", the whole experience feels cheap and wishy-washy- A weak story or bad vibes can usually be forgiven if a game has a fun gameplay loop, but Aspire: Ina's Tale doesn't get that quite right either. Don't get me wrong; the puzzles are competently designed and some were even quite clever. But it doesn't matter when the "platformer" half of the "puzzle platformer" nomen feels so awful to play- Ina constantly feels like she's running underwater. Doing literally anything in this game feels sluggish and awful. I have no idea why she moves so slowly, but I constantly found myself grinding my Steam Deck's analog stick against the housing in an subconscious attempt to speed things up- The sludgy movement becomes glaringly obvious when enduring chase sequences or completing puzzles requiring quick or precise timing. Things slow down even harder when you have to push blocks or wait for doors to open.- I'm not going to be back for the achievements or collectibles. Seeing the credits roll was a bit of a relief- Nice background art and a great soundtrack can't save this one. I've played very few platformers that made basic movement and environment navigation feel so awful- Seeing as how the game is in no rush to get to where it's going, it won't tax your system too badly. It played well on the Steam Deck- . Even with perfectly snappy controls, this title would still feel a little generic. As it stands with the existing controls, calling the experience a chore would be charitable
_childDocuments_.name: Aspire: Ina's Tale

_childDocuments_.review: The games selling point is the art. The story is enjoyableThe gameplay is simple enough for anyone who has played a puzzle platformer before to not have any troubleThe music is good and has a nice mystical whimsy feel to it, A few gripes:Would've been nice to have a bit more gameplay with mixing the different ability types.the length of the game is short but isn't all that bad, too much longer and it could easily have felt too drawn out.For a $13 game I'd recommend it to a friend that's looking for something to relax and kick back with, but doesn't have the time to commit to a longer game
_childDocuments_.name: Aspire: Ina's Tale

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR; If you're looking for a good puzzle platformer, look for something else. If you're only interested in aesthetics and don't care about the rest, this could be your fit.Overrated. Expected something similar to GRIS, although not quite as polished. Unfortunately this game has nothing going for it except for it's art style and presentation, which is really good to be honest.Sadly the gameplay is totally bland. Your character feels slow, the controls are clunky and the puzzles are not at all engaging. For a puzzle platformer i expect the platforming to feel nice and intuitive. It's unfortunately not the case for this gameAfter the first chapter i thought it's short enough, might as well just finish it. But then i decided that it doesn't make any sense to stick with a game i don't have fun with.
_childDocuments_.name: Aspire: Ina's Tale

_childDocuments_.review: Aspire: Ina's Tale is a beautiful puzzle platformer featuring atmospheric music that is brought down by its frustrating controls and mediocre storyline. Saying it is a knock-off version of Gris is doing a disservice to both games - while the similarities are there (beautiful artwork/atmosphere, great soundtrack, female protagonist, puzzle platformer, etc) - Gris does them with style and skill that Aspire lacks. Yet, Aspire is still a fun, beautiful game in its own right that simply has some problems Gris doesn't - namely, frustrating controls (being unable to change direction when jumping in a platformer is annoying especially when the jump you are given is pretty tiny to begin with) and a just-ok storyline that is begging to be explored in greater depth. All in all, it was fun to play and I'm glad to have bought it, but the storyline and controls take what could be a great game into good territory.
_childDocuments_.name: Aspire: Ina's Tale

_childDocuments_.review: This game is absolutely frustrating for a "simple" plat-former game. Convoluted for jumping, switching and running, all while "beating" an invisible timer. Then when you loose it, the save game system does NOT save at the last checkpoint rather I've had to replay the same sequence 4 times and each time, the reload puts me way back in the story, that I've started to memorise all the dialogue. Needless, there was NO!!! reason for this game to be this difficult or convoluted. I'd rate the game maybe 3/10
_childDocuments_.name: Aspire: Ina's Tale

_childDocuments_.review: Something of a nice short story, but barely qualifies as a game.It's a very easy puzzle linear platformer. 4 "secret" rooms to add a few lines of dialog with NPCs and that's about it.I do recommend the game, but be aware of these points: it's short, easy and linear.It could be easily be substituted with a short comic.

_childDocuments_.review: Good story,great visuals,amazing music and some very challenging puzzles (I dont usually play puzzle games so I had to look for a video guide for a few puzzles),funnily enough the Ina Jones achievement (complete all the rope/chain sequences without falling) took me longer than The Watchful eye achievement (dont die during the last boss),because I skipped one of the 2 ropes next to each other during the first few chapters,and you need to have it fall to the ground for the achievement. Overall this is a great game and I definitely recommend it,even to those who don't usually play this genre.
_childDocuments_.name: Aspire: Ina's Tale

_childDocuments_.review: Aspire: Ina’s Tale is a surprisingly nice puzzle platformer game. The game looks beautiful and together with the lovely music it creates a nice, tranquil vibe. Ina’s story is abstract and inspirational, which I really like. The characters you meet along the way all have their own personality and I really liked that. Even though you don’t see them for very long, I feel like I know them. There’s one gameplay issue I encountered: I had difficulty picking up some of the small moveable blocks, especially in the dungeon area. Next to that, I would have liked the game to be a bit longer, since it’s so good. I would have loved to see more areas of the tower, since we only really got to see three. The puzzle elements were very nice, though, and I liked the various crystals needed to progress through the puzzles. Overall Aspire is a very enjoyable game.
_childDocuments_.name: Aspire: Ina's Tale

_childDocuments_.review: Aspire: Ina's Tale is a platforming side-scrolling game where we play as a princess who has the power to control spirit to move, extend or light up platforms to escape from a Tower that is stealing the dreams from people within. For me, this game was a lot of fun to traverse to fix the Tower by solving some interesting puzzles that get progressively harder and a little bit more complex as we get closer to the end. The boss chase was also intense, it really put your knowledge of the mechanics to the test, even though, (at least for me) my frame rate dropped during the chase it was still a decent one, not as fast pace as Ori and the blind forest first chase of course (mostly due to the music), but still up there with how they incorporated the mechanic in it.For me, this game was a nice, colourful invention with unique crystallize patterns design and a variety of dungeon creations, if anyone is curious about getting this game, maybe wishlist it and wait for the discount along with the artbook as it seems a few people completed it around the 2 hours mark, ignoring my playtime.

_childDocuments_.review: is a “cinematic” platformer with light puzzles and a few chase sequences. The story follows the titular character, Ina, who is trying to escape from the crumbling sci-fi-esque magical Tower. The story is linear, the dialogue options do not affect anything, and there is no exploration. The non-playable characters appear once to say a few lines and to be shown again only during the credits. The story significance of the spirits goes against their gameplay usage - they are energy sources to activate platforms and to be left in those platforms or at the barriers between the puzzles, which is deeply ironic, considering that the main character is a priestess who spends a few minutes narrating that she is going to save them. The platforming part clashes with the cinematic animations - the character is slow, clunky, and uncomfortable to control. While the controls are partially rebindable (can’t rebind the movement keys), some actions use the same key with the difference being tapping and holding it. The graphics, while very lovely, also prevent from seeing clearly whether a platform has been activated or not or whether something is an obstacle or a part of the scenery. The few early-game chase sequences are very easy and require only holding the movement key away from the foe. The actual issue is the timed puzzles which, as mentioned, do not work well with the character controls. During one of them, I struggled to determine if I got the logic wrong or just could not perform the actions quick enough (it was the latter). The music became rather annoying at that point, so I turned it off. The final boss, on the other hand, was generally fine - it did not kill instantly and there was enough time to pull/push/climb all the blocks. The game saves the progress on the generously-placed checkpoints and it is possible to roll back to any of the previous ones. While the game itself is rather short, about 2-3 hours, the quality of the gameplay and the story makes it a positive quality.
_childDocuments_.name: Aspire: Ina's Tale

_childDocuments_.review: What an amazing experience, Halfway through my playthrough I felt compelled to write a review for this game, but I held off until I experienced everything this game had to offer. I went in with a pretty open mind, expecting a simple puzzle game with some gimmicky mechanics or graphics, but this game far exceeded my expectations. I've never been so invested into a game on my first playthrough, I'm extremely happy I decided to play this.The gameplay is fairly surface level, I can definitely tell this game isn't really focused on the gameplay elements more than the story and environments. It was still enjoyable but there wasn't really anything challenging and I never found myself getting stuck anywhere.The graphics, wow. Absolutely stunning, and one of the greatest looking games I've ever played. The massive almost otherworldly looking structures and objects paired with the music creates a sense of scale with just how big the tower really is. I found myself stopping multiple times just to admire the backgrounds and scenery. This artstyle is beautiful, and I hope to see more games like this in the future.The music, oh my god. This has one of the most beautiful soundtracks. Each song has such an impact that it will really resonate with you after your playthrough. The music is incredible. It compliments everything going on in the game perfectly. The sense of curiosity, fear, hope, feeling overwhelmed, the music portrays all of these emotions at the perfect moments in the game, especially during the last part, I was really feeling the panic and stress there.I haven't felt a special feeling of immersion in a while, this game brought that feeling back to me. Do not play this game for just the gameplay, play it for the experience, letting yourself follow the story, admire the scenery, talk to each character and listen to how they express themselves and the stories they have to tell. I cannot recommend this game enough, and it is well worth playing.
_childDocuments_.name: Aspire: Ina's Tale

_childDocuments_.review: Aspire: Ina's Tale is a mellow, thoughtful little puzzle platformer, which brings some interesting philosophical writing, that all too often veers into quasi-intellectual wank.Positives:  -Music-  It won't win any awards but it wins over your ears by virtue of being meditative and subtle, without huge theatrical swells.  Again, nothing really special, but it accentuates the gameplay without getting in the way.-Graphics-  Not fancy at all, but highly evocative and with some occasional flourishes and effects that don't come across as gilding the lily but rather as genuinely special touches.  These are stylized by the way, not photo-realistic, but if that's your jam you'll really enjoy the visual palette.-Gameplay-  Some may lambaste it as being too samey and too easy.....but I just had a really good time, even if I was only occasionally "challenged".  Not everything has to be a white-knuckle battle between you and the  a quiet, story-based platformer, non-stop action and rapidly escalating skill requirements would seriously detract from the enjoyment.Meh:-Plot-  It doesn't really get much past the surface of the storyline and it is just a bit too vague and up its own rear-end (it seems to think it's deeper and more intellectual/philosophical than it actually is) to be 100% enjoyable.-Controls-  For the most part tight as a drum, which sure is what you want in a platformer....but occasionally it's a little too floaty, especially in the last "battle", where some heretofore unseen mechanics and gameplay themes come into play.All in all, it's very enjoyable, but it's a little bit less than the sum of its parts.  Recommended with minor reservations.
_childDocuments_.name: Aspire: Ina's Tale

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic game, beautiful levels that are pleasing on the eye. Game itself is not too difficult but offers enough of a challenge to keep it interesting from beginning to end. It won't take up too much of your time and is definitely worth a purchase to waste away a quiet afternoon. Definitely recommend! 👍

_childDocuments_.review: A fun plat former game with cute graphics and a sweet story. It doesn't take very long to complete, and the only difference in dialogue comes from not retrieving certain stories. Otherwise, it's fairly quick to play, and it has some challenging moments. _childDocuments_.review: A really nice puzzle platformer. The visuals are stunning and it gives off this really somber feeling that is so beautiful. It's not very challenging, but it also isn't supposed to be. I only have a couple issues regarding some readability of some of the puzzles but it's fairly small and arguably is on my end. It only takes like 2-3 hours to complete and I think it's worth a playthrough. It might not knock your socks off but it definitely was an enjoyable time.

_childDocuments_.review: Great art style and good music.  Short but sweet game.  Story is somewhat vague, and the gameplay is solid for the most part.  Could use a bit of polish, but perfectly acceptable for an indie game.  Had a difficult time with the final boss, because I kept dying faster than I could deduce where I was supposed to go.  Kinda wish the path was more apparent, because the environment often blends together.  That being said, definitely pick this game up for the Autumn or Winter Sale.
_childDocuments_.name: Aspire: Ina's Tale

_childDocuments_.review: I kind of have mixed feelings about this game. First of all, it was really short. I love puzzles and this game had quite a few of them, though they seemed pretty easy to me and I got the hang of them very early on. I would've liked it more if there were more complex or tricky puzzles (like the ones we had toward the end) and if it wasn't so short.The next thing that makes me so unsure of my feeling toward Aspire is the story. I kind of expected it to be deep or at least emotional, but it didn't leave me with such impressions at the end. I liked the characters and conversations they had with Ina, and I liked the world too, but I feel the story and the message it tried to convey weren't as polished as it should've been.But I gotta say the art was beautiful and the soundtracks were amazing. There were also lots of save points that made backtracking super easy. Overall, I enjoyed it and had fun working on the puzzles and meeting the characters. So, yeah. I recommend it but treat it as something casual, or you might feel a bit disappointed at the end.
_childDocuments_.name: Aspire: Ina's Tale

_childDocuments_.review: While this is by no means the best puzzle platformer ever conceived it is still one worth playing, because even though there's some shortcomings in terms of gameplay & technicalities, there's still a work of art underneath. Let us dissect.Just one glance at the trailers or screenshots should be enough to convince you wether or not to pick up this game, as visuals really are the main appeal here. I for one found them to be absolutely gorgeous from start to finish, especially in the more verdant midgame area. Every screen has something nice to look at, wether it's odd geometric shapes, gorgeous godrays or just nice compositions. The artists really knocked it out of the park here. It really reminded me of Gris at times, which is a testament to how good the game looks. However not only the visuals but the designs of the characters and environments are awesome as well. With the architect and guiding light designs being my favorite. In terms of music; the score, while not as memorable as something like gris or inmost, is still beautiful and fitting. I'm going through loss currently so the soothing soundtrack helped me relax and find some peace in a time where i'm needing it most. These are the game's biggest positives, and in my opinion, reason enough to pick up the game.However there's also some issues that plague the game, mainly gameplay. This game's main puzzle mechanics are really basic and as a result so are the puzzles. I wasn't really engaged or challenged solving the puzzles because of this, and if you don't care about visuals but do about good puzzles then this may not be for you. The story was also not as engaging as some others gems found within the genre.Lastly there's polish and while the game was bug free for me the loading times were, for such a simple game, really long. Failing a jump or anything else that would reset you made you go through a 5-10 seconds loading screen. I know that's still pretty short but most puzzle platformers have near instant respawns. In the end this isn't a dealbreaker as the game has different strenghts and is short enough to keep you engaged without the load times ever getting too much to bear. It's a nice, beautiful and short game that's decently priced for what it is.

_childDocuments_.review: Most of my praise is directed to the game's aesthetics. It's just so gorgeous! On par with Gris, methinks. But unlike Gris, this game has actual gameplay.Most of the puzzles are enjoyable, with a frustrating few. For a puzzler that involves timing, the controls shouldn't be this finicky and there could've been more wiggle room for some of the timed puzzles. Doable, but still. The story was a little meh too.All in all still enjoyable, but walk away if you don't want timed puzzles.

_childDocuments_.review: In my review of Aspire: Ina’s Tale I won’t be revealing any plot spoilers. I’ll only provide a brief synopsis of the story and I’ll discuss the plot and characters featured in the first half hour of the game. I’ll also explain game mechanics introduced later in the game, but I won’t be spoiling how the protagonist obtains these powers.In Aspire: Ina’s Tale you control Ina, a young woman who needs to escape a mysterious area known as the Tower. Her goal is to get back home, to a town called Kamiura, where she lives with her father. Ina is a priestess and she learned the profession from her father. She had a lot of responsibility in her hometown, from performing prayers, conducting ceremonies in front of people, and even fasting all day.As she journeys through the Tower she meets a wide variety of characters. You can talk to these NPCs as you travel through different areas, and there are branching dialog options that allow you to respond positively or negatively. Your dialog choices don’t change the story, but it is certainly interesting to see different kinds of responses.One of the earliest encounters you’ll have in the game are with two NPCs named Thief and Joker, who help explain more about what the Tower is exactly and how Ina can escape it.Two of the earliest characters you’ll meet are Thief and Joker, who each have their mannerisms and quirks.. These NPCs have a lot of personality, from their artwork to their animations. For example, the Joker acts as flamboyantly as possible and his artwork and animations reflects this. On the other hand, the Thief is extremely reserved. The Thief prefers hiding and not giving away any unnecessary details. As you interact with them more and more, they both slowly open up more to you. There are many other characters you meet along the way, but I’ll leave them all as a surprise for you to meet.Where the game really shines is in its artwork. All of the characters have very colorful 2D designs. The 2D animations are also very well-made, and you can feel the weight when Ina swings on a rope, as well as when she jumps and lands. You need to take your time when swinging on a rope because you need to build up momentum to jump and land on the next platform. In fact, you need to be careful when jumping from tall heights, otherwise Ina will take extra time to recover which can be dangerous if an enemy is chasing you.The game is not trying to have the latest graphics of course, it’s just a small indie title. For the scope of what the game is trying to achieve it has a surprising amount of details. One small detail I really liked was how Ina has a reflection off of many kinds of surfaces. There’s areas with dozens of crystals, and as you walk or jump by them you can see Ina’s reflection off of each crystal.The game has very beautiful backgrounds. As you progress through the game, there are three major areas: the starting area which looks like a utopia that was destroyed, a beautiful garden area which is now unkempt, and a mechanical area meant to feel very cold and industrial. Each of these different settings have their own hazards to watch out for too.The soundtrack of this game is also very well done. The main theme of the game feels very mysterious, but also relaxing at the same time. The soundtrack really reflects the atmosphere and mood of the game and it kept drawing me in more and more. Many of the tracks in the game feature Asian instruments as well which go well with the cherry blossom garden environment.Don’t mistake this game’s colorful appearance and fun soundtrack with only happiness though. The game features a lot of lore and backstory, and the game does have many serious plot events and somber moments.Underneath this game’s colorful artwork there is a lot of sadness to uncover.Both Ina and the NPCs have a lot of internal conflict that they need to overcome and you’ll actually get a great plot out of this game.The gameplay is very addicting, and is also easy for newcomers. Aspire features no combat at all. It’s a 2D puzzle platformer, so a lot of the gameplay involves avoiding obstacles and enemies. You can move around and jump like any other platformer. Sometimes Ina will need to swing on a rope to jump across platforms and Ina can also climb up ladders.What makes Aspire unique is that you can absorb blue energy to deactivate machines, and you can give the energy back to reactivate them. Many of the puzzles involve finding energy and giving it to a particular door.Although Ina starts out using blue energy, she will be able to use green and purple energy later in the game which allows her to do different actions. Ina can give energy to certain platforms, which can either increase the size of the object (green energy) or move it vertically or horizontally (purple energy). When you put all of these elements together, the result is very fun puzzles that you need to solve to get through the game.The game starts off with easy puzzles to get your feet wet, and they get harder as you progress through the story. Even so, the puzzles near the climax of the game don’t get too hard at all. Even the worst puzzle would only take me 5-10 minutes of thinking, and the puzzles in this game are easier than similar indie platformer titles. The puzzles are made in a way such that you can’t permanently mess them up and there are only so many things you can do. It really is meant to be a relaxing game most of the time with a few sections in-between that’ll make you scratch your head.In one of the earliest puzzles, Ina has to push a crate with a rope attached so that she can swing across the rope to get to the energy source. You can’t jump over the box at first due to a low ceiling, so you’ll need to move it to on of the ends, jump over it, and then pull the box back towards you.The game also features plenty of checkpoints that you return to if you die. I’d typically see a checkpoint every 5 minutes or so which was very reasonable. You’ll likely die many times from just exploring, be it from pitfalls or enemies attacking Ina, but it’s easy to try again using the nearby checkpoint.My only criticism with this game is that it’s a tad short. My playthrough of the game took only three hours and it certainly is possible to beat the game in one sitting. There are a few optional memories of the NPCs you can find throughout the levels (referred to as Stone of Memories) which also contain information regarding lore of the world, but otherwise there aren’t really any collectibles or optional content in the game. Although all of the NPCs were extremely well-made and nuanced, there are only one or two NPCs per region which some people may find to be underwhelming.As well, the route through the game is very straightforward, with only one branching path per region to collect the optional memories. I do like that the game has a small scope and that it features tightly-woven gameplay, but at the same time there is a lack of substance and there isn’t any reason to go through the game again except to experience the plot again.Although my criticisms may sound harsh, don’t take it to heart because the game is very charming and fun. I’d say to definitely give this game a try if you like other 2D indie puzzle platformers. Aspire: Ina’s Tale definitely stands tall among other similar games such as Limbo, Inside, or Little Nightmares. If you enjoyed any of those titles I can guarantee you’d enjoy Aspire as well. Aspire is brimming with great artwork and animations, and is really worth a playthrough despite having a few shortcomings.
