_childDocuments_.review: Warning: strong Steins;Gate vibes detected.The Entropy Centre is a first person puzzle game developed by Stubby Games. The best way I can describe this game, is that it's a love letter to the Portal games. But I think this game differentiates enough from the Portal games to be it's own game. Let's see if this is a puzzle game worthy of your attention.The game is set in the far future, when humans discovered the technology to reverse entropy, which is used to prevent cataclysmic events and help Earth to course correct to avoid the cataclysms. To reverse entropy, entropy energy is used, which is harvested by completing time-based puzzles. Solving time-based puzzles became a job for specialized people, and it's established that only solving the puzzles for the first time generates entropy energy. Another thing the game establishes is that no entropy energy is generated when people know how to solve the puzzles, which contradicts the first rule I mentioned, because the puzzle gets solved regardless of if the people solving them know the answer beforehand. But the game kinda corrects itself when it's established that knowing the answer beforehand generates less entropy energy than in normal circumstances, but that creates conflicts with another rule, which states that each puzzle generates a fixed amount of entropy energy, which cannot be the case, because different conditions generate different amounts of entropy energy. So, yeah, the worldbuilding is a bit of a mess in this game.The plot kickstarts with a similar scene that in the first Portal game. At first, the main character, Aria, doesn't know what's going on, and she is instructed to solve puzzles, because Aria is a puzzle operative at the Entropy Centre. But later, the plot switches gears, and became a race against time to avoid a cataclysmic event. The ending of this game heavily reminded me of Steins;Gate, because of how worldlines and attractor fields work on that game (if you played Steins;Gate, you'll know what I mean), but above all, for the fate of the main character. The ending was properly foreshadowed, albeit a bit heavy-handed, with on-point setups and payoffs. The pacing is consistent and the tone is similar to that of the Portal games. Overall, the plot is one of the strong suits about the game.There are only two characters in this game: Aria, the playable character, and Astra... the gun, because Aria uses a sentient gun, or what appears to be sentient. Unfortunately, Astra is like a discount version of GlaDOS. It's evident that the writers attempted to replicate that iconic character from the Portal games, but failed to give her spunk and an interesting personality. One of the things that made Portal 2 great was the characters, GlaDOS, Wheatley and Cave Johnson. They had unique quirks and personalities, and that allowed them to carry the dark humor of that game, all that compounded with outstanding character writing. Aria seems like a fine character, but, at the same time, is a bit bland. In some instances, the game pretends to depict a strong bond between Aria and Astra, but wasn't earned whatsoever. There is not enough development between the two to create that bond, and that makes one of the scenes where Aria is separated from Astra rather forced. Definitely, the characters aren't a strong point in this game.The gameplay is very similar to the Portal games, but with a twist. Instead of creating portals, the game plays with time. The game relies on rewinding objects in time to solve puzzles. There is a maximum time that objects can be rewinded, which is 30 seconds. The tools available are similar to the Portal games, but there are tools unique to this game. Also, there are enviromental tools, which add variety to the gameplay. The platforming also relies on rewinding objects to reach places unreachable by normal means. There is also combat in this game, and this is something Portal doesn't have, aside from the boss fights in both games. The player can rewind projectiles or use explosive cubes to defeat enemies, or they can grab the enemies from behind and launch them into another enemy. Cool! But, for a game that relies on time to solve puzzles, there is next to no time management, aside from the final levels. The fact that there is a time limit to rewind objects is an idea that has ample opportunites for the player to use lateral thinking to solve puzzles, which leads to the main drawback of the gameplay. The game doesn't allow the player to think outside the box to solve puzzles, which would allow for more than one solution. It's a more mechanical approach to puzzles, and with time-based puzzles, that seems like wasted potential.The game definitely looks better than the Portal games, since it uses a newer engine (UE 4). It's not a stunner, but it's very good nevertheless, which is more than enough. I didn't found problems with the sound design or the background music, but the voice acting of Aria could have been better. It's as if the VA was bored voicing her character. Astra's voice is more lively and at least sounds convincing. The performance was good, most of the time, because there are still frame drops in some scenes, and for someone using an RTX 4070 at 1080p max settings on an UE 4 title, it's not a good look in the optimization department. Also, I need to mention that playing this game caused me nausea, perhaps because of the gun motion. Keep in mind that's my personal experience, and it may not apply to you.In conclusion:-Strong plot.-Interesting premise for a puzzle game.-Solid gameplay and innovative platforming.-Poor worldbuilding.-Uninspired characters.-Wasted potential for gameplay opportunites.I said at the beginning that this game is a love letter to the Portal games, and I still think that. The problem is that is a love letter with some spelling errors, but some spelling errors is far better than a completely nonsensical letter. I think there are enough elements to like about this game, but I also think that, with a bit more polish, it could have been a great game. If I'm to describe my experience with this game, is that this game is a raw diamond. Still, all in all, I still recommend this game if you are willing to ignore the aformentioned issues and just dedicate to puzzle-solving action.
_childDocuments_.name: The Entropy Centre

_childDocuments_.review: While the comparisons to Portal are obvious, unfortunately it's not nearly as good as a game.The visual are nice enough, if nothing spectacular, but the UX of the game is lackluster. Puzzles don't seem to be built in a way to give you a good mental map of them, puzzle elements (boxes, jump pads, etc.) don't stand out nearly enough, and there's just generally a lot of clutter around the area that makes everything harder to see. The people who made Portal put a LOT of effort into making sure all of this stuff worked smoothly (without the player even noticing), and most of that is unfortunately missing from this game.They tried to lean pretty heavily into the story and worldbuilding, plus the cute robots/AI companions thing that seems to be trendy in indie games these days. Unfortunately it's way too weak to work as satire, if that was even the intent, and it's too cookie-cutter to be interesting straight.So if you want to play this game for the puzzles, you'll just get frustrated by all the nagging little things. And if you want to play for the story or visuals, they're just not good enough to stand out. I'm sure some people will enjoy it, but I felt disappointed.
_childDocuments_.name: The Entropy Centre

_childDocuments_.review: There is clearly a lot of similarity to Portal 2, however the puzzle mechanics of The Entropy Centre help it stand apart from its inspiration. Portal's puzzles seem to focus more on movement and timing while Entropy has far more focus on sequence of events. For each object, you effectively get a 30 second window of time that you can manipulate the object back and forth, and you shouldn't need to get too close to that time limit if you're planning the sequence of moves/stops effectively.Otherwise, Entropy is a good, but not great game.  It has some humor, but nothing too memorable.  It has some world-building (the environments are interesting and the notes give you a sense that this was an active centre prior to everything going to ruin) but its still largely empty-feeling.  And it has an interesting story, but you need to piece it all together yourself from the notes you read throughout the game.  If you don't have the patience to find and read all of the notes, you miss out.  And if the ending is what I thought it was?  That's a refreshing change and very well done.
_childDocuments_.name: The Entropy Centre

_childDocuments_.review: I really hate that I have to give this a negative review. It's a lovely concept for a game, and it's lovely to look at from a distance. However, the deeper you get into it, it becomes clear that the development team are way too ambitious for what they can actually accomplish. In line with the gameplay itself, they feel like they design most puzzles backwards. They create the problem, and then make a solution for it. They take many shortcuts which cheapen the experience, and seem far too confident in their physics system which is not exactly cut out for the job they are asking of it.The story as well, while engaging, is very predictable and cheap, and can easily be guessed before any of it really happens. Any remaining secrets or questions are not actually addressed, and it more becomes a medium of exploring the nuances of the situation you're already in, rather than any investigation of how you got here, or any way to resolve it.In all, if you just want a puzzle game without having to think too much, this game can do it well. But if you want to actually focus and think about the intricacies, the base game may frustrate you more than it helps.
_childDocuments_.name: The Entropy Centre

_childDocuments_.review: I REALLY wish I could recommend the game. The characters are great, especially E, our special little bot buddy. The chemistry between Aria and Astra feels authentic and you genuinely begin to care about the characters and their predicament. The story is cool, an interesting concept that is explored well in the "hidden" intel parts. The puzzle concepts are cool, and keep the gameplay somewhat fresh.However.The mechanics aren't amazing at times, there were a handful of levels I found myself only able to complete by manipulating the cubes (especially the jump and spring) to hop on the edges of the map to circumvent parts of the puzzle area.Dying has a habvit of setting you further back than you'd expect, often leading to you having to listen to the same dialogue exchange for the fifth time, including some of the incredibly drawn out tannoy announcements.The main reason I can't bring myself to recommend the game however, is the ending. It is so incredibly disappointing.I get the thinking behind choosing that as the ending, its set up constantly through the game and I get how it makes sense.  But considering how much time and effort you have to put into the game to get to it, its basically being slapped in the face and told "well done" in a mocking voice.If the game was half or even 3/4 as long, the ending would be alright, it would fit the story arc and feel like an alright pay off. Yet, I've spent 13 hours slogging through it, going insane with the pain that came from some of the levels, and it just feels like a waste of time.
_childDocuments_.name: The Entropy Centre

_childDocuments_.review: Don't like to leave a negative review, but technical imperfection are grind my gears: * 38 seconds to unroll sometimes is not too much, all sequence should be recorded almost flawlessly for some levels* jumping mat has a small hitbox and very low character control in air* jumping on a beach on rocks is very tedious, also about collisions but now about the rocks and there is no a hint for a jumping mat position* if you missed a jump at the end, all sequence should be started from scratch* some puzzles are not working with first attempt with a correct solutions, looks like you can lose impulse sometimes* when you realized how to solve the problem it's not too fun to implement it; I guess it's related to time unwind mechanics in comprising with forward solvable puzzles like all portals, turing test...* also sometimes you can unwind a little bit too much and it also can lead to restartSome of this problems I suppose can be fixed
_childDocuments_.name: The Entropy Centre

_childDocuments_.review: Definitely hits that "Portal-abandoned-Facility" spot, the voice acting as well as the soundtrack were peak.The puzzles are pretty good, the elements are introduced one-by-one which I liked very much, although sometimes I felt like there was an intended solution but I had to cheese it because I saw no other way.The lore that is scattered around the game is very, very intriguing and made me wish for more of the story in some form outside of the game.Also:cat.cat. cat. cat.
_childDocuments_.name: The Entropy Centre

_childDocuments_.review: Excellent game, I would recommend it to anyone looking for a puzzle game in a similar style to Portal. Some elements are certainly heavily inspired by Portal, but the game manages to do something interesting and different with them. The story is more heartfelt and mysterious than you might expect. The characters are likeable and the writing features a few cheesy jokes but it was so much better than I would expect from what's primarily a puzzle game.I think there are about 75 formal 'test chambers', with new puzzle elements introduced about every 5, and there are transition sections between some of them that have mild time pressure and/or enemies along with more puzzles. There are also some optional collectables which contain more story information, I did my best to find them all and only got about 2/3rds so that's definitely something to look out for if you like that kind of thing. It took me about 10 hours to complete and while I didn't find any of the challenges overly difficult they were still very engaging and satisfying to solve. The game doesn't use too many moving parts at once so it's not too difficult to keep track of the different timelines of all the movable objects. I've not even touched the level editor and community content, where I'm sure there's a lot of much harder puzzles if that's what you're looking for.Ran fine on my (now quite old) i5/GTX1060 PC on Ultra, only a few minor stutters when loading large areas, and the game looks great. Didn't encounter any bugs and only very minor physics engine jank, which comes with the territory for a physics puzzler really.Considering the very small dev team on this, it's an extremely impressive effort to be on the same level as Portal. I'll be looking forward to any kind of follow up or other games by the studio.Overall, definitely worth full price if you enjoy puzzle games, and I would recommend it to anyone considering it when on sale.
_childDocuments_.name: The Entropy Centre

_childDocuments_.review: The portal inspiration is pretty obvious from the moment the game starts, from the way the puzzles are presented to the familiar feeling testing chambers, to the robot that occasionally insults you... I was actually kind of surprised that there doesn't seem to be any portal easter eggs in the game of any kind, not even a 'The Cake Is a Lie' scribbled somewhere. But nevertheless, the game lives up to the comparison. The main mechanic of time gave me the same feeling I got the first time I was ever asked to Think With Portals.I do, however, think the game could have done with just a bit more polish, as there was a lot of clipping in places that you weren't meant to go, but were very easy to get to, and as the game went on more windows that led to completely empty rooms. It also could have been fun if there were more non-puzzle related objects you could interact with, like maybe restacking a fallen mess of papers or watching a ping pong ball go from the floor to bouncing back and forth on a table. The apple near the beginning of the game made me think there would be more interactions like this, but from what I experienced it never did. But all that's just extra, the game excels at everything that's important, beautiful scenery, great puzzles, fun dialogue, and a story that's one of the best that I've experienced in a while. This game scratches that puzzle itch that Portal 2 left me with so long ago, but at the same time makes me wish for Portal 3 all over again.
_childDocuments_.name: The Entropy Centre

_childDocuments_.review: short but fun puzzles, crashed once and a few glitches(a dialogue line would play after a death that was not played before the death), some amount of jank such as seemingly unintended solutions and sometimes wonky physics but nothing at all game breaking. most of the puzzles flowed from one to the other but only a few times more than one element can be introduced at a time which can make finding out how some mechanics work difficult or the "introduction" seemed to happen after you found it. the game was also somewhat short feeling which could have just been because i did not go for collectables which (the few i found) had a somewhat explorative element but seemed to easy to find but some of them that i did not find may have in fact have been a challenge. the secrets themselves also had some  additive story from before the start of the game. in the end i give the game a 7.5/10 as it is a very good game with some small to moderate hangups.
_childDocuments_.name: The Entropy Centre

_childDocuments_.review: Slightly recommend. The puzzling is pretty good. Somehow new mechanics are constantly introduced throughout the entire game. Some of them get used frequently and some of them clearly didn't fully pan out. Difficulty was a little on the easy side, most of the difficulty came from trying to execute the solution due to some janky physics. Voice acting is phenomenal and the story telling  (through computer messages) was pretty good. The "combat" was extremely frustrating and didn't add much to the game, but there was not much of it to wade through. Overall a good, not great game. Pick it up if you have already exhausted the top-tier puzzlers.
_childDocuments_.name: The Entropy Centre

_childDocuments_.review: Picked this up from a humble bundle and it depresses me that it never came up on my radar before. If you enjoyed portal, then I suspect you will also enjoy this one. The puzzles are interesting, though once you have your head around the mechanics not the hardest in the world, the story though is what's keeping me engaged, and the attention to detail in the world setting...**chef kiss**I do recommend this one.
_childDocuments_.name: The Entropy Centre

_childDocuments_.review: I really liked this, it has it's moments where it drags on a bit long, the physics are a bit weird, and almost all the concepts are stolen from portal, but nevertheless it's a great game. The story is engaging, the characters are decently well written, the puzzles get quite challenging at the end, and the visuals are very good!Overall 8/10
_childDocuments_.name: The Entropy Centre

_childDocuments_.review: Earth is facing a catastrophic extinction event and the only human potentially left alive is on the Moon. Aria is a junior puzzle operative for the Entropy Center, a humanitarian company that generates renewable energy and whose headquarters is, for perfectly normal reasons, in space. Alone and with amnesia, Aria and her AI entropy device Astra must generate enough energy in an attempt to save Earth from its destruction and investigate why she’s been left behind. 8-15+ hours to complete, The Entropy Center is a post-apocalyptic half puzzle-platformer half walking-sim where you rewind objects in time to solve puzzles. Explore a gigantic abandoned space station overgrown with plant life and search through crumbling buildings for information to discover how you ended up alone on the moon. Overall, I had a very lovely experience as it’s a graphically beautiful game with a storyline that’s fun to think about. The only two cons I would note are that I wish there were more unlocked rooms to investigate and that the plot twist was less obvious. There are time-sensitive sections and enemies that appear in and past Act 7, but nothing is terribly difficult or frightening. I highly recommend The Entropy Center, especially if you are fond of abandoned places.
_childDocuments_.name: The Entropy Centre

_childDocuments_.review: Visually stunning but lacking identity. Entropy Centre is a game that is heavily inspired by portal. It's incredibly obvious. But is it good? The main plot follows Aria whom has woken up in a facility alone. The game then presents the main goal of the game. The earth has had a calamity and you need to complete puzzles using a time rewinding device to generate energy to reverse said cataclysmic event. One of the strongest parts of this game is its theming, it's story and the visuals. Honestly I hope that if we ever get a Portal 3 it looks halfway near as good as this game. Some areas are just a spectacle to behold. The game also constantly reminds you of your goal both directly and indirectly as the Earth is in full view looming over the facility (Which is on the moon) as the shockwaves hit areas of the facility causing damage to areas as you progress. It gives that same looming threat feeling as something like the moon in Majoras mask and it's just great. Without spoiling any of the story, some of the beats here are really fun with some little revelations along the way. I honestly prefer the overarching story here to what is presented in either portal game. Character wise, the few characters you encounter and leftover memoirs are engaging and enjoyable with the Entropy gun and the main character having some fun dialog to break things up. One place where I do feel the game falls a bit flatter is in its decision to look so similar to portal as well as directly lifting a number of elements. Whilst the facility is overgrown, it's a lot of white walls with some damage to it akin to Portal 2. Honestly I wish the game distanced itself a little more in this regard and went with more interesting environments which at times do pop up. Portal had a reason for looking the way it did whereas this game doesn't need to in order to communicate interactivity to the player. In regards to gameplay, a lot of elements seem copy and pasted. Cubes, light bridges, fans that push and pull you, bouncing areas (Gel)  laser cubes and turrets. It doesn't feel very fresh and I really wanted the game to do something more. A stand out for me is the transforming gates and conveyors which felt much more unique to this game as well as their interactions. Most of the puzzles generally revolve around moving a block of some kind in reverse of what you need and then playing through the level reversing what you did with said block. I feel like puzzle diversity is something that is lacking here which is largely due to the entropy gun having the single utility. It also meant that for me personally, the puzzles were generally quite easy with only a few around the 10th chapter or so providing much challenge. I think if the game perhaps mixed up the elements more or gave more utility to the entropy gun it would have allowed for more puzzle diversity such as being able to throw cubes or be able to fast forward objects or having more to interact with. By no means are the puzzles bad and some people may get more out of it than me but overall they're probably the weakest part of the game. All in all I commend the solo developer that made the game. I think they made a really well polished, well presented game with an engaging plot and characters and a really nifty mechanic. I just hope that any future projects provide more innovative gameplay so that the gameplay can be more interesting and engaging.
_childDocuments_.name: The Entropy Centre

_childDocuments_.review: Initially, I thought that The Entropy Centre would be some basic Portal lookalike, but I was very quickly proven wrong. The puzzle design is unlike what I've mostly seen prior to playing this game (had a lot of fun playing around with alternative and probably unintended solutions to some puzzles in the endgame), the environment tells an interesting story (albeit it's kind of hard to wrap your head around it), and the interactions between the main character and Astra in random situations never failed to cheer me up. My only complaint was towards some of the achievements, but, other than that, I'm happy to give this game a score of 9/10!
_childDocuments_.name: The Entropy Centre

_childDocuments_.review: I've been playing for almost 2 hours but I can't keep going because there isn't really any puzzles in this game from what I've seen so far. The puzzle rooms are just too easy to complete. You get into the room, you see the pattern in 10 seconds and then you just spend time moving blocks around and rewinding time. So you get 10 seconds of thinking and 2 minutes of moving things around. You do that a couple of time and then you get 10 minutes of walking to the next floor. After almost 2 hours of this, I'm totally not hooked in. I could try to keep playing, but I'm not having fun and at this point I won't risk it and ask for a refund.Maybe the puzzles get interesting later on? But how long do I have to do boring manual tasks and walking around before I can get an interesting puzzle?Also, between puzzle rooms, you get those walking section where you just hold W while listening to the robot talk. Sometime you'll get events happening in those sections, but it's always just "something blew up in front of you, hold M1 to rewind time on that object, good, go back to pressing W. Oh no, something blew up in front of you....". Again, no thinking involved at all, just walk on and do manual tasks.Before I stopped playing, I got to a part where you have to fight enemies, but all they do is slowly shoot a ball at you, you hold M1 to return the ball to them and they die. I don't get the point of that. It's not difficult to do and it's doesn't add anything to the puzzle element of the game, why is it in the game?
_childDocuments_.name: The Entropy Centre

_childDocuments_.review: Good if you want to scratch that Portal itch - the levels aren't super difficult for the majority of the game but there's a few that had me thinking for a little while. It took me a little under 10 hours to finish including stopping by and reading the computer consoles that I could find (extra lore). I thought the story was pretty interesting as well.
_childDocuments_.name: The Entropy Centre

_childDocuments_.review: The Entropy Centre has a very familiar feel if you have played the Portal series. To be clear, it is not the same, even if I wish it were. The humour is very different, but the concept of going through a large number of puzzles with an overarching purpose is very much the same, even if there is not an evil robot overlord insulting you at every opportunity.The puzzles are reasonable in difficultly, sometimes being very obvious, and other times, you overthink the heck out of it, but your mileage may vary.If you like puzzle based games, with some perhaps silly humour and reasonably good voice acting, this is for you.
_childDocuments_.name: The Entropy Centre

_childDocuments_.review: Great game. Just needs a little work with the level editor, like a update. I like the beach theme but at least give us the option to have a blank template, like in the trailer. Also i just want more puzzles and elements in the level editor. We can also add a tutorial, we also should get structures that can be reversed, we can also add a event trigger to make things break. we could also add structures that bots can break, and we can repair. Another thing i would love to see is the doors, not puzzle doors, but office doors, we should be able to have them locked and we have to turn on a puzzle button to unlock them. I really think this would be a cool update so please add this.
_childDocuments_.name: The Entropy Centre

_childDocuments_.review: Great puzzle game !Somewhat mix of Portal / Relicta / Stanley Parable but with it's own story and unique concept, based around the entropy of things and the ability to reverse it through a device. Concept which was made famous with the Tenet movie by Christopher Nolan.I finished the game in 11H during the course of 2 days. Lovely and challenging just enough. Some puzzles do require some thinking, but overall the progression and challenge was just right.Lovely graphics, simple controls, cute stories in the computers emails, ...
_childDocuments_.name: The Entropy Centre

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a very well done homage to Portal and other FPP puzzle games. It's got an intriguing story and setting to top off some puzzles that really do make you sit and think for a while to complete them. If you're at all interested in puzzle games, especially games akin to the two Portal games, this is one you shouldn't miss out on.
_childDocuments_.name: The Entropy Centre

_childDocuments_.review: Overall a very fun game that deserves lots of love. 2 suggestions to the devs for improving future installments: 1. Give a little "funneling" onto jump pads, similar to how Portal does for portals. Make it toggleable if you want. Nothing made me want to put the controller down more than when I knew how to solve the puzzle, got everything in place, then missed a jump forcing me to restart the whole thing. 2. In a similar vein to #1, give better "checkpoints" in puzzles. Something where when you solve one part of it (e.g., getting a second cube), if you lose that cube, don't make us re-get it. Have some mechanism where when you get to it the first time, you can open a door or raise a ramp or something to make getting back to it easier. The puzzles are a ton of fun, once. After knowing how to solve them, solving them again does nothing for me. I don't want to be too negative in this review, I criticize the relatively minor things that made me like your game less. The writing, music, environment, graphics, and gameplay are all excellent. Smooth out those rough edges and its an easy 10/10
_childDocuments_.name: The Entropy Centre

_childDocuments_.review: Before I start: Please ignore my "time played" because I was not connected to steam while playing.Review: Pros:- Easily one of the best games, I've ever played. - For me, it's perfectly balanced – challenging but not too challenging (only a headache towards the end ;) ). - The story is awesome! - If you are able to think ahead, you won't need a guide/walkthrough. - The puzzles change between easier and harder. That's great because if you take long solving one puzzle, the next one will probably be easier for you and you won't get frustrated. - The more progress you make the more mechanics will be added to the puzzles. In my opinion there's more variety in this game than there is in Portal (and I love Portal).- After you solve a bunch of puzzles there will be some exciting story elements so you won't get bored.- The "world" you walk through and the "things" you see will be epic....Cons:- There could have been more easter eggs or variety in level design between puzzles. You will see the same posters, the same offices/desks etc. over and over again. Apart from the main game you won't have much to discover. There are many areas you can explore but there will be nothing to discover/nothing new to see. - There could have been more dialouge/reactions from the main protagonist- One time I got stuck between a wall and some boxes and I had to restart.
_childDocuments_.name: The Entropy Centre

_childDocuments_.review: 6.5/10the inspiration with Portal series is more then obvious, but the quality and polish is just not there.I can recommend it to anyone who love Portal for it's post-apocalyptic feel and quirky humor. But if you pick this up maily as a puzzle game, you'll probably be disappointed. There are a lot of puzzle levels as well as some pathfinding between them, sufficient amount of diverse puzzle elements are gradually introduced, BUT they are all very simple with like 3-4 step solutions and the difficulty/complexity scales super slowly. It's not until like 70% of the game where the puzzles get interesting and you get to think a bit instead of seeing the solution right away. Around that time also the story ramps up. It's a little shame there is potential for larger more complex puzzles and better scaling.Finally I have to mention the respawns, the conversations and humor are great and all but when you hear them again every time you die it quickly gets annoying. And die you will because as much as the deterministic physics of destruction is impressive, you'll get randomly crushed by the rubble when reversing quite often. Also waters kills you misstep from a narrow bridge and so on, you get the point, dying often = fine, hearing the same conversation 10 times...Technical notes:- with some persuasion runs on Steam Deck- multi-platform sync works great, maybe even too well as you'll be fighting the syncing settings- 100% achievements is doable, but be wary, one of them (all the collectibles) is presented only as a number so either look extremely well to find them all in your 1st playthrough or just ignore them entirely and do a 2nd run, my semi-observant playthrough where I wound like 90% was pretty much just lost time as the rest could have been anywhere throughout the levels.
_childDocuments_.name: The Entropy Centre

_childDocuments_.review: I've played through this game. I've played Portal, Portal (and a lot of its mod maps), Talos 1/2, Qube 2, and many more. I paid $7 for it, and for that price, it's fine. However, I don't like the main game mechanic. Essentially, you always reverse what you've done. The save points are subpar. The puzzles aren't particularly impressive. I didn't quite grasp the story, but that might just be me. Still, if you've played all the Portal games and all the Talos games and are looking for something new, this game offers 13 hours of fun. Otherwise i would recommend those games.
_childDocuments_.name: The Entropy Centre

_childDocuments_.review: Joins Q.U.B.E. 2 as another easy recommendation for fans of the genre; it has more personality and a lighter tone than Q.U.B.E. 2, and I found the story more engaging too, but the Portal games are still safely in a league of their own. The lack of any run/sprint functionality is as frustrating as usual, but this design choice seems to be common in all other games I've played in the genre for some reason. Enjoyable puzzles which are never cheap and rarely frustrating, however the difficulty throughout is relatively low; could perhaps have been made either  shorter or more difficult. Overall very good.
_childDocuments_.name: The Entropy Centre

_childDocuments_.review: A wonderfully inventive puzzle gameThoroughly enjoyed this experience from start to finish. I was surprised by how it stayed fresh and surprising throughout the runtime. The story and writing were excellent as well, it usually bothers me when decent portions of the story are communicated through text logs, but the emails are so well written, I ended up looking forward to them. Getting extra bits of context for the world of The Entropy Centre.Well worth the price of admission, at full or sale price. _childDocuments_.review: My quick review: Portal without the polish.Something I noticed after playing this is that Portal has clever little touches that help you out. For instance, notice how you rarely miss the portal you're jumping into. This game doesn’t have those tweaks, meaning you will often have to redo a tedious puzzle because you failed to hit a box. Do that a few times in a row and you'll start feeling rather annoyed.Another irritation is the audio. There is something with the mixing that causes the voices to drown in background noise. Again, a little thing Portal got right.As for the puzzles, they aren't exactly bad, but they lean towards tedious. Meaning, you don't want to experiment or try things, as you feel you get punished for it. The game also keeps introducing new puzzle elements in a way that feels unnatural, like here is a box that forms a bridge. Again, a little thing that Portal does so much better.Fortunately, the story seems interesting, but I'm smelling a typical "you're in a timeloop" ending. I'm sure someone likes those endings, considering how common they are, but prefer to feel like the character actually accomplished something.

_childDocuments_.review: I've played the demo when it came out and thought that it was an interesting concept, but probably not worth the money, so I've waited for a sale later down the road. Later down the road is now, and 9 chapters in I would say that my initial feeling was right, and even discounted it's still... something. If I had to name this game as something, I would like to say it tries hard to be Portal 2, in both setting and aesthetics, but falls short. Not so much on aesthetics, but definitely on the gameplay.The main game mechanic is the selling point, but also annoying: A good chunk of puzzles involves  backtracking. You can't see the entire puzzle solution in one go for some levels, because parts are hidden behind doors, on other levels, or both. So you're starting to solve it to the best of your abilities, only to then figure out that you need one step at the beginning and can do it all over again. The puzzle difficulty is, from my point of view, varying wildly. Most puzzles are rather trivial, some are annoying to set up, and rarely you have a really hard/non-obvious puzzle, smashed between two trivial ones. There's no real difficulty grade that I could see. It's a bit all over the place.The puzzle elements are also rather rough and in my opinion not very well done. For example, the jumping box is super small and puzzles that involve jumping from one platform to another repeatedly get incredibly frustrating because you can't really strife while in air - so you better hope that your initial jump and placement of the boxes was correct, otherwise you can return to the beginning, set up the puzzle, and do it all over again. I didn't expect this to be a precision platformer.What makes it even more frustrating is the save system: There's no way (that I could find) to save or quicksave a level. The game dictates when it wants to save, and it's not super obvious when this happens. I've had finished some levels, quit the game, only to find out that I had to do them all over again - because I hadn't hit the autosave point.Then we have the... really weird combat levels that happen sometimes. In-between two puzzles with unlimited time and no stress, you're suddenly in a cutscene, then some chase, then some fight. Of course, if you die, you can restart the entire level, because as mentioned before, save points aren't really happening inside a level. Meaning: You can run away for two minutes, miss a jump, fall through a gap, fall to your death, and re-do the entire thing from scratch. Several times.The story seems neat, although I'm not entirely sure about it at this point, especially about the find-all-clues bits. The aesthetics are nice and well-made, but they can't make up for the previous points.It's an interesting concept, but when compared to Portal 2 and its mods (some which deal with "time" as a concept too, and much better in my opinion) and workshop maps, or games like Talos Principle, the Entropy Centre is just not enjoyable.
_childDocuments_.name: The Entropy Centre

_childDocuments_.review: The very definition of we have Portal at home.My wife’s boyfriend says it’s like if Portal and Singularity had a baby.I absolutely adored my time with it. This is a really great game that everyone that enjoys puzzlers should check out. It's aesthetically and structurually similar to Portal but with less focus on humor and tongue in cheek writing.The Entropy Center seems light-hearted, with innocent puzzles, references to cats, set in what seems to have been a healthy work environment, complete with "cute" robots and friendly AI characters. But this facade quickly decays into what is one of the most terrifying stories I have ever experienced in a video game.The setting and atmosphere of the game is absolutely incredible, it's like if you took the Oldest House from Control (in terms of the concrete and geometric shapes architecture) and combined it with that of Mirror's Edge Catalyst, and then slapped on some next gen lighting; over all that then drape the overgrown areas of Portal 2 or the pristine look of Portal 1. I seriously couldn't stop looking at the architecture and design of the rooms.I really, really enjoyed it! The puzzles stumped me a couple of times but never for too long, I felt like a genius all the way through. The dialogue between you and the cute little Al you talk to (Astra) never got old, and the story was mind boggling with the emails providing more detail without being necessary to enjoy it. I could see how the ending can be polarizing, but I loved it.You don't always get the exact thing you want/ are expecting, nor do you always get closure or a secret ending based on 100% the game. Thought provoking all the way through without over staying it's welcome.For about the 15 hours to completion it took me, I’d say it had enough value despite not being the most replayable. I really enjoyed it and only a few puzzles frustrated me by being a little more focused on dexterity than on ingenuity. Additionally, there’s a solid amount of “combat” that I know will really annoy some people, but only one small section of that I’d say was bad. Feels like a great spiritual successor to Portal.TBH I'm quite glad to see the Portal genre catching on. I can think of only a handful of other games that followed suit after the surprise success of Portal. But it gives me hope when I see publishers still willing to make these types of games. We need more Portal, and I think this game will give me my fix.Overall it’s a very fun puzzle game with great visuals, great characters and dialogue, fantastic story that’s kept me invested and guessing what’s going on, and fun puzzles. All in all it was really nice to have a game that gives you both an appealing presentation and a solid value for your money. I highly recommend it.8/10

_childDocuments_.review: Excellent game! Very Portal-esque puzzler, substituting the portals for time manipulation.The time rewind mechanic is really interesting, and definitely a good fit for the genre. Unfortunately, I think just learning the basic mechanics contributes to most of the difficulty in this game. New puzzle elements are introduced frequently throughout the game, and figuring out the nuance of each element is where most of the challenge arises. Beyond grasping the mechanics, the rest of the puzzle becomes simple order of operations. All you need is a good vantage point to visualise the puzzle, then plan backward from the exit. The last few puzzles leading to the end, explicitly labelled as 'extremely hard' puzzles, were some of the easier ones purely because I was already familiar with all the elements at that point.The underlying narrative is great! The concept of rewinding time for the planet in order to avoid apocalyptic endings with prepared planning is a genius plot. To see that implemented into a game so elegantly makes for an enjoyable experience. Avoiding spoilers, I would still like to recognise the interesting mental state of the main character portrayed through the back half, and how her aimless determination descends into a moral abyss as a result of hope in the face of constant hopelessness. Rare to see a person's character challenged so directly by introspection.Regarding the characters: I love Astra, the situational commentary combined with artificial obliviousness makes them a really humorous and likeable character. While Aria has a hint of likeability to her personality as well, her passive attitude requiring constant guidance lets her down a bit. It feels contradictory to play a character so impressionable through a plot that casts her as absolutely single-minded.Lastly, the collectable achievement in this game is a horrific experience due to the lack of a record tracking which intel you have and have not found. There's no way of telling when or where you may have missed one without referring to a guide or playing through the entire game again with the sole intention of searching every last nook.I can recommend this game for at least one good playthrough. Beyond that, perhaps the integrated mod support will carry the weight of delivering more replayability.

_childDocuments_.review: Of note, you can get portal 1 and 2 for less than this game costs, and I would recomend both of those before recomending this as they both have more interesting gameplay and fun to them.SPOILER WARNING:Having just finished the game I must say I found it very lacking. All stackes are completely scripted until you do a thing which completely falls apart once you get close to the end where they will mention incredibly low times, like "catastrophic colision in 20 seconds" only for the walk you need to go taking more than that and nothing happened. This really should not have been the case, firstly. If the time you claim is less than a minute you better make sure what you are claiming actually happens. and secondly. The fact that you can't even get to where you need in the given time is really bad imo. There is also a few pewes i have, one being the placement of some items the the games more broken down sections. This game has areal fate plates. Its very obvious they arent suposed to be where you find them yet they happen to line up perfectly with the next part you have to reach every time. It just makes no sense and does bring me out of the game with how incredibly gamey it feels. The game even had a great option to replace them which would have been way less obvious. _childDocuments_.review: The Entropy Centre was a game that I didn't realize I needed in my life or an experience that I needed. I went into this game knowing that I am not the best at puzzles. I struggled immensely with the Portal series, but I still loved the series, regardless of my struggles. The Entropy Centre is  Portal-inspired, with exceptional level design and a huge mind f**k of an ending. Some levels left me dumbfounded and stumped, but I ended up loving the design once I cracked the puzzle. That being said, if you're someone who is not great at puzzles, please don't let this scare you into thinking you won't be able to beat this game! There is Google to help you if you ever get stuck, and don't feel bad or ashamed if you Google an answer. I will say that figuring out the puzzle yourself is the best feeling you'll ever have. So gratifying. I highly recommend this game to all people who enjoy the Portal series or even just a great puzzle solving game with a vastly realistic and intriguing storyline.The Entropy Centre is a strikingly gorgeous game, and this was yet another game that I found myself taking countless screenshots throughout my entire playthrough just because everything was just so f***ing beautiful. I couldn't help myself. Take your time and enjoy the scenery. The characters introduced to you during the game are just so easily likeable and charming. I loved the main character, Aria, and your Entropy energy gun that you carry around through the game; an AI is attached to this gun (P.E.A.). Her name is Astra! She was possibly one of my favorite characters, as she reminded me so much of a nicer and friendlier GLaDOS with her quirky humor and snarky comebacks to everything. I found myself laughing recurrently at Aria and Astra's interactions with each other, and it was just the cherry on top of the whole game, in my opinion.There are 27 achievements, and they seem  to achieve. So, this might be a great game for my fellow completionists out there who like to achievement hunt and 100% games, like myself. There was a sort of "collectible" to keep an eye out for, and this was basically lore or notes that you found on computers or terminals. There are 76 "intel" that you can find, and I actually really enjoyed trying to find every single one and reading all the entries! It will provide you with an abundance of information about the world and the research/projects being carried out at The Entropy Centre. I recommend looking for them and reading them if lore is something that you're into! I did not find all of them through my first playthrough; I believe I finished the game at around 56/76 intel, which is pretty good for a first run, and I felt like I scoured for them, so there must be lots of secret rooms that I just didn't find!I never experienced anything related to framerate issues at all. I can recall one negative review towards this game, complaining about framerate that apparently made the game unplayable, but the game ran like butter for me. Maybe this person didn't have a great GPU, but I have no clue as they did not put their specs in the comments of their review, *even after the developer asked for these details as well to try and solve their problem*. The game feels very optimized, which is phenomenal for launch day! But again, this was my experience, and others' might be different, so read around for some other reviews! To follow with this, the only thing I didn't really enjoy about the game was the saving system. Sometimes you would die by mistake and it would load back up—not an annoying amount—but if you kept dying, you would have to walk to a puzzle room again and collect any intel you collected previously again, as it would reset anything you collected before death. Like I said, it wasn't too bad, but it wasn't something that I loved at the same time. This might make it hard to gather some of the intel (collectibles) through another playthrough because you won't be able to just load a chapter, gather the intel, save, and load another chapter. It will require another full playthrough (and this is okay). I love replayability!All in all, The Entropy Centre was an amazing experience, and it will definitely give you food for thought; it is thought-provoking in more ways than one. I definitely recommend this game, especially at full price. You will fully enjoy the story it has to tell and fall in love with the concept. I hope you enjoy it as much as I did, and thank you so much for reading my review!Rating: 9.5/10

_childDocuments_.review: I wanted to like this game, but I spent way too much time being frustrated to give it a thumbs up.  I'm about two thirds of the way through the game, judging by chapter numbers, and I just can't make myself play any more.First problem, the physics are janky.   You'll really, really come to hate the jump pad, which is a key puzzle element that makes you try to hit a postage stamp from great heights, and then spend a couple minutes resetting all the components EVERY SINGLE TIME when you invariably miss it 10 times in a row.  Oh, and I should mention that the devs  like the rule of threes a lot, so you'll find yourself trying to hit that postage stamp three times in a row.  (This could be solved if the devs just made you land where your cursor points.)Second problem, the saves are not generous enough.  I rage quit after the third time I had to do a double postage stamp puzzle, and then died later in the level, requiring me to repeat those postage stamps.  I'm guessing it was 30 or 40 total postage stamp attempts by the time I finally successfully executed all the components of the level.  There really, really needs to be save on demand, just to save the (sometimes) minutes it takes to re-setup your components if you miss that postage stamp.Third problem, it's too easy to die, and there are areas that look accessible but aren't, killing you.  There are some bonus content pieces that require you to be precisely positioned in order to execute them, so get prepared to die six or seven or more times in order to successfully execute the trick.  (As to why dying is bad, one big reason is there are collectibles that don't get saved across deaths, so it's easy to miss a collectible if you die and forget to grab it again.)Fourth problem, lockdowns.  I'm trying to be spoiler-free, but imagine having to do puzzles while having tennis balls lobbed at your head.  Oh, and two tennis ball hits kill you.  I *hated* lockdowns.Fifth problem, chase sequences.  This is kind of a spoiler, but there are sections where you run while interacting with the game's main mechanic.  As I mentioned before, the physics are janky.  If you press the button, there's no guarantee that the game mechanic will kick in, and so you stand there a couple seconds wondering why nothing is happening.  I've had to hit the button three or four times before the mechanic kicks in.  Now add a timer to that.  I really hated the chase sequences as well.Sixth problem, it's too dark in too many places and you don't get a flashlight.  Not much more to add to that.Cumulatively, these six annoyances made the last half of my seven hours invested in this game a chore rather than fun.  So I'm gonna recommend skipping it unless you have a high threshold for jank.

I'd say to buy this game once it's on sale, It's got hours worth of gameplay, and a good story to boot. It's 100% overhated for being classed as a portal copy, even if it reuses assets.

_childDocuments_.review: Great game, enjoyed it a lot.If judging it as a standalone game (not comparing it to Portal. or similar experiences), it's really cool, not sure how much time or money it took to develop it, but it's a solid 8-9 hours for one play through.Puzzles are enjoyable, although maybe racking up in difficulty a bit too slow, since you really start to turn gears in your head more in about last third of the game. The variety of mechanics for puzzles was really appreciated and it didn't feel stale, with few somewhat original ideas (at least for me, but I didn't personally play a lot of puzzle games).Story is fine, nothing too exciting, but I guess enough to justify the stuff happening in the game, although I didn't like ending too much, it was sort of underwhelming and predictable, and didn't really lead to anything.Visuals are great in quality, but a bit lacking in visual style and design I'd say, and seems to be all over the places on some occasions.If comparing it to Portal, I'd say it'd still hold up pretty good, but I feel like level storytelling, as well as narrative through visual design in general is lackluster. Almost everything has this overgrown post-apocalyptic look to it, as if it was untouched for hundreds of years, and it stays like that through whole game, with very little changes and mix-ups (the most notably probably being )On technical side, had 1 crash and 1 game freeze (when I was switching windows) through whole playthrough so I'd say it's stable.On R5 5600X, RX 6900XT, 16 GB of 3200MHz RAM and PCIe gen 4 SSD, game was running good, in 1440p had 120FPS locked on Ultra settings everything, only there were couple of stutters every time there was (I assume) level streaming, especially in the very beginning of the game, before any loading screens, but it wasn't anything game-breaking.
_childDocuments_.name: The Entropy Centre

_childDocuments_.review: Good game!(Though landing on the jump boxes from a high spot has been a pain like 90% of the tries)(Really, you finally have the solution of the puzzle, execute it, and then yo have to repeat because your invisible feet didn't touch the damn box for less than a meter)(By the way, what worked for me was to aim (totally) down while falling and make the circle at the center of the screen to "touch" the box)(And still managed to miss a couple of times)
_childDocuments_.name: The Entropy Centre

_childDocuments_.review: Entropy Centre was an enjoyable experience to play through, for the most part. The things that really sold me on the concept was the idea of temporal puzzle solving, and clear portal inspiration. However, Portal this isn't...The puzzles, as mention by other reviewers, are generally all samey and quite simple; Not really taking full advantage of most puzzle elements (Which might be a benefit for the god awful water physics). Say for some of the later puzzles, they really just equate to doing the solution in reverse to solve it. Also, for me at least, I found most of the puzzle rooms unintuitive as puzzle elements like cubes and the springboards were usually hard to spot among the scenery (More so the springboards, as a faffed about in a room until I eventually notice a springboard a couple minutes in my confusion).Physics were janky at worse (Water physics were awful), but still worked. Those 'combat' encounters were too frequent and tedious And those sudden deaths thanks to rewinding structures and objects awkwardly were infuriating.However, aside from that I found the story interesting, the environment and music great, and the whole entropy gun the best part of the game. If you can power through some low points, its a definite recommend but for the others just play the demo and see if you like it.
_childDocuments_.name: The Entropy Centre

_childDocuments_.review: This game does enough to differentiate itself from Portal in concept, yet it provides the feeling of a "sequel in spirit".The story is compelling enough and the puzzles in the later levels left me scratching my head.My only complaint is that I can't play it for too much more than an hour without feeling motion sick.EDIT: I'm pretty sure that the motion sickness came from either the FOV setting or the first hour of the game. Either way it wasn't a problem for most of my playthrough. Although the game feels story-light and repetitive from the halfway point to near the end, I still recommend it.
_childDocuments_.name: The Entropy Centre

_childDocuments_.review: An okay game. Visually feels like an asset flip with the same bush and vine copy pasted a million times. Portal and it's followers had a feeling of starting in a clean research center and later breaking into a backstage with creepy corridors. Here you start in a backstage, killing the vibe of breaking the rules and exploring something you shouldn't. Base mechanic is boring - it's not about actual time rewind - it's about rewinding certain objects on their path... until it's not. 90% of the puzzle rooms are: place the box on plates in reverse order, then fire your gun. Puzzles are extremely, like 1 y.o. toddler level easy - every new room takes you 15 seconds to figure out which cubes do you have, then 15 seconds to solve the puzzle in your mind, and another 3 minutes to actually do it because the rewind function is so slow, The gun really needs an option to hold another button to speed up the process to at least x3 speed. Also after the introduction of bridge cube you can skip about 70% of the remaining puzzles just by placing it on some slope and building yourself a staircase to the exit. And I'm not like a speedrunner or bug hunter, these game breaking moments are obvious and so easy to do. This is just bad level design. And for some reason there are so much action sequences which are, again, boring and slow.
_childDocuments_.name: The Entropy Centre

_childDocuments_.review: The Entropy Centre is a great first person puzzle game that involves spacial and temporal awareness, lateral thinking, and a lot of logic. It is right there on the sweet spot of games I like most, such as Portal 2, The Talos Principle, QUBE 2, etc. But ultimately, it lacked some polish and playtesting that would have placed it in the same category as those. This review might contain some small spoilers, but anything significant will be spoiler-tagged.: The gameplay is fluid and easy to get, and the controls are intuitive, and everything runs smoothly. I did miss a crouch feature, but that's mainly from me being used to it. The jump specifically felt rather short (I can't get on top of regular cubes, for example), but that might've been due to puzzle limitations. One thing that severely bothered me, however, was how often I'd get stuck on weird geometry, or how some boxes would clip through platforms, etc. Some more intensive work on playtesting would've been nice on that front, especially in areas where I could get physically stuck, or have a difficult time moving around in. I have also managed to very trivially access some areas the game clearly didn't want me getting close to, such as dead end corridors and little crevices in natural landscape. One other thing that became apparent as the game progressed was how often the game would use broken catwalks for navigation, to the point where any time the room would shake, I'd immediately go scavenge-hunting for the next catwalk to rewind.: On the visuals side of the game, everything looked spectacular! Given the small team and budget, the game looks very polished and well thought out, with high quality assets and interesting level geometry and decoration. Some assets could have used some subtle texture variation, just so they wouldn't look so obviously copy-pasted (like all the lockers in the game being labeled "C4"). The early areas of the game look very believable and lived in, but as you progress through the campaign, you start to see more places where the visuals and level design were cut short. Near the end of the game, there were several, easily accessible offices (so not those far away ones you can barely see) that were completely empty, just a box with lights on the ceiling. There were also bizarre choices for prop placements at times, such as having those bulky tube monitors with logs sitting on top of a very modern flatscreen control panel (with a perfectly good office desk nearby where it could've been). Some puzzles had very, very extreme lighting and fog, to the point where everything looked white and opaque and difficult to comprehend and navigate.: The puzzles were amazing! Many of them had me thinking and planning for several minutes at a time, and the puzzle elements were very inventive! I especially like the departure from Portal 2 in that puzzle elements are primarily attached to puzzles, which meshes really well with the game's mechanic. Unlike in Portal 2, where you bend space to access fixed elements, in here you bend time to access mobile elements. Brilliant! Most of the puzzles were also very logical and easy to execute. As a puzzle designer and level designer myself, however, the main issue I had was readability. The early puzzles were fine in that regard, but late puzzles had the exit tucked away in hidden corners, had (mild spoiler for a late puzzle element) completely invisible in the equally grayscale floor surrounded by foliage, and later yet puzzles completely forewent having tracks for moving platforms to ride on (they would just float from point A to point B, clipping through anything in the path). Another major gripe for me was the time limit in the gun's time recording ability. A lot of puzzles - especially the late ones - involved a lot of steps, and having only 38.1 seconds at our disposal meant that, in some puzzles, I had to be extremely efficient with how I handled objects. I'd reset them at the start of their path, then make the most straightforward and linear moves towards their next destination, and would rewind them to correct for any idling in-between. And even then, in one particular puzzle, I had to solve it all over again twice because, despite all the optimization in timing, I still lost time!: This is where I'll probably disagree with most players. I'm already pretty accustomed to first person puzzle games, so the game was probably overall significantly easier for me than it was for most players. Especially up to chapter 6, I genuinely felt like I was solving the same puzzle over and over, with some very small variations. Once you inherently understand the way the time mechanic works, you can easily figure out those puzzles by playing them in reverse in your head. And since most of them are just about the order of execution, then the challenge became less about finding the catch and more about memorizing the actions you gotta do. I wish there were more elements like (mild spoiler for a late puzzle element). The late late puzzles, especially past chapter 10, significantly improved the challenge of the puzzles, and some of them really had me stumped for a while, but still, some of them just felt like "advanced" versions of the early puzzles, in that it was easy to solve but difficult to execute. I was also not very fond of the (mild story spoiler for late game) sections, as I felt like they completely detracted from puzzle solving and didn't fit the gameplay style at all.: I will be frank, the story isn't the strong suit of this game. It's an interesting premise, and has some compelling characters, but it overall wasn't too inventive or captivating. There wasn't much of a deeper meaning, or theme to explore, outside of the superficial ramifications of the setting itself. But, in all honesty, that didn't matter too much to me, since the story didn't really seem to be intended to be the main focus, but rather served as a platform to keep the game going and to justify the puzzles. I encountered several seeming loopholes and contradictions in the narrative - but I guess that's what happens when time travel shenanigans are involved - and at times it felt like the game tried to overexplain some details to its detriment (for example, when one email chain tried to explain déjà-vus with technobabble, when it could've given it an air of mystery and given more room for the player's imagination to fill in the blanks). But by far, the thing that bothered me the most was the way that reading emails and logs didn't really mean anything in the game. It just served as a "collectible" of sort, and while it did provide some funny jokes and gags, the exposition it gave didn't really seem to influence the gameplay. For example, prior to getting the entropy gun, I read an email that described it (even explaining what the "PEA" acronym meant). But when I did get the gun, my player character still questioned it like I hadn't literally just read about it less than a minute prior. I also wished that more of the story was told via audio logs, paper logs or just environmental storytelling. I don't want to just read about The Entropy Centre, show me more about it! Immerse me in the story!In summary, my rating for this game would be a 7.5/10. Solid puzzle game, really enjoyable for the most part, and excellent overall production quality! Could have used some more playtesting and feedback. I would really like to be able to make puzzles for it myself, there is a lot of untapped potential here! I still recommend this game because, despite the nitpicks and issues, it's still a very enjoyable, very fun puzzling experience. If you can, buy it on a sale. Lengthier review:

_childDocuments_.review: Overall It's really good, however;The game never gets 'hard' it's always pretty straight forward to get to the solutions of the puzzles, so much so that the first third of the game were an absolute chore to play because of how easy and repetitive the puzzles were.I'm not that keen on a voiced protagonist, she doesn't add much besides trying to put thoughts and feelings into your head...it's a show don't tell kinda thing.Finally the ending is nice, if predictable but the lack of agency in the outcome is disappointing even if that is half the point8/10
_childDocuments_.name: The Entropy Centre

_childDocuments_.review: I thought I was going to like this game at first honestly. Decent graphics, solid easy to understand mechanics and concept, and and somewhat interesting plot. And for a while it went pretty smoothly.But then the game makes the same exact mistake that every other game attempting to rip off portal does: It doesn't know when to STOP. There is no getting around the fact that if you keep trying to pad out the gameplay too long the puzzles get repetitive, then boring, then outright frustrating. I've only gotten through level 7 so far, I'm sick of the puzzles now and I want the plot to make some bloody progress...and apparently this isn't even the halfway point for the game.And while the narrative isn't bad... we've all seen this kind of writing before. Sci-fi that messes with time loops and attempts to "think outside the box, you know like every other sci-fi puzzle game" and in doing so does exactly what you expect it to do as a result, with pretty predictable plot twists, etc.I don't want to keep playing anymore. That's the review.

_childDocuments_.review: Short: Recommendation for everybody who miss Portal. Best Portal successor ever created.1) Sensible price.2) Simple, but reasonable plot (ideal balance, like in Portal).3) Good diversity of mechanics and thir utilization.4) Game doesn't trying to drown you in endless variations of the same idea to increase it's length (F you, The Talos Principle).5) Ideal complexity. I never even thought aboth watching a solution in the internet, but sometimes there was something to think about (F you, The Talos Principle. Again.)
_childDocuments_.name: The Entropy Centre

_childDocuments_.review: I have never been so wrong about a game before in my life. I was reluctant to buy what appeared to be a Portal copy with cheesy smiling robots. And for the first two hours of gameplay, that's what it seemed to be, just a literal attempt to copy the opening of Portal 2 with ugly lighting, walls that looked prefabbed from the level editor, jumps that were easy to miss, bad checkpoints, and the same puzzle over and over....But then I got to chapter 4. I don't want to spoil anything. But nearly everything after that point was excellent. Gameplay. Story. Visuals. Length. No bad language anywhere. Only I wish you could interact with a few more objects.If it weren't for the opening chapters, I would give this game a perfect 10/10 score. This is the best puzzle-platformer that I have ever played.
_childDocuments_.name: The Entropy Centre

_childDocuments_.review: After beating the game, I feel.. mixed about positive or negative review. Game looks and runs great on PC. But from the beginning I expected the game to be more "open world" puzzles, not like Portal and test rooms.  By that I mean it felt like lab (and yes, story explains why..) but  enviromental puzzles would be great. Also got bad feeling when 3/4 of the game and yet another game mechanic is introduced and started to feel overwhelmed. Or that the game is puzzle after puzzle with little breathing room. More story breaks or shortening puzzle chapters would be enough (since last chapter and charging entropy energy to 100% felt neverending) On the other hand, characters were great, voice acting same and I would love to see sequel (even tho review seems to be negative).

_childDocuments_.review: Okay, look... I really like the general setting of the game and the core concept as well. But solving puzzles in this game feels like doing chores. Too much of them feel like they're there just to fill the space and stretch the game time a bit. Many of them have quite repetitive core ideas, just applied on a different scale.
