_childDocuments_.review: Portal 2 has been and still is my favorite game of all time and The Entropy Centre does a fair job of being a comparable experience. The concept of the gameplay mechanics are interesting and well executed. Some of the puzzles toward the end become decently challenging and felt really rewarding to complete. I will say that as I got toward the end, I started to get a little fatigued with the puzzles. One of the things that Portal 2 did really well was avoiding that kind of puzzle fatigue by making some of the later puzzle solving incorporated into navigating the environment in general. The Entropy Centre does have some of that, but when it is there, the puzzles were typically dumbed down and were very easy to work through, while the dedicated puzzle rooms were significantly more difficult in comparison. In terms of the story, I really enjoyed the world that was built throughout the campaign. I love that more of the lore and world is built through the terminal messages that you find throughout the centre. I also really liked ASTRA and the dynamic between it and Aria. ASTRA is really cute and helped lighten the mood throughout the game. The ending is a little disappointing to me because it just felt somewhat underwhelming, however, the ending sequence of the game was done really well and I thought conveyed the ending really well. I do wish there was a menu option that would let you look at a list of all the terminal messages in the game. Look back at the ones you've unlocked and see what chapters the ones you missed are in. I think I finished the game with 69 out of 76 and I don't really want to go back and try to get them all because I have no clue where the ones I missed are and I don't want to replay the whole game just to look for all of them lol. Overall, I really enjoyed this experience. I loved the story, environments, puzzles, and characters. I'd love to see more games like this :)
_childDocuments_.name: The Entropy Centre

_childDocuments_.review: It was almost a tie on whether I enjoyed this game. There was clearly a lot of detail put into the level building and 3D modeling, but the core mechanic of the game is extremely simple and grows repetitive fast. The tie-breaker was the constant obnoxious dialogue you're subjected to between the character and her gun every minute or so. It feels like the game designers gave up halfway, and instead of adding more lore building in the world, they had to shove it in your face with overly obvious and pointless dialogue.
_childDocuments_.name: The Entropy Centre

_childDocuments_.review: I normally don’t review games but I felt like I needed to do so for this one… The Entropy Centre is such a beautiful game. There is a lot of comparisons to Portal but I personally feel like it’s unfair to compare TEC with Portal. Although they share similarities in play style, TEC is a one of a kind game that sucks you in from the start. Yes they are both puzzle games and yes they both use “guns” to solve the puzzles but TEC is so so much more than that. It’s similar enough to satisfy any Portal fan while also giving you a fresh experience. The story and the lore behind TEC is emotional, heartbreaking, but yet captivating and original. What gets me the most is how much some of the events that take place in the game could actually become possible in our timeline. I highly recommend this game to anyone who enjoys ‘portal-esque’ genres. Even if you don’t; the story and the gsmeplay is unique enough to leave an impression on any puzzle loving gamer
_childDocuments_.name: The Entropy Centre

_childDocuments_.review: I have waited my whole life for a game like this. The parallels to Portal are obvious and though some might see it as lack of originality, I see it as a love letter. The developers may have borrowed certain elements from Portal but they have expanded on them into something fresh and exciting. Aside from the Portal franchise, some other games I can see they might have pulled inspiration from include Braid and Singularity for the time manipulation puzzle solving, Prey and Control for the deep lore and the looming architectural aesthetic, and even a little Bioshock and Dead Space in the way side characters we never actually meet still enrich the world with slices of life in the form of diaries or in this case emails you find on PCs throughout your journey. The plot is fascinating, the characters have fun and witty personalities, and the soundtrack is “Oops, All Bangers.” I went into this game with no expectations and it absolutely blew me away. It’s an instant treasure!
_childDocuments_.name: The Entropy Centre

_childDocuments_.review: The game is fine. There are just a few problems from making it really worth playing1. Every puzzle starts to feel the same. You place blocks on buttons in reverse order and then rewind.2. Action portions are low stakes because you can instantly rewind any threat before it gets even slightly close to you3. The main plot element that's meant to give you a sense of urgency happens in act 3 and there are 12 acts after it. By act 8 there wasn't any progress in the story and it had lost any pressure.4. Every piece of lore I've had to go out of my way to find, really thinking outside of the box, have been mundane and uninteresting. Making it across an impossible chasm to open up a computer and be told "2 for 1 taco Tuesdays are cancelled until further notice."
_childDocuments_.name: The Entropy Centre

_childDocuments_.review: One of the most substantial Portal-likes I have encountered so far. The puzzles revolve around reversing time for certain objects, which is a great premise, since it often forces you to figure out the entire room and then execute parts of the solution requiring puzzle elements in reverse.Now. the tonal dissonance between the bleak plot and the dialogue, which occurs between your assistant AI Astra, the embodiment of the "haha, machine doesn't understand nuance and human social cues" trope, and the player character, who is unfortunately 25% on her way toward That Quippy Marvel Attitude Which You Really Do Not Want, can be a bit grating. Thankfully. I did end up liking their rapport for the most part. How could you get mad at chipper Astra's emoticon expressions?
_childDocuments_.name: The Entropy Centre

_childDocuments_.review: Entropy Centre is a game that takes so many pages out of Portal's book. From its puzzle mechanics, to its theme and setting there are links that tie the two everywhere. Many moments throughout the game its hard to sake the feeling that you're not playing a modded version of portal. If any of these sound like negative criticisms to you, then you are wrong. In fact, I'm more than happy that they did so as it led to the core mechanics of the game to be quite solid.Graphically, the game is stunning and performing. Even though it was developed in the UE4 engine, I can happily report that performance was great even at Ultra settings with no noticeable stuttering which. My only wish for the future is Ray-tracing support. Since this game heavily relies on the use of Screen-Space reflections for its brutalist style architecture, ray-tracing support would benefit this game greater than others. The story in this game is also very endearing to play through. While the ending was good, I felt a secret-ending could've been implemented with satisfying results. Overall, a very solid game that does a fantastic job of reaching its goals.
_childDocuments_.name: The Entropy Centre

_childDocuments_.review: this game looked super cool but unfortunately it's not for me. maybe it's just because my computer isn't quite powerful enough to run the game properly, but I did not find this game enjoyable. it might help if there was an option to turn off constant plant motion considering how many rooms are full of plants that are always moving. as it is though i don't find the game compelling enough to keep me playing through the performance issues. maybe when i get a better computer I can come back and leave a better review
_childDocuments_.name: The Entropy Centre

_childDocuments_.review: Finished it moments ago— a really enjoyable puzzle experience. It’s heavily inspired by both TENET and Portal, featuring time-reversal mechanics via a gun.Pros:-The story was charming, with companion characters that were present but not overly distracting.-Movement was smooth, not particularly 'clunky', and allowed for some unintended puzzle shortcuts.-The length was just right; it didn't overstay its welcome, and there are definitely some puzzles I'll revisit because they were so fun to solve.-The voice acting was good—not groundbreaking, but certainly not poor.-The music was great as well, shout out to whoever made the OST.Cons:-Some puzzle elements introduced later on felt a bit 'meh' and didn’t make the later puzzles feel any more challenging (this is just from my experience).-The story was a bit hit-or-miss for me; it was okay but a bit cliché.-I experienced one crash in a later level and had to restart at the final encounter because jumping wasn’t disabled, allowing me to exit the on-rails segment.Overall, I’d give it a solid 7.5. I’d definitely recommend it if you’re a fan of Portal and/or relaxing puzzle experiences.
_childDocuments_.name: The Entropy Centre

_childDocuments_.review: If you played Portal 2 and thought "Yes, I want 5+ more hours of this", this is the game for you. Depending on who you are, that might be a good review, or it might be a bad review.The time reversing mechanics are well developed. This game has a high production value and a lot of polish.This game feels like a mod of Portal 2; maybe that's how it started development. They take so, so, SO many things from it. From its plot, from its puzzles, from its environment, from its asthetic, from its humor. The only puzzle elements that are unique to this game, Transformers and Collapsible Boxes, are under-utilized.
_childDocuments_.name: The Entropy Centre

_childDocuments_.review: I loved Portal so I decided to give this game a chance. In my opinion, the puzzles are way harder than the Portal puzzles and I really struggled, because there are more puzzle mechanics than in Portal. Had to look up some solutions on YouTube because I was not able to solve them on my own. Also the game felt a bit lengthy. There were some combat mechanics too and I have to say that for me they felt good. Nothing too special, but they loosened up the game and added an extra element. Story was fine.
_childDocuments_.name: The Entropy Centre

_childDocuments_.review: I do not really know how to grade this game. On one hand it could be a worthy successor to Portal, on the other it misses the mark. Impressive work as for one-man team and I like the idea behind this game, but not its execution.Portal, the inevitable comparison standard, can be called a "pure puzzle game" in that it is all about the discovery and next "aha!" moment. Many games tried doing the same and few succeded.Entropy Centre has the "big task", some lore, companion, puzzles, interesting main mechanic and enemies. Focusing on the puzzles alone and disregarding its story (it is a loop anyway, Owlman quotes galore) there is not that much to say about them. You can cheese some (of course), slog through others, but at the end it is all the same. It feels the same.Besides that, the tedium mostly boils down to one thing - checkpoints. They are too far apart, forcing players to go through the same sequence again, again and again if they fail. Fun fact: collectible email lore bits are not permanently saved, prepare to read them again if restarting from checkpoint.Overall game feels too long. It is as if after half the game we haven't really gotten anywhere. Nothing really changes. Entire game is like one or two gigantic levels and not a set of "testing rooms". Again, I like the concept, but playing through this is... for now not what I would like.
_childDocuments_.name: The Entropy Centre

_childDocuments_.review: Portal crossed with Control with time reversal as a puzzle mechanic. The characters are charming, the story is a wonderful existential sci-fi horror, the puzzles are challenging at first glance but never feel impossible. I cried, I felt existential dread, I felt triumph. Artistically excellent in so many ways.It's not flawless. The combat sections are a bit clunky, The nature of the puzzle mechanics means that enacting your solution usually involves several minutes of holding left mouse button and waiting for objects to reverse, and if you made a mistake you usually need to redo the entire sequence from the start (or from the reverse-end?). This could perhaps be helped with some sort of fast-forward-to-a-checkpoint tool?Even with the flaws, an undeniable success, especially for a solo developer.
_childDocuments_.name: The Entropy Centre

_childDocuments_.review: It's not a great game, but not a bad game either. The polish is there, but the potential in the rewinding is lost on confined puzzle mechanics where random destruction and physics based would have been far more interesting. The reuse of assets wears down the environment until it all blurs together and the story, like the mechanics, is not fully realized and instead feels shallow and unearned.But, bottom line, if you like puzzle games it's worth a play through.
_childDocuments_.name: The Entropy Centre

_childDocuments_.review: The american voiceovers with "jokes" aimed at that audience are going to annoy you immensely.Sometimes, the physics are far too punishing. Where a box will have to go over a conveyor, but the RNG of the physics engine makes it turn and shift position, and then it bumps in to something to the side, that you have no control over.This is something that should have easily been avoided.I'm about halfway through now, and these things are starting to be more and more of a problem, so far.Other than that, it's a Portal-like puzzler and it is okay.Those downsides are a huge deal in a puzzler like this, though, so I can't say I can recommend anyone else getting it.

_childDocuments_.review: I love first person puzzle games, and felt that it had been a while since a new one had come out. I found this game advertised a few weeks before it came out and waited eagerly since it seemed to fit the type of game I like. The story is interesting and kept me engaged for the most part. Hit some good beats towards the end. Mechanism-wise, it feels like it took a big inspiration from Portal 1/2 and the Talos Principle. Not that Portal has a monopoly on cubes on buttons, but additionally the laser redirection cube, light bridge, talking assistant similar to GLADOS/potato GLADOS, fans that work similarly to the excursion funnel, bounce pad that works similar to the blue paint, the game hits a lot of similar notes. Combine this with the time record / copy mechanic from Talos Principle and that's what the game felt like to me. Which isn't a bad thing!The object rewind mechanic is novel enough though and provides for interesting puzzle design and interactions. Some of the later puzzles had me stumped for a bit. Often times I know exactly what I need to do, it's executing the correct sequence of events that ends up taking me some time. Some of the puzzles can be cheesed (in particular, I found myself using the light bridge cube at specific angles and just walking up to the higher-up doors, not sure if any of them were intended), but I like when I can find unintended solutions. Overall, the game's been a good amount of fun. Not a lot of new FPS-Puzzle games in recent memory, and I'm always glad to play another.
_childDocuments_.name: The Entropy Centre

_childDocuments_.review: Very buggy, pretty sure half the puzzle solutions I came up with were unintentional, would really have liked to have had the ability to move faster or have some movement tech. But I had fun. Despite the over ambition and jank of a project like this from a solo dev/small team it hits the mark. Only recommendation would be to let me bhop in your next game.Do Recommend

_childDocuments_.review: Very creative design game - if you enjoyed any of the Portal games this will be right up your street!Skill wise the game never got to the point I needed to google for the solutions so very rewarding, but still gives a little brain ache! Good use of commentary throughout the game to keep it interesting without constantly chattering in your ear as you are trying to concentrate.Only issue I had was sometimes it needs you to do a little jumpy puzzle bit, and it seems a little unpredictable where the player is going to land. It was a little annoying to have figured out the puzzle but couldn't get the jumps right. I would however still give this game a solid rating, its well worth adding to your collection. some replay-ability too with level creation/editors plus community downloads if you need that extra fix....

_childDocuments_.review: I wasn't captivated by this idea, I played the first few minutes of the game but unlike Portal where every surface felt like a new opportunity, once I realised that nothing could be interacted with I felt kind of like a prop in a very pretty and atmospheric world. I didn't play very deeply into the game so it's entirely possible that the gameplay improves, but I felt like it would have worked better if it didn't tie itself so closely to Portal and instead focused on a different way of using the time rewinding mechanic.The puzzles didn't feel very inspired in the first few rooms and the random broken scenery felt like a weird show-off of a mechanic that didn't interest me.
_childDocuments_.name: The Entropy Centre

_childDocuments_.review: A fun puzzle game that knows exactly what it's trying to do and was well worth the experience of playing it. It has two main characters that have absolutely great chemistry and listening to them banter was a massive highlight of the game. There were plenty of bits that earned some very good laughs from me.The central conceit of working in reverse became very intuitive after the 2nd act (of many more) and solving puzzles was very satisfying with both the companion and the boards that show you your time stats.Some of the puzzle mechanics don't feel like they got used to their full potential, but the game definitely feels complete -- it's more that there's room for the content creator mode to do some really interesting things with it. And potentially an expansion or dlc to do something? idk -- I'd like to see more from these devs in the future.

_childDocuments_.review: Nice Puzzle Game. Cannot Deny it tries to be a Portal Clone with the humor and some of the atmosphere within the game. The story is good but not paced well. Basically you have to solve puzzles to generate some special sauce called entropy to save earth! It ties well with the current situation we are in but does not go too deep but there are a lot of messages scribbled across walls and computer messages if you would like to spend time there. SO coming to the meat of the game which is basically you solving puzzles involving a mechanic of reversing time. There are many puzzle elements from boxes,lasers,fans,switches.Nothing unique if you have been playing puzzle games. The time reversal mechanic I think might be the first time done in a 3d puzzle game. The puzzles are not difficult and just require some logical thinking once you get used to thinking about time going backwards! The only problems with the game are some puzzles very few do not obey what you have been taught throughout the game and also the physics is very janky which might lead to the need to repeat processes again as there are no quick saves. Other than that new puzzle elements are introduced at proper times but it does get a bit repetitive towards the last 30 percent of the game. Overall 15 chapters with about 4-5 puzzles each with the last half having some tedious puzzles which get frustrating due to the janky physics and no quick saves. There are a few action sequences which are passable but still fun. Still worth a buy as it is not a full prized game and if you like first person 3d puzzlers this is a must buy.Just a note I did have some minor bugs which simply require you to load a previous save but there were hardly 3-5 in my entire playthrough. I did have some crashes but that might be down to my old laptop.
_childDocuments_.name: The Entropy Centre

_childDocuments_.review: A truly enjoyable experience. The game looks great, the puzzles (for the most part) play great, and as an atmosphere junkie, I am happy to say this game is a master class in environmental storytelling. My only real issues were as follows: -While I did get softlocked in a few spots due to my habit of trying to get into every area I can possibly reach even if I'm not "supposed" to be there, the checkpoints are generally good and you can be back in action in a minute or two tops.-There were a few puzzles, namely in chapter 11, that were truly annoying (and I feel like I cheesed my way through after 30+ minutes trying to figure them out), and started to make me dread puzzle segments throughout the rest of the game (though the dread was unfounded; future chapters' puzzles were pretty much all great).-After completing the game, finding all the files, and taking a good amount of time pondering the story, some plot holes open up which irk me. For instance, (MAJOR spoilers): This and other similar discrepancies (mainly caused by the various entries on computer terminals) have lived rent-free in my head since completing the game. But a review isn't the place for story discussion.However, these are pretty minor nitpicks. At no point while playing did I start wishing for the experience to end, which as far as I'm concerned is the mark of a great game. I loved taking in the solitude and the bleak atmosphere, checking out all the fine details of each room, enjoying the banter between Aria and Astra, listening to the striking ambient soundtrack, and getting all the thought-provoking puzzles I was hoping for. You can tell a lot of love and passion went into this game and it's a joy to play... as long as exercising your mind is something you enjoy, that is.8/10
_childDocuments_.name: The Entropy Centre

_childDocuments_.review: I loved both Portal games and both Talos Principle games and found The Entropy Centre to be a good game, in the same likenesses of these other titles, that I could complete in around 8 hours. The puzzles were for the most part easily accomplished after one or two attempts but I still came away with a good feeling of accomplishment and when I came across a couple of the more demanding puzzles I felt that I had worked for it.The story is good, again think Talos Principle 2 or either of the Portal games. It has a good amount of mystery that makes you want to search for extra information to build the storytelling. I especially liked it when the story gave a touch of atmosphere that really drew me in  . On my fairly good spec PC (10th Gen i7, 3070, 32Gb DDR4) the game ran flawlessly.Overall if you like accessible puzzlers (Portal not Myst...) give The Entropy Centre a go its a good one.

_childDocuments_.review: I love this game. People who liked Portal and Portal 2 will definitely enjoy this, and it's a nice introduction to physics puzzle games as well. Take this with a grain of salt as I haven't beaten it yet, but the game could use some more difficult levels (I've beaten most of them so far in less than 10 minutes), but they've got some pretty interesting elements to them. _childDocuments_.name: The Entropy Centre

_childDocuments_.review: Not too challenging but diverting first person puzzler. I'd say it's a moderate recommend for me. The game does go on a bit too long for my interest in the mechanics. I feel like time manipulation as the main mechanic doesn't really work as well when you're having to manually manipulate each object in a puzzle. If you're good at planning you should be able to map out the solutions, but as a hands-on kind of thinker with a predilection to want to walk out an area I found the need to constantly reset if a small part of the solution went awry gets fairly tedious towards the end.Hostile enemy sections are more aggravating than interesting.The story is alright, though all the supplementary exposition through computer inboxes really makes the flow of the game awkward and too often you come across a screen while some dialogue is playing. Nothing here approaching a definitive moment in gaming narrative, but that might be for the best as I think most players will be happy not to feel obligated to play to the end and simply stop where they are satisfied.
_childDocuments_.name: The Entropy Centre

_childDocuments_.review: It wears its Aperture Science influences on its sleeve, but this is absolutely a worthy entry in the Portal-like subgenre of puzzle games. The fact that this was developed by a single person is mind-boggling!My main critique of it is that the core to every puzzle's solution feels very same-y. Once you identify the final step in a certain level's sequence of required actions, everything falls into place easily, for the most part. I still had fun figuring it all out, though; and a few levels rose to the challenge that I would have preferred seeing across more of the game. (I never had to use a walkthrough or look up answers, for the record.)7/10
_childDocuments_.name: The Entropy Centre

_childDocuments_.review: I got this because it was from the creators of Portal and looked to be in the same vein.  It was an okay game in it's own right, but it was not as good as portal was.  The puzzles were fine, some had mildly creative solutions. Keep reading for more detailed description, but ultimately if you like Portal only for the puzzles you might enjoy this.   But if you liked Portal because of the story, and the hidden eastereggs and the witty comments, wait for a good sale to get this one. (Honestly, just wait for a sale no matter what)I see 2 major flaws in the game. The Entropy gun is only able to work on specific aspects of the puzzle area (specific elements meant to solve the puzzle with, or the occasional broken wall ect.) and this means you have very clear pieces right away.  And it's not hard to find what you can use as they all glow with an orange highlight when you aim at them making them easy to spot. This means solving the puzzles is always pretty easy. I never had to look up a solution and the only puzzle that took longer than 3-5 minutes was more or less because I has a hard time making a well placed jump or fall. A solution to this is give free reign over shooting the gun. You can already repair parts of the facility so, let us repair everything. Shoot the grass and nature? It revers grows and its gone. Allow the entire building to be fixed (and give an achievement for it!)  Make more thing like the fans that interact with the gun in small meaningless ways but at least give the feel of freedom.  And get rid of the orange highlight. This means you can do more with unofficial puzzle solving outside of game rooms, and even have puzzles that should have been more easy, suddenly more difficult because the room is broken in strange ways.2nd big problem is the story.  The story is very lacking and predictable.  There's really no mystery and it's pretty obvious whats going on from the start.  I'm not looking for deep plot, but at least Portal had GlADOS.  Give some kind of antagonist besides literally 2 types of robots I can't even use my cool gun to fight directly, instead having to repeat the same tired reverse their own energy back at them way too much.
_childDocuments_.name: The Entropy Centre

_childDocuments_.review: I've seen enough.Ultra repetitive jank and then they throw in extremely unfun action sequences.  But ultimately I quit just because of poor level design.There is one puzzle repeated as nauseam in the game: put the blocks / lasers / bridges in the last spot they need to be in, then the 2nd to last, etc until they are in the first spot they need to be in, then execute by going through the puzzle and rewinding things to hit switches in the proper order.  Changing how annoying it is to set up this sequence or how many different elements are needed does not make it a more interesting puzzle.  It just makes it a longer more tedious puzzle.Frequently you would only have access to part of a puzzle room at the beginning and can only predict the last couple places the objects will need to be.  In these cases, you need to do half a puzzle, realize you didn't place all the objects properly to begin with once you can ACTUALLY see everything, go back and reset and start setting it all up again.This is made even worse by janky puzzle setups where the physics can easily send an object in the wrong direction and force you to reset the whole puzzle again due to no fault of your own. There was an early puzzle that I had to do no less than 5 times because a block kept bouncing the off the switch.  Was this playtested at all?If you like wasting hours on completely uninteresting puzzles in what is probably the worst Portal ripoff I have ever played, this game is just what the doctor ordered.

_childDocuments_.review: I really really wish I could recommend this game, I've been waiting on it excitedly since it was announced, but there's one huge problem that I just can't get past. I rarely write reviews, but this one needs to be written.I want to preface this by saying that Portal 2 is one of my all-time favorite games, I have almost 150 hours in it. Hopefully that provides some context for other parts of this review.This isn't as much part of the review as it is something I really wanted to discuss (don't worry, the actual review is below). You can't look at The Entropy Centre and argue that it wasn't very heavily inspired by Portal. While some might see it as a blatant rip-off, I honestly love all of the references. The beginning of the game feels like a Portal 2 mod, and honestly I think it might be intentional.Some of the first EC puzzles are essentially identical to the first P/P2 puzzles. The now iconic cube-and-button mechanic is ever present throughout the game. Virtually every mechanic Portal has (aside from the, you know, portals), EC has their own version of. From laser cubes to fans as tractor beams, or bridge cubes as hard light bridges to entropy bots as turrets, or even bounce cubes as repulsion gel and conveyor belts as propulsion gel, the inspiration is obvious. The talking gun is essentially a much nicer version of GlaDOS, and walking around feels like talking to PotatOS or holding Wheatley while the ever-present announcer talks in the background. There's too many little references to count, but I just really want to shout them out because I love them and think the devs did a great job. (Was the "nine nine nine nine nine..." sound bit pulled straight from P2?)With all that said, in my opinion the EC is still very original, and the Portal references remain just that- references. The time travel mechanic is unique and the story is actually really engaging once you get into the later acts.I really want to start the actual review portion of this review with what I liked about the game, because honestly there's a lot to love.- As I discuss in detail above, the Portal references are really cute- The soundtrack and overall sound design is incredible- The talking gun is adorable and I found myself emotionally attached to her throughout the game, but she's still really funny- The story is really engaging, and gets super interesting in the final third of the game- like wow that ending really makes it all worth it- I appreciate the relatively regular introduction of new puzzle mechanics- The runner levels and exploration levels are pretty fun- The visuals are (mostly) beautifulThere's a lot to love about this game, but one huge issue I can't get by: as small as it may seem, the bounce cubes are, without a doubt, the worst game mechanic I have ever experienced. Allow me to explain.I know I discuss Portal a lot, but bear with me here. I'm not sure how common this knowledge is, but Portal uses something the devs called "funneling", which means that as you're falling into or flying towards a portal the physics engine cheats a little to guide you into it. In short, if you jump of a ledge into a portal, as long as you jumped near it you will fall through the portal if you don't touch any buttons while you're in the air. You get funneled towards it.The bounce cubes are in desperate need of a funneling mechanic, and in all honesty if they had one I would be able to confidently recommend this game. Sure, I have other issues with it, which I discuss below, but this one is the only deal-breaker for me.For context, the puzzles in this game aren't particularly difficult. I was able to mentally solve nearly every puzzle within a minute of entering the room, and then it was merely a matter of executing the solution. All you have to do is work backwards through the puzzle in your head and then move the cubes around so they can be rewound, it's not that hard.But that's where the problems come in. In a puzzle game, the challenge should be figuring out what to do, not actually doing it. Portal doesn't require any significant gaming skill- you rarely need to aim precisely or think fast. When executing a puzzle solution it's difficult to mess up.Unfortunately, in EC, it takes gaming skill to complete puzzles. If you're good at platforming it probably isn't hard but I'm not. One of the most frustrating experiences is to spend several minutes setting up a puzzle solution, only to need to make one more big jump to the exit door, and when you make the jump you fall right next to the bounce cube you were aiming for, requiring you to go back to the start and tediously set everything up again. It's not difficult, it's just really annoying (especially when you can't run and you walk at a snail's pace). I found myself putting on YouTube videos in the background while I attempted long, multi-step puzzles four or five times because I kept missing a bounce cube.There are a few other minor things I'm not a huge fan of:- The entropy robots are REALLY annoying. In Portal 2, you never have to worry about turrets really because they sit still. Entropy bots move around, and can only be destroyed by launching an explosive at them or by rewinding their pellets. It's really frustrating to be in a lockdown puzzle trying to find a button to unlock the door when a robot sneaks up behind you and nails you in the back with an energy pellet at the same time as his friend and you die. They're a pain in the butt and I don't like them. The runner levels are fine, but the combat/lockdown levels are endlessly annoying.- This might be more of a bug, but occasionally you need to stand on a fallen walkway or whatever and rewind it to lift you up in the air. Well, it's really obnoxious when part of the walkway swings into place and crushes you. I wish it would just push you out of the way instead of killing you just because you didn't see it coming (turns out predicting how things will fall in reverse is hard!)- The puzzles are REALLY repetitive. I know it's weird to say I want the game to be shorter, but they get old so fast. The new elements are nice, but it really feels like you aren't making any progress when every puzzle is essentially the same, and the only difficult part is the execution not the solution.- The areas between the worlds really break suspension of disbelief sometimes. It feels too much like a game, like a puzzle, it doesn't feel real. Am I expected to believe that some quarters have bounce cubes in them, complete with a button to spawn a new one? And wow, how convenient that that walkway is not only destroyed, but rewindable!- A lot of the animations are pretty janky. The launch things (EC equivalent of faith plates), for example, just bounce up. Compare that to Portal's intricately designed plates and it just feels sorta sad and empty. I'd love to see refinements on the animations. To the dev's credit, though, the destruction animations are solid.Man, that was a big wall of text. Hopefully it's useful to some of you. Long story short:- I love the game, very pretty, engaging, and a solid storyline with lovable characters- The bounce cubes not funneling break the whole thing for me- It still needs a little work in some areas- If it weren't for the bounce cube issues, I could easily recommend this game- Oh yeah, the puzzles are pretty easy, good for beginners

_childDocuments_.review: The actual Portal 3 we never got. (if you count Stories: Mel then Portal 4?) As someone who is a bit of a portal super fan, aperture science is my key chain, my bumper sticker, and I own a mini companion cube for my desk. Oh, and I've played pretty much every decent portal map ktmk. One would say I know Portal when I see it; and this, this is portal. Q: Does it have GLaDOS? A: No, it has ASTRA, and she not trying to kill you, but she's a snarky A.I. none the less. Q: Does it have Turrets? A: No, it has roving droids that will shoot you on site, or worse tase you to death. Q: Does it have a Portal gun? A: No, it has an Entropy gun, and she talks to you, see previous reference to ASTRA? ThEn iT's nOT PoRTaL! To which I say, if it looks like Portal, makes my brain engage and go AHA at every puzzle like Portal, if it keeps me coming back for more and unable to pull away once I turn it on like Portal, then by Jove it's Portal to me. Or my name isn't Cave Johnson, though it might be Tannoy. I've played every portal knockoff, ripoff, and homage under the sun, and none of them have felt as Portal as this. It just has that je ne sais quoi, that Portal did. The Entropy Centre feels like a subsidiary of Aperture Science Labs, or maybe they're owned by the same parent company. Either way, this game captured the soul of Portal more than any other game has since Portal, without actually being portal. It solidly stands on it's own. Now, we just need a Chell and Aria dual play cross over somehow... VALVE Make it Happen!

_childDocuments_.review:
An extinction level event has set the world ablaze. You appear to be the last remaining person alive. Mankind's only hope lies at the core of the Entropy Centre. The Entropy Centre is a mind-bending puzzle adventure where you reverse objects through time to overcome seemingly impossible obstacles and conundrums. Manipulate time to your will and solve ingeniously challenging puzzle rooms, each one taking you closer to the heart of a colossal space station in orbit of Earth.

Deviously challenging with razor-sharp witty writing and outstanding voice acting performances, The Entropy Centre merges a brilliant puzzle game with an epic adventure.

name: Klonoa Phantasy Reverie Series
detailed_description: KLONOA is a 3D side-scrolling action game series whose first title was released by Namco in 1997. Set in a unique universe populated by a range of original characters, the game follows the hero, Klonoa, as he sets off on a journey to save the world. Commemorating the 25th anniversary of the first title in the series, we are pleased to announce the release of the KLONOA Phantasy Reverie Series, a remastered title combining both KLONOA: Door to Phantomile and KLONOA 2: Lunatea’s Veil! The world of the games and their gameplay elements remains unchanged, while the graphics have been upgraded. Adjustable difficulty settings have also been introduced to make the games more accessible to first-time players. Enjoy a nostalgic trip down memory lane playing this new and improved KLONOA. Included: ・Main game ・KLONOA Costume Set: Moo Costume Set KLONOA Costume Set: Moo Costume Set This costume allows the Player to dress as the enemy character, Moo. *Design, content, and specifications may be changed without prior notice. *Costume DLC is added to the main game. *Bonus features may be released separately at a later date. *After being downloaded, bonus features may be equipped from Costumes under Options.

_childDocuments_.review: I certainly recommend this game, however  These games are very short. Door to Phantomile can be completed 100% within 4 hours or so, and Lunatea's Veil can take around 7 hours to complete. They're perfect games to play through when you have an afternoon to kill, however if you're more of a "one-and-done" type of person I'd recommend waiting and getting the game when it's on sale. While the games are HD remasters and have pretty decent graphics, the game audio is ripped directly from the original PS1/PS2 games, so be aware that there will be some instances of compressed sound effects and voice audio (especially with Door to Phantomile's cutscenes). While I love this game, do NOT purchase the DLC. As far as I know it only includes a few bonus costumes for Klonoa to wear, plus maybe a couple extras. Whatever is included, it is certainly not worth the asking price.That being said, Klonoa has always been a series that holds good memories from when I was a kid, and Phantasy Reverie Series is perhaps the best and easiest way to experience two of the best 2D platformers of the PS1 and early PS2. Of course, the stories of these games are the most noteworthy aspect. Very simple and straightforward, but with very charming characters and unforgettably emotional endings. I absolutely hope this game's success gives Bandai-Namco the incentive to keep Klonoa around as a series and not be left to be forgotten again.
_childDocuments_.name: Klonoa Phantasy Reverie Series

_childDocuments_.review: To start with, I do recommend everyone get this, since the series deserves all the love and attention it can get. However, there's some huge caveats.Put simply: This is NOT a good remaster. On the Door to Phantomile side:The voice quality is horrible, since they used the compressed PS1 audio instead of sticking to the Wiimake script or getting the voice actors back for a clean recording. There's also visual errors such as Nahatomb's body looking like they forgot to smooth the normals, and visible seams in some models. Reverse mode is also absent, as are all the  Wiimake alternate outfits.On Lunatea's Veil:Shadows are missing in parts, and there's this odd clockwork-esque sound that happens after inflating enemies that wasn't there in the original. Overall though, it's clear this side of the collection had the most attention paid to it.I will say, I don't blame the developers at Monkeycraft; it's clear they did their best, and it definitely seems like this was a case of them not being given enough time/budget by Bandai Namco. As of this writing, there have been no patches or updates to the game, which is sad since many issues would be simple to fix. But again, this is clearly the fault of the publisher; they've treated this series horribly since the very start, and this is no exception.However, I still encourage as many as people to get this, especially if you've never experienced these games before. I just believe this deserved to be so much more than what we were given.

_childDocuments_.review: Review of both games from someone who has played the original versions:Klonoa 2: Lunatea's Veil:The port of Klonoa 2: Lunatea's Veil makes the purchase of this collection worth it (even though the asking price of this collection is a little too high in my taste). Klonoa 2 is a solid game with a cast of memorable characters combined with fun platforming that fairly increases in difficulty as the game progresses. Compared to Klonoa: Door to Phantomile, the bosses are much more varied and unique and are a blast to fight. I noticed no difference in the way Klonoa controlled in the remaster of Klonoa 2 and had no issues while playing the game. The remastered environments and the addition of widescreen allow the game's world to feel more alive than ever before and are a vast improvement over the PlayStation 2 release. The small issues I have with this port of Klonoa 2 come down to lighting and animations. Some particle effects and character animations are just absent from this release (ex. Klonoa's dynamic face during gameplay) that can make some aspects of the cutscenes seem a little off. The lighting of the game is also very static and not as dynamic as the original release, which makes some areas of the game lose their intended atmosphere. If I were to nitpick, there was one animation in a certain cutscene that was absent in this version of the game that took a way from an emotional moment that led me to be disappointed. Klonoa: Door to Phantomile:The remaster of the Wii remake of Klonoa: Door to Phantomile included in this collection is a decent way to experience the game, but has some issues that should be noted. The game's story is identical to the PlayStation version with it's charming characters and locations that made the game a cult classic, while it's gameplay is a fun blend of puzzle platforming that is fairly easy for the majority of the game.  I appreciate the developers bringing back the original script from the PlayStation version of the game to give Klonoa more agency in the plot, as well as remodeling several characters to restore their original appearances compared to how they looked in the Wii version.However, using the original script of the game meant that the developers had to use the super-compressed voice lines from the PlayStation version of the game, which clash with the HD presentation. Also, compared to the remaster of Klonoa 2, it seems that many assets and textures in Klonoa: Door to Phantomile have been simply upscaled from the Wii version rather than remade from the ground up. This can make some areas seem visually inconsistent with the assets that have been remade. Additionally, on Normal difficulty, Klonoa's wind bullet just feels too short, and makes the game way more challenging and sometimes downright unfair at times when doing precision platforming or fighting against certain bosses. Hopefully this will be patched in the future, but it would be best to play on the Easy difficulty for this game as it makes the radius of the wind bullet larger.Finally, the impact of the story and the cutscenes of this game are hampered by broken lighting and animations in certain places of the game. The cutscenes in the PlayStation and Wii versions of Klonoa: Door to Phantomile are framed and shot in a very cinematic fashion that increase tension and allow the drama of the narrative to play out in an engaging manner. It seems that the developers tried so hard to make this game try to emulate the bright and colorful style of some parts of the original PlayStation game, that they forgot that certain parts of Klonoa's cinematography are meant to be dark and atmospheric. For unaware players, these cutscenes might be serviceable as they might just think that the developers are being faithful to the original vision of the game. However, what is missing here to me is a core part of what makes the storytelling in these games so great and it's really disappointing.Additional Content:The DLC is not worth it for this game for the price they are asking for it. The small amount of costumes you get are purely cosmetic and don't change anything gameplay wise. Additionally, though the contents of the artbook and the soundtrack are nice, they are not given to you in a .pdf and .mp3 format, but a Unity application to view them in. There is no way to view these bonuses outside of the program, and it's ridiculous that Bandai Namco would do this in 2022 considering most other games have this type of content available for download right from their Steam pages.Overall:Despite some flaws, this collection has the definitive way to play Klonoa 2: Lunatea's Veil even if it has its flaws. The version of Klonoa: Door to Phantomile is a decent way to experience the game but has flaws that need to be addressed in a patch. After beating Klonoa: Door to Phantomile, I would highly recommend watching the FMV cutscenes from the PlayStation version of the game as they are well worth your time. I hope this collection means more Klonoa in the future and I hope new fans will get to share the same joy I had playing these games for the first time. Wahoo!

_childDocuments_.review: A little rough around the edges, but the core gameplay is just as great as it ever was. Some people experienced stuttering, but I guess I got lucky. All I experienced was getting re-used to the game after decades of wishing for a new one.It's not all sunshine and rainbows; the lighting and shading engine used in the remake of the first game is completely broken. I haven't seen graphical comparisons between 2 and its remake, but I wouldn't be surprised if that one had broken visuals too. That's the biggest slap in the face about the collection; some of the charm of this otherwise extremely charming platformer is lost to a lackluster port job. Part of me is hoping Bandai Namco sees that there is demand for this series and that putting time and money into it will be worth the effort, and maybe comes back and fixes these issues (though I'm not holding my breath).They also used the original voice sounds from the PS1 and PS2 games, which are noticeably lower quality than the rest of the sounds and music. However, as a fan of the gibberish voice acting, I found it preferable to the English dub we got with the Wii remake (no offense, English VA crew).Everything else is uphill from here. The music is retouched - that's a very subjective topic but I liked it (the audio mixing seemed a bit off sometimes though. Turn the music up and the sound effects down a little in the Options menu).The games play great, and that's the most important part. The controls are tight (which is good because the games demand precision on normal difficulty) and the games strike a good balance difficulty. There don't seem to be any wild difficulty spikes or anything.The stories are pretty great too. Not mind-blowing world-shattering (well, maybe the first game, kinda) epics, but short and bittersweet tales of a brave boy just trying to help and getting way in over his head. I just applaud the first game for having the balls to follow through on some of its darker story beats.Overall I recommend it, especially if you don't have the originals. If you have the original games though, it's a bit of a tougher sell. The convenience of having the game on modern consoles might be enough to convince many people to buy it if they aren't hardcore retro gamers.EDIT: The second game is not held back by the technical limitations of the first. It looks much nicer than the first, and I'm hoping the first gets (at the very least) the shaders fixed.Both games should be experienced by everyone, either by playing the originals or this collection.

_childDocuments_.review: The fact that Lunatea's Veil has finally made it off the PS2 is enough to recommend Phantasy Reverie. Klonoa's now more available than ever; no matter my negatives, that's fantastic.Thing is, Door To Phantomile is my favourite game. Ever. Period. It's arguable PR would've never satisfied me but I want to bring up a number of issues not present in the original:- Klonoa's jump height is fixed. In classic, you could control this and manoeuvre him through obstacles, with level design clearly built around it. PR flings him to his maximum no matter what and makes for a MUCH more fiddly platforming experience.- The wind bullet (your attack) has a smaller hitbox. If you're standing on a slope, Klonoa will fire directly in front of him and shoot cleanly past any enemy above or below him, making for some really annoying sections where before it wasn't an issue.- The switch to 3D models over the original's sprites lends a significant amount of input delay. Klonoa's animations now have to be taken into account when moving and neuters the excellent pixel-perfect feel from classic DP. Granted it's not a major sticking point if you're new, but the later stages aren't nearly as fun because of it and weakens one of DP's strongest elements.- Klonoa lost his drop shadow for some reason. In a PLATFORMER.- While I won't knock PR's total makeover as it's both subjective and based on the 2008 Wii remake, the presentation isn't up to snuff. Music doesn't loop properly and is mixed quieter, facial expressions are jittery and somehow less consistent than the sprites. Dialogue is ripped directly from the original and the audio quality clashes hard. Classic DP's cutscenes (especially a certain one) are the emotional drive of the game, it's very disappointing seeing them in a lesser state. Needless to say, I think the original looks WAY better but different strokes on that front.As for Lunatea's Veil, it does play closer to its PS2 counterpart but sadly carries over a few audiovisual issues, namely the looping and facial animation. Other than that, I've not seen anything as egregious and is definitely the better of the two, even if I miss the cel-shading.Idk. I'm conflicted. To see Klonoa get a new lease on life and in the hands of more players excites me more than anything. EVERYBODY needs to play these games, regardless of version. None of my qualms truly ruin the experience and in fairness, I'm in the minority.That's the rub though. I can't separate the pedestal I keep the PS1 original on from Phantasy Reverie and at best, all I see is my favourite videogame in a far less appealing form. It could've been so, so much more than it is. I still recommend these remakes, especially for the chance to play Lunatea's Veil, but I'm publishing this review from my perspective. I'm biased.

_childDocuments_.review: First I'd like to say I didn't play the original games on PS1 and 2. If you feel like that should invalidate my review go ahead and hit that thumbs down, steam wouldn't put that there if they didn't want you to use it.Klonoa is cute and colorful although it does that current trend of having whiplash from the dull late 2000s era of gaming where now where the colors are too white for both games. Stages are challenging but not to the point where you're grinding for 30 minutes beat or collect everything. The soundtrack feels like one of those dreams where everything is pristine and calm but still mysterious. The gameplay is unique for a 3D 2D platformer. I like how enemies have different contextual meanings to the player. One could be helicopter, the other times you have to precisely chain together jumps with enemies to access certain parts of the level. Despite levels also being "course clear" objectives many of them are nonlinear in design and are quite fun to navigate. It's got that vibe that kirby has with it's atmosphere and character designs. I don't want to say that it's "so dark guys lol" but it's got a neat story for both games that lightly messes with you. I 100% achievement it and as you can tell by my hours it's quite a short amount of time to do that. I played it all on my Steam Deck and it runs flawlessly if you're wondering. I had a certified "WAHOO!" moment with this game!

_childDocuments_.review: YES YES YES ITS FINALLY HERE!!!!!!!This is one of those few releases I've been anticipating on having pretty much daily since announcement. The only others of that kind for me are the System Shock remake and Wrath Aeon of Ruin. ANYWAYSYeah so this is a review specifically on the remaster itself, instead of the game. There's tons of reviews out there on the game you can watch or read. Though I will say that I personally really love this game and have since I first played it a year or two ago. I have no nostalgia attached to the game. And don't let its cutsey nature fool you! This game is extremely solid despite its simplicity. Story is great, and the characters are all lovable. The ending shocked me at first and without spoiling any plot details, I'd have to say it's one of the most depressing endings to any game I've ever seen. At least the first one - I haven't finished the 2nd one yet. Moving on to the remaster. You're probably immediately wondering about that price tag. That is quite pricey for a remaster. 40 dollars for a 25 year old game is pretty steep. Though it is a remaster of TWO games and not one, but that's still pretty high. And there's a dlc that should be maybe 5-10 dollars, but for some reason it's 20 here. So it's 60 for the full package, the price of a normal brand new game. Which is kinda horrible. But I bought the full thing anyways to show the devs there are people out there that really care. The first game is one that's been needing a proper rerelease for a long time, as it, since the early 2000s, has been the most expensive game on PS1 physically. Not sure if it got a PS3 digital rerelease but it did get a remakster thing on the Wii and a Sequel on the PS2. Neither of those which have been rereleased, but that WII version of 1 and the ps2 game are both of what have actually been remastered and included here. The visuals are very crisp, colorful, smooth, and fluid, and yes, better and more refined than their original counterparts. All the polish with today's tech, while keeping all the charm that played a big part of making the originals so lovable. The movement and mechanics are solid as they always have been and are pretty much untouched. Luckily on PC I have a 240hz monitor, so being able to play these games at that framerate has been an absolute treat to say the least. Not a ton of customization options, but that's pretty much expected as far as remasters go. The levels so far seems to be the same without anything new added, though this version does have extra costumes and achievements and whatnot, even though alot of the costumes are part of that expensive dlc. This version has local splitscreen which is awesome, though I haven't tried it yet nor do I know how it works. The music seems uncompressed which is awesome, though in a strange move they kept the original compressed PS1 audio. I'm not sure if that was intentional to keep the spirit of the og game, or it was an oversight but it's definitely a bit strange. Not necessarily a good or bad thing to me. Personally I loved the audio, it's just weird hearing that with the newer crispier visuals.And don't let my hours fool you either, I've played the original for at least a hundred or so hours (which is alot considering it's a short game), so I noticed the changes immediately. TLDR; If you enjoyed the original games, this is a great remaster and probably the best way to play the games now. If you want to show the devs that people still care about this series, I'd suggest buying this too and playing the crap out of it. If you've never played these games before, you're missing out! And if you haven't played them but want to try them out before dropping the cash, you can just emulate the originals and see what you think. Despite the price, it was worth it in my opinion. So happy to finally be playing these!
_childDocuments_.name: Klonoa Phantasy Reverie Series

_childDocuments_.review: This game is aaahhh how do you say....like reconnecting with your best friend from childhood after not seeing each other for years. What can I say, except that game really does reopen those nostalgic childhood memories that have  been exploited thousands of times by those greedy corporate fat cats. It is a welcoming experience just as how you remember it. Now if you never played this before you will probably overlook it as it is a pretty simplistic game. Hell truth be told there are way better platformers out there. But if you are like me and Klonoa has a special place in your heart as you remember those few good moments of your childhood than this is for you.

_childDocuments_.review: It's okay to remember to be sad. Klonoa's a bubbly game with some of the best platforming I've ever had the joy to go through. But in a lot of ways, it's more than that to me. What initially starts as an innocuous journey of a little cat thing trying to fight darkness and sorrow becomes something so much deeper. There's a level deep into the sequel, a game that holds for me as one of my top PS2 titles of all time, called the Maze of Memories. It's a place where people spend their entire lives reminiscing on the good times they had, no longer building what was new.  It hit me hard as a kid and still hits me hard now. It's a reminder that even though we attempt to distract ourselves from harsh realities and sorrows of the present, we can't just pretend it doesn't exist.  Klonoa is probably one of the best things Namco's ever made in my eyes. It's a sharply designed game with graphics that hold up even now... But it also possesses a heart that few games have ever been able to attain. If there's one thing this story deserves is a chance to give Klonoa a chance to find his way home. Wahoo.
_childDocuments_.name: Klonoa Phantasy Reverie Series

_childDocuments_.review: Oh brother... i have mixed feelings here, i will mostly focus on Klonoa 1 here since it's the one i finished and to be honest, the more special game to me.First things first, it's an ok way to experience these games, hell i'd argue it's a great way to experience  of these games.Don't expect a Crash Bandicoot N. Sane Trilogy level of remake here, you are getting at best two PS2 games with some spit shine applied to 'em, this works well for Klonoa 2, since that was a PS2 game originally and i'd argue it mostly looks better than the original even tough i've played very little of it.Klonoa 1 on the other hand, oh boy, this was a PS1 game and to be honest, the PS1 version is still the best way to experience this game, this part of the remake fumbles. The original game might've been a PS1 game but it wasn't a pushover when it comes to graphics at the time and it had a consistent look, this part of the remake honestly wouldn't look impressive even on the PS2, and its so inconsistent, some levels look very good, some look bland, and animations during cutscenes are consistently stiff, more on that later. I will however compliment the character designs, they do capture the style of the original very well and probably save Klonoa 1 from being a total disaster graphically in this remake.The classic Klonoa gameplay is mostly intact, 2.5 platformer, you interact with elements in the background and foreground, however the new graphics i feel hurt Klonoa 1 here, unlike Klonoa 2, the first game was not designed with full 3D graphics in mind, in the original, your character and the enemies were 2D sprites, only the levels were 3D, as a result, it was very easy to tell when enemies were in front of you, in the background or the foreground, with the new graphics is not so easy and i sometimes tried to grab enemies that were actually in the background, that being said the gameplay is 95% intact, its not really a deal breaker on this aspect, and the game is super easy anyways, mistakes like this wont generate too much frustration.Now here's the thing, if you've heard of Klonoa 1 before, you probably know it as "that cute platformer that gets surprisingly sad towards the end", i'd argue the story of Klonoa 1 is crucial for the experience and the remake drops the ball HARD here, nearly every single dramatic cutscene is sabotaged by stiff character animations, SPECIALLY stiff facial animations, something very sad might be happening on screen and the characters might have a smile on their faces because animation is hard and someone was very lazy during development, this issue is compounded by the audio which was taken directly from the original, and while that's a plus for the music, which is as great as ever, its been horrible for the character voices which are bit-crunched to hell and back, everyone sounds as if they recorded their lines in a basement and underwater, the fact character talk is gibberish prevents this issue from getting worse, atleast you know you are not supposed to understand anything.Here's the thing tough, i recognize few people will care as much as i do, this is a game that made me feel sad as a kid and that was rare, it stuck with me, someone who didn't grow up with this game isn't going to give a damn, they will still be getting a decent platformer out of Klonoa 1, albeit a short and easy one, Klonoa 2 while not as emotionally impactful to me, is the better game in terms of gameplay, longer, harder and looks much better overall in this remake.i suppose the package as a whole is worth it so i recommend it, even tough i believe this is not the best way to play Klonoa 1.

_childDocuments_.review: The Klonoa games are special to me. Klonoa 2 in particular is one of my favorite games. And it saddened me knowing that in the twenty one years it had been out, the game had no re-release in any form. So seeing the game, along with the original game being re-released for every modern console and the PC made me pretty happy. I booted up 2 immediately and while I thought the game looked really nice in terms of the environments and updated character designs, all the little details seemed to have fallen to the wayside.Facial expressions have generally become worse looking and are outright missing in some cases. You have a couple scenes where a certain character is supposed to be smiling, but isn't. Part of what made the game so special to me is how expressive the characters are, and seeing that taken away almost ruins a few scenes. Apparently, a lot of the files that were ported over didn't transfer correctly and were overlooked. Music cues for certain cutscenes have been broken, so music plays over moments where it's supposed to stop in order to emphasize certain moments in the cutscenes.Background elements like the crowds in Joilant are incredibly low-poly creating a jarring disconnect with everything else.Random parts of the script got changed which leads to weird moments where characters repeat what they've just said and certain lines got replaced by ones that just sound awkward.As for DtP, the game is essentially a shinier port of the Wii remake from back in 2008, but with updated character models to keep in line with the original PS1 game's aesthetic. It tries elements of both via using the PS1's audio files in conjunction with the Wii's cutscenes, which creates a rather jarring disconnect. Still better than the Wii's terrible English dub, but not by much.Overall, this is not a very good remake and frankly I feel the Klonoa games deserved far better than this. It's frankly a sloppily made product. I would hold off on buying the game until Namco Bandai polishes the game some more via updates or until somebody decides to mod the games to try and fix the issues these games have.

_childDocuments_.review: Delightful remake of the first two Klonoa games,  (from the PlayStation 1 era) and its sequel  - which is still one of the PlayStation 2's most highly rated games with a Metacritic score of 94 at launch. I fondly remember playing both at the time so I was delighted that Namco's furry mascot was getting a new lease on life on all modern platforms for his 25th anniversary. What surprised me the most about both games was how well they both hold up considering they came out between 1997 and 2001. Platformers have seen a creative renaissance over the intervening years thanks to the budding indie scene, so it was surprising to see both hold up so well against the more modern games in the genre. To say both games in the collection have aged beautifully is an understatement and this is only amplified by the loving restoration done by Monkeycraft on these lost platforming relics so that hopefully an entire new generation can discover them.  If sales are buoyant enough, hopefully then there is the possibility we see a third mainline entry into the series. Simple yet delightful to play,  is gorgeous visually, oozes charm, has clever level design that often allows the player to approach it from various angles, and is a winner for fans of the genre. Recommended.

_childDocuments_.review: It’s been a long time since the last time I played this saga, probably somewhat around 20 years ago but I always wanted to return to both Phantomile and Lunatea, something got stuck in my head and those were lovely memories from easier and past times. Now let’s jump to the year 2022, the impossible happened, Klonoa is coming back with a remastered version of the main two games, Door to Phantomile and Lunatea’s Veil, with this Phantasy Reverie collection. Is it worth your time? Do they still hold up for modern standards? Let’s find out.Let’s start talking about both stories with Door to Phantomile which is the beginning of our story. We are Klonoa, a young boy from Breezegale, a small village from Phantomile. One day we experience a strange dream in which a strange ring drops from the sky and a strange entity appears, Huepow. To your surprise it seems that it wasn’t a dream and it really happened but things are about to start now, a strange aircraft crashes near your village, once you go inspect the incident you discover a strange figure and its minion are kidnapping a little girl, our mission will be saving her as we discover the truth of what’s going on.We don’t know what happened after our adventures in Phantomile, however, we are about to start a new adventure in a new land, Lunatea. We wake up in this world without knowing what happened but we (as players) know we are being observed by someone. Almost immediately after you wake up, both Lolo and Popka, our new friends in this adventure, will tell us where we are, who we need to talk with and what they think it’s going on. What started as a small adventure will lead into a much bigger one sooner rather than later.Both stories are quite liviane, keep in mind both games were designed with younger audiences in mind, however, I find both quite enjoyable no matter your age. In both cases there’s a great setup with their own rules, Phantomile and Lunatea have different sets of rules however, by the own nature of this saga, you will soon find shared elements between both places, it works as a bigger picture than their respective worlds. Characters are also extremely enjoyable in both cases.Huepow, Lolo, Popka, even villains like Joka or Tat (which, for some reason, I always loved the way she talked) are all not that deep but deep enough to enjoy their presence. Main characters do have enough presence to know them better and some side-ones too.Make no mistake, while both games were created with younger audiences in mind, that doesn’t mean they are exclusively for kids, in both cases there are dramatic moments, some extremely iconic nowadays as they were completely unexpected.There’s little more I can say about the narrative side without spoiling things but, What about visuals in both cases?Well, you see, Klonoa Door to Phantomile was a PSX game with a very peculiar but rather amazing visual style with 2D sprites and a somewhat 3D look, however, it got a remake treatment for the Wii which redo all the assets from the ground (likely got some inspiration from PS2 Lunatea’s Veil) and this remaster surprisingly drops in the middle of those two.Phantasy Reverie’s version is clearly redone, it’s clean but at the same time tries to emulate the original more than the Wii version. Klonoa’s character looks more like the original, backgrounds are less detailed than on the Wii and I think the reason for this is that they want to go after the original visual feeling. It’s more colorful and has a pixel filter that is great and confusing at the same time. I used it for a few levels but ended up using the vanilla visuals.When it comes to Lunatea’s Veil, you will immediately notice that it doesn’t look like the original, that’s correct. While no assets seem to be different, the visual filter changed to make it more streamline with the Door of Phantomile, that’s a good way of not making a huge difference between the two in the same collection. Lunatea’s Veil also has more details, more effects and in general it feels like a natural evolution for a game that came out 5 years after the original and on a completely different platform, If you ask me, Lunatea’s Veil is extremely beautiful at times, I might be biased given how I remember it when I was a kid and what I experienced but in general it is a great step up.Both games hold really well today and their level design is still extremely engaging. The way it moves as a 2D platformer but in a 3D environment makes it an extremely compelling experience, I don’t think there’s anything else like Klonoa right now and that’s something to consider as an achievement.Music is also a great part of the game and I’m happy to say that it sounds as good as the original movie sequences, there are great themes in both games, they too hold really well.I could say the same about the gameplay loop. There are two main actions to consider in this game: grab and hold an enemy to use it and jump/ hold in the air. As you can see it’s really basic but the way they designed the levels makes it an extremely engaging experience, sometimes there’s no room for a mistake, you do it or you don’t. You will notice this a lot if you try completing these games at 100%, mostly trying to get all the gems per level, you need to focus and jump correctly, run at the requested speed and not get hit during the process, and there’s also the side levels which are meant to be beaten only by those who are used with the controls and the movement, they are challenging but really gratifying once you beat them. Going after the 100% sure is an experience.I think it’s a good moment to talk about performance. I completed both of them on the Steam Deck, do not worry, they run perfectly out of the box, as a matter of fact, thanks to the pre-compiling shaders I think it eliminates some little stutters present on the windows version of the game. Battery held really well, performance was steady at 60fps with all settings at max and in general I would say I enjoyed it more playing them on a handheld than on my main computer, I guess they are that kind of game that for some reason I tend to enjoy more on a smaller screen due to memories.And I think that’s about it, Klonoa Phantasy Reverie collection was all I wanted for a proper comeback. Visuals are great, gameplay is still engaging and it transported me to my childhood playing them on the Playstation. Usually I would say “it’s not a game for everyone” but f*** it, I will say this is a great game for everyone, for those who want to revisit this old saga, for newcomers, for kids and for adults.Klonoa is back and for that I’m thankful, from the deepest part of my heart, thanks Bandai Namco for bringing back this old friend from past days, I’m glad to say that the final result is well worth your money and your time, heck, I went after all the achievements and the 100%, that shows you how much I loved this.I hope you enjoy it at least half of how much I enjoyed it, my best wishes to all of you.Thanks.

_childDocuments_.review: Its been almost two years since its released so I think its finally time to actually talk about the quality of these games in the package they come in. First off, I want to say that these games alone are fantastic on their own right, but you are much better off emulating the original games than playing them via Phantasy Reverie. The quality of these remasters are comparable to the quality of Sonic Adventure DX: Director's Cut. In terms of the game's visuals, it looks like they only saw the complaint about the wii remake being desaturated and decided to over-saturate the entire game which in fact made it look worse than the wii remake at times. This includes the second game as well. In addition, there are missing effects, broken textures and lighting, missing animations, poor audio mixing, alongside with some other new bugs introduced. To make matters worse, It also doesn't help that the first thing the games asks for when you boot it up for the first time is your location and to collect your data for a single player game of all things. You can easily get around that by disabling the games internet connectivity via your firewall settings. Regardless, there is absolutely zero reason for a single player game of all things to be asking to collect your data and you can't play the game if you reject it either.  I genuinely wish this remaster had more development time and wasn't treated as a rush job like most of Bandai Namco's recent remakes/remasters. Part of me wishes that they just brought over the first two games via emulation rather than a botched remaster if this was the quality we were going to receive. While this remaster sold decently enough in almost two years, I genuinely hope that if there is another Klonoa game in the near future, it gets the time and attention it truly deserves. It's a shame things turned out the way they did and that the most accessible versions of these games happen to be inferior versions when compared to their original counterparts.
