_childDocuments_.review: This is a tough one, but generally as I’m a glass-half-full kind of person, I’m going to give this a recommend. I was originally interested in buying this game because it shares various similarities to the metroidvania game,  and therefore, it looked like something that I might enjoy. However, after playing it now for around eight hours, I am slightly conflicted with whether I really like this game or not. This is mainly because it has no story at all and a frustrating death mechanic that resets nearly all but a slight amount of progress upon dying. At first, I found this mechanic to be quite frustrating, and if it weren’t for some solid gameplay mechanics, it would have been a deal breaker for me. But, as I’ll explain, there are many positive elements to this game too that still make it worth playing overall in my opinion.  Have you ever wanted to play as Death, claiming souls with the hack-and-slash of a scythe that has cool animations and upgrade pathways? Great! Because this game lets you do that, and it is honestly the best part about this title.The gameplay is honestly the only thing that made me open up the game again after my initial disillusionment with it after realizing that progress is mostly reset upon death. The combat feels fluid, challenging and satisfying and there is a genuine sense of progression when it comes to getting better at it. There are three available weapon types that you can equip Death with: the cloak weapons, spells, and the main weapon, the scythe. All of these weapons feel meaningfully different from each other and using them in tandem can create the opportunity for interesting combos that add some variation to the gameplay. The feeling of deciding to keep fire arrows equipped so you can have a long-range option for a particular boss while using a cloak item such as daggers for a close attack option genuinely adds a nice layer of nuance to the gameplay which feels satisfying when executed correctly. The whole thing feels fluid, responsive and balanced. So, it’s great! And no other complaints there.(The same goes for the art style, which, although in early access, is still really gorgeous and looks markedly different for each area). The only real problem that I have with this game, then, is the repetitiveness. This game is REALLY repetitive (at least in its current early access stage). I don’t see how a game developer in 2022 can expect their player base to play through the same levels just to end up dying to lose their progress and do it all over again. It’s strange. Especially when you consider that there are so many games out nowadays (many of which are free) that offer the opportunity for emergent gameplay upon each playthrough and many of which actually reward the player with permanent items that have more of an impact on gameplay than those  do. Runs usually go this way: start off by killing a bunch of low-level mobs, get curses which unlock branching powerups, collect weapons through the various sub-levels, beat the end of area boss to buy heals, and then do it all over again for a different area with a different end of area boss. This formula would be okay if there was a genuine sense of reward at the end of each run, but there kind of isn’t. After the completion of a run all the player gets in return is a few gold pieces that they can use in a shop to purchase items such as cloak weapons that can be unlocked on the next run or food that gives certain powerups for a small duration. I really would have liked something permanent in return for my progress in this game, even if it’s just a cosmetic item such as a new robe for Death or something. I think that this would have broken up the monotony of repeating the first levels and added some much-needed meaningful variation to the game. is a game with fun mechanics, a solid identity, and a lot of promise. However, due to issues such as lack of meaningful rewards and the requirement to repeat the same bosses, it just doesn’t feel complete enough at this stage. Hopefully, this will be resolved when the game launches fully, which should bring much more dimensions into the game for hopeful players such as myself to tuck into. However, despite its feeling of incompleteness and sometimes frustratingly repetitive gameplay, the game is fun. I would like however, to see in the future more variation in terms of bosses, levels, cosmetics, and weapon upgrades to add more variation to the gameplay because it desperately needs it. In short, I would say that if this game is in the sale, then buy it, if it’s full price though, then it still just about justifies a purchase (for me).

So basically every run is the same, with the only difference being "having unlocked more weapons", which as I said, doesn't make much of a difference except visually.Overall, I see this as a huge waste of talented artists' efforts, solely due to the lack of fun. I find the movement, weapons, and bosses really good, but the game forces you to be patient while having fast combat and quick enemies. Play this game if you are a big fan of roguelites but this game really dragged out my patience. There were a lot of things I liked about this game despite it not being in my genre, so I would still recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: I think this game is pretty good, but it took me a little bit of time to get used to the mechanics and the health system.The health system seems to be what people complain about the most, but after playing for a decent amount of time I found it to actually not be too bad. I think the biggest thing a player has to do is acquire curses that allow them to build their defense, give them life steal abilities, or increase their health, as well as visit certain floors that will grant them more health and mana.In almost every play through, I will skip the store, I don't find it rewarding to spend a prisimium (sp?) to upgrade the store either. I only go to the store when I need an Anima. I usually skip thanagers as well since I have unlocked every weapon and food item in the game.After clearing floors, you'll have the task of choosing which floor to go to next, and the reward from each floor is represented as seen in the icon beside the floor. Ex: Weapon storage has an axe. therefore there will be a weapon on that floor as a reward of clearing it.The builds are fun, and the more you play the more weapons you unlock. The weapons you unlock can be upgraded to make them stronger, and will also unlock more abilities for that weapon. I found some weapons don't get any effects applied to them even when fully upgraded though.I find the break rooms in between floors to almost be irrelevant. You are only allowed to take 1 item from the fridge per playthrough, and the only time I take items from the fridge is when they award me pure heals or fill my Anima bar. I think it would be nice if you were given an item per break room fridge, and if that were to decrease the difficulty of the game substantially, then decrease the effects given from the items in the fridge.All-in-all, for an early access game I find this to be fun and I imagine that it only gets better from here.Thanks for listening to my TED Talk.EDIT: Animas are healing orbs.Also to elaborate on the health system, it is almost like you have two health bars. One health bar, "The foreground health bar" is the total amount of health your character has. If this health bar decreases to 0, your character dies.The other health bar, let's say the "background health bar" decreases the total amount of health that your character can recover when your character takes any damage. The only way you can recover this health is if you can acquire a yellow anima. or find an item that gives you a "pure heal".Sorry if this seems convoluted.

_childDocuments_.review: Have a Nice Death is a very unique game, offering many different ways to play, while also providing a fair challenge to those who are looking for it. I received this game as a gift from a friend way back before the official release, and the developers, Magic Design Studios, have shown nothing but love for their creation as shown by their willingness to allow Early Access to their game and swift handling of various issues that they have then ironed out with ease, a practice not done to even the highest of budgeted "Triple-A" video-games as of late.While my hours on the game as of writing this may be low, don't be fooled, as it felt like I've been playing it for days. The game-play requires focus and engagement, along with swift reaction times and basic skill. And while the story is basic the characters scattered across Death Inc. are brimming with various attitudes and personalities! The story of the game is very straightforward but has more than proven that it's more meat than bone, that being it's packed with all sorts of weapon combos, types, and branching paths for various upgrades within the game-play itself. Paired with the "Rouge-Like" properties found in other titles like "The Binding of Issac", it is able to provide a different experience each time you play, keeping the player hooked as they hope the next time will be the run to the finish!Have a Nice Death is also an amazing pairing with the Steam Deck released by VALVe as the size of the game is fairly small, the graphics are not too demanding, and the native controller support allows for a quick jump into the game right after it's installed.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall the game is... fine... BUT it is early access so there are obviously going to be some issues.The art style of the game is gorgeous, although the art is strangely low rez? This becomes very clear when the game has closeups on characters and they are VERY pixelated. The assets in the health UI appear to be horribly low rez for some reason too. Characters like Death and his book however look great during gameplay, the various animation also helps liven up the world.The gameplay is a good start but needs vast tweaks. There is a large delay that often comes in for dashing and causes more frustrations with the controls than an actual challenge from gameplay. The upgrades are fun, although there are clearly some that are just objectively "better" than others leading to most of them feeling very disappointing.The health system is just bad... the desperation to save health encourages you to just run through areas without fighting to save health, which in turn reveals that most levels are empty and pointless.I have high hopes for this game as all of the issues are very solvable, and some of the issues are pretty standard for early access. Not only this but the combat is most fun when it works correctly and the art is VERY good (when it's not looking broken), but as it is right now... it's just not particularly fun.This does not mean the game is in any way bad! I love the character designs but this game has some of the most god awful writing I have ever tried to read.  Maybe you have to have worked in an office setting to get 90 percent of the humor, or maybe translating from French speaking devs just didn't work out.  It has been fun and I'll beat it a few more times to see if it expands but as is I would try to buy it on sale and not expect too much replay value.  There are better options out there but this is a solid one!

_childDocuments_.review: I wanted to like this game so I even bought it on Switch too for I no longer have a PC but since the early access and the released product I see no difference, like many said before animation and art style are great but thats really what I can come up as defense for Have a Nice Death. Levels are bland, fighting is not that great either as its just boils down to hitting and dodging, I know most rougelike is just this but the other titles in this ballpark have some flow to the combat like Flinthook, or they offer something else outside of the usual grind like Cult of the Lamb with its town building part, I played a lot of of this genre before but for me this doesn't really stand out in any way except for the graphics ofc. My other complaint is about the soundtrack, as I sometimes feel like its not even there like its too smooth to notice, if I have to remember one it must be the elevator song which says a lot. In this state the game for me is an okay ish title and I'll look back in a couple of months.

_childDocuments_.review: The visuals of the game is good but that’s kind of where it ends for me.I spent 8hrs on this game, might say more just because i left the game on idle. i do not enjoy starting over. The builds are not fun, your limited access to gaining abilities or basically “cool stuff” is very stingy.   You also don’t need to kill anything in the levels other than 1 or 2 areas that force you to fight in each level.  The levels are quite long and become annoying platforming chores overtime to traverse. There’s nothing to get excited about in future runs when I compare my time playing Hades and Skul. Each run was refreshing and a chance at a novel experience. But with this game each new run after the first handful became a bigger and bigger slog. If it weren’t for podcasts and other content on youtube to distract myself… I  doubt i’d even put in the hrs I did. It’s definitely a very nice looking game but it’s not very fun nor is it satisfying to kill enemies.

_childDocuments_.review: This game fails the rougelite formula. I'm three and a half hours of tries, and the power growth that I'm expecting to help me through things as I bash my head against the wall isn't showing up. It's a fun base game, and it's frustrating that I feel like, while I am getting better, the game isn't giving me the sort of power growth that you'e come to expect from games like Hades or Dead Cells.

_childDocuments_.review:
Have a Nice Death is a 2D action roguelike where you play as an overworked Death, whose employees have run rampant, completely throwing off the balance of souls - and his vacation plans. In order to restore order, you'll have to grab your trusty scythe and show your employees who's boss. 

Since Death can't die, use what you've learned and earned to overcome the numerous minions and bosses in each department of Death Incorporated... over and over. A performance review after every run guarantees that you'll unlock interesting items and upgrades that will help you progress on your journey.

name: Sam & Max: Beyond Time and Space
detailed_description: Join the Freelance Police on a bizarre adventure from the North Pole to the Fountain of Youth, from outer space to Hell and back. Sam & Max: Beyond Time and Space is a remastered version of Telltale’s second season of episodic Sam & Max games, lovingly updated by a small team of the original developers. Sam is a six-foot canine detective with a nose for justice. Max is a hyperkinetic rabbity-thing with a taste for mayhem. Together, they’re the Freelance Police—an irreverent comedy duo whose esoteric crime-fighting style has been entertaining comic book and video game fans for more than thirty years. In this five-episode collection of interconnected cases, Sam & Max are back on the crime beat in a showdown with Santa Claus, a race to subdue a giant volcano, and a face-off with a Eurotrash vampire. And then things get even weirder. Is paranoid shopkeeper Bosco on to something with his talk of a grand conspiracy? Is diner proprietress Stinky hiding the truth about what happened to her grandfather (also named Stinky)? Will flaky neighbor Sybil Pandemik ever find true love? Did someone say… BIRTHDAY?! Hop into the DeSoto for a hilarious outing that won IGN’s Adventure Game of the Year award the first time around and now looks and sounds better than ever, with gorgeous HD graphics, overhauled lighting and lip-sync, finessed cinematography, remastered audio, and eight all-new musical tracks featuring live jazz musicians. Zombies will dance. Mariachis will sing. A giant battle robot will trash the streets. And when their friends’ lives are on the line, Sam and Max will risk their very souls to set things right. Features: An adventure game that makes you laugh: Explore unexpected places, chat with eccentric characters, and tease out brain-tickling puzzles in an interactive story that has a joke hiding behind every hotspot. Beautifully remastered: Lighting, lip-sync, cinematography, audio, music, and more have been updated and enhanced to bring Sam & Max’s second episodic season up to modern standards. No walkthrough required: The game detects when you’re stuck and provides subtle contextual hints. Hint frequency can be customized to accommodate all playing styles. Optional driving mini-games: Take the wheel of Sam & Max’s 1960 DeSoto convertible for fun diversions from the story. The hood decals and car upgrades you win carry over across episodes. Localization: English voice with subtitles in English, French, Italian, German, and Spanish.

_childDocuments_.review: I guess it's only fair to compare remaster of second season to the previous remaster. And I gotta say, it feels even better!- DeSoto mini-game progress now works better (decals progress is saved properly and you don't have to play episodes in order), that progression checklist is also pretty nice.- Personally, Bosco's VA perform better than first season. And I don't think it's just because I got used to his new voice.- Quite a handful of areas got revamped with new decor and actual lighting. New lighting is especially nice to look at in zombie factory and night time streets. Pleasant references for true S&M fans sprinkled everywhere.- Nipple keyring is back.- Most obscene (and therefore hilarious) original jokes didn't get cut so I assume nothing else got cut too (as promised by Skunkape devs) - New music is really great! And don't worry, you'll get to hear all original compositions too!- I didn't notice at first, but I'm glad they added skip button for closing credits so you can see original post-credits scenes!- And I also gotta thank Skunkape Games for letting me beta test the game and report various bugs and oddities. Thought I was dreaming when I was first offered to volunteer. Honored to help such a chill, responsive and positive crew with polishing my most favorite game series!

_childDocuments_.review: Originally released back in late 2007 through 2008,  is the second season in Telltale’s trilogy starring the beloved, somewhat niche, crime-solving duo.For a little more than a year now, it has been available with a fresh coat of paint, exceptionally remastered by Skunkape Games, a team founded by ex-Telltale developers back when the you-know-what hit the fan at the ol’ office. Skunkape has since been the home of the six-foot, fedora-wearing dog and his "hyperkinetic rabbity thing" buddy, and it is thanks to their hard work that the duo’s worst adventure can now be enjoyed on modern systems, with improved visuals, audio, and an updated soundtrack.Hold up! "Worst adventure" yet a positive review? Look, If you’ve got four games in a series, it only follows that one of them has to be the worst. It's just that you can’t pin it on the original LucasArts darling that gave these two their first time in the spotlight, and it can’t be the game that brought ‘em back, nor the dramatic sendoff. Therefore, the title of “worst” has to fall in the middle, even if the game to bear it is quite alright. But I've got gripes!The second season follows the freelance police on their most colourful journey of ‘em all. Through five episodes, each with its own outlandish location and bizarre villain, you’ll be battling (pointing & clicking through puzzles until the credits roll) the supernatural, urban legends, and none other than Santa himself. It’s going to be a bit hard to take a step back and evaluate  on its own merits when it so clearly wasn’t designed for newcomers to the franchise. Usually, the cases Fido and his lagomorph pal take on are one-offs; standalone stories without explicit continuity between ‘em. You don’t need an overarching plot hanging above the entire series for good seasonal storytelling, yet Season Two picks up a couple of background tidbits from  (Season One), cranks ‘em up into a proper plot, and rounds off some fan-favourite characters. In that sense, it’s quite bold to try and build something new and cool off of what was left over from the previous game. The execution here is narratively satisfying, yet it lets the past have too much hold over everything new, to the point where it feels conflicting.Point & click adventures live and die by the writing, but more often than not, they die by repetition. offers a lot to appreciate. Its writing is as biting as ever, surprisingly relevant, and most importantly, unrelentingly hilarious. It's a more cohesive whole than , making it all the more suitable for a solid binge. Still, “is repetitive” is a recurring item on the “Cons” lists of almost every review of a game from this genre written since the dawn of time.  was served those same complaints when it was released, but managed to rise above ‘em because of how fresh it was.Even with all the new bits showing that  has more than enough ideas to be its own thing and keeping in mind that its story is building up on  foundation, there are  so many reused characters and locations that are hard to take in earnest. Almost every time something from Season One comes back around, it feels like a cost-cutting technique, rather than necessary continuity in a trilogy of games. Even worse, the centrepiece puzzle of every episode follows the same pattern, including a repeating, ridiculously easy minigame.  Anyone who thought Telltale started abusing tried-and-true methods only after  is in for a surprise.To someone who’s hooked on the storyline connecting these two seasons, getting over the cardinal sin of point-&-click adventure games that’s been committed here might not be a tall order. The same goes for Sam & Max fans, especially those who’ve gone through the necessary hours of bludgeoning yourself with a hammer to be on board with this kind of humour. However, they might be turned off for different reasons, depending on how intimately familiar they are with what makes these characters work.The world these characters inhabit is one of finely-balanced absurdity. Everything goes. Animals are anthropomorphized, store owners sell mundane items for billions of dollars, giant stone statues run for the presidential office, cockroaches serve in the military, self-help gurus build bases on the Moon, wars erupt over forgotten birthdays… Yet, it’s paced and delivered in a manner that never feels overbearing or incoherent. leans a tad too hard into that absurdity and puts the pedal to the metal until you’re desensitised. It becomes farcical; as if whoever's in the writer's chair is just thinking up ludicrous scenarios with little regard to anything else. Travelling to the Easter Islands, where Amelia Earhart has been kicking it back with DB Cooper ever since the two had disappeared seems a lot less clever when the previous episode had you  over to the North Pole to deal with a rogue Santa Claus. Following that up with an episode where you battle disco-dancing zombies in an old German castle turned night club seems like a downgrade. I don’t want to go “Ah, okay, right, that makes sense—I’m playing a  game”, but rather “Oh, that’s right, this is a  game!” when weird things happen.Aside from the sharp writing style, this is where most of the humour comes from. The slight disconnect is needed to make the game work as the satire that it is. The joke isn’t that Sam & Max are doing all these weird things, it’s that they’re doing them within the logic of a point & click adventure game, where MacGyvering it goes unquestioned. You’re not supposed to accept it, even when making sense of it is necessary for the solution of most puzzles, but rather laugh, ponder, or flinch from the downright cruelty it usually implies when it comes along.My dislike of the tone is passed on to the soundtrack, a lot of which is rearrangements of tracks from the previous season, to go along with those same old locations you’ll be revisiting. While new music was again contributed as part of the remaster by the original composer and legend that is Jared Emerson-Johnson, neither it nor the rest is as memorable or catchy as what was in . The silver lining is that it still makes for some enjoyable jazz, except for the quietly mixed title track that has just a tad too much nervous energy, with its bongo beat and sudden blares of trumpets. Even the dark and gritty third season had the guts to include something fun, like a theremin!An ambivalent tug of war that pulls strong enough in neither direction,  travels between past and present so much it ends up in a chaotic loop, eventually spat out somewhere in the middle of the road—six outta ten, five on a bad day. With three whole other games in the same series, each offering a better experience, it wouldn’t be hard to pass up were it not part of a trilogy and a well-written bout regardless.Speaking of the trilogy, the third season should be getting its remaster at some point this year, and I’d much rather we go out with a bang rather than a whimper. Just thinking about it gets me all tingly, or maybe that’s the intracranial hematoma from all the hammer blows acting up.

_childDocuments_.review: This remaster is perhaps not as striking as the one for Season 1, but the eye candy is fantastic and there are fewer reasons to want to go back to the original this time around. Ogie Banks' performance as Bosco is markedly improved from Save the World, to the point I hardly miss the original voice.The new music is fantastic and I enjoyed 100%ing the game for the first time, as before it never seemed worth the trouble. Now with added controller support, the minigames are more fun and easier on my fingers.As of this moment, there are some minor issues I experienced. The new City Streets music is missing in Episode 5, and some dialogue that should have effects applied doesn't for whatever reason. And there is a bit of clunk still left in the game design that could have been ironed out a bit. Still, this is an easy recommendation and the best way to experience Season 2.

_childDocuments_.review: The second enhanced version of Sam and Max TellTale adventures hits the spot, nor only does provide the same benefits as the previous season enhancment, but this time around the changes are way more noticable. Besides that, season 2 is as strong as it ever was, it´s easy to forget it and remember the first because it started it all, and the third due to the outstanding ending and clever new ideas for episodes, but seaon 2 is the one that honestly has some of the best jokes of the whole series, and the one that had the most fun with the limitations of the game. If you enjoyed season 1, this is gonna be a blast, and a good apetizer for the upcoming enhanced version of season 3.

_childDocuments_.review: Beyond time and space is an exceptional remaster, and not just because it brings this 2007 relic to modern platformsThe developers have clearly put their heart and soul into making this remaster as great as it can be, making it easier for new players to get into and understand the game as well as giving long time fans a reason to play the game again if they played the 2007/08 original. The Save the World remaster was all about reinvigorating season 1 and while Beyond time and space does this as well for season 2, the changes this time round are also about re-imagining certain scenes in the game. This is best seen with the new lighting, where STW sought to only make the game look nicer and modern with the real time lighting, the new lighting in beyond time and space is often more stylistic. The best example of this is in episode 2, 'Moai Better Blues' where the gloomy, overcast appearance of streets contrasts nicely with the other main setting of the episode, Easter island. Not only that, but the changes and additions to the game also allow beyond time and space to distinguish itself more from Save the World. With the original release of Season 2, A lot of content was re-used from Season 1. Most likely to keep the series releasing as quickly as it did in 2006-2008. However, this to me always made season 2 seem less like a proper sequel and more as DLC. Additional episodes that told a different story from Save The World while also reusing the same assets, music, etc. There were new things, however, it always felt as if the re-used content outweighed the new content just based on it's prevalence within the game (Even though there technically more new set-pieces, music, etc used in the game than re-used). However, this remaster removes this feeling entirely from the game. There still is re-used content, but it's now usually only reserved to small sections of the game you may only visit once or twice. The new music alone makes all the difference, with the new City Streets theme making the streets feel completely different compared to the original STW theme (Which is should considering the streets are torn apart in the opening of the game). Another area the game differs itself is Camera angles. From what I've played, I'm pretty sure every recurring location from Save the World is now shot differently to give an alternative perspective on the room you're in. Whether it being looking through Flint's office into Sam & Max's office to being able to see more details on the back wall of Sybil's office. The game now feels complete unique from Save the World, having a more consistent theming with recurring motif's (Like the portals) that weren't really front and centre in the original. On top of all the usual QOL changes, updated controls, improved inventory and UI, new easter eggs, this is a top quality remaster (Especially so, considering the recent reputation of remasters in the past year)

_childDocuments_.review: If you liked the previous remaster of "Sam & Max Save the World" you're gonna like this.I think the biggest improvement besides character models has to be the lighting,  it's beautifully crafted and breathes new life into the game. Artistic choices like camera framing in gameplay, new additions to cutscenes, lots of little details and even certain effects have been added to enhance the overall experience while still being faithful to the original. For example, in Moai Better Blues, it's now overcast gloomy weather when Sam and Max are in the city, which helps juxtapose the beautiful sunny and vibrant colours of Easter Island when travelling back and forth between them. Skunkape Games really did a fantastic job and I can't wait to see what they do with the Devil's Toybox. Overall fantastic work, it looks slick and modern which is a testament to the artists considering it looked dated even by 2008 standards when it initially released. Disclaimer: Yes, Bosco still got the new voice actor, I've liked his performance better in Season 2, he's doing his best, but if you weren't sold in the first one, this one won't change your mind.

_childDocuments_.review: It maintains the cleverness and quality of the previous game. The puzzles are more difficult but mostly remain in the "solvable with time" realm. There is greater variety in the environments.TECHNICALThe game slightly slowed down in the third chapter, as it features rain effects. I did not encounter any crashes, glitches, or anything of the sort.AUDIOVISUALThe microphones are more consistent, but not wholly consistent, with some characters having slightly worse microphone quality between lines. Aside from this the quality of graphics and sound is the same as the previous game. GAMEPLAYThe puzzles are harder. A good portion of this is because some of them are "hunt the object" puzzles where the solution involves finding an obscure prop object. Some of this is due to legitimately requiring more thinking. I think each episode is also longer, but I don't know if that's a matter of more stuff to do or harder stuff. Something interesting here is the presence of car minigames: one per episode. They aren't just there for puzzle purposes, but also to obtain optional collectables in the form of car decals. It's interesting as a concept but the games themselves are rather boring. WRITINGThe writing in this is a bit better than in the prior game, but the prior game had great writing, so there wasn't much to improve on. While the previous game had some distinctly 2000s jokes, this game is more timeless, though some lines can all but carbon date it. Aside from this, the only thing to note is that this game is slightly more politically incorrect, but I doubt it would actually offend anyone. Like in the previous game, the overarching plot is nothing deep, but it seems that there was more focus put on creating something cohesive. There's foreshadowing for later episodes, for example.

_childDocuments_.review: As with Save the World, the visual presentation is simply fantastic, and a huge step up from the original. The new camera angles, the models, the colors, the lighting, it's all so beautiful.The writing is sharp, sharper than I remember! I played this with a couple of friends and we were laughing quite a bit. This is definitely the best writing in the TTG trilogy, in my opinion.The music is as outstanding as ever, with a handful of new tracks by the boys over at Bay Area Sound, and they're all just as good, if not better than the original compositions! ("Maimtron 9000's Pancake Breakfast" is a standout one for me, it's so damn good!)Overall, I think Skunkape have outdone themselves with this one, it's an expertly crafted remaster of an old classic, they just simply knocked it out of the park.Thank you so much for keeping Sam and Max alive!
_childDocuments_.name: Sam & Max: Beyond Time and Space

_childDocuments_.review: I haven't gotten through all the episodes yet, but yet again, this seems like a worthy update much like the Save the World remaster was. Improved visuals and lighting, new music, quality of life improvements etc. For those of you who weren't happy with the minor line rewrites for Bosco in the first season, none have been changed this time. (I really don't think it was ever a big deal, but I assume some would want to know.)I can't wait to see what Skunkape does with The Devil's Playhouse, since that season was a whole different vibe. I imagine it might take a bit longer to come to fruition, so in the meantime, I'm happy to get back into the games that made me fall in love with the genre. This season is probably my favourite of all the Sam & Max games - there's just so much to enjoy, from Santa Claus, to zombies to time travel and even to hell itself. It's up there as one of my favourite adventure games of all time.So yes, highly recommended.

_childDocuments_.review: 2020's Sam & Max Save the World was a fantastic way to cap off that nightmare of a year. It's developers, Skunkape Games(despite some controversy), made, in my opinion, the definitive way to experience the Freelance Police's first season of their Telltale exploits.Now, just a little over a year later, they've done it again with the follow-up Beyond Time and Space, the fresh new reprint of Sam & Max’s second season.Much like Save the World, the base game is largely unchanged. It's still five episodes of unfiltered chaos as Sam & Max face-off a killer robot, tango with Santa, become volcano gods, and rap battle a vampire as they descend further and further into hellish madness. As always you're still pointing, clicking, and using an inventory system to solve various puzzles, alongside the occasional dialogue tree, wrapped together with the same never-miss dialogue that'll probably have you cackling like a damn hyena. Each episode is about one or two hours long to complete if you know what you’re doing. If you don’t know what you’re doing, then don’t worry too much, as there’s a handy hint system that can guide you in the proper direction.Before getting to the presentation, let's start with the writing, because those allergic to inconsequential changes will be happy to know that absolutely NONE of the dialogue was cut or altered in any form or fashion. Even the more obscene topical stuff, like Timmy Two-Teeth and his coprolalia, have been untouched.Bosco's new voice has also improved significantly. While still being voiced by Ogie Banks, his direction and delivery are way better than in Save the World. He conveys much more emotion and energy this time around, making him sound like a proper paranoid maniac.The presentation is still on top, like last time, with updated textures, lighting and character redesigns with input from Steve Purcell, and a live jazz soundtrack packing eight new tracks that are absolute FIRE.This extends to the more technical changes too. There’s new camera angles and interface tweaks, uncompressed voice clips, the driving minigames are now optional, the decals you can earn in those minigames are a lot easier to keep track of, there's just a lot of great changes to make the experience more cohesive.Overall, Sam & Max: Beyond Time and Space is another great remastering of another great graphic adventure. With a ton of new bells and whistles, this makes for the finest way to play the funniest Sam & Max adventure yet. (And if you’re still on the fence, you can still play the originals, in all their janky-ass glory.)

_childDocuments_.review: OK, so I so far have played "Sam & Max Hit the Road" and "Sam & Max Save the World", but this game, "Sam & Max Beyond Time and Space" has the best jokes/gags so far! It seems like the banter between Sam & Max in the first two tried to carry the humor, but it just didn't seem all that funny to me. This game seemed to let the other characters provide some of the humor, which I did enjoy! The robot quoting 80's music lyrics I enjoyed, and little Timmy (or was it Jimmy) with turrets I though was funny, and I did catch myself laughing out loud with the parking break gag! Is the game perfect? No, so far it had the best jokes/gags. Some of the puzzles/solutions were like, "WTF?", but at least there are plenty of guides out there, although I couldn't find the perfect guide for me that included just the right amount of information to help me solve the puzzles. I started to use a Youtube video walkthrough, but they were clicking on every item possible, which I can find and do on my own, so I abandoned it and found a text and picture walkthrough guide, but it looked like it was translated from Russian, so there was some bad grammar and it seemed like it left out some details, so I had to go back to the Youtube video to visually see how exactly the puzzle was solved. I was going for all the achievements, which the "Desoto Dominator" was the one that gave me the most problems in obtaining, since it spanned 4 of the 5 "episodes". Since this is a point and click game, I was using the mouse and keyboard on my computer, but I found that a game controller seems to make the driving mini games easier, especially on one of the games where the left stick can not only move you right or left, it can also speed you up or slow you down, depending on if you push up or down while moving left or right. After I finished the game, I thought I did everything to get the "Desoto Dominator" achievement, but it did not pop up for me. I used the poster next to the Desoto to check to see if I was missing any decals, and noticed that none of the decals from Episode 1 got transferred over to the final episode. Also, upon further investigation, I noticed that the very last sticker will turn "gold" when you reach a certain threshold (run over x number of Torture Me Elmers, deliver x number of discs to zombies, etc.). I had to go back to episode 1 and redo all of the decal challenges, and go back and do the bagpipe challenge until the sticker turned gold. If the last decal for each season isn't gold, then you still need to complete the next threshold challenge. You will need to obtain the gold decals in order to get following DeSoto upgrades: Ep1: Turbo Charger, Ep2: Dashboard Hula Girl, Ep3: Flame paint job for DeSoto, Ep4: None/NA, Ep5: Demonic Grill Teeth/Super Upgrade:Police Lights. I thought these only applied to the console versions of the game, but they are in the PC version as well!

_childDocuments_.review: Sam & Max: Beyond Time and Space is a wonderful continuation of the first game. The humor is still top notch and the charm is as good as ever. However I'm going to have to place this game a bit lower than Save the World, purely because of the way the puzzles are handled in this game. Season 1 had absolutely solid puzzles that made sense and were reasonable enough for you to figure them out. Season 2 however I found the puzzles were more troublesome and confusing, especially in Episodes 2 and 3. The Moai island was probably the worst time I had with this game purely cause of how often I got stuck.Another unfortunate thing about Season 2 versus Season 1 is that there is one less episode, which is compensated by increasing the length of each episode. While in Season 1, you could finish each episode in one sitting which gave me great satisfaction, Season 2 takes multiple sittings to get through each episode which is probably also a consequence of the worse puzzles this game had. Both the actual duration of the episode and puzzle troubles increase the time it takes to complete each episode.With all that being said, Beyond Time and Space is still a good Sam & Max experience and well worth it. I just wish the puzzle solutions weren't as obscure and confusing. And now that I finally completed this, I'm greatly looking forward to The Devil's Playhouse remastered!

_childDocuments_.review: It's weird, silly, and complete with charm. Get it for the music alone!I will say that the writing + narrative this season feels much less cohesive -- even if they deliberately try to tie in elements like the Mariachis, Santa / Satan, etc. -- and makes for a deliberately more ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ insane product. Which has plenty of solid jokes... but also, a lot of misfires or awkward moments, hampered by some irritating voice acting and sound effects esp. from the season's overarching antagonists. I know that Sam & Max is an inherently irreverent brand; this season just gets a little TOO irreverent for my liking. And the Devil's Playhouse ups the stakes by keeping the irreverence, but also adding some stakes + poignancy so you get more invested; here, it's all so flippant that it can be really grating at points.But beyond that -- it's still fun puzzle-solving. The best episode is the Moai episode; I think Jurgen's is my least favorite. There are plenty of excellent challenges to figure out -- even when some border on purely frustrating. (I hate that rib puzzle in the 5th episode, man). I can't wait for the third season.

_childDocuments_.review: Skunkape Games are back at it again with the Second Season of Sam & Max: Beyond Time and Space. Now completely remastered; this season takes our freelance duo to new heights now with the the world rules being laid out in Save the World. Sam & Max will go all over the universe in this next journey which will take them to the likes of the North Pole, Bermuda Triangle and even Germany! All of this spans five-episodes of brain teasing spine chilling fun.Once again, the game is a standard point-and-click adventure just like the last Season. In fact, a lot of familiar elements from Save the World are retained in this second outing, meaning that everything should feel at home if you're jumping in from the first season's remaster. All control schemes from the last game are still present in this version.The graphics have gotten a great facelift. Even with the production of a sequel, the graphics back in 2008 were nothing to write home about. All the graphical improvements you've experienced in the last season is here and accounted for, even including some flashing effects which were never present in the original game (these can be turned off in the accessibility settings). The new lighting and model touch ups help to bring new life into Beyond Time and Space, just as much as it did for Save the World.The presentation as always is top notch. All sorts of additions have been made to make this season even cooler than before, like the bigger hole in the Office wall for example, which gives us an intriguing view of the office. There are a sprinkling of new Easter eggs to find this time around.  And since I might not get to mention it elsewhere, the new soundtrack pieces are a delight to listen to. The new street theme is enthusiastically toe-tapping and the addition of new music tracks for action scenes and different time periods is a very welcome change.With the arrival of this second season comes even more ballistic writing. The jokes get raunchier this season thanks to the wider variety in locales and the overall story is as wacky as ever, even getting meta at more times than not. It's best you experience it for yourself, trust me. There's a lot more visual gags to giggle at too. The arrival of Banang was imminent, but the famous recurring jokes in Telltale's Games has come back to grace us in it's original appearance.On the subject of original appearances, some of you may be highly miffed on the return of Ogie Banks as Bosco. You definitely won't have to fear this time as despite his involvement, no other change had been made to anyone's voices, or even the script for that matter. All that raunchy dialogue you've come to love is still here. And Ogie's improved performance makes up for it even more. The voice direction definitely has a noticeable improvement over the first iteration heard in Save the World. If you still don't sit right with the voice change however, a mod to restore the original versions of the lines is available.(And don't worry about any changes for Season 3, Bosco isn't in the next season at all)Overall, this was another great effort from the devs at Skunkape Games to reintroduce the gaming public to another chapter in the story of Sam & Max. This version comes highly recommended from me, the changes to visuals and presentation are too good to pass up. Season 2 in general is a great step up from Season 1. I'm highly anticipating the final chapter in this remastered trilogy, The Devil's Playhouse, the best possible conclusion to the Telltale Saga. But until then, the best version of Season 1's continuation awaits you! Experience Telltale at their next peak (before all the other ones)!

_childDocuments_.review: While I did enjoy my time with this series, Season 2 was not major improvement over the first season. Despite it's attempt to spice things up, you still have to visit the same handful of locations and talk to the same few characters in the same street to get things done, this can make things feel small and inconsequential. However, Skunkape's modifications to the lighting and atmosphere of each chapter made everything feel like time had passed between each episode and that things were actually happening.Unlike with the comparatively more primitive first season, It's much harder to tell what the new changes and additions are (minus the most obvious ones). Things like new external building shots and similar are mostly redundant due to either not needing them or already having them. This suggests one way this season is better than the original.Definitely worth a look if you are a fan of the series.

Join the Freelance Police for a second season of adventure, crime-fighting, and chaos. Sam & Max Season Two starts with a giant battle robot attack and never lets up, taking our valiant crime-fighters on a gut-wrenching mission from the North Pole to Easter Island, from outer space to Hell and back.
Babies will dance. Mariachis will sing. The undead will roam the streets. And Sam & Max will risk their souls to bring you the most fun you've had playing a video game. Ever.
